articles.title: How Natera designed an agentic AI system for lab ops with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Natera designed an agentic AI system for lab ops with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
At Natera, a leader in cell-free DNA (cfDNA) testing, keeping lab instruments up and running is critical, because equipment downtime disrupts sample processing. Natera’s lab engineering team, led by Ariel Jirau worked with AWS to build SWARM (Systematic Workflow Analytics and Resolutions Manager), an agentic AI system for lab operations.
This post walks through how the Natera team built an agentic AI system for lab operations using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that captures and deploys institutional knowledge at scale. It describes the full architecture, from knowledge base construction to automated system deployment and evaluation, so you can apply the same patterns to your own operational workflows.
SWARM delivers about 130x faster first response time and 96.2 percent automated coverage across support tickets, giving engineers immediate access to institutional knowledge the moment a ticket arrives.
The challenge: Knowledge continuity
Natera’s lab operations rely on a wide range of precision instruments spanning multiple equipment families, each with its own failure modes, vendor documentation, and resolution patterns. The service engineering team responsible for maintaining this infrastructure is organized around deep individual expertise rather than standardized playbooks. When a senior technician who had spent years diagnosing a particular instrument family departed, the institutional knowledge they carried was effectively lost. No system existed to capture, organize, or deploy that expertise at scale.
With over 65 tickets per day across three Jira queues and an average first response time of 17.4 hours, instrument downtime delayed lab samples and patient reporting. Hiring more engineers couldn’t keep pace. SWARM had to respond in minutes, deliver accurate diagnostics across a wide range of equipment types, and improve continuously through a structured evaluation loop.
Why Natera chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
The Natera team chose to build SWARM on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a fully managed, extensible service by AWS designed to build, deploy, connect, secure, and operate AI agents at scale. Three core requirements drove the decision:
- Autonomous processing of high-volume support tickets without human intervention.
- Deep integration with existing operational tools such as Jira and Confluence.
- Built-in security and observability (encryption, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) integration, and distributed tracing) without requiring the team to build and maintain custom infrastructure.
“We needed a managed runtime that would let us focus engineering effort on diagnostic accuracy rather than infrastructure plumbing—AgentCore gave us that, along with built-in identity management and the flexibility to swap models without rewriting agent logic,” Jirau said.
AgentCore provides native integration with services including Amazon DynamoDB, a fully managed NoSQL database service, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), and AWS X-Ray, a capability of Amazon CloudWatch.
How SWARM works: Two agents, one skill library
SWARM uses two complementary runtimes sharing a single skill library. The swarm-agent autonomously generates structured diagnostic reports before an engineer opens a ticket, while engineers use swarm-hive to interact in real time, upload images, and explore alternative troubleshooting paths.
“The system does not replace engineers—it gives them access to the full depth of institutional knowledge the moment a ticket arrives,” Jirau said.
Four layers connect the architecture:
- The event layer routes Jira tickets through Amazon EventBridge and Amazon SQS.
- The agent layer hosts swarm-agent, swarm-hive, and the skill library, and delivers diagnostic reports back to engineers.
- The context layer draws on vendor manuals, historical tickets, and operational data.
- The observability and delivery layer captures traces, logs, and metrics.
Security architecture
The Natera team’s first architectural decision was where to run the agents. The team required a managed runtime that would handle container orchestration, scaling, and security without requiring them to maintain custom infrastructure. They chose AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, because it hosts both swarm-agent and swarm-hive in a secure, managed environment with built-in identity management and monitoring, avoiding the need to build and operate a custom agent execution layer. You can adopt this pattern regardless of the framework you choose.
The team chose a keyless deployment model because SWARM runs in a clinical environment where credentials exposure is unacceptable. OpenID Connect (OIDC) and AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) generate temporary credentials scoped per deployment, with no long-lived keys in the pipeline. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) enforces least privilege at the component level. Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) with private subnets and VPC endpoints keeps traffic off the public internet. AWS Secrets Manager rotates the few credentials that exist on an automatic 30-day cycle.
GitLab CI runners authenticate to AWS by presenting an OIDC token to an IAM identity provider configured in the account. AWS STS exchanges the token for short-lived credentials scoped to the deployment role (no long-lived access keys are stored in the pipeline). For setup details, see the IAM OIDC provider documentation.
The following example illustrates the pattern: an IAM OIDC trust policy for GitLab CI follows this structure:
These infrastructure-level security controls work in concert with SWARM’s data governance policies. Together they form the full compliance posture required for operating an AI system in a regulated clinical environment.
Compliance and data governance
SWARM runs on HIPAA-eligible AWS services under a Business Associate Agreement (BAA), reflecting Natera’s obligations as a clinical laboratory operator. Every agent invocation is audit-logged (a searchable record that satisfies data access traceability requirements). No patient-identifiable information touches the vector index or the language model. Tickets contain only equipment and workflow metadata. Teams building under HIPAA or similar regulatory frameworks should confirm BAA coverage and data separation requirements before designing the knowledge base pipeline.
Knowledge base and document pipeline construction
Early prototypes using general-purpose retrieval without equipment-specific metadata produced inconsistent results, so the Natera team built a custom document processing pipeline tailored to technical equipment documentation. Amazon Titan Text Embeddings generates vector representations for semantic search, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), converting documents into embeddings stored in batches of 100, a size chosen to balance indexing throughput against API rate limits. For heavily structured source documents with tables and diagrams, investing in a custom parsing pipeline rather than relying on default chunking compounds accuracy gains across every diagnosis.
Amazon Bedrock services, including Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore are available in multiple AWS Regions. For the latest information, see Amazon Bedrock supported Regions and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore supported Regions.
The Natera team uses the tiktoken tokenizer with the cl100k_base encoding to measure chunk boundaries. The following example illustrates the pattern, the chunking configuration follows a standard structure:
For more on batch ingestion patterns, see the Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases documentation.
“Diagnostic accuracy is a data quality problem first,” Jirau said. “Adding missing vendor manuals for the lowest-scoring instrument family lifted accuracy from 71% to 75% with no model changes.”
This shaped the Natera team’s improvement approach: when accuracy plateaus, the team checks data coverage before model tuning, because gaps in vendor documentation are the most common cause of missed diagnoses. The pipeline reprocesses new or updated documents and refreshes the vector index without disrupting active operations.
Skill library architecture
The Natera team faced a key architectural choice: embed logic directly in agent prompts, or build a separate, versioned skill library. Natera chose the library approach because it makes SWARM auditable and improvable.
“When a diagnosis is wrong, we need to point to a specific skill rather than debug the whole system — that’s why we built a versioned skill library from the start,” Jirau said.
The library contains 33 skills: 24 instrument-specific skills covering the full range of equipment families Natera supports, plus 9 cross-cutting workflow skills that apply broadly across ticket types. Each skill has a defined interface, is independently testable, and is evaluated against the same standards as the overall system, treated as production software, not embedded prompt logic.
The skill architecture follows a clear split: Python handles deterministic tasks such as parsing Jira fields or formatting HTML reports, while large language model (LLM) skills handle language reasoning such as interpreting symptoms, matching vendor documentation, and generating diagnostic narratives. For teams building a multi-skill agent, this split between deterministic Python skills and LLM-powered reasoning skills is one of the highest-impact decisions to make.
Agent runtime deployment
Natera split diagnostic work into two distinct runtimes because autonomous background analysis and interactive engineering collaboration have fundamentally different latency and context requirements. The swarm-agent is built for throughput. It selects skills based on equipment type and symptoms, queries the knowledge base, and produces a structured HTML report with a lead cause hypothesis, ranked troubleshooting steps, and a confidence label. The report is delivered to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and linked to the Jira ticket within minutes. Swarm-hive is designed for depth: engineers can engage in interactive follow-up, upload images, and explore alternative paths, with AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, retaining per-engineer conversational context across sessions.
Because swarm-hive accepts free-form engineer input, prompts are routed through Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for content filtering.
Event-driven Jira integration
SWARM integrates with Jira through Amazon EventBridge Scheduler and a polling AWS Lambda function, a serverless compute service that runs code in response to events, avoiding webhook configuration. Verified tickets enter an Amazon SQS queue for reliable delivery. DynamoDB handles deduplication using the ticket ID as a partition key with time-to-live (TTL) based expiry, and stores per-run metadata such as status, cost, and token usage to feed the evaluation loop. This EventBridge-to-SQS pattern decouples the agent runtime from the ticketing system’s availability.
The following example illustrates the pattern. The deduplication table uses a minimal schema with TTL-based expiry:
Observability design
Agentic systems with many interacting components are difficult to debug without per-invocation traces, so the Natera team built observability into SWARM before the first production deployment. If you’re running agents in production, per-invocation tracing is non-negotiable: without it, debugging a bad diagnosis means guessing which skill misbehaved.
In a clinical lab environment, where instrument downtime directly impacts patient reporting, the ability to trace, alert on, and audit every agent action isn’t a “nice to have”. It’s a regulatory and operational requirement.
SWARM’s observability stack uses Amazon CloudWatch to capture searchable logs for every run, providing a clear record of operational health. AWS X-Ray traces each run from ticket intake to diagnostic report, recording time and cost per tool call so the team can pinpoint the specific skill responsible when something is slow or expensive rather than guessing. Amazon Simple Notification Service delivers failure alerts by email, while a Slack tracker gives the entire team real-time visibility into agent activity.
Continuous evaluation methodology
SWARM uses a continuous evaluation loop rather than testing once at deployment, which is especially critical for systems handling changing documentation or evolving workflows. On every ticket processed, the agent provides a lead cause hypothesis, ranked troubleshooting steps, and a self-rated confidence label. Engineers record what they found and fixed, and an evaluator grades each response as Accurate, Partial, or Wrong, broken down by instrument family. Results are reviewed to identify where the agent is underperforming, the fix is applied (typically by updating the knowledge base), and the evaluation set is re-run to confirm improvement.
SWARM’s self-rated confidence labels show a directional relationship with actual accuracy. Tickets labeled High confidence achieve 74 percent accuracy across 154 evaluated cases, while Moderate and Low confidence tickets both achieve 65 percent across 78 and 37 cases respectively. Note that Moderate and Low currently share the same accuracy rate. The Low confidence sample size of 37 cases is too small to draw statistically meaningful conclusions, and the Natera team expects the two tiers to diverge as the evaluation dataset expands.
The separation between High and the remaining tiers gives engineers a useful signal for how much weight to place on each diagnosis at the point of reading a diagnostic report.
SWARM performance
The Natera team evaluated SWARM across 524 support tickets to establish a performance baseline. Of the 524 tickets in the evaluation set, 269 received a High, Moderate, or Low confidence label and had a corresponding engineer-verified resolution available for comparison. The remaining tickets were either labeled none or lacked a verified resolution at the time of analysis.
Average first response time dropped from 17.4 hours to roughly 8 minutes (about 130x faster). These measurements were collected from Jira ticket metadata over a 90-day production evaluation period. Coverage matters just as much: 96.2 percent of tickets get an automated first response without an engineer having to initiate the diagnostic process. Coverage was measured as the percentage of incoming tickets that received a SWARM-generated diagnostic report before engineer review.
Lessons from building agentic AI in production
Several architectural decisions in SWARM translate directly to teams building similar systems.
- Treat chunk size and overlap as tunable parameters. The right values depend on how your source documents are structured.
- Build traceability into your skill library from the start. When a diagnosis is wrong, you want to point to a specific skill, not debug the whole system.
- If your workload mixes batch processing with interactive querying, separate them into distinct runtimes.
Getting started
Try these patterns yourself with the AgentCore samples repository, Building Agentic systems on AWS or the Getting Started with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore guide for deploying agents securely at scale. Healthcare and life sciences organizations facing similar challenges with institutional knowledge loss, high-volume operational workflows, or clinical compliance requirements will find that the architectural patterns Natera developed with SWARM provide a replicable, production-tested foundation for building agentic AI systems on AWS.

articles.title: 3 ways AI is changing the healthcare revenue cycle - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
3 ways AI is changing the healthcare revenue cycle
The healthcare revenue cycle depends on teams investigating denied claims, checking payer rules and deciding which problems need a human’s attention. AI agents could take on some of that work, but the harder question is how to fit them into the way health systems operate.
For Mount Sinai Health System Inc., that starts with clear workflows and accountability when automation encounters an exception, according to Salonia Brown, system vice president of revenue cycle at Mount Sinai. Without those foundations, adding AI could make existing problems harder to manage.
“If you don’t have your workflows down pat, if you don’t have operational owners, when something kicks out, when you use AI, if there’s no ownership over that or accountability, then what you’re in essence doing is kind of digitizing dysfunction,” Brown said in an interview with theCUBE. “It’s very simple and easy to inject AI, but to do it the right way, making sure there’s governance [and] that the economics make sense? That takes a little bit of time.”
Brown and Akash Magoon, co-founder and chief executive officer of Adonis Technology Inc., along with other industry experts, spoke with theCUBE’s host Gemma Allen for the Adonis Reimagining Claim to Cash interview series on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI agents can handle claims work, how health systems govern exceptions and where human judgment remains essential. (* Disclosure below.)
Here are three insights from this exclusive interview series:
1. Mount Sinai brings AI agents into the healthcare revenue cycle.
Adonis is building agents to investigate denied claims and reduce the manual work involved in pursuing payment, according to Magoon. The company uses voice AI to call insurers for claims information and makes tens of thousands of those calls each week on behalf of its partners.
At Mount Sinai, Brown’s team helps determine which tasks can be automated and which require critical judgment. Employees need to trust the technology and know who is responsible when an exception arises, he noted. The goal is to free staff from repetitive administrative work so they can focus on more complex cases.
Watch the full interview on theCUBE.
2. Rush asks frontline staff what AI should take on.
Adonis distinguishes between frequent, repetitive tasks suited to automation and complex work that calls for better information and decisions, according to David Unger, managing director of health system sales at Adonis. For a high-value appeal, that can mean helping a team decide whether to pursue it and what evidence may improve its chances.
At Rush University System for Health, frontline employees help identify time-consuming steps that add little value, according to Blake Evans, system vice president of revenue cycle at Rush. Their firsthand knowledge helps the company decide where to automate and has made staff advocates for further changes.
Get the complete story on theCUBE.
3. Panoramic Health weighs AI’s promise against healthcare’s rules.
Adonis aims to identify revenue-cycle issues as they emerge and recommend a response, according to Doug Pickett, chief revenue officer of Adonis. An issue might call for automation, or it might reveal an upstream coding or provider-credentialing problem that a health system needs to fix before it grows.
Clinicians and operating teams are increasingly asking for AI tools that could reduce administrative burdens, according to Sap Sinha, chief executive officer of Panoramic Health. Yet rules governing billing, documentation and interactions with insurers have not kept pace with the technology. How those rules evolve could shape whether and how providers and insurers can use AI agents to interact over claims.

articles.title: Muse can now place calls to US businesses — if you pay | TechCrunch
articles.text:
After initially testing the feature in September, Meta’s consumer AI agent Muse is now able to place calls to U.S. businesses on behalf of its users. However, only paid subscribers have access to the feature, the company says.
Meta’s Muse, which now has over 10 million users, the company said last month, has been working to make consumer AI a mainstream product for everyday users. Placing calls is one of the ways it aims to get there, as it could handle another task on people’s to-do lists.
Notes Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer and head of its Superintelligence Labs division, the feature could be used to take care of calls people don’t want to make, like those to their cable company, the DMV, or to a restaurant that doesn’t offer online reservations.
Previously, only a select number of Muse early adopters were able to try this feature after asking the AI for access. Now, anyone who pays for Muse can make this type of request. Currently, Muse subscription plans start at $20 per month for 500 million Muse tokens per week. Heavier AI users can opt to pay $100 per month for 3 billion tokens.
Muse is not the only AI agent able to place calls to businesses; the startup Instinct has been offering a similar option, as has Google’s Gemini. However, while the AI tools are now certainly capable of handling the task, the reception on the other end of the line can be mixed. Many businesses and receptionists hang up on calls from AI agents as soon as they identify that it’s not a human on the phone. But with AI now better able to mimic a real human voice, being able to tell the difference between a customer and an AI working on the customer’s behalf will get tougher.
Despite the challenges, this feature is one that could appeal to consumers who have grown frustrated with the state of customer service over the years. For too long, customers have been forced to navigate complex phone trees, and then sit on hold waiting for a human representative to pick up. If they’re lucky, that person can actually help them, and not transfer them to another department. Now, those consumers could potentially use their AI, with its infinite patience, for this tedious task instead.
While calls remain a paid-only feature for the time being, the recently added option to make a Muse email address will soon roll out to free users, Wang said this week.

articles.title: The Elder Scrolls' most obscure adventure gets a 4K PC makeover
articles.text:
So, you think you’re an Elder Scrolls superfan? You say you’ve been there since The Elder Scrolls Arena on MS-DOS and have logged hundreds of hours in The Elder Scrolls Online? You say you’ve bought all of the roughly 5,000 re-releases and remasters of Skyrim that have been made available in the last 15 years?
Tell me, then: What do you think of The Elder Scrolls Travels: Shadowkey?
What’s that? You’ve never played Shadowkey? You weren’t there day one back in 2004, Nokia N-Gage in hand, ready to experience the game’s 176 x 208 resolution mobile hack-and-slash RPG combat for yourself? And you call yourself a real Elder Scrolls fan?
Well, don’t worry. Now you can fill in this crucial gap in your history without even having to track down functional, decades-old N-Gage hardware. That’s thanks to Shadowkey: Reforged, a free fan-made PC port that pairs updated art with the original game files and scripts for an upscaled, 4K experience that runs natively on PC, no N-Gage or emulator needed.
A few decades of upgrades
Moving from a pre-iPhone mobile game to a modern PC obviously comes with major graphical upgrades, powered by a completely rewritten PC graphics engine. What was once a cramped portrait orientation on the N-Gage has now been expanded for a 16:9 monitor standard that displays at up to 120 fps (though the game’s logic still matches the original game’s 25 fps). In addition to newly retextured character and environmental models, the new port also sports small touches like bloom lighting, rippling water, and an upgraded interface with sharper text rendering than was possible on an ancient mobile phone.

articles.title: Shipping giant Maersk confirms data breach as hackers demand $5 million ransom
articles.text:
Shipping giant Maersk confirms data breach as hackers demand $5 million ransom
World, say 'hi' to WhiteArmor, a new ransomware player on the block.
- Maersk discloses cyberattack on a legacy system from an acquired logistics company, with attackers allegedly stealing 100GB of data
- A ransomware group is demanding $5 million and threatening to leak records, passwords, and logistics information
- Maersk says core operations remain unaffected while investigating the breach and assessing the validity of the stolen data claims
One of the world's largest shipping and logistics companies, A.P. Moller–Maersk (often just called Maersk) has confirmed it recently suffered a cyberattack in which it lost sensitive data from one of its earlier acquisitions.
The criminals are now trying to pressure the company into paying a ransom, threatening to release all of the stolen information on the dark web.
Maersk issued an incident report, saying cybercriminals broke into a unnamed company it had previously acquired which reportedly operated a legacy system that the attackers managed to pierce.
“Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed,” Maersk said, “The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI.”
WhiteArmor takes the blame
The company said it does not expect the attack to disrupt its operations, and told its customers they can continue using its platforms to book and manage their shipments as usual.
But just because the data has not yet leaked, it doesn’t mean it won’t happen. According to BleepingComputer, a hacking group calling itself WhiteArmor added Maersk to its data leak site and told the company to pay $5 million in bitcoin - or else.
"Your contract-logistics arm, the former LF Logistics, runs fulfillment for many of the world's largest consumer brands. Five million dollars is roughly four hours of that EBITDA," the threat actor said. "You have 30 days to contact us and pay USD 5,000,000 in bitcoin."
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Companies usually don’t jump on the opportunity to pay the cybercriminals, so it’s safe to assume Maersk will ignore this invitation, and the data will leak.
However, we now know who it was stolen from - LF Logistics. This was an independent Hong-Kong-based third-party logistics company specializing in warehousing and ecommerce fulfillment. Maersk bought it in 2022 for $3.6 billion and integrated it into its own global Logistics & Services division, where it effectively ceased to exist as a separate entity.
Risky business
WhiteArmor claims to have stolen 100GB of data, including almost 30,000 driver records, passwords in plaintext, 33 SUPER_ADMIN accounts, signed delivery receipts, and 14.44 inventory rows with purchase orders and Advance Shipping Notices (ASN). Furthermore, it claims to have nabbed 27,842 mobile device logs containing phone numbers, email addresses, and even IMEI numbers.
If the claims are true, then this could be a major issue for Maersk. Passwords in plaintext and SUPER_ADMIN accounts means the company’s IT team will have to rotate all secrets to secure their premises. If any of the passwords are also used elsewhere, those services are at risk, as well. Details such as phone numbers and IMEI numbers are ideal for phishing and vishing attacks which have proven, time and time again, their destructive potential.
As one of the world’s largest container shipping companies, Maersk employs more than 100,000 people and generates more than $50 billion in revenue, as its global network includes more than 60 terminals and over 500 warehousing facilities.
In 2017, cybercriminals utilized the infamous NotPetya attack to wreak havoc on Maersk and bring its entire global network to a standstill, leading to damage that cost the business between $250 and $300 million.

articles.title: Elon Musk says it ‘would be an honor’ to hire ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — possible projects could include Terafab, SpaceX’s planned GPU manufacturing, or Tesla’s AI accelerators
articles.text:
Elon Musk says it ‘would be an honor’ to hire ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — possible projects could include SpaceX’s planned GPU manufacturing, Terafab, or Tesla’s AI accelerators
Jensen Huang still possesses valuable knowledge despite his departure from Nvidia.
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO two weeks after his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy was revealed by intelligence sources and a day after his affair with an Nvidia vice president became publicly known. But hours before this move, when it was just rumored that the Nvidia board was planning to oust him, Elon Musk had already stated his willingness to hire the former Nvidia chief on X. A random X user posted, “Elon please hire Jensen,” to which the billionaire replied, “That would be an honor.”
Despite the scandals that Jensen is currently facing, he still has the engineering know-how, deep knowledge of the industry and its inner workings, plus multiple connections across the world, which would be extremely valuable for any company looking to break into the semiconductor industry.
This is exactly what Elon Musk is doing with his Terafab project, which he first mentioned in November 2025. Jensen Huang even warned that this was going to be a challenge, pointing out that “the engineering, the science, and the artistry of doing what TSMC does for a living is extremely hard.” Nevertheless, Musk poured his resources into the project, with construction on the Terafab facility in full swing and with plans to hit volume chip production by the second half of 2028. Musk himself said that the site targets a production capacity of a million wafers a month by 2032. Tesla has an ambitious AI accelerator roadmap, and SpaceX has even touted making its own GPUs in the future.
We still don’t know what Jensen Huang’s plans are, but even though he’s no longer a part of the Nvidia board and its leadership, Jensen and his wife, Lori, still jointly own approximately 800 million Nvidia shares through various trusts and LLCs, while Huang himself personally owns around 70 million Nvidia shares.
Aside from that, he still has an outstanding invitation from Congress to discuss Nvidia’s security protocols, which could turn into a subpoena if he snubs them, although we don’t know how his resignation would affect the closed-door meeting. There’s also a reported FBI investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive who was allegedly instrumental in the import of $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia AI GPUs into China and is suspected of working with China’s Ministry of State Security.
Jensen Huang is just the latest in the long list of executives who resigned or were ousted from their leadership position because of a relationship or an affair with a subordinate. This includes former Boeing CEO Harry Stonecipher in 2005, HP CEO Mark Hurd in 2010, Intel CEO Brian Krzanich in 2018, and former McDonald’s CEO Steve Easterbrook in 2019. Musk himself is known to have had relationships with subordinates from his various companies, and that he has even fathered four children with Shivon Zilis, a top executive at Neuralink who started working at Tesla in 2017, through IVF.
It’s still not confirmed if Musk’s reply is a serious offer for Jensen Huang. But if the former Nvidia chief ever decides to work for Musk on his Terafab project, then Jensen could put his effort and expertise into turning it into a formidable competitor to Nvidia.

articles.title: „Anhaltend enttäuscht“: Sam Altman kritisiert die Gen Z in KI-Debatte
articles.text:
Sam Altman vs. Gen Z: Warum der OpenAI-Chef die Jugend kritisiert
Die KI-Revolution sorgt schon jetzt dafür, dass die Zahl der Stellenangebote für Berufseinsteiger:innen rapide abnimmt – auch in Deutschland, wie eine Analyse des Jobportals Indeed kürzlich gezeigt hat. Vor allem Angehörige der sogenannten Gen Z, also zwischen 1997 und 2012 geborene Personen, fürchten, durch den zunehmenden Einsatz von KI-Tools ersetzt zu werden.
Sam Altman: Anhaltend enttäuscht von Gen Z
Sam Altman will solche Sorgen nicht gelten lassen. Im Sommer 2025 prognostizierte der OpenAI-Chef Uni-Absolvent:innen einen Arbeitsalltag der Zukunft, in dem dank KI „einfach alles besser“ ist – „astronomische Gehälter“ inklusive. Die Gen Z teilt Altmans Begeisterung offenbar nicht, was diesen „anhaltend enttäusche“, wie Fortune berichtet.
In einem Interview mit der Stanford Graduate School of Business erklärte Altman, dass die Studierenden lieber machten, was vor fünf Jahren cool war statt etwas Neues auszuprobieren. Dabei, so der KI-Verfechter, sei genau jetzt die richtige Zeit um neue Wege zu gehen.
KI-Revolution bietet auch Chancen
Es sei vollkommen richtig, dass KI eine große Zahl von Dingen, die heute noch Menschen erledigen, künftig besser, günstiger und schneller mache. Zudem übernehme die KI große Bereiche aktueller Tätigkeiten komplett. Aber: Der Umbruch biete auch Chancen für ambitionierte Arbeitskräfte, so Altman. Dazu müsse man aber bereit sein zu überlegen, welche neuen Geschäftsmodelle sich mithilfe von KI entwickeln ließen.
Die Ausgangslage sei so offen wie nie zuvor. Die KI öffne Unternehmer:innen ein seltenes Zeitfenster, um Bereiche aufzubauen, die noch vor wenigen Jahren schwierig oder gar unmöglich gewesen seien, so Altman. Auf Basis der Technologie, so der OpenAI-Chef, ließen sich Unternehmen entwickeln, die weitaus größer und bedeutender sein könnten als OpenAI selbst.
Karriere in Zeiten des größten Wandels
„Wenn ihr euch jetzt in die Welt hinausbegebt, um an etwas zu arbeiten – dann beginnt ihr eure Karriere vermutlich in einer Zeit des größten Wandels“, gab Altman den Stanford-Studierenden mit auf den Weg. Menschen mit großem Potenzial, Tatendrang, Ideen, einer neuen Sichtweise auf die Dinge sowie neuen Fähigkeiten kämen tendenziell besonders gut zurecht, „wenn der Boden am stärksten bebt“.

articles.title: Elon Musk podría incorporar a Jensen Huang a una de sus empresas tras su salida de Nvidia: “Sería un honor”
articles.text:
Elon Musk abrió la posibilidad de incorporar a Jensen Huang a alguna de sus compañías después de que el empresario dejara la dirección ejecutiva de Nvidia, uno de los principales fabricantes de procesadores para inteligencia artificial. El fundador de Tesla y SpaceX respondió que sería “un honor” contratarlo, luego de que un usuario de la red social X le pidiera sumar al ejecutivo a su equipo.
La declaración se produjo el miércoles 11 de noviembre por la noche, cuando todavía se especulaba sobre el futuro de Huang dentro de Nvidia. El comentario llegó después de que el diario The Wall Street Journal informara que la junta directiva de la compañía preparaba una reunión para analizar su continuidad al frente del fabricante de chips.
Horas después, durante la mañana del jueves 12 de noviembre, Nvidia confirmó la renuncia de Huang como director ejecutivo. La empresa designó a Colette Kress, quien hasta entonces se desempeñaba como directora financiera, como CEO interina mientras busca un reemplazo permanente.
Aunque la respuesta de Musk generó comentarios sobre un posible movimiento profesional, no existe una confirmación de que haya presentado una oferta formal a Huang ni de que ambos empresarios hayan iniciado conversaciones para concretar una contratación.
Qué dijo Elon Musk sobre contratar a Jensen Huang
El intercambio comenzó cuando la cuenta del blog financiero ZeroHedge publicó un mensaje dirigido a Musk en X: “Elon, por favor contrata a Jensen”. El empresario respondió: “Eso sería un honor”.
La breve contestación despertó interés debido a la trayectoria de Huang y al papel que desempeñó en la transformación de Nvidia. Durante más de tres décadas, el ejecutivo convirtió a la compañía en uno de los proveedores más importantes de tecnología para inteligencia artificial.
La posibilidad de que Musk incorpore a Huang también resulta llamativa por los proyectos tecnológicos que dirige. Tesla trabaja en el desarrollo de sistemas de conducción autónoma y robots humanoides, mientras que SpaceX impulsa infraestructura espacial y xAI desarrolla modelos de inteligencia artificial.
Todas estas iniciativas requieren capacidad de procesamiento y tecnologías avanzadas para entrenar y ejecutar sistemas de IA. Sin embargo, el comentario de Musk no especificó a cuál de sus empresas podría incorporarse Huang ni qué funciones tendría.
Por qué Jensen Huang dejó Nvidia
La salida del empresario ocurrió después de que trascendieran informaciones sobre una investigación relacionada con sus vínculos personales y posibles implicaciones para la seguridad tecnológica de Estados Unidos.
The New York Times informó sobre una relación extramatrimonial entre Huang y Alice Huang, una ejecutiva de negocios que, según funcionarios de inteligencia estadounidenses citados por el medio, habría sido identificada como una presunta agente vinculada al Ministerio de Seguridad del Estado de China.
La mujer trabajó anteriormente en Megaspeed International, una empresa de computación en la nube con sede en Singapur investigada por el Departamento de Comercio estadounidense por presuntamente facilitar el desvío de procesadores avanzados de Nvidia hacia clientes chinos. La compañía negó las acusaciones.
Según información de The Information citada por Reuters, la relación habría facilitado el envío de al menos 7.500 millones de dólares en chips de Nvidia a empresas chinas. El Departamento de Justicia de Estados Unidos investiga si se incumplieron las normas de control de exportaciones.
Nvidia había iniciado una investigación interna y contrató al exfiscal federal Joon Kim para conducirla. La empresa sostuvo que no tenía motivos para creer que se hubieran comprometido sus secretos corporativos o la seguridad nacional estadounidense.
Qué pasará con Nvidia después de la salida de Huang
La renuncia de Huang representa un cambio importante para Nvidia, que se convirtió en una pieza central de la industria de inteligencia artificial gracias a sus unidades de procesamiento gráfico (GPU).
Estos componentes son utilizados por empresas como OpenAI, Microsoft y Google para entrenar y ejecutar modelos capaces de generar textos, imágenes y otros contenidos. Su demanda impulsó el crecimiento financiero de Nvidia y la convirtió en una de las compañías más valiosas del mundo.
Tras la salida de su cofundador, Colette Kress asumió la dirección ejecutiva de manera interina. La ejecutiva trabaja en Nvidia desde 2013 y conoce las operaciones financieras de la empresa, aunque la junta directiva todavía debe elegir a quien ocupará el puesto de forma permanente.
La crisis también tuvo consecuencias en los mercados. Las acciones de Nvidia cayeron más del 8% en las operaciones posteriores al cierre de la jornada en la que se conocieron los reportes sobre la posible reunión de la junta directiva.
Mientras la compañía enfrenta el proceso de transición, Musk dejó abierta, con una breve respuesta en X, la posibilidad de que Huang continúe su trayectoria en otra empresa tecnológica. Por ahora, no hay indicios de que esa contratación vaya a concretarse.

articles.title: Mittal says India must hold the satellite 'kill switch', warns against reliance on one company
articles.text:
Mittal says India must hold the satellite 'kill switch', warns against reliance on one company
The kill switch is the ability to cut off, throttle or restrict a satellite network's service, whether for a single terminal, a region or an entire country, from the operator's control systems and ground gateways.
Bharti Airtel Founder and Chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal said India must keep control of the "kill switch" for satellite communications on its own soil, as the government weighs security conditions that will decide when satellite broadband goes live.
"The kill switch, as we call it, should not be sitting somewhere else," Mittal said in an interview with PTI marking Bharti Enterprises' 50th year. "India must have control over its own space destiny."
He did not name a company in that remark.
The kill switch is the ability to cut off, throttle or restrict a satellite network's service, whether for a single terminal, a region or an entire country, from the operator's control systems and ground gateways. In satellite broadband, user terminals connect to satellites, which relay traffic to ground stations and then to the internet, so whoever runs those control and gateway systems can in principle disable users or reroute their data.
Governments see it as a security tool. It would let them shut down service quickly in a conflict, during a security threat or to enforce lawful orders, and it would let them monitor and intercept traffic.
The implications cut both ways. If the switch sits with a foreign operator or abroad, a country's military, emergency and civilian users can lose connectivity because of a decision made elsewhere, which Mittal calls losing control of "its own space destiny."
If it sits with the government, that same power can be used to cut off access in national emergencies or for strategic reasons.
It is for these reasons that security clearances, in-country gateways and monitoring requirements will shape who can launch satellite broadband in India and how fast.
Mittal pointed to Ukraine, saying that "if Ukraine is using Starlink, it's also using OneWeb now".
Last month, Ukraine accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself by cutting connectivity speeds, disrupting military operations. Those restrictions, rendered some Ukrainian strike and interceptor drones virtually unusable.
Whether the government's scrutiny of satellite operators is justified, Mittal said it is. He argued that warfare is moving to space. "Whether it's drone or it's cyber issues, or indeed guided missiles and all, they're all going to be managed from space," he said.
"Everybody in the world needs to have control over its security," he said. "There India will need to have guardrails. It'll need to secure itself."
He said India should not lean on a single provider. "Importantly, it may need to have different players. You can't just depend on one country or one company," he said. India must also ensure "the security of the apparatus, of the equipment, the communications coming down into the ground to be monitored," and "everything should be routed through India," he added.
He said Eutelsat OneWeb is building a secure European communications network, in which he said the EU is spending 14-15 billion euros, and that this has drawn attention to the company.
Mittal said OneWeb's service already works in India. "The government occasionally uses their terminals for emergency services," he said.
As an example, he said economic adviser Sanjeev Sanyal took a terminal on a boat trip to Oman.
"He was streaming all the way through," Mittal said. "It is, right now, fully available. We can just switch it on soon."
"We were the first licence given by the government. We have satisfied all their needs, and we just now wait for their signal," he said. "I still hope we'll get the first approval."
Three companies hold satellite communications licences in India: Jio, OneWeb and Starlink. The government has said all three operators hold provisional spectrum and are at a similar stage, and that final launch depends on security clearance.
On the spectrum debate, Mittal said satellite spectrum is shared. "Everybody dips into the same spectrum," he said, with operators at different orbital heights having to coordinate. He said OneWeb has "the highest priority on the KU band, and therefore others have to coordinate with us," and that the regulators understand the debate.
Mittal said satellite will not replace mobile networks. "For the foreseeable future it will remain complementary. It's very expensive. Satellites need to be replaced every five, six years," he said. "Where there is fibre, radio cannot compete with it. Where there is a radio, satellite cannot compete with it. But together all of them... will coexist."
He said the case for satellite is coverage. There are still "dark spots" in "deep rural hinterlands, in the forests, in the hills, mountains, in the high seas, in the ocean and of course in the air," he said.
Satellite links would connect a phone user in the mountains with no signal, he added.

articles.title: « Un problème au niveau d'iOS » : Binance alerte sur une faille de l’iPhone qui menace tous les portefeuilles crypto
articles.text:
Binance tire la sonnette d’alarme. Dans un message publié sur X, la plus grande plateforme d’échange de cryptomonnaies indique que la faille de l’iPhone permet à des « applications malveillantes de lire les fichiers locaux d’autres applications, mettant en danger les phrases de récupération, les clés privées et les identifiants de connexion dans l’ensemble de l’écosystème ». D’après la plateforme, les mises à jour iOS 26.7.1, iOS 27.0.1 et iOS 27.2 sont concernées.
 A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.…
— Binance (@binance) November 10, 2026
Binance souligne que le problème ne vient pas de son application iOS. Yi He, cofondatrice de la plateforme crypto, met bien en avant qu’il « s’agit d’un problème au niveau d’iOS ». En clair, tous les portefeuilles crypto installés sur un iPhone vulnérable sont potentiellement concernés. Notez que la faille d’iOS n’a rien à voir avec le piratage de Binance, dont le butin est toujours en cours de blanchiment sur les blockchains.
Une faille qui fait tomber les cloisons de l’iPhone
Sur iPhone, chaque application fonctionne normalement dans un espace isolé du reste de l’OS, appelé le « bac à sable » (sandbox). Une application ne peut donc pas fouiller dans les fichiers d’une autre application, pour des raisons évidentes de sécurité. La faille worse_query permet justement de contourner cette protection. Découverte par deux chercheurs, @0xjohnny et @forcequitOS, la faille a fait l’objet d’une démonstration sur GitHub. Il est bien possible d’exploiter la faille pour s’emparer de données confidentielles, ou supprimer les informations d’une app.
Sur le papier, des pirates pourraient se servir de la vulnérabilité pour pénétrer dans le portefeuille crypto des détenteurs d’iPhone, en subtilisant la phrase de récupération dans une application. Pour arriver à ses fins, l’attaquant doit mettre au point une application iOS malveillante, programmée pour exploiter la défaillance.
« Un attaquant devrait toujours parvenir à installer un logiciel malveillant sur l’iPhone ciblé, par exemple en convainquant son propriétaire d’installer une application provenant d’une source non fiable », explique Bitdefender dans un rapport consacré à l’incident.
Le risque concerne donc surtout les utilisateurs qui installent des applications en dehors de l’App Store. Par ailleurs, la faille « n’expose pas automatiquement tous les portefeuilles crypto ». Le risque « dépend de la façon dont chaque application stocke et protège ses informations sensibles », nuance l’éditeur d’antivirus.
Pour Charles Guillemet, directeur technique de Ledger, ce type de faille « était autrefois très coûteux et réservé à des attaquants disposant de moyens importants ». Son coût tend désormais « vers zéro, et elles sont désormais exploitées à grande échelle », vraisemblablement à cause de l’essor de l’intelligence artificielle. « Ne stockez simplement rien de précieux sur votre mobile, surtout pas vos phrases de récupération crypto », recommande le responsable.
 Unfortunately this kind of vulnerability used to be very expensive and reserved to high potential attackers. Their cost is trending towards zero and are now exploitee at scale.
Simply don’t store any valuable in your mobile, especially not your crypto seeds…
— Charles Guillemet (@P3b7_) November 10, 2026
Une faille toujours béante
Il y a quelques jours, Apple a déployé iOS 27.2.1, une mise à jour truffée de correctifs. Neanmoins, Apple n’a pas corrigé la faille pointée du doigt par Binance. Ni iOS 27.2.1 ni la première bêta d’iOS 27.3 ne corrigent la faille. Bonne nouvelle, aucun vol de cryptomonnaies exploitant la vulnérabilité n’a été signalé pour le moment.
En attendant un correctif, Binance recommande de supprimer toutes les applications installées depuis des sources non officielles. Si vous soupçonnez une intrusion, transférez vos fonds vers un nouveau portefeuille, créé au besoin sur un appareil sain, puis déconnectez toutes vos sessions actives. Évitez aussi de conserver votre phrase de récupération dans une capture d’écran ou une note sur votre téléphone. C’est la meilleure façon de se faire dépouiller.
 👉🏻 Suivez l’actualité tech en temps réel : ajoutez 01net à vos sources sur Google, et abonnez-vous à notre canal WhatsApp.
Source : Bitdefender

articles.title: Claude-Update sorgt für Ärger: Warum die KI jetzt legitime Projekte blockiert
articles.text:
Anthropic verschärft Regeln: Warum Claude jetzt Games blockiert
In der Spielebranche sorgen KI-generierte Kopien zunehmend für Unruhe. Dazu kommt, dass sich im Vorfeld von Veröffentlichungen geäußerte Ideen oder verbreitete Demos mit KI-Support zur Game-Entwicklung missbrauchen lassen – inklusive entsprechender Erpressungsversuche.
Nachbau existierender Games verboten
KI-Anbieter Anthropic will dem jetzt einen Riegel vorschieben. Im Systemprompt seiner Modelle Claude Code und Claude Opus 5.5 findet sich ein Passus, der den „Nachbau spezifischer existierender Games“ untersagt. Das soll auch dann gelten, wenn die Entwickler:innen für das Ergebnis einen anderen Namen wählen, wie Tom‘s Hardware berichtet.
Weiter erlaubt sein soll Anthropics KI-Modellen aber die Hilfe bei der Entwicklung von Games, wenn die Nutzer:innen dabei ihre eigenen Designs und Materialien verwenden. Das Unternehmen hat die Änderung bestätigt und dabei auf mögliche Verletzungen geistigen Eigentums verwiesen.
Schutz vor möglichen Urheberrechtsklagen
Diese, so Anthropic-Mitarbeiter Addy Osmani via X, verstießen gegen die Nutzungsrichtlinien. Zudem dürfte das Unternehmen damit versuchen, sich vor möglichen Verfahren wegen der Verletzung von Urheberrechten zu schützen.
Allerdings scheint es im Zuge der strengeren Regeln auch zu Problemen bei legitimen Entwicklungsprojekten zu kommen. So soll Claude auch eigentlich unbedenkliche Versuche, Games per Reverse-Engineering zu analysieren, blockieren. Im Visier scheint demnach unter anderem das vielgenutzte Tool Reverse Engineer Anything zu stehen.
Claude soll legitime Projekte torpedieren
Auf GitHub häufen sich laut Tom‘s Hardware Meldungen von Nutzer:innen, dass die Anthropic-KI die Zusammenarbeit auch bei der Nachbildung von Spielmechaniken oder beim Patchen von Game-Code verweigert. Die Weigerung trifft laut Berichten auf Reddit und anderen Plattformen auch andere Entwickler:innen aus anderen Bereichen, die etwa einen Windows-Crash analysieren oder Junkware von einem Smart-TV entfernen wollten.
Inwiefern es sich bei allen Beschwerden um legitime Anliegen handelt, ist derweil nicht zu belegen. In einigen Fällen sollen aber bekannte und glaubwürdige Entwickler:innen Protest eingelegt haben.
Regeln zu streng? Anthropic will nachjustieren
Hat Anthropic also die Zügel zu eng angezogen? Der KI-Anbieter hat angekündigt, entsprechend nachjustieren zu wollen, um „ein Gleichgewicht“ zu finden. „Falls Claude in der Zwischenzeit etwas ablehnt, das dir gehört, dann schick es mir“, schrieb Osmani via X.

articles.title: Avant même le Black Friday, Amazon fait descendre l’ampoule connectée Tapo L520E à 7,59€
articles.text:
Rendre une lampe de bureau ou un plafonnier pilotable à la voix ne demande ni pont domotique ni installation, à condition de choisir une ampoule Wi-Fi au bon culot. En pré-Black Friday, Amazon affiche la Tapo L520E à 7,59 € au lieu de 10,99 €, une ampoule E27 à la lumière du jour de 4000 K, pensée pour les pièces où l’on travaille plus que pour les ambiances tamisées.
La gamme Tapo de TP-Link, que nous croisons souvent pour ses caméras de surveillance, compte aussi des ampoules pilotées depuis la même application. La L520E en est la version la plus simple : un culot E27, une seule teinte de blanc et une intensité réglable. Amazon la propose à 7,59 € au lieu de 10,99 €, soit 31 % de remise sur le prix conseillé, dans le cadre de son opération pré-Black Friday.
L’offre parle d’abord à ceux qui veulent goûter à la maison connectée sans investir dans un écosystème complet, ou équiper une pièce de travail d’un éclairage programmable.
L’ampoule connectée Tapo L520E passe à 7,59 € au lieu de 10,99 € chez Amazon, avec la commande vocale Alexa et Google Assistant sans hub à ajouter.
Pourquoi choisir la Tapo L520E ?
- Aucun pont à acheter : Elle se connecte directement à votre réseau Wi-Fi 2,4 GHz, sans hub domotique. Le prix affiché correspond donc au coût total de l’installation, ce qui n’est pas le cas des systèmes qui passent par un pont Zigbee.
- La voix ou le smartphone : Elle répond aux commandes d’Amazon Alexa et de Google Assistant, et se pilote à distance depuis l’application Tapo. Vous pouvez ainsi l’éteindre à distance si vous l’avez oubliée en partant.
- Des automatismes utiles : Programmation horaire, minuterie et calage sur le lever et le coucher du soleil évitent d’y penser au quotidien. Le mode absence allume et éteint la lampe pour donner l’impression que le logement est occupé pendant vos congés.
Du bureau à l’entrée, là où cette lumière du jour trouve sa place
Une température de 4000 K donne une lumière neutre, ni jaune ni bleutée, qui convient à une lampe de bureau, à une cuisine ou à une salle de bain. Avec 806 lumens au maximum, soit l’équivalent d’une ampoule classique de 60 W, elle éclaire correctement une petite pièce ou un plan de travail. La gradation permet de la baisser le soir sans changer d’ampoule, et son angle de diffusion de 220 degrés répartit la lumière autour du luminaire. Dans une entrée, la programmation calée sur le coucher du soleil allume la lampe avant votre retour.
Le profil type est celui d’un premier équipement : vous avez une enceinte Echo ou Nest à la maison et voulez commander une lampe à la voix sans rien installer d’autre. Elle convient aussi aux locataires, puisqu’il suffit de la visser à la place de l’ancienne ampoule. Elle est en revanche moins indiquée pour un salon ou une chambre, où l’on cherche souvent un blanc plus chaud en soirée : sa fiche technique n’annonce qu’une seule température. Les utilisateurs d’iPhone qui comptent sur Siri et l’app Maison n’y trouveront pas leur compte, TP-Link ne citant qu’Alexa et Google Assistant.
Wi-Fi sans pont ou écosystème complet : où se situe cette ampoule
Dans notre comparatif des meilleures ampoules connectées, nous rappelons que des systèmes comme Philips Hue passent par un pont Zigbee, plus complet mais plus coûteux à l’entrée. La Tapo L520E se place à l’opposé : une ampoule Wi-Fi autonome, sans couleurs ni nuances de blanc, qui fait l’essentiel pour un prix très bas. Le même comparatif retient la WiZ Color E27, autre ampoule Wi-Fi sans pont, pour qui veut des couleurs. Dans la gamme Tapo, la L530E joue ce rôle multicolore, et nous en avions déjà relayé une promotion en mai 2025.
✅ Les points forts
- Connexion Wi-Fi directe, sans hub
- Compatible Amazon Alexa et Google Assistant
- 806 lumens, équivalent 60 W, intensité réglable
- Programmation, minuterie, lever et coucher du soleil
- Mode absence pour simuler une présence
❌ Les limites
- Une seule température de couleur, 4000 K
- Wi-Fi 2,4 GHz uniquement
- Pas de compatibilité Apple HomeKit annoncée
- Classe énergétique E
Avant le Black Friday, Amazon vend la Tapo L520E 3,40 € sous son prix conseillé, de quoi équiper plusieurs pièces à petit prix.
À 7,59 €, la Tapo L520E apporte la commande vocale, la programmation et le mode absence sans aucun équipement supplémentaire. La remise de 31 % reste modeste en euros, mais à ce prix, équiper trois lampes de bureau ou de cuisine coûte moins de 25 €. Pour un foyer déjà doté d’une enceinte Alexa ou Google, c’est une façon simple de mesurer l’intérêt de la domotique au quotidien.
Elle ne remplacera pas pour autant un éclairage d’ambiance. Pour un blanc chaud ou des couleurs, la L530E est plus adaptée, et pour l’app Maison d’Apple, mieux vaut choisir une ampoule qui affiche explicitement la compatibilité HomeKit, comme le conseille notre guide. Pour une lumière franche là où vous lisez, cuisinez ou travaillez, elle fait exactement ce qu’on lui demande.
Comment profiter des offres exclusives du Black Friday ?

Retrouvez tous les bons plans du Black Friday 2026 sur la page dédiée à l'événement.
Pour les aficionados de X, n'hésitez pas à suivre notre compte Clubic Bons Plans pour être au courant en direct des meilleures offres.

articles.title: New worm-like 'SCKit' malware targets MSPs in ScreenConnect attacks
articles.text:
A new worm-like malware toolkit named SCKit was deployed in the recent ScreenConnect attacks targeting managed service providers (MSPs), designed to spread from infected customer devices to MSP technicians' computers and compromise additional managed networks.
The malware toolkit uses a worm-like technique that exploits a previously patched ScreenConnect vulnerability, CVE-2026-84869, to execute malicious code on a technician's workstation when they connect to an infected device.
However, researchers at Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber say they have not observed successful exploitation of this flaw during the attacks, with Blackpoint confirming that the exploit failed in testing against a patched ScreenConnect client.
The findings follow yesterday's widespread ScreenConnect attacks, in which attackers gained unauthorized access to cloud-hosted ScreenConnect environments and used the platform's Run Command feature to install rogue ScreenConnect remote-access clients on customer endpoints.
ScreenConnect is a remote access and support platform used by MSPs and IT teams to remotely manage and troubleshoot customer devices.
According to an updated Huntress report, the attacks compromised at least 288 endpoints across 48 organizations, with all of the affected devices targeted within 90 minutes. Approximately one-third of those systems were affected within the first 10 minutes.
Huntress also believes the initial access was through RMM+, a third-party ScreenConnect extension that lets external management tools interact with ScreenConnect sessions without using the standard technician console.
The researchers found that RMM+ versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 contained an authentication flaw that could allow attackers to execute commands without authenticating to ScreenConnect or completing multifactor authentication.
RMM+ uses a shared access key to authenticate requests rather than ScreenConnect's normal user accounts and authentication mechanisms. However, the vulnerable versions allowed the access key to remain blank if an administrator had never configured one.
When this occurred, an attacker could supply an empty access key and pass the extension's authentication check, allowing them to issue remote commands through the ScreenConnect environment.
Huntress says this matches the activity observed during the attacks, where commands were executed across multiple ScreenConnect instances without corresponding user login activity, and logs linked the commands to RMM+.
As part of its response, ConnectWise disabled five potentially related third-party extensions across approximately 400 partner environments. The company stressed that the presence of these extensions does not mean those environments were compromised.
SCKit attempts to spread through ScreenConnect sessions
In separate analyses, Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber examined SCKit, a collection of 16 scripts and components developed to establish persistent remote access and spread between systems managed through ScreenConnect.
Blackpoint Cyber's Adversary Pursuit Group (APG) recovered the malware's loader directly from attacker-controlled infrastructure and decrypted subsequent stages to obtain the complete loader and a ScreenConnect installer used in the attacks.
The attackers first deploy additional ScreenConnect Access clients configured to connect to servers under their control for persistent remote access even if the original MSP ScreenConnect session is terminated.
However, SCKit's more novel capability is its attempt to turn a legitimate MSP remote support session into an attack against the technician initiating it.
The toolkit includes a component called RelayTrap, which is designed to replace the legitimate ScreenConnect Guest process running on an infected endpoint and wait for an MSP technician to establish an interactive connection.
Rather than dropping a precompiled executable, the attackers store RelayTrap as a C# source code file named RelayTrap.cs on their infrastructure.
The source code is then downloaded to compromised devices, where a PowerShell script compiles it locally into an executable.
A separate component called TrapWatch monitors ScreenConnect services and prepares the replacement Guest process to intercept incoming support sessions.
When an MSP technician connects, RelayTrap attempts to send a malicious file in the opposite direction of a normal remote-support operation, from the infected customer endpoint to the technician's workstation.
The technique attempts to exploit CVE-2026-84869, a critical ScreenConnect client-side file-transfer vulnerability that ConnectWise patched in version 26.6.5.
Under normal circumstances, ScreenConnect allows technicians to send files to managed endpoints and execute them remotely. Instead, the vulnerability potentially allows a malicious Guest to send a file back to the technician and have it executed.
The recovered source code also contains extensive comments explaining its functionality, compatibility workarounds, and previous coding errors, giving it the appearance of LLM-generated code.
Huntress also noted that RelayTrap appears to have been generated using a large language model.
Once running on a technician's workstation, other SCKit components attempt to steal ScreenConnect authentication cookies from web browsers, which could allow attackers to hijack the technician's authenticated management session without requiring their credentials or a new MFA challenge.
The malware then attempts to use the technician's existing ScreenConnect permissions to enumerate accessible endpoints and distribute malicious commands through legitimate management features, including the platform's Shared Toolbox.
This creates a worm-like infection chain in which a compromised customer endpoint could infect an MSP technician's workstation, steal their management session, and use that access to compromise additional endpoints across other customer organizations.
However, Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber have not seen this worm-like behavior succeeding during the current campaign.
Blackpoint researchers Sam Decker and Nevan Beal told BleepingComputer that they reproduced the toolkit's attempted exploit against a current ScreenConnect client and found that the existing security fix prevented execution.
"The Guest side queued the transfer, but the current client never requested or ran the payload," the researchers explained.
"So we have confirmed what the toolkit is built to do, and we have no evidence of successful exploitation and no evidence of a bypass at this time."
Huntress similarly reported that the console takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log it examined.
MSPs are urged to disable the affected third-party extensions, update ScreenConnect clients, investigate unauthorized remote-access installations, and review Run Command and Toolbox activity for signs of compromise.
Both research teams also recommend avoiding interactive ScreenConnect sessions with potentially infected endpoints and instead using separate security tools to investigate systems.

articles.title: Four Amazon Bedrock inference choices that affect cost | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Four Amazon Bedrock inference choices that affect cost
Your Amazon Bedrock inference bill can keep climbing after you tune prompts and application logic. Request-level choices can still change how many tokens the service processes and the rate applied to them. Cache duration, service tier, reasoning effort, and maxTokens can affect cost without changing your model or prompt.
Each choice depends on the model and workload. This post shows how we tested each choice and how to verify its effect from response metadata, logs, and billing data.
To try these settings yourself, start with the Amazon Bedrock Samples notebooks Mixed TTL Caching and Tenant Isolation with Prompt Caching. For maxTokens and reasoning effort, see the 01-low-effort folder of the sample-code-for-genai-cost-management-workshop GitHub repo. Each sample sets its own model ID, so change it, and the inference parameters, to match the model you call. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Models at a glance. For broader decisions such as model selection, batch inference, routing, and distillation, see Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock.
Where inference cost comes from
Every Amazon Bedrock response carries usage metadata. Input and output tokens bill at the rate for the model and tier that served the request. Cache reads and writes use separate token counters, and reasoning tokens count as output tokens.
Prompt cache duration
Repeated system instructions, tool definitions, or reference context can be processed again when the cache expires before the next request. The Prompt caching for faster model inference guide lists 5-minute and 1-hour time-to-live (TTL) values for supported Anthropic models. It also lists a 30-minute minimum TTL for supported GPT-5.6 models. Support and API fields depend on the model, so check the current support matrix before selecting a duration.
For supported models, Amazon Bedrock also offers implicit prompt caching, which attempts to reuse eligible prompt prefixes without cache controls in your request. Because implicit caching is best effort and doesn’t guarantee a cache hit, the duration choices in this section apply to explicit caching.
This Converse API signature requests a 1-hour entry on models that support it:
For supported Anthropic models, InvokeModel places the same ttl value in cache_control.
A longer duration is not automatically cheaper. The Amazon Bedrock Pricing page lists separate rates for 5-minute writes, 1-hour writes, and cache reads. For Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 and Anthropic Claude Opus 5 on Amazon Bedrock, a 5-minute write costs 1.25 times the input rate. A 1-hour write costs 2 times, and a cache read costs 0.1 times.
These rates set the break-even, assuming each request reuses the exact prefix and each cache read refreshes the TTL. A 5-minute cache pays back on the first reuse within 5 minutes. When requests for the same prefix arrive more than 5 minutes apart, it rewrites at 1.25 times on every request. The 1-hour cache is then cheaper from the second request within the hour.
Cache rates and checkpoint minimums differ by model. Check the Amazon Bedrock Pricing page and the prompt caching guide for the model you call. Rerun the comparison for your model, then confirm it with cache read and write tokens after rollout.
Keep stable content before dynamic content, meet the model’s checkpoint minimum, and use on-demand inference because prompt caching doesn’t work with batch inference.
Changing a cached prefix, including a system instruction or tool definition, causes a miss and a new write. Checkpoints are evaluated in the order tools, system, then messages, so a change in an earlier section also invalidates the later ones. Version prompts that change often so each version gets its own cache entry. We ran six calls on Claude Sonnet 5 with a 1-hour checkpoint, changing the system prompt once and the tool definition once. Each change produced zero cache reads and a new write.
AWS describes cache entries as scoped to your account and Region, not to your tenants. In a multi-tenant application, prepend a tenant-specific SHA-256 hash to the cacheable prefix. The Optimizing cost and latency with Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for Anthropic models post describes this pattern. Enforce tenant authorization before you build the prompt. The hash partitions entries inside one account. If a regulated workload needs a hard data boundary, keep each tenant in a separate AWS account.
Keep the 5-minute default for frequent reuse. Move from it to a longer supported duration when the same prefix recurs at least twice an hour with gaps longer than 5 minutes. To beat no caching at all, the 1-hour cache needs three requests an hour.
Service tiers for latency-tolerant workloads
Background jobs, evaluation harnesses, nightly summarization, and backfills don’t always need the latency profile used by interactive requests. For models that support Flex, select it with this request signature:
Use default, not standard, to request the Standard tier. You can also omit serviceTier:
Tier support is model-specific, so record support by exact model version. The Amazon Nova 2 Lite and OpenAI gpt-oss-120b model cards list Flex as supported. The cards for Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 and Anthropic Claude Opus 5 on Amazon Bedrock list it as not supported. A Flex request to an unsupported model fails with a ValidationException instead of silently running on Standard. Our request to Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 returned that error.
If your policy allows Standard as a fallback, catch the unsupported-tier error and retry once with default. Don’t retry every ValidationException, because malformed requests raise it too. Cap application-level retries. The bounded retry strategy of the AWS SDK handles throttling and transient errors.
Set your own deadline for Flex requests. A supported response reports the resolved tier, which you can also verify with Amazon CloudWatch ResolvedServiceTier. See Service tiers for optimizing performance and cost and the Amazon Bedrock Pricing page for the exact model you call.
We tested Flex on Amazon Nova 2 Lite with 200 default requests and 200 flex requests, sent in interleaved pairs. Both tiers processed the same number of input and output tokens. All 400 requests resolved to the requested tier, and the median latency difference was too small to separate from noise. At the time of writing, the published Flex rate for Nova 2 Lite in us-west-2 is half the Standard rate, and our bill reflected that. Check the Amazon Bedrock Pricing page for current rates. Keep latency-sensitive traffic on default.
Adaptive thinking effort
Reasoning tokens bill as output tokens. Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5 use adaptive thinking at high effort by default, even when a request omits the thinking field. An application moved from Claude Sonnet 4.6 without changes starts billing thinking tokens, and maxTokens now caps thinking plus response text. Claude Haiku 5.5 defaults to medium. All three models support low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. Lower the effort for a task with this request signature:
Keep effort in output_config, not inside thinking. Check Adaptive thinking whenever you change models.
We tested a tool-calling agent on Claude Opus 5. Its three tasks follow the design in Build long-horizon agents with Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock, and each has one correct answer. We ran each task eight times at every effort level. The table shows median output tokens:
| Effort | Correct runs | Median output tokens | Change from low (95% interval) | 
| low | 24 of 24 | 936 | baseline | 
| medium | 24 of 24 | 1,484 | +59% (50% to 78%) | 
| high (default) | 24 of 24 | 2,521 | +169% (112% to 190%) | 
| xhigh | 24 of 24 | 2,964 | +217% (170% to 260%) | 
| max | 24 of 24 | 3,762 | +302% (180% to 402%) | 
Accuracy at lower effort depends on the model and the task. Measure on tasks shaped like yours.
On the Amazon Bedrock Samples Invoke Bedrock model for code generation workload, median output tokens were 676 at low and 743 at high, a difference within run-to-run variation. The programs we graded passed at each effort level.
Use per-request output-token counts, CloudWatch AWS/Bedrock OutputTokenCount, invocation logs, and a task pass rate to evaluate the choice. Start below high for routine, well-bounded tasks. Keep high where your quality tests show that the task needs it. A token reduction that breaks the task is not a saving.
Output token limits
maxTokens is an application output ceiling. It limits the output that a bad prompt, regression, or loop can produce before the request stops. The quota rule is documented in How tokens are counted in Amazon Bedrock. Amazon Bedrock deducts your input tokens plus maxTokens when a request starts, so an oversized value reduces concurrency.
An output ceiling isn’t a safety control. Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails as a standard responsible AI control in production generative AI workloads. Guardrails can filter content, detect prompt attacks, and check grounding on supported inputs and responses. See Detect and filter harmful content by using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.
Set maxTokens per task type after observing a representative output-token distribution:
See Inference using Converse API for the request parameters.
In our test on Claude Sonnet 5, five normal outputs peaked at 103 tokens, so we set an illustrative fence of 155 tokens with headroom. We then sent the same deliberately verbose prompt with adaptive thinking disabled, once under a 2,048-token ceiling and once under the 155-token fence. The first request generated 2,048 output tokens and the second generated 155, so the fence avoided 1,893 output tokens. Both stopped at max_tokens, so both responses were truncated. The fence limits spend but does not make an unsuitable prompt useful, and in a multi-turn or agentic chain a truncated turn can break the steps after it.
For production calibration, compare the 95th and 99th percentiles (P95 and P99) for each task type and add headroom to the selected percentile. With adaptive thinking on, maxTokens also caps thinking tokens, so calibrate with thinking enabled. P95 limits exposure more aggressively but accepts more truncation risk. P99 preserves more valid long-tail responses at a higher ceiling. Monitor max_tokens stops and investigate the request before raising the task’s limit.
Putting it together
Use the same test loop for each setting: confirm model support, change one request choice, measure tokens or cost, and track quality or completion. If you route across models, keep a capability record for each model version, Region, and API: supported cache duration, service tiers, reasoning levels, and output ceiling. Validate each request against that record before you send it, then check the response for the resolved tier and cache counters.
| Setting | Default or permissive state | Result | Risk to accept | 
| Cache duration | Model-specific TTL | From published Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 rates, a 1-hour cache wins from the second request per hour when gaps exceed 5 minutes | A 1-hour write costs 2 times input, so low reuse loses money. Partition tenant prefixes | 
| Service tier | default | At the time of writing, Nova 2 Lite Flex was published at half the Standard rate, and our bill matched | Longer processing. Set your own deadline and a fallback | 
| Reasoning effort | high on the tested adaptive model | Low to high: +169% median output tokens on the agent test, no reliable difference on code generation | Quality can drop near the task’s capability boundary. Track pass rate with tokens | 
| maxTokens | Permissive 2,048-token cap | An illustrative 155-token fence avoided 1,893 output tokens in one test | Truncation can cascade through multi-turn or agentic chains. Check stopReason before raising the limit | 
Signals to watch
| Setting | Symptom | Verify with | First response | 
| Cache duration | Repeated context does not produce the expected latency or cost benefit | Application latency and cost telemetry | Check prefix stability, reuse interval, and model support before changing TTL | 
| Service tier | The requested tier is unsupported or the serving tier differs from expectation | Response serviceTier and CloudWatch ResolvedServiceTier | Use a supported tier or return latency-sensitive traffic to default | 
| Reasoning effort | Output tokens rise while quality holds | Per-request response telemetry, CloudWatch OutputTokenCount, invocation logs, and task pass rate | Lower effort for that task class and rerun its quality test | 
| maxTokens | stopReason is max_tokens | Response stop reason and task-scoped output-token distribution | Inspect the prompt and task fence before raising the limit | 
Derive P95 and P99 for each task type from task-tagged application telemetry or invocation logs.
Conclusion
All four choices live in the inference request. Recheck support when you change models, then change one setting at a time and measure the result in your application.
Use these resources to evaluate the choices for your workload:
- Amazon Bedrock console: console.aws.amazon.com/bedrock.
- Prompt caching: Prompt caching for faster model inference.
- Service tiers: Service tiers for optimizing performance and cost.
- Adaptive thinking: Adaptive thinking.
- Responsible AI controls: Detect and filter harmful content by using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.
- Related reading: Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock.
- Related samples and posts: Invoke Bedrock model for code generation and Build long-horizon agents with Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock.

articles.title: El Black Friday de Sihoo deja la Doro C300 Pro V2 a precio mínimo histórico: una silla ergonómica perfecta para casa u oficina
articles.text:
El Black Friday es uno de los momentos más importantes del año para hacer compras en todo tipo de dispositivos, especialmente de tecnología. No obstante, hace tiempo que todo tipo de tiendas y marcas se unieron a esta fecha. Una de ellas ha sido Sihoo, una marca que destaca especialmente por sus sillas ergonómicas. De hecho, la marca ahora mismo tiene en promoción la Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2. En este momento, la marca tiene disponible la silla por 484,99 euros.
