articles.title: Logitech offers 7,000 employees a paid day off to play GTA 6
articles.text:
The takeaway: Ahead of next week's GTA 6 launch, Logitech has announced a novel initiative called Logi Game Day, giving all of its employees one paid day off to play video games. While the move is unusual for a tech company that isn't a game developer or publisher, game studios and publishers are known to host company-wide launch parties and gaming sessions as part of major launch-day events.
Logitech explained that the program applies to all 7,000 full-time employees and interns globally, who can take the time off to play any video game of their choice, not just GTA 6. The company also clarified that the day can be used anytime between now and November 2027, and doesn't have to coincide with the launch of GTA 6.
In a statement, Logitech CEO Hanneke Faber said the Logi Game Day initiative is intended to challenge the perception that gaming is unproductive. "It's time to retire the stereotype that gaming is a waste of time," she said, adding that as a company that designs both enterprise and gaming products, Logitech believes that "engagement in one sphere supports performance in the other."
The initiative follows Logitech's Ctrl Tomorrow study, in which 81% of gamers agreed that "gaming builds real-world confidence, reduces anxiety, and correlates with stronger day-to-day work performance."
A separate Logitech study of enterprise IT decision-makers (ITDMs) found that 98.8% of respondents believe gaming skills translate directly to workplace capabilities, such as problem-solving and performing under pressure.
Faber said she plans to join the Logi Game Day festivities on November 19, when the company will host a gaming event at its San Jose office, with workspaces converted into gaming lounges to celebrate the much-awaited launch of GTA 6. The event will also be streamed online for fans.
The data cited by Logitech contrasts with some estimates suggesting the US economy could lose up to $1 billion in productivity on November 19 as 1.5 million workers call in sick to play GTA 6. However, the figures have been disputed by Victor Matheson, an economist at the College of the Holy Cross, who argues that any short-term loss will be made up for in the long term.
GTA VI will launch on November 19, 2026 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series consoles, with a PC version rumored to arrive sometime next year.
The game is available for pre-order starting at $80 for the standard edition and $100 for the "ultimate" edition. Rockstar is also selling a whopping $400 Collector's Edition, but that box is merchandise only and doesn't include the game.

articles.title: Shares of AI cloud operator Nebius drop 16%+ despite strong earnings results - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Shares of AI cloud operator Nebius drop 16%+ despite strong earnings results
Shares of artificial intelligence cloud operator Nebius Holdings NV dropped 17% today after it posted third-quarter financial results.
The company’s adjusted profit and revenue topped expectations. The selloff may have been sparked by its full-year forecast, which fell short of the consensus estimate. It’s also possible the sudden departure of Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Jensen Huang contributed. Nvidia is an investor in Nebius and many other AI and cloud companies.
Another possible factor: Nebius increased its full-year capital spending guidance to $27 billion. According to CNBC, that’s $4.15 billion higher than what Wall Street had expected. The company’s plan to invest between $40 billion and $45 billion in data centers next year surpassed the consensus estimate by an even wider margin.
The surging expenses may be related to its shift away from colocation facilities. Today, about 90% of the company’s infrastructure is located in rented data centers. In contrast, the next 2 gigawatts of computing capacity that it plans to bring online will be mostly powered by internally operated data centers.
“Our focus remains on building a healthy, profitable business for the long term,” said founder and Chief Executive Officer Arkady Volozh. “We will continue to invest across the business – in our capacity and infrastructure buildout, in our platform and products, and in the team that takes this to market.”
Nebius swung from a $100.4 million adjusted loss a year ago to a $90.9 million adjusted profit. The latter figure breaks down to adjusted earnings of 31 cents per share. The company’s profitability surprised analysts, who expected a loss of 69 cents per share.
Revenue growth was another bright spot. Sales jumped 517% year-over-year, to $980.8 million, which put the company well ahead of the $907.5 million consensus estimate.
One of Nebius’ main growth drivers is its Token Factory service for running open-source AI models. Developers use it to host both post-training and inference workloads. Nebius says that the offering, which launched a year ago, is nearing a “multi-hundred-million-dollar run rate” after logging a 17-fold quarter-over-increase in contract value.
Nebius’ largest customers played a particularly important role in its strong quarterly performance. The company signed $12 billion worth of contracts in the three months ended Sept. 30. The haul included multiyear deals with Snowflake Inc., Databricks Inc. and other major tech firms.
The company uses customers’ contract prepayments to finance its data center projects. The company says that the value of the prepayments it received in the third quarter exceeded its capital expenditures. However, the ratio of prepayments to capital expenditures is expected to decline as Nebius ramps up its data center spending. That detail may be yet another factor in today’s stock selloff.
Nebius expects its full-year revenue to be “at the low end” of its $3 billion to $3.4 billion target range. Analysts expected $3.37 billion. For 2027, Nebius is forecasting $12 billion to $13 billion in revenue.

articles.title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security.
U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.)
Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported.
The story took a sudden new turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang, and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.
By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee.
The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities.
As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.
November 12, 2026: Huang was having a third affair with another Nvidia employee, according to Reuters
After Huang was already ousted from Nvidia, we continued to learn more incriminating claims about the former CEO. According to Reuters, Huang had a third affair with an additional, unnamed employee of Nvidia.
November 12, 2026: Jensen Huang resigns, CFO Colette Kress named as interim CEO; Huang agrees to testify before Congress
Nvidia confirmed in an SEC filing on Thursday that the board accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress, will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang.
Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993.
Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26.
“Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.”
The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed.
November 11, 2026: Nvidia’s stock drops as board reportedly preps to oust CEO Jensen Huang
After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days.
Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said. The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan.
November 11, 2026: Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, NYT says
The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO.
According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year.
November 11, 2026: Congress plans to subpoena Huang to answer questions about affair
Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed.
November 9, 2026: Huang pulls out of various speaking engagements
The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum.
November 9-10, 2026: Details emerge about the business relationships between Nvidia and the alleged spy
Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported. The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips.
Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported. Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang.
In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported.
November 8, 2026: Trump shows support for Nvidia CEO, calls him a “fine person”
On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO.
“I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said.
When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia, Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.”
November 8, 2026: Huang admits to affair in public message to Nvidia employees; Nvidia board of directors begins investigation
Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife.
“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.”
“Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote.
Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day.
November 5, 2026: Three Republican committee chairmen ask Huang for closed-door briefing
Three Republican congressmen — Chairman John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Chairman Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Chairman Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence — sent a request to Huang for a closed-door joint briefing with their three committees.
“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People’s Republic of China]’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.”
October 29, 2026: Jensen Huang publicly revealed to have developed ‘close relationship’ with suspected Chinese spy
U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year when the New York Times broke the story in late October that the two executives also had a close relationship.
An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary.
“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.”
Spring 2026: A secret memo circulates in the Trump administration about Nvidia CEO’s alleged relationship with Chinese spy
U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo.
Late 2025: President Trump briefed on U.S. surveillance of Alice Huang and her relationship to Nvidia CEO but does not take action
Around the same time, per the New York Times’ report, U.S. President Donald Trump was briefed about intelligence findings that possible Chinese spy Alice Huang had formed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Trump did not act on this information.
The Nvidia CEO, an ally of Trump, has repeatedly advocated for the U.S. government to let Nvidia expand its business in China.
October 2025: U.S. and Singapore each investigate Megaspeed over possible Chinese export violations
Megaspeed was confirmed to be under investigation by both the U.S. and Singaporean governments in October 2025. As a customer of Nvidia, Megaspeed was suspected of helping Chinese companies get around American embargoes on chip exports.
Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service.
Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born.
These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.”
“NVIDIA visited multiple Megaspeed sites yet again earlier this week and confirmed what we previously observed — Megaspeed is running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules,” the Nvidia spokesperson said at the time.

articles.title: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Hydrogen, finally replacing 3.8 Flash
articles.text:
Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen. These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen’s purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google’s ecosystem use.
With Google’s recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers. Even when general availability began, Google restricted access to users paying for its most expensive AI subscription. The limits for Hydrogen are much more relaxed, with access beginning immediately. This model has replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across the company’s products.
Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it’s 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces “fabricated claims” by more than 5x, according to Google’s analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash’s score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon.

articles.title: US data center power demand outpaces supply by 10x and could bring the AI boom to a grinding halt by 2030
articles.text:
US data center power demand outpaces supply by 10x and could bring the AI boom to a grinding halt by 2030 — with AI companies funneling millions into gas turbine generators and modular nuclear reactors to stay online
The AI boom is facing a massive bottleneck
- United States data center power demand currently outstrips supply by ten times
- The problem could cause the AI boom to collapse by 2030 if new power sources are not brought online
- AI companies are turning to nuclear reactors and gas turbine generators to bring new developments online, but they have their own issues
The demand for power from the US data center boom is currently outstripping current capacity by ten times, with many developments looking for alternative sources of energy to keep their hardware online and the AI boom… booming.
But with Democrats now in control of the House and Senate, the Trump administration may encounter some obstacles in continuing its attempts to turn on dirty sources of power while exempting them from environmental controls.
Some AI companies have taken matters into their own hands, spinning up onsite gas turbine generators or decommissioned nuclear reactors, with a $25 billion debt on the health of Americans left to future generations to solve.
Big grid upgrades needed to continue AI growth
The huge surge in AI demand requires billions in infrastructural investments to continue. Similar to the dot com boom where the main bottleneck was fibre cabling, the current bottleneck for AI is energy.
A new report from insurance broker Howden estimates that in order to continue the current rate of data center expansion without increasing grid usage, up to 58% of power demand will need to be sourced from alternative sources.
Looking at data from the US Energy Information Administration and the S&P Global since the year 2000, Howden found that data center power demand has increased by 19% year on year, while actual electricity grid expansion has only increased by 2% each year. Total grid capacity from data centers in 2025 reached 5%, whereas in 2000 it was just 0.1%.
While there is significant demand on hardware for data centers — which has caused computer components such as GPUs and RAM to skyrocket — new supply chains and manufacturing is expected to ease constraints by late 2027 or early 2028. But the current growth of data center power demand could halt new data center construction by 2030, as highlighted by a Gartner report in June.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Grid expansion is typically funded through ratepayers, meaning the price rises experienced by working class Americans are going towards funding new grid expansions and connections for data centers, leading experts to predict power costs in some states could rise by as much as 50% by 2030.
Alternative energy could help, but it might be too little too late
There are a number of alternative sources of energy that data centers are considering. Anthropic recently revealed that it is investing $3.4 billion in onsite gas turbine generators to supply the power necessary to get new sites online, but that has its own issues.
In this case, Anthropic may be trading one energy crisis for another. In dodging the lack of grid capacity by turning to turbine generators, the AI company has found itself heavily reliant on natural gas supplies. The conflict in the Middle East hasn’t helped at all in this regard as other industries turn away from supply constraints placed on oil and increase their consumption of natural gas, spiking the price across the board.
Gas turbine generators are not popular alternatives for those living in close proximity to data centers. Given how much power some hyperscale sites consume, some data center campuses have been equipped with ranks of gas turbine generators that emit sound levels comparable to an international airport, and the low hum has caused unexplained illnesses in local residents.
Other AI companies are turning towards nuclear power to get their data centers online. Palisades Nuclear Plant in Michigan, Crane Clean Energy Center in Pennsylvania, and Duane Arnold Energy Center in Iowa are set to receive a total of $4.4 billion in federal grants to be recommissioned, with Microsoft and Google first in line to receive energy from the sites.
Amazon is looking to purchase over 960 megawatts of energy from 12 small modular reactors planned to be constructed in Iowa at a cost that will likely exceed $1 billion, but the sites are yet to be approved and may not be operational until the mid-2030s.
To that end, the US has just recently approved plans for the first data center-specific small nuclear reactor to provide power in Tennessee, with each modular reactor providing up to 300MW.
But nuclear power is not a simple solution to the constraints placed on the US energy grid. New reactors are expensive to build, and recommissioning existing reactors requires significant investment to ensure the lifespan of a facility will meet the expected operating lifetime, with billions of dollars needed to ensure old facilities meet new and existing safety requirements.
Continuing data center expansion, and the AI boom for that matter, will therefore require billions more to be invested.

articles.title: Corsair HX1000i Shift Crystal power supply review: 1000W Platinum efficiency with an eye-catching transparent aesthetic
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
Built by CWT, the HX1000i Shift Crystal is a showpiece that backs its looks with real substance. Efficiency is excellent, regulation and ripple are tight, and the fanless window covers half of its rated output at room temperature. Taiwanese capacitors, a noisy hot run and a 200 mm long chassis are the compromises, while the ten-year warranty and iCUE LINK integration add genuine value.
Reasons to buy
- + Excellent overall efficiency
- + Cybenetics Platinum certified
- + Tight voltage regulation
- + Low ripple
- + Fanless up to 500W
- + Striking transparent design
- + Integrated iCUE LINK hub
- + Per-pin 12V-2x6 protection
- + 10-year warranty
Reasons to avoid
- - Taiwanese capacitors
- - Long 200 mm chassis
- - Loud when hot
- - Needs side clearance
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
Corsair needs very little introduction to anyone who has built a PC over the past two decades. Founded in California in 1994 as a manufacturer of memory modules, the company has since grown into one of the largest brands in the PC component and peripheral market, with a catalog that covers cases, cooling, keyboards, mice, streaming gear, and of course, power supplies. Corsair entered the PSU market in the second half of the 2000s and built its reputation there by choosing its OEM partners carefully rather than manufacturing in-house. Channel Well Technology (CWT) has been one of the most important of these partners, producing a large portion of the RMx and HXi units over the years. The HXi series in particular has long been Corsair's high-end, digitally monitored family, positioned just below the flagship AX models.
We take a closer look at the HX1000i Shift Crystal to see if it deserves a spot in our best power supplies list. The HX1000i Shift Crystal is a bit of an odd bird, and Corsair is clearly fine with that. First shown at Computex 2026 and launching on November 12th, it combines the side-mounted connector layout of the SHIFT models with the digital HXi platform, and then wraps everything in a chassis with clear polycarbonate panels on three sides, turning the internals of the PSU into a part of the build's aesthetics. Beneath the show, the platform is built by CWT. It holds a Cybenetics Platinum certification at both 115 VAC and 230 VAC, and it is fully compliant with the ATX 3.1 and PCIe 5.1 design guides. It also integrates an iCUE LINK System Hub and Corsair's PinProtect+ per-pin current monitoring for the native 12V-2x6 connector. The 1000W model that we are reviewing today is rated to deliver its full power output continuously at ambient temperatures up to 50°C and comes with a ten-year warranty.
Specifications and Design
| Corsair HX1000i Shift Crystal Power specifications ( Rated @ 50 °C ) |  |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RAIL | +3.3V | +5V | +12V | +5Vsb | -12V | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MAX OUTPUT | 25A | 25A | 83.3A | 3A | 0A | 
| Row 1 - Cell 0 | 150W | 150W | 1000W | 15W | 0W | 
| TOTAL | 1000W | Row 2 - Cell 2 | Row 2 - Cell 3 | Row 2 - Cell 4 | Row 2 - Cell 5 | 
| AC INPUT | 100 - 240 VAC, 50 - 60 Hz | Row 3 - Cell 2 | Row 3 - Cell 3 | Row 3 - Cell 4 | Row 3 - Cell 5 | 
| MSRP | $ unknown | Row 4 - Cell 2 | Row 4 - Cell 3 | Row 4 - Cell 4 | Row 4 - Cell 5 | 
In the Box
The HX1000i Shift Crystal ships in a very large and sturdy black cardboard box, with a large render of the unit on the front that does a good job of showing off the transparent panels and the lit fan. The model name is printed in big yellow and white letters across the bottom half, while the badges in the top right corner - ATX 3.1 with PCIe 5.1 and 12V-2x6 support, the Cybenetics certifications, and the iCUE LINK logo- tell you most of what you need to know before even opening the package.
The bundle is rather spartan for a product of this class. Inside the box, we found the AC power cord, four mounting screws, a handful of black cable ties, and a leaflet with safety and compliance information. There are no Velcro straps, no cable combs beyond those already on the cables, and no other accessories of any kind. It is not a deal breaker by any means, but a premium unit like this that is focused on aesthetics could have been a little more generous in this department.
All of the cables are fully modular and black, with individually sleeved wires and low-profile cable combs. There is a 24-pin ATX cable, two 4+4-pin EPS cables, three PCIe cables carrying four 6+2-pin connectors in total, and a native 12V-2x6 cable rated for 600W, alongside two SATA and two Molex cables with four connectors each. Eight Molex connectors on a modern 1000W unit is extremely generous, frankly more than any reasonable build will ever need. Corsair also supplies two iCUE LINK cables of different lengths and a USB cable that connects the PSU's monitoring interface to the motherboard.
| Corsair HX1000i Shift Crystal |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Connector type | Hardwired | Modular | 
| ATX 24 Pin | - | 1 | 
| EPS 4+4 Pin | - | 2 | 
| EPS 8 Pin | - | - | 
| PCI-E 5.1 | - | 1 | 
| PCI-E 8 Pin | - | 4 | 
| SATA | - | 8 | 
| Molex | - | 8 | 
| Floppy | - | - | 
External Appearance
With dimensions of 150 x 86 x 200 mm, the HX1000i Shift Crystal is a long ATX unit, which is a non-issue if you are getting the matching Corsair 4500X case anyway. In any other case, you will need to check your case's specifications before buying one. The side-mounted SHIFT connectors also require some free space next to the PSU, as the cables plug into the side of the unit instead of its face, which is great for cases with a hidden PSU compartment but not suitable for every chassis. The design is unlike anything else on the market. The steel frame is black, with Y-shaped cutouts forming the fan grille and a debossed pattern of the same shape on the opposite panel, while three of the sides are clear polycarbonate panels that reveal the white fan frame, the bulk capacitors, the coils, and the white PCBs. With the RGB fan lit, the unit very much looks like a piece of display hardware rather than a power supply.
The rear of the unit is a little more conventional, with the AC receptacle, a rocker on/off switch marked with the "HX1000i SHIFT" logo, and a large perforated area with the same Y-shaped cutouts for the exhaust. The modular connector bay is on the side, behind the clear panel. The face opposite the AC receptacle hosts the white control PCB, also visible through its clear panel, with two iCUE LINK ports, a USB Type-C port, and a small port marked "TACH". The hexagonal specifications sticker is on the solid steel top side of the unit and is an envelope-type that can be closed to hide the text.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The CRYSTAL is fully compatible with Corsair's iCUE software, which can be used to monitor the PSU, adjust its fan speed, and switch the 12V overcurrent protection between single- and multi-rail modes. Corsair also integrated an iCUE LINK System Hub that, according to the company, supports up to 24 iCUE LINK devices without the need for a separate hub. The most interesting addition, however, is PinProtect+, Corsair's per-pin current monitoring for the 12V-2x6 connector. If the current on a pin exceeds a user-customizable threshold, the PSU cuts power to the connector, and the RGB fan lighting turns red to signal the fault. Given the history of melting connectors, this is a genuinely useful feature rather than marketing fluff. We can confirm that it is working as intended, as we tried pulling 20A from a single wire of the 12V-2x6 connector and the PSU shut down instantly.
Internal Design
Cooling is handled by a 140 mm Corsair NR140HL-RGB fan. Corsair calls it a magnetic dome bearing design, and in practice it is a rifle-bearing fan with a half-domed shaft magnet, rated at 0.55A on 12V. The fan is white with addressable lighting, which also doubles as the visual alarm for PinProtect+. It is a decent fan, and the magnetic shaft should help with longevity, but it is worth mentioning that the regular HX1000i SHIFT uses a fluid dynamic bearing fan, which we would normally consider the better choice for a premium unit.
The OEM behind the HX1000i Shift Crystal is Channel Well Technology (CWT), Corsair's long-time partner for its HXi units. Almost every part inside the unit has been relabeled as "Corsair", including the capacitors and the magnetic components, so the OEM is not obvious at a glance, but the Cybenetics report confirms it. The layout is extremely clean and obviously optimized for aesthetics, which also explains the excessive length of the chassis. The bridge rectifiers have their own heatsink, the APFC components sit on another large heatsink, and the primary switchers have their own heatsink as well, while the secondary side components are on a vertical PCB right after the main transformer. All heatsinks are of good size and quality.
The transient filtering stage has four Y capacitors, three X capacitors, and two filtering inductors. Two bridge rectifiers sharing a large heatsink feed the APFC stage, which relies on two Infineon 60R099P6 MOSFETs and two fully encased filtering coils. The APFC stage also includes two bulk capacitors, one Corsair 560 μF / 420 V capacitor and one Corsair 470 μF / 420 V capacitor, for a combined capacity of 1030 μF. According to the Cybenetics report, these capacitors are supplied by Elite, a relatively reputable Taiwanese manufacturer, and they are rated for 105°C. They are not capacitors that we frequently encounter in anything above mid-tier, though, and we feel they are not a great match for a premium unit.
The primary inversion stage uses two more Infineon 60R099P6 MOSFETs in a half-bridge LLC resonant topology. On the secondary side, ten Infineon 014N04LS MOSFETs handle the synchronous rectification of the 12V rail, and the minor rails are derived from DC-to-DC converters. All of the capacitors on the secondary side are rebranded as Corsair, with black and white sleeves that match the color scheme of the unit, and are also made by Elite. These are mostly good parts, but it is a bit ironic that Corsair advertises 105°C Japanese electrolytic capacitors for the regular HX1000i SHIFT, while the version built to show its capacitors off uses Taiwanese ones.
Cold Test Results (25°C Ambient)
Cold Test Results (25°C Ambient)
For the testing of PSUs, we are using high-precision electronic loads with a maximum power draw of 2700 Watts, a Rigol DS5042M 40 MHz oscilloscope, an Extech 380803 power analyzer, two high-precision UNI-T UT-325 digital thermometers, an Extech HD600 SPL meter, a self-designed hotbox, and various other bits and parts.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
At 25°C ambient, the HX1000i Shift Crystal is a very efficient power supply. It averaged 92.1% at 230 VAC and 90.5% at 115 VAC across the nominal load range, with the efficiency peaking at 93.6% (230 VAC) and 92.2% (115 VAC) at around 40% load. The curve is relatively flat after that, with the unit still achieving 91% at 230 VAC and 88.5% at 115 VAC while delivering its full 1000W. The efficiency at very low loads is good as well, at just over 88% with a 50W load on 230 VAC. These figures are in line with the unit's Cybenetics Platinum certification at both input voltages. There is no 80 PLUS certification for this unit.
The acoustics at room temperature are very good. The fan stays completely off up to 50% load, so a typical gaming system with a powerful graphics card will rarely ever wake it up. Once it starts, the unit registers 31.6 dB(A) at 500W, and the fan ramps up very gently, staying around 33 dB(A) at 700W and below 37 dB(A) at 900W. Only at full load does the noise climb to about 39 dB(A), which is still a low figure for a 1000W unit. Thermal performance gives no reason for concern at all, with the primary and secondary heatsinks reaching just 55°C and 58°C respectively at full load.
Hot Test Results (~45°C Ambient)
Hot Test Results (~45°C Ambient)
Inside our hotbox, at roughly 45°C ambient and still within the unit's 50°C rating, the HX1000i Shift Crystal hardly lost any efficiency at all. It averaged 91.7% at 230 VAC and 90.1% at 115 VAC, a drop of just 0.4 percentage points compared to the cold test. The peak efficiency dropped to 93.3% and 91.9%, respectively, and the full-load efficiency to 90.6% and 88.1%. That is a very strong result that shows how well the platform tolerates high ambient temperatures.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The fan is the part that changes its behavior the most in the heat. It starts spinning a bit earlier, at about 400W, registering 32.2 dB(A), and the noise climbs relatively fast to about 36 dB(A) at 600W and 39.5 dB(A) at 700W. Beyond 800W, the fan profile becomes much more aggressive, with the unit reaching 45.7 dB(A) at 900W and 46.8 dB(A) at its maximum output. That is definitely loud, though it takes very adverse conditions to get there. Internal temperatures rose considerably, with the primary heatsink reaching 84°C and the secondary heatsink 89°C at full load, figures that are high but comfortably within what the platform can handle.
PSU Quality and Bottom Line
Power Supply Quality
Voltage regulation is very good. Across the 20% to 100% load range, the 12V rail deviated by 1%, from 12.10V down to 11.98V; the 5V rail by 1% as well; and the 3.3V rail by just 0.7%. These are not the sub-0.5% figures of the very best digital platforms on the market, but all of the rails are well controlled, and the 12V rail stays very close to its nominal voltage across the whole load range. The ripple suppression is excellent. The 12V rail peaked at 48 mV under maximum load and 44 mV during the 12V cross-load test, while the 5V and 3.3V rails both topped out at 26 mV. Compared to the ATX design limits of 120 mV and 50 mV, that leaves a margin of 60% on the 12V rail and about 48% on the minor rails, which is very comfortable headroom for a 1000W unit.
During our thorough assessment, we evaluate the essential protection features of every power supply unit we review, including Over Current Protection (OCP), Over Voltage Protection (OVP), Over Power Protection (OPP), and Short Circuit Protection (SCP).
All protection mechanisms were verified and triggered correctly during testing. With the unit hot, OCP tripped at 148% (37A) on the 3.3V rail, 144% (36A) on the 5V rail, and 132% (110A) on the 12V rail, with OPP shutting the unit down at 130% of its rated output, or 1300W. These thresholds are on the high side, especially for the minor rails, but they are not unusual for an ATX 3.1 unit.
| Main Output |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Load (Watts) | 201.85 W | Row 0 - Cell 2 | 503.24 W | Row 0 - Cell 4 | 749.85 W | Row 0 - Cell 6 | 999.1 W | Row 0 - Cell 8 | 
| Load (Percent) | 20.18% | Row 1 - Cell 2 | 50.32% | Row 1 - Cell 4 | 74.98% | Row 1 - Cell 6 | 99.91% | Row 1 - Cell 8 | 
| Row 2 - Cell 0 | Amperes | Volts | Amperes | Volts | Amperes | Volts | Amperes | Volts | 
| 3.3 V | 2.27 | 3.38 | 5.66 | 3.38 | 8.5 | 3.36 | 11.33 | 3.36 | 
| 5 V | 2.27 | 5.05 | 5.66 | 5.03 | 8.5 | 4.99 | 11.33 | 4.99 | 
| 12 V | 15.1 | 12.1 | 37.75 | 12.07 | 56.62 | 11.99 | 75.5 | 11.98 | 
| Line | Regulation | Voltage Ripple (mV) |  |  |  |  |  | 
| Row 1 - Cell 0 | (20% to 100% load) | 20% Load | 50% Load | 75% Load | 100% Load | CL1 12V | CL2 3.3V + 5V | 
| 3.3V | 0.7% | 16 | 18 | 24 | 26 | 20 | 26 | 
| 5V | 1% | 18 | 20 | 20 | 26 | 20 | 24 | 
| 12V | 1% | 24 | 30 | 36 | 48 | 44 | 34 | 
Bottom Line
The HX1000i Shift Crystal is a power supply designed to be looked at, and that is not something we often get to say. Corsair took a CWT-built HXi platform, cleaned up its layout to the point that it can be shown off, and placed it behind three polycarbonate panels with an RGB fan on top. The result is unique, and it is backed by a genuinely modern feature set, with ATX 3.1 compliance, full iCUE support, an integrated iCUE LINK System Hub, and a native 12V-2x6 connector with PinProtect+ per-pin current monitoring. The latter is more than a bullet point on the box, as the unit shut down instantly when we pulled 20A from a single wire of the 12V-2x6 connector.
Most importantly, the looks did not come at the expense of performance. The efficiency is excellent, with averages of 92.1% at 230 VAC and 90.5% at 115 VAC, and it barely moved when we raised the ambient temperature to 45°C. Voltage regulation is tight on every rail, and the ripple suppression is excellent, leaving a large margin against the ATX limits. At room temperature, the fan does not even spin up before the load reaches 500W and it stays quiet all the way up to the maximum output.
The compromises are few, but some of them are hard to ignore on a unit like this. The capacitors are all made by Elite and rebranded as Corsair. Elite is a relatively reputable Taiwanese manufacturer, but its capacitors are not something we frequently encounter above the mid-tier, and they are not a great match for a premium unit when the regular HX1000i SHIFT advertises Japanese capacitors. The fan uses a rifle bearing with a magnetic shaft instead of a fluid dynamic bearing, and it becomes loud under heavy load in a hot environment. The bundle is also spartan for an aesthetics-focused premium product. Finally, the 200 mm long chassis and the side-mounted connectors mean that not every case will accommodate the unit, although most buyers are likely to pair it with Corsair's matching 4500X case anyway. On the bright side, the ten-year warranty covers the unit for a period that very few users will ever need, and it makes the component choices easier to accept.
At the time of this review, Corsair had not made the price of the HX1000i Shift Crystal public, which makes a definitive value judgment impossible. The regular HX1000i SHIFT is the obvious comparison, as it offers the same side connector layout, iCUE integration, and iCUE LINK hub for $339.99 at Corsair's own store, along with a fluid dynamic bearing fan and Japanese capacitors. Compared to other showy high-end units, such as the Asus ROG Thor 1000W Platinum II or the Lian Li Edge 1000, the CRYSTAL is the only one that actually puts its internals on display, and its Cybenetics Platinum efficiency and tight electrical performance mean that it does not need its looks to justify itself. If it arrives at a reasonable premium over the regular HX1000i SHIFT, it is an easy recommendation for anyone building a showcase system, and a well-performing 1000W unit for everyone else who simply likes how it looks, as long as they can live with its parts selection.

In the early 2000’s, he delved deeply into overclocking Duron and Pentium 4 processors, liquid cooling, and phase-change cooling technologies. While he has an extensive and broad engineering education, Dr. Fylladitakis specializes in electrical and energy engineering, with numerous articles published in scientific journals, some contributing to novel cooling technologies and power electronics. - quorm Are Taiwanese capacitors really still inferior in 2026? Is it still hard to make a reliable capacitor? Seriously asking.Reply
- EmmFyll quorm said:Are Taiwanese capacitors really still inferior in 2026? Is it still hard to make a reliable capacitor? Seriously asking.
Not inherently, no. Some Taiwanese makers are very good, and plenty of “Japanese” capacitors are actually made in China or Southeast Asia anyway. Making a reliable electrolytic capacitor is still hard though. It comes down to foil purity, electrolyte chemistry, sealing, and keeping it all consistent from batch to batch. The top brands have the longest track record of doing that over many years. Elite is a decent manufacturer and I do not expect these capacitors to fail early. My criticism is about positioning: on a premium unit that literally shows its capacitors off, and when Corsair advertises Japanese capacitors on the cheaper regular HX1000i SHIFT, buyers can reasonably expect better. articles.title: Hackers compromise 4,800 GitHub accounts to steal cloud credentials
articles.text:
Tens of thousands of GitHub repositories were targeted in a campaign dubbed ‘wfx-loot’ that uses malicious workflows to steal GitHub Actions secrets and cloud credentials.
Although not all repositories ran the payload, researchers confirmed that the threat actor stole secrets from at least 1,835 targets.
The threat actor used thousands of compromised GitHub accounts to open pull requests against repositories those accounts could access, testing whether they had sufficient write permissions to inject malicious code.
Some of the compromised accounts belonged to Fortune 100 organizations, the US General Services Administration, the French government, Nextcloud, and WebdriverIO.
According to researchers at application security company Aikido, about 50 of them appear to have publishing rights on other open-source software ecosystems and package indexes such as npm, PyPI, Go, crates, and Packagist.
Attack details
Aikido says the wfx-loot campaign began around 12:45 UTC on November 10, when the attacker used stolen GitHub credentials from 4,837 compromised accounts to probe 61,764 repositories for write access.
The threat actor opened pull requests titled ‘docs: dependency audit notes,’ disguised as dependency audit notes.
Of those pull requests, 92% remain open, Aikido reports, suggesting the legitimate repository owners did not notice the activity.
They then delivered a 1,500-line credential-stealing shell script by modifying an existing GitHub Actions workflow, adding a new workflow on a short-lived branch, or planting an npm install hook.
The script attempts to collect the following data:
- GitHub Actions and variables, the workflow’s GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC, and Actions runtime tokens.
- Cloud credentials for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, including credentials exposed through instance metadata on self-hosted runners.
- Developer and infrastructure credentials from Git, SSH, GPG, Docker, Kubernetes, npm, PyPI, Vault, and Terraform.
- AI service and developer-tool credentials for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Hugging Face, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot.
- Other sources of secrets include environment variables, .env files, private keys, keystores, shell histories, process memory, repository files and recent commits, and workflow artifacts.
The script also supports cloud privilege escalation by exchanging GitHub OIDC tokens for temporary AWS, Azure, and GCP cloud sessions.
In AWS, it can chain into additional IAM (identity and access management) roles present in the repository "to create long-lived credentials for IAM users." It also uses collected service-account credentials to impersonate identities in GCP.
Aikido notes that capabilities include establishing persistent access by creating long-lived credentials or modifying cloud identity and trust policies where permissions allow.
The script compressed the collected data into tarballs and exfiltrated it via HTTP POST to one of two attacker-controlled endpoints.
In the final stage, the attacker quickly reverted their changes and deleted workflow runs and logs. Aikido says this was completed in under a minute.
Automated publishing carried the payload into Packagist’s digitalelvis/neuronai-studio 3.14.3 and two versions of the Go module github.com/onuragtas/docker-env, v1.0.278 and v1.0.280.
The researchers believe the threat actor's primary objective was to steal CI secrets, while the package releases were a byproduct of automated publishing.
The researchers also found certain overlaps with the 2025 GhostAction campaign.
Repository owners are advised to look for the ‘wfx-docs’ branch, the probe pull request, and gaps in workflow run numbers.
Where payload execution is confirmed, all secrets and cloud roles available to the affected workflows should be considered compromised and rotated immediately.

articles.title: One stack, not three silos: How Stelcore’s leaders want Indian brands to go global
articles.text:
One stack, not three silos: How Stelcore’s leaders want Indian brands to go global
At TechSparks 2026, Stelcore’s Bharat Mandot, Percy Avari and Navin Mistry explained how brands can turn compliance, tech and supply chain into one growth engine.
Selling abroad once meant stitching together a marketplace, a freight partner, and a compliance consultant, and hoping the pieces held. For India’s next wave of brands, that patchwork is giving way to one connected commerce stack.
That shift was the focus of a session at TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s flagship event. Navin Mistry, Strategic Partner, Stelcore Commerce, was speaking with Bharat Mandot, Founder & Chairman, Stelcore Group, and Percy Avari, Co-Founder, Stelcore Supply Chain, about how technology, trade and supply chain can work as a single layer.
Mistry kept the conversation informal, with the aim of giving D2C founders a clear sense of the integration layers, process layers, and mindset needed to build a brand in India or beyond.
Why silos hold brands back
Mandot started Stelcore in 2011 as a management consultancy. The business turned to compliance in 2016, when Amazon began taking Indian sellers global and merchants needed help making their products compliant. Today the group covers compliance, trade enablement, and payments across 14 countries.
Avari, who has spent 35 years in logistics, including 29 years at Aramex, said the old model was the problem. What he saw over those decades, he said, was that “commerce, technology, and logistics were operating in silos”.
Avari added that the goal now is to bring all three into one ecosystem, so Indian brands can go cross-border in an effortless, intelligent and compliant way.
Prove demand, then fix compliance
Asked how a founder should sequence the journey, Mandot put the customer first. “Customer acceptance is the most important part,” he said. A brand can test through a marketplace or even social channels, then bring in compliance, logistics and payments once buyers keep returning.
He advised making only the top-selling products compliant at the start, since certifying an entire catalog pushes up launch costs. Mandot also pointed to inventory placement as a growth challenge. The Middle East can be served within a day, while the US is far larger, so stock must be spread across locations. His advice on scale was patient: win one country, build loyalty and healthy margins, and only then replicate the model in the next.
Avoiding the first-shipment trap
Avari said compliance has eased considerably over the past decade, but destination rules still catch new exporters out. Many first shipments, he noted, get stuck at foreign customs because founders skipped the homework.
Stelcore Supply Chain now builds this knowledge into its technology, so a seller is warned about required documents while creating a shipment. “If you don’t look at all three together, you cannot grow your brand in a profitable way,” he said.
Mandot described two tools for founders. One is a compliance assessment that shows the rules for a category across several countries in minutes. The other is an order management system linking warehouses and last-mile partners across countries, so no brand depends on a single facility.
From dropship to forward fulfillment
On when to move beyond third-party fulfillment, Avari said most brands begin with dropshipping, with 85-90 % of orders in year one. Demand data then shows which SKUs deserve forward fulfillment from regional hubs such as Dubai. By years two or three, he said, dropshipping can fall to 10-20 % of orders.
Mistry added that no single formula fits every brand: “There’s no universal answer, but it’s a mixture of both.”
The MSME opportunity
Avari called small businesses the backbone of Indian exports and said Stelcore aims to move 25,000 MSMEs from domestic to cross-border trade within five years.
Mandot expects export opportunity to grow roughly tenfold in three to five years, helped by government support. For tech founders, his advice was simple: build “the product for which we are willing to pay”.
From the audience
Audience questions covered customer acquisition and delivery economics.
Mandot said Stelcore acts as an introductory partner, connecting brands with marketplace teams to gauge market potential before they commit.
Avari said unit economics improve over two to three years as brands shift from dropshipping to regional forward fulfillment, though a long tail of SKUs will always stay on dropship. He suggested holding inventory in free trade zones across a few regions to keep costs in check.
The takeaway from Stelcore’s leaders was that cross-border growth depends less on any single tool than on aligning compliance, technology, and logistics from the first order.

articles.title: « La prochaine version du smartphone » : Sam Altman dévoile sa vision du téléphone à l'ère de l'IA
articles.text:
Le 31 octobre dernier, Sam Altman, PDG d’OpenAI, a rencontré une cinquantaine de dirigeants de Samsung en Corée du Sud. Si nous savions que cette rencontre était centrée sur l’avenir de l’intelligence artificielle et de son intégration dans les entreprises, peu d’informations nous sont parvenues, les échanges étant restés relativement confidentiels. Cependant, plusieurs médias sud-coréens ont aujourd’hui rapporté des échanges qui ont eu lieu durant cette rencontre initiée par Samsung. Sam Altman a notamment partagé sa vision de l’avenir du smartphone.
Sam Altman imagine un appareil qui remplacera nos smartphones
Lors de la rencontre entre Sam Altman et une cinquantaine de dirigeants de Samsung qui a eu lieu en Corée du Sud, une session de questions-réponses a également été organisée. L’un des dirigeants de Samsung lui a posé la question suivante : « Quel type d’appareil deviendra, selon vous, un compagnon doté d’intelligence artificielle ? ». Sam Altman lui a alors répondu que cet appareil « sera la prochaine version du smartphone ». Il n’est donc pas ici question de smartphones de nouvelle génération intégrant l’intelligence artificielle qui viendraient remplacer les smartphones tels que nous les connaissons (plein d’applications), mais d’« un appareil ».
Mais quel type d’appareil ? Sam Altman précise : « Je souhaite un appareil aussi discret que possible, où l’IA, et non des applications, accède et gère proactivement nos vies physiques et virtuelles. […] Les appareils de nouvelle génération collecteront des informations provenant du monde physique ». Autant dire qu’à l’heure actuelle, ce sont les lunettes connectées qui correspondent le mieux à cette description. Nous pourrions aussi imaginer un pendentif ou un petit appareil à clipser sur soi, mais il faut rappeler que le Humane AI Pin a été un fiasco, tandis que le Muse Charm, le pendentif IA de Meta, ne s’annonce pas vraiment comme une révolution.
Pour l’instant, les lunettes connectées et les smartphones intégrant pleinement l’IA, comme le NaviX Ultra et le Cyclon, correspondent le mieux à la vision de Sam Altman : celle d’un appareil portable et discret, qui ne nécessite pas d’application.
Sam Altman annonce vouloir collaborer avec Samsung
Toujours dans le cadre de sa rencontre avec Samsung, Sam Altman a expliqué vouloir travailler avec le groupe sud-coréen afin de concevoir un appareil commun, soit un appareil Samsung intégrant pleinement ChatGPT. À l’heure actuelle, nous ne savons pas de quel type d’appareil il pourrait s’agir.
Pour rappel, OpenAI travaille depuis maintenant plusieurs mois sur un smartphone intégrant pleinement ChatGPT, et donc sans application. De son côté, Samsung lancera à la mi-décembre ses premières lunettes connectées qui intègrent Gemini (Google). Pour l’instant, aucune collaboration annoncée donc, mais cela pourrait changer prochainement.
