articles.title: Telegram
articles.text:
Telegram is a messaging app with a focus on speed and security, it's super-fast, simple and free. You can use Telegram on all your devices at the same time – your messages sync seamlessly across any number of your phones, tablets or computers.
With Telegram, you can send messages, photos, videos and files of any type (doc, zip, mp3, etc.), as well as create groups for up to 200,000 people or channels for broadcasting to unlimited audiences. Plus, you can share videos up to 2GB, send multiple photos from the web, and forward any media you receive in an instant.
Can you use Telegram without sharing your phone number?
You do need a phone number to create a Telegram account, but after setup, you can control who sees it. You can also use a username to connect with others without sharing your number. Some users use virtual numbers or secondary SIMs during registration for additional privacy.
Is Telegram really private and secure?
Telegram offers some privacy and security features, but it is not as private by default as many people assume. Only "Secret Chats" use end-to-end encryption. Regular cloud chats are encrypted between your device and Telegram servers, which means Telegram technically has access to the content. Users looking for maximum privacy should use Secret Chats.
How do I back up my Telegram chats?
Telegram regular chats are stored on Telegram's servers, so no manual backup is needed – they sync automatically across devices. However, Secret Chats are device-specific and cannot be backed up or synced. If you want a local copy of your chats, you can use Telegram Desktop, which allows you to export chat history, go to: Settings > Advanced > Export data.
Why do people use Telegram instead of WhatsApp or Signal?
People often choose Telegram for its advanced features, large file sharing, support for groups with thousands of members, bots, channels, and cross-device syncing. However, it is important to remember that privacy-conscious users may still prefer Signal for its stronger encryption policies.
How do I delete my Telegram account?
Telegram accounts can be deleted via the official Telegram account deletion page. Deleting the app won't delete your account. Be aware that deleting your account will erase all messages, groups, and contacts.
Are Telegram groups and channels safe?
Groups and channels are as safe as the people managing them. Content is not end-to-end encrypted, and administrators can see your profile if you interact. Public groups and channels may expose your username to anyone. Many users recommend caution when joining unknown or large public channels.
What's the difference between Telegram groups and channels?
- Telegram Groups are for two-way communication where all members can chat and interact.
- Telegram Channels are for one-way broadcasting where only admins can post and subscribers receive updates.
If you want discussion, use a group. If you want to share info to an audience, use a channel.
Can I use Telegram on my phone and PC at the same time?
Yes, you can use Telegram on your phone and PC at the same time. Telegram is designed for multi-device support and your cloud chats will sync across devices. You can start a conversation on your phone and continue it on your PC seamlessly.
Is Telegram better than WhatsApp?
That depends on what you value most. Telegram is more feature-rich and flexible, while WhatsApp is more secure by default and more universally adopted. If privacy is your top priority, Telegram's Secret Chats are end-to-end encrypted, but normal chats are not. WhatsApp uses end-to-end encryption for everything by default.
What's New
Bot API 10.4
Widgets
- Added the class Widget and the field widget to the classes Message and ExternalReplyInfo for messages with HTML widgets.
- Added the method sendWidget, allowing bots to send messages with HTML widgets. Currently, in the production environment, widgets can be sent only to private chats, and sent widgets automatically have protected content and therefore can't be forwarded.
- Added the method sendSharedWidget, allowing bots to send again shared widgets created by the bot.
- Added the class WidgetQuery and the field widget_query to the class Update for queries sent to the bot by widgets in messages sent by the bot or via the bot.
- Added the class SharedWidgetQuery and the field shared_widget_query to the class Update for queries sent to the bot from forwarded messages with shared widgets.
- Added the classes WidgetQueryType, WidgetQueryTypeData, WidgetQueryTypeSignData, WidgetQueryTypeSentTransaction and WidgetQueryWallet, describing the type of a query from a widget. A query can contain data for the bot together with the TON wallet card of the user, data signed by a TON wallet of the user, or a notification about a transaction sent from a TON wallet of the user.
- Added the method answerWidgetQuery, allowing bots to answer queries from widgets.
- Added the method editMessageWidgetData, allowing bots to change data of a widget in a message.
- Added the method editSharedWidgetData, allowing bots to change public data of a shared widget.
- Added the classes InputWidgetMessageContent and InputSharedWidgetMessageContent, allowing bots to send widgets in response to inline queries. Currently, widgets can't be sent in response to inline queries in the production environment.
- Widget messages can't be copied using the methods copyMessage and copyMessages.
- The right can_send_other_messages in the classes ChatPermissions and ChatMemberRestricted now also allows sending widgets.
Ephemeral messages
- Allowed bots to send ephemeral replies to callback queries in any chat except channel direct messages chats by specifying callback_query_id without receiver_user_id in the parameter ephemeral_message_parameters of the methods sendMessage, sendRichMessage, sendAnimation, sendAudio, sendContact, sendDocument, sendLivePhoto, sendLocation, sendPhoto, sendSticker, sendVenue, sendVideo, sendVideoNote and sendVoice.
- The field receiver_user_id of the class EphemeralMessageParameters and the parameter chat_id of the mentioned methods are optional now.
Quotes from rich messages
- Added the field rich_texts to the class TextQuote for quotes chosen from a RichMessage.
- Added the field quote_rich_texts to the class ReplyParameters, allowing bots to quote rich messages.
TON wallet
- Added the classes TonWalletCard, TonWalletCardSticker, TonNft and TonNftAttribute, and the field ton_wallet_card to the class ChatFullInfo.
- Added the class TonWalletTransfer and the field ton_wallet_transfer to the class Message for service messages about transfers with a TON wallet.
- Renamed the class StoryAreaPosition to AreaPosition, because it is now also used to describe the position of stickers on TON wallet cards.
Chat share themes
- Added the classes ChatShareTheme, ChatShareThemeEmoji and ChatShareThemeUniqueGift, and the field share_theme to the class ChatFullInfo, describing the theme of the screen for sharing a link to a user or a chat.
- Added the classes EmojiType, EmojiTypeEmoji and EmojiTypeCustomEmoji.
- Added the classes ChatShareThemeBackdrop and ChatShareThemeBackdrops and the method getChatShareThemeBackdrops.
Gifts
- Added the method getUniqueGift, allowing bots to get information about a unique gift by its name.
- Added the method deleteBusinessAccountGift, allowing bots to delete regular gifts owned by a managed business account without receiving Telegram Stars for them.
General
- Allowed users with a Telegram Premium subscription to assign secondary usernames ending with "agent", "ai", "app", "game", or "gay" to up to 2 owned bots. Such usernames can be suggested in the field suggested_username of the class KeyboardButtonRequestManagedBot.
- Added the class RichTextTonAddress representing an address in the TON blockchain in a RichMessage.
- Added the type "ton_address" to the class MessageEntity for addresses in the TON blockchain.
- Added the type "bank_card_number" to the class MessageEntity for bank card numbers.
- Added the parameters custom_description_parse_mode and custom_description_entities to the methods verifyUser and verifyChat.
- Added the class PaidMessagesWaived and the field paid_messages_waived to the class Message for service messages about the sender using a link which allows sending messages without paying Telegram Stars.
- Added the ability to create links to topics in private chats with the bot in the format https://t.me// . Such a link opens the topic only for the user in the private chat with whom the topic exists.
Android
- Fix context menu double activations.
- Fix text rendering in animating bubbles.
- Fix possible crash in audio playback speed menu.
- Fix possible crash in forum or bot topic deletion.
- Show active auctions above chats list.
- Add star sending effects in live stories.
- Fix back button in group member profile view.
- Export separate topics message history.
- Export audio files saved to profile.
- Many different crash fixes.
- Improved support for gift auctions.
- Reorder stories in stories albums in My Profile.
- Bug fixes in new profile cover design.
- Add your Saved Music to data export.
- Reorder saved music in My Profile.
- Fix new cover overlapping information in My Profile.
- Fix opening stories from My Profile.
- Fix media viewer breaking after viewing Live Stories.
- Fix several possible crashes.
- Support for Gift auctions.
- Support for Live stories.
- New profile pages design.
- Highlight links in contact notes.
- Show menu with screen share controls in wide group call mode.
- Fix possible crash in saved music removing.
- Fix crash in theme editor.
Music on Profiles, Stickers Mini App, New Profiles, and More
In today's update, you can add music to your profile, choose a default profile tab, set unique chat themes based on your collectible gifts, help your friends upgrade their gifts – and more.
Music On Your Profile
Audio files from any of your chats can now be added to your profile with a single tap in the media player. Once on your profile, the track appears in a stylish bar beneath your photo.
As you add tracks to your profile, it automatically creates a playlist that includes the previous ones.
To add music to your profile, tap the 'Add to Profile' button in the media player or select that track and tap Save to... > Profile.
Stickers Mini App
Telegram users can create custom stickers with a built-in editor and manage packs through the @Stickers bot.
Starting today, the new Stickers Mini App lets you create stickers and emoji, manage your packs, and view detailed usage statistics.
Any user can create, send and share custom artwork using Telegram's open platform for stickers and emoji.
New Profile Design on Android
Thanks to a recent contest, profiles on Android now feature a sleek new design with scrolling animations first introduced on iOS.
Telegram regularly hosts contests for developers, designers, content creators and more – some of which offer the opportunity to join the Telegram team.
Default Profile Tab
Now you can choose which tab appears first when someone opens your profile – to better highlight your saved stories or your gift collections.
To change the default tab on your profile, go to Settings > My Profile, hold down on a tab and select Set as Main Tab.
Gift Themes
Since 2021, Telegram users can apply themes to individual chats. Today we are adding dozens of new dynamic chat wallpapers based on Telegram gifts – which their owners can now set as a custom theme in any private chat.
The only way to unlock these wallpapers is by owning a gift. Each wallpaper is based on gift attributes, using the model and backdrop to create a unique theme for every collectible. One gift unlocks one theme for one chat.
This currently works with Plush Pepes, Precious Peaches, Durov's Caps and Heart Lockets.
Upgrading Gifts for Other Users
You can now send Stars to cover the cost of upgrading a gift on someone else's profile – in case they're low on Stars or didn't know it could be converted. If the user later decides to upgrade their gift, this will be free for them.
The new 'Upgradable' filter filter makes it easy to find gifts that can be upgraded. And with the 'Upgrade Next Gift' button, you can upgrade multiple gifts back-to-back.
To make unboxing collectibles even more exciting, our designers added extra suspense to the upgrade animation.
Gift Value
Users can securely trade collectible gifts in the Gift Marketplace within Telegram.
When viewing a gift's attributes, the new 'Value' field shows its approximate resale price. You can expand it to view more statistics like the average sale price of other gifts in the same collection.
Public Post Search, Story Albums, Gift Collections and More
Today's update introduces global search for public posts on Telegram, sorting stories into albums and organizing gifts into collections, managing bots via a new stylish mini app – and so much more
Public Post Search
Search now has a 'Posts' tab, where you can see relevant results from public channels. This makes it even easier to find specific information and browse a variety of sources in one lightning-fast interface.
Story Albums
Your favorite vacation stories, pet pictures and more can now be organized into story albums on your profile – to create highlight reels of your best adventures and favorite memes.
Gift Collections
You can now group gifts on your profile or channel into custom collections – based on theme, rarity, or any other trait.
The same gift can appear in multiple collections, letting you create unlimited combinations. Collections also support granular filters for easy browsing.
Profile Rating
Telegram profiles now show a badge with a numerical rating based on the total volume of successful transactions they've made with Telegram Stars.
It highlights your Telegram level and helps channel owners see that you can be trusted for Suggested Posts and other requests.
Premium Gifts
Telegram Gifts are so popular that new releases sell out in minutes. While you can always buy gifts from others on the gift marketplace, we want more people to get gifts right at launch.
Soon, you may see a new type of gift – available only to Telegram Premium users, with each person able to buy just a limited number. Stay tuned!
BotFather Mini App
Developers of Telegram bots and mini apps can now manage them in the new @BotFather mini app – from creating bots to updating settings, icons, and descriptions.
Any developer can create sleek mini apps that support full-screen mode, subscriptions, home screen shortcuts, geolocation, motion tracking – and more.
Checklists, Suggested Posts and More Monetization Options for Channels
Today's update introduces checklists to help teams and individuals track tasks without leaving Telegram. We've also added suggested posts – a safe, easy way to organize partnerships and promotions with channels, opening new opportunities for creators to crowdsource and monetize content.
Checklists
Premium users can now create collaborative checklists in any chat to track tasks and coordinate teams – or manage shopping and to-do lists.
Checklists have granular permissions letting you control if others can mark tasks as done or add more items to the list.
Suggest Posts in Channels
Subscribers are now able to submit content to their favorite channels as suggested posts through a transparent and automated interface.
Suggested posts are sent to channels via direct messages – and can be anything from fan art to promotional videos, product reviews and more.
You can set a specific date and time for the post – or select 'Anytime' to let the channel owner choose.
Funding Suggested Posts
When suggesting a post, you may offer Telegram Stars or Toncoin to the owner in exchange for posting the message.
Toncoin can quickly be added to your Telegram account via Fragment – which allows for larger purchases.
The channel owner will receive their reward 24 hours after posting – if the post is removed earlier, Telegram will automatically return the full amount to you.
Monetizing via Suggested Posts
Suggested posts give channels of any size a way to crowdsource content and participate in affiliate marketing – all from inside the Telegram app, protecting creators from scams and preserving their privacy.
When you receive an offer for a post, you can suggest edits to the post before accepting – to modify the text and media or change the price. Once both parties approve the post, it can be instantly posted or automatically scheduled for a specific time.
Unsend Messages
We hope everybody had a great celebration. We at Telegram certainly did. One of our engineers got so excited about the new year that he mistakenly shared awful stickers with his Mom. To fix this, he quickly added a way to unsend recently sent messages. This smart move saved his morning, and it can still save yours! If you use Telegram v.3.16 or later, you can now unsend any weird messages you shared within the last 48 hours.
Shareable Chat Folders
Chat folders can now be shared with a link - inviting your friends or colleagues to dozens of work groups, collections of news channels, and more. With one tap, they will add the folder and instantly join all its chats. Each chat folder supports multiple invite links allowing access to different chats. When creating a link, select the chats you'd like to include - and give it a unique name to match, like Interns or Managers. If you add more chats to your folder and update its link, members will see a suggestion to join the new chats.
Previous release notes
Today's update gives content creators and public figures more control over their privacy while offering new ways to monetize their popularity. Now you can filter incoming messages, protect your peace of mind, and earn Telegram Stars – all while staying connected with your audience.
This update also introduces an info page for new chats to prevent scams, the option to gift Premium with Stars, and Verification Platform 2.0, helping startups save on user verification – plus much more!
Stay in Control of Your Inbox with Star Messages
If you receive a high volume of messages, you can now set a fee for incoming messages from users outside your contacts. This ensures that only those who truly value your time can reach you – giving you full control over your inbox while allowing you to earn Stars for your attention.
With this feature, you can:
- Filter out unwanted messages and avoid inbox overload.
- Ensure that every message you receive is meaningful – strangers can only contact you if they're willing to send Stars.
- Monetize your popularity while safeguarding your privacy and peace of mind.
- Stay open to new conversations while protecting your account from spam and message floods.
This setting can also be applied to group chats and channel discussions to keep interactions focused and free from spam, helping group owners monetize their community and earn Stars from meaningful conversations.
Flexible Controls & Instant Refunds
Star Messages come with customizable settings – you can allow certain users or members of specific groups to message you for free. And if you ever need to make an exception after a message is sent, you can instantly refund the Stars with a single tap.
How to Enable Star Messages
* In private chats: Ensure you have Telegram Premium, then go to Settings > Privacy and Security > Messages.
* In groups: Enable 'Charge Stars for Messages' in the Permissions section.
Take control of your messages, protect your time, and turn your popularity into an opportunity – all while keeping your inbox safe and manageable!
Know Who's Messaging You with Contact Confirmation
Now, when someone outside your contacts messages you for the first time, you'll see a detailed info page that helps you spot scams, avoid impersonators, and verify who you're talking to – before you even reply.
This page gives you essential insights about the sender, including:
- Their country (based on their phone number).
- Any shared groups you have in common.
- When they joined Telegram – so you can spot fresh accounts.
- When they last updated their username or profile picture – a handy way to detect sudden identity changes.
- Clear indicators showing whether the user is an official account, has third-party verification, or is just a regular user.
With this new feature, you're in control of who gets your attention – no more second-guessing unknown senders or falling for impersonators. Whether you're chatting with a potential collaborator, a fan, or a new friend, you'll have the info you need to decide whether to engage – effortlessly and with confidence.
Gift Premium with Stars
Now you can use your Telegram Stars to share Premium perks with others. Use your balance to gift Premium to friends – all without spending extra money.
Earned Stars from Star Messages? Use them to celebrate holidays or congratulate contacts with a Premium subscription: exclusive features, faster downloads, custom emoji and more – all powered by your Stars!
Withdraw Stars via Fragment
Users and groups that earn Telegram Stars through Star Messages can withdraw these Stars via Fragment, converting Stars into valuable rewards. These rewards can be instantly used to purchase Telegram Ads, collectibles on the TON blockchain and more.
Manage Group Star Balances
Group owners who receive Stars from Star Messages can now view and manage their group's Star balance directly from the group's profile, making it easier to track and utilize earned Stars.
Pin Gifts on Your Profile
In addition to wearing your favorite gift, you can now pin up to 6 other gifts to showcase them both on your gifts tab and on your profile cover.
Stream to Chromecast on Android
Android users can now cast videos straight to their Chromecast devices – whether you're watching memes with friends or presenting important content in a meeting, enjoy it all on the big screen!
Save Even More on User Verification
Telegram Gateway is a cost-effective and privacy-focused solution for user authentication, allowing businesses to verify their customers' phone numbers through Telegram at a fraction of traditional SMS costs.
Telegram's Verification Platform was already 9x cheaper than other services, and now it's 20% more cost-effective! Today's update lets developers set a max delivery time – if a code isn't delivered within the window, it's automatically refunded.
SMS verification elsewhere can cost $0.50 or more per message, while Telegram Gateway offers authentication for just $0.01.
It's completely free to test – letting startups cut unnecessary costs and focus on building great products. Learn more in our detailed guide and start saving today.

articles.title: Nebius tests the neocloud playbook with $40 billion in planned spending | TechCrunch
articles.text:
In its third-quarter earnings call Thursday, the neocloud company Nebius laid out $40 billion in planned spending for 2027, far more than Wall Street had expected. It’s an ambitious plan, but it rests on a string of planned projects that are already starting to show cracks.
Nebius plans to fund the buildout by relying on customer pre-payments and loans backed by customer contracts — essentially using the future value of its data centers to finance their construction. But that can be a risky strategy if those projects get bogged down by delays or cancellations.
“Building at this scale is hard, and delays are part of our industry right now,” CEO Arkady Volozh said during Thursday’s earnings call. “We are not immune.”
The earnings announcement comes on the heels of reports that Microsoft is cooling on neocloud deals that aren’t delivering on time. That’s a problem for companies like Nebius, whose financing strategy is becoming more dependent on repayments. Because if it can’t get to capacity on time, it will keep piling on costs while revenues slip.
One of Nebius’ largest customers is Microsoft, which is paying for AI computing capacity at a Vineland, New Jersey, data center that is now months behind schedule. Nebius’ contract with Microsoft is worth up to $19.4 billion, but it’s already letting deadlines slip. Only just over half of the Microsoft capacity is now planned for delivery by the end of the year, with the rest coming in Q2 2027.
The delay is because DataOne, the third-party operator of the site, “decided to wind down the temporary generation faster than it was expected,” according to Andrey Korolenko, chief product and infrastructure officer, as the site switches over to Bloom Energy fuel cells.
Still, that transition wasn’t entirely by choice. In August, the investigative site Floodlight identified at least 45 natural gas generators in operation at the DataOne site, even though it had not received any permits for operating gas generators. New Jersey regulators fined the DataOne facility $1.1 million in response, finding that the use of the generators violated federal law.
DataOne is also facing a noise-complaint lawsuit from nearby residents over a constant humming noise allegedly emitted by the data center.
According to Nebius’ summary of its Microsoft contract, Microsoft can terminate affected service after a grace period if dates are missed and no alternative capacity is offered. The tranches were originally meant to be deployed in 2025 and 2026, so a Q2 2027 delivery date falls well beyond that window. The contract also includes financial penalties for late delivery.
Nebius said that Microsoft “has been part of the planning process.” Nebius did not say whether Microsoft has agreed to the new dates, but Microsoft has not publicly canceled anything.
TechCrunch has reached out to Nebius, Microsoft, and DataOne for comment.
On the call, Marc Boroditsky, Nebius’s chief revenue officer, said the company’s deals with Microsoft and Meta both came with significant prepayment, which arrived long before delivery. But Bloomberg reported last week that Microsoft is tightening oversight on projects run by third parties, including Nebius, IREN, and Nscale, and debating whether it’s worth signing new agreements. Microsoft also sent employees to the site in New Jersey, per Bloomberg.
In its own quarterly earnings report, Microsoft noted that its capex spend was lower than expected due to third-party delays. The company is clearly not above pulling back from planned agreements where its partner doesn’t meet its share of the bargain. Bloomberg also reported that Microsoft won’t use an option to more than double its Nscale agreement for a Texas data center and recently stopped being an anchor customer for Nscale’s planned Essex site after power delays.
Nebius says the delays it faces are coming from sites it doesn’t control, with the data centers it is building itself coming online on time or ahead of schedule. Those, Nebius says, will supply most of its new capacity from 2027. New deals signed in Q3 came with prepayments that more than cover the cost of building capacity behind them, says Boroditsky. Nebius ended the quarter with $7.4 billion in cash.
Total prepayments plus asset-backed financing of investment-grade contracts are expected to cover up to 85% of the $40 to $45 billion 2027 capex spend. CFO Maria Del Dado Alonso Sanchez named Microsoft and Meta as contracts that can be financed this way. Boroditsky also said Nebius could “tap prepayments to shore up any additional cash requirements.”
Nebius forecast 2027 revenue of $12 to $13 billion, and said it expects to break even on a pre-tax basis by the fourth quarter.
Nebius reported third-quarter revenue of $981 million, up 571% from a year earlier. Roughly a third of that was a one-time payment tied to a new partnership model. Nebius cut its 2026 revenue forecast by $200 million to $3 billion, citing delays to third-party sites like New Jersey. Shares ended the day down 17%.

articles.title: Ukraine says it can’t stop Russian strikes because Starshield is limited again
articles.text:
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said today that Starshield has again been disabled on fast-moving drones in Ukrainian territory occupied by Russian forces, and that the US has provided “very little” information about the return of the restriction.
“We have detected speed restrictions on Starshield on our Ukrainian territory again, in the temporarily occupied parts of Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in a speech at the 9th European Political Community Summit in Ireland. “The speed limit is back at 161 kilometers per hour—that’s 100 miles per hour.”
Zelenskyy’s allegation is that Starshield—the military variant of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service—stops working on Ukrainian military drones when they travel above 161 kilometers per hour.
SpaceX today denied Zelenskyy’s allegation. “This is false. There has been no change,” SpaceX’s media relations department told Ars today when asked if SpaceX has any response to Zelenskyy’s statement that Starshield is being restricted again.
“This means more Russian strikes get through”
SpaceX has received multiple Pentagon contracts to give Ukraine access to the military-focused Starshield. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said last month that any decisions on Starshield restrictions are made by the US government. The Pentagon inspector general’s office has since declined a request from US senators to investigate who ordered the restrictions.
Ukraine officials reportedly said today that they believe the limit was reinstated to put pressure on Ukraine in the latest round of peace talks with Russia. Zelenskyy said in today’s speech that without satellite connectivity on its drones, Ukraine cannot intercept Russian drones that fly in from the occupied parts of Ukraine.

articles.title: Google lanza Gemini 4 Hydrogen y lo integra con su buscador para dar respuestas más completas e inteligentes
articles.text:
Gemini 4 Hydrogen es la última adición a la familia de modelos de lenguaje insignia de Google. La firma de Mountain View lanzó su nueva IA este miércoles, sumándola a Gemini 4 Argon y Carbon, que debutaron en octubre.
De acuerdo con Google, Gemini 4 Hydrogen no está pensado para tareas que requieran de razonamiento profundo y extendido como las otras dos variantes. Por el contrario, la inteligencia artificial fue especialmente preparada para la ejecución rápida de tareas en flujos de trabajo destinados a agentes.
Más allá de los benchmarks y las capacidades que desbloquea Gemini 4 Hydrogen, la novedad realmente interesante que trae este modelo es su integración con el buscador de Google. Esto le permite a la plataforma brindar respuestas más rápidas e inteligentes, ampliando drásticamente la experiencia de búsqueda actual.
Los de Mountain View afirman que la llegada de Gemini 4 Hydrogen implica la actualización más importante que ha recibido el buscador web en materia de modelos de IA. El objetivo de la compañía no solo es enriquecer el contenido de las respuestas, sino también mejorar la comprensión de matices, intenciones y modismos incorporados en el lenguaje natural de los usuarios.
Gemini 4 Hydrogen ahora impulsa al buscador de Google
Entre las mejoras que llegan al buscador de Google de la mano de Gemini 4 Hydrogen, destaca la habilidad de la IA de entender consultas complejas o directamente mal escritas. Esto se debe a que el modelo de lenguaje puede detectar más fácil qué es lo que quiere decir el usuario, incluso aunque la pregunta tenga varias partes pero no esté dividida de forma apropiada o tenga errores de ortografía muy severos.
Por supuesto que esto es un arma de doble filo. Después de todo, Google le va a estar facilitando la vida a ese amigo o pariente que escribe con faltas ortográficas horribles porque sostiene que así "se entiende igual". Fuera de eso, puede ser una salvación si cometes errores involuntarios durante una búsqueda rápida.
Gemini 4 Hydrogen también promete mejoras en la ramificación de consultas, así como en el ofrecimiento de enlaces más útiles. Por otra parte, la inteligencia artificial incorpora más elementos gráficos en los resultados del buscador de Google. Esto no solo implica la inserción de imágenes o enlaces con vistas previas de multimedia, sino también de mapas, gráficos, tablas y más.
La integración de Gemini 4 Hydrogen con el buscador de Google se está desplegando desde hoy a los usuarios de todo el mundo. Para acceder al nuevo modelo cuando realices una búsqueda, tienes que pulsar el botón "+" que aparece bajo el recuadro de búsqueda y seleccionarlo desde allí. Si todavía no lo ves, es posible que se habilite en las próximas horas y/o días.

articles.title: I spent 8 days with an Apple HomeView in my kitchen and another on my wall — and they've made me reach for my iPhone less
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Apple's first smart display is a strong start. The HomeView combines a beautiful design, surprisingly powerful sound, thoughtful personalization, and a much smarter Siri into a device that fits naturally into everyday life. It's not perfect — third-party app support is limited, and some Siri requests still take longer than I'd like — but after eight days living with two HomeViews, I've found plenty to love. Most importantly, it's useful when I need it, and happily fades into the background when I don't.
Reasons to buy
- + Modern, thoughtful design with excellent clock faces
- + Excellent sound quality from the tabletop model
- + Personalized experiences and genuinely useful Siri AI
- + Seamless smart-home controls and FaceTime
Reasons to avoid
- - Limited third-party apps
- - Requires an iPhone to set up, with newer models needed for the full experience
- - Siri can be slow to respond to some requests
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Apple HomeView: Two-minute review
Apple's first smart display is a strong start, even if it's a somewhat strange first-generation product. The HomeView gets a lot right, from its distinctly Apple design and excellent audio to its personalized experience and genuinely useful Siri AI capabilities. And after eight days of living with two HomeViews, I really like what Apple has delivered.
First and foremost, though, the HomeView is for folks already invested in the Apple ecosystem. You'll need an iPhone to get the most out of it, and ideally an Apple Intelligence-enabled model to take full advantage of Siri AI and Personal Context. This integration is what makes the HomeView special, letting Siri find information in your messages, control your smart home, and surface personal content without you constantly having to reach for your phone.
The hardware is excellent, with a compact, premium design and a vibrant 7-inch display. I've been using the speaker-mounted 'countertop' HomeView in my kitchen, and the wall-mounted version in my entryway, and both fit naturally into my daily routine. I especially love the Photos clock face, which intelligently cycles through pictures of my dog Rosie, family, and friends.
Audio is another standout. The standard HomeView delivers surprisingly powerful bass, a wide soundstage, and enough volume to fill my kitchen and living room. Music support is so strong that I've actually been occasionally using it as my main speaker.
Siri AI is impressive, too, particularly when tapping into Personal Context, though it's not always the fastest. Simple smart-home requests are generally quick, while more complex tasks can take 10 to 15 seconds. Still, the ability to ask Siri to find a song a friend recommended in my messages and then play it is pretty neat.
There are some limitations, though. There's no App Store at launch, third-party apps are restricted, and video options are limited. While I'd have liked to see more flexibility, I suspect Apple's curated approach is intentional. HomeView feels designed to be a more mindful, ambient device that surfaces information when you need it rather than another screen constantly demanding your attention. That being said, I wouldn’t be shocked if, when WWDC 27 rolls around, a dedicated 'home' OS is announced, and the app experience opens up.
At $299 / £299 / AU$449, the HomeView certainly isn't cheap, but it also doesn't feel like an unfinished first-generation experiment. It's already great for FaceTime calls, quickly checking messages, playing music, controlling smart home devices, and displaying personalized clock faces. These are the kinds of everyday interactions that make it easy to appreciate having the HomeView around, rather than feeling like you're searching for reasons to use it.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Ultimately, the Apple HomeView feels like a natural companion to your iPhone, giving you a reason to leave it in your pocket rather than constantly reaching for it. It's a smart-home controller, digital photo frame, surprisingly capable speaker, and personal assistant rolled into one, but it's also perfectly happy just showing you the time or a favorite photo. It's not perfect, but Apple has delivered a thoughtful, genuinely useful first-generation product that feels like a very strong start, especially if you're already deep in its ecosystem.
- Value score: 4 / 5
Apple HomeView: Design
- Premium, distinctly Apple design with a vibrant 7-inch Liquid Retina display
- Two designs: tabletop and wall-mounted, with the same core features
- Excellent customizable clock faces
The HomeView comes in two distinct styles: standard and wall-mounted. The standard HomeView will likely be the more popular option, and features a square 7-inch Liquid Retina display with soft, rounded corners that sits on an arm extending from a domed, circular base.
It's smaller than you might expect, and pretty cute. It comes in four colors: Starlight, Space Gray, Rose Pink, and Silver. I've been testing Starlight, which looks like an airy gold or more silver depending on how the light hits it. Apple also includes a color-matched USB-C cable and wall adapter, making physical setup straightforward.
The design is distinctly Apple, with a premium aluminum build combining brushed finishes and polished accents, particularly around the hinge connecting the display to the base. At first glance, it's almost like an oversized Apple Watch — perhaps an earlier generation thanks to the fairly thick bezels. There's also a bit of the iconic, potted-plant-like iMac G4 in its DNA, and I quite like that.
The display can tilt up or down, but not left or right. For that, you'll need to manually turn the entire HomeView, though the rubberized bottom, similar to a HomePod or HomePod mini, keeps it firmly planted. And while it’s easy enough to turn it left or right with the display, a swivel mechanism built in here would have made this more seamless.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
I've been testing the standard HomeView in my apartment, where the kitchen flows right into the living space, and I've found a natural home for it on my kitchen island. Thanks to its compact size, I can easily slide it around or turn it to face wherever I am, whether I'm making coffee, cooking dinner, or hopping on a FaceTime call. Center Stage does a good job of keeping me in frame, but it can only follow me so far before I need to turn the display manually. A motorized arm would be pretty dope, and I'm holding out hope for one in a future generation.
The 7-inch Liquid Retina display looks great, with clear text, vibrant photos, and plenty of brightness, though its glossy finish can still catch reflections even when the brightness is cranked up, and I would be surprised if Nano-Texture or a similar coating might be ushered in a future generation.
Apple says it can dim down to just 0.3 nits, the lowest of any display in its lineup, which is likely handy for bedrooms and helps ensure it’s not glowing in the middle of the night or in dimmer conditions. It's excellent for displaying photos, album artwork, or lyrics in Apple Music, and I've never had an issue reading text.
It's also noticeably thicker than an iPad or even Apple's now touch-enabled MacBook Pro, though that's understandable given everything packed inside. Above the display sits a 12-megapixel Ultra Wide camera, while tiny microphone openings are dotted around the frame, including near the camera, along the sides, and on the rear. You won't find any physical buttons or a camera shutter, though, as Apple is betting almost entirely on touch and voice. The only port is USB-C for power.
The base is where much of the audio hardware lives, with dozens of precisely drilled holes around its lower half. There are two full-range drivers built into the display section, while the base houses a downward-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators. I'll dig deeper into sound quality below, but it's surprisingly robust for something this small, with plenty of low-end punch without causing HomeView to vibrate excessively or topple over.
Overall, HomeView feels a good bit more premium than older Echo smart displays or Google's Nest Hub, though it takes a markedly different approach from Amazon's newer Echo Show 8, 11, and forthcoming Echo Show 16. It fits neatly into Apple's broader design ethos, even if the colors, somewhat ironically, don't necessarily match those of the HomePod or HomePod mini.
I've also been testing the second version, which Apple calls HomeView (Wall Mounted). While the standard model is more versatile, there's a lot to like about having Apple's smart display permanently positioned on a wall.
Unboxing is considerably simpler, as you're essentially getting just the display, without the arm or speaker base. On the back is a USB-C port, which is designed to work with compatible mounts, including those from Schneider Electric, which were developed specifically for HomeView.
Importantly, you're not sacrificing the core experience. The wall-mounted version has the same processor, display, cameras, sensors, and software as the tabletop model. The biggest hardware difference is audio, handled by two custom drivers rather than the more elaborate speaker system in the standard HomeView. It's by no means tinny and still offers a surprisingly wide soundstage, but there's less oomph, particularly in the low end.
I suspect most folks opting for the wall-mounted model will want to wire it directly into the wall for the cleanest possible look. But as a renter, I went with Schneider Electric's USB-C wall mount, and it was one of the simplest mounting experiences I've had with a smart home device. Two drilled holes, anchors, screws, and probably less than 15 minutes later, it was on the wall. From there, I connected the lengthy USB-C cable to a power adapter, which you'll need to supply yourself.
I've been using the wall-mounted HomeView in my entryway, and it's a great fit. Walking in to see photos of my pup Rosie, my nieces, or family and friends is a lovely touch, while the customizable Smart Home face turns it into a central control panel. I'll dig into that experience, including some surprisingly useful features, more below.
Ultimately, the standard HomeView likely offers better overall value thanks to its more powerful audio system and flexibility to move between rooms. But the wall-mounted version feels especially well suited to an entryway, kitchen, or another central location where you want information and smart home controls available at a glance. Both feel thoughtfully designed, and Apple has delivered two distinct approaches to what a smart home display can look like.
- Design score: 4 / 5
Apple HomeView: Performance
- Siri AI and Personal Context deliver genuinely useful, personalized experiences
- Excellent sound quality, responsive smart home controls, and impressive FaceTime performance
- Limited third-party apps and streaming options, and complex Siri requests can be slow
I've been living with two HomeViews for eight days, with one serving me well on the entryway wall of my apartment, and the other primarily living in my kitchen. The standard model has also spent some time in my office and even the bedroom, and I've been putting both through their paces.
HomeView is built around your iPhone, and that tight integration is central to the experience. You'll also want an Apple Intelligence-enabled model to get the most out of Siri AI and Personal Context. Thankfully, it all works quite well.
I've used HomeView for everything from music and FaceTime calls to smart home controls, checking messages, and displaying photos. I've even watched some Apple TV, though it's hardly the ideal screen for that.
Setup feels familiar if you've ever paired an Apple Watch or AirPods with an iPhone. Plug HomeView in, wait for it to boot up and say hello, then bring your iPhone nearby. From there, you scan a graphic to pair the devices and follow a few steps, including choosing who you're setting it up for.
HomeView is designed to be communal, sitting in a shared space where multiple people can use it, but also personal when the situation calls for it. It supports up to six registered users, and adding someone starts on HomeView before handing the process over to their iPhone. They'll also need to be part of your Apple Home.
The personalization works particularly well. For instance, while I was viewing my messages, my dad walked into the camera's view, and HomeView immediately stopped showing my personal content until it could recognize me again. It's a clever safeguard, especially for a device that's meant to live in a shared space.
It does mean, though, that some items you’d think would be shared among users are missing. For example, there's no calendar — likely because it might contain confidential items, and Apple wants to make sure those are shown to a registered user. But that does mean the HomeView doesn’t offer a shared calendar like, say a Skylight or an Echo. One solution would be a shared calendar that is shared with each person (up to six) who is registered on the HomeView.
The HomeView runs custom software, not HomeViewOS, that borrows heavily from iOS and watchOS. The app grid, including its tint and customizable widgets, feels like iOS, while customizing the clock faces is more akin to watchOS, complete with complications. It's a bit of a Frankenstein-like approach, but it works.
And speaking of clock faces, they're one of my favorite parts of HomeView. Snoopy is especially delightful, with custom-designed artwork and animations separate from what you'll find on Apple TV. You can even tap Snoopy to trigger an animation, which is an adorable little touch.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The Photos face is equally impressive, and really shows how personal HomeView can feel. You can select people, places, or pets, and HomeView will intelligently surface and cycle through relevant photos. I chose my dog Rosie during setup, and I love seeing different photos of her throughout the day. You can even tap the screen to see when and where a particular photo was taken.
I could easily see HomeView being a great gift for parents or family members for this feature alone, especially since you can use a shared photo album as the source and have new photos appear as they're added. It turns what could have been a pretty ordinary clock face into something much more personal.
There's also the Modular face, which lets you customize the display with widgets and complications, putting useful information and controls front and center. Between that, Photos, and Snoopy, Apple has done an excellent job making the clock faces feel like more than just a way to tell the time.
In terms of responsiveness, HomeView generally feels quite snappy. Apple's A18 chip is under the hood, complete with the Secure Enclave, which plays an important role in the device's privacy protections. Apple handles processing on-device when possible, while more complex requests can be handled through Private Cloud Compute.
You'll still need your iPhone for the more personalized experiences, though, as HomeView draws on the content and apps connected to your device. And that's what enables some of its most impressive tricks.
For instance, I asked Siri which Dave Matthews Band song my friend Benjie wanted me hear. HomeView took a moment to think — probably around 10 to 15 seconds — while displaying updates at the top of the screen as it searched through my messages. It eventually came back with the answer: "Ants Marching."
I then asked Siri to play it, and since I have both Spotify and Nugs connected through my iPhone, it asked which service I wanted to use before starting playback.
It's an impressive interaction, even if Siri takes its time, and I appreciate seeing updates on what it's working on. I could also ask Siri to look at my calendar, find an event in the city, and figure out when I need to leave based on traffic. It's another multi-step request that isn't instantaneous, but it gets me to the answer.
Response times can vary quite a bit, though. When I asked Siri to play Ghosts by Bruce Springsteen, it took about 12 seconds before the song started playing through Apple Music, complete with album artwork on the display. A simpler request, like checking the weather in New York City, took closer to two or three seconds.
Smart home requests, thankfully, are considerably quicker. Asking Siri for the temperature in my apartment, pulling data from both HomeViews, multiple sensors, and my Nest thermostat, takes about two seconds, if not less. I can also quickly turn on my Philips Hue lights or adjust the temperature, and those everyday interactions have worked well.
Of course, you don't have to rely on Siri to control your smart home. The HomeView has a dedicated Home app that's similar to what you'll find on your iPhone or iPad, but it's the Home Modular clock face that really turns it into a smart home control panel, especially when wall-mounted. You can customize it with blocks showing key information, like the temperature or readings from connected sensors, alongside easy touch controls for lights, thermostats, and other smart home devices. Everything is in one place, and I've found it especially useful on the HomeView in my entryway, where I can quickly see what's happening around my apartment or make an adjustment without reaching for my iPhone.
You'll also find automations you've previously created in the Home app, but the HomeView takes things a step further by letting you create new ones simply by asking Siri. These can be single actions or more complex, multi-step routines. For instance, I asked Siri to create an automation that raises the smart blinds in my apartment and turns on the lights every morning at 6am. It handled the request, and just like that, I had a new morning routine without setting it up manually in the Home app.
The broader smart home ecosystem remains somewhat confusing, particularly around compatibility. HomeView works with Apple Home and supports Matter, with Thread connectivity built in, but there's no native Zigbee support. That doesn't rule out Zigbee devices connected through a compatible bridge, though. It's worked well with my existing devices — Philips Hue lights, Google Nest Learning Thermostat 4th Gen, Eve Cam, an Anker Eufy camera, and Ryse Shades — and Apple's own Home Collection is set to arrive in December. Still, it's worth checking which devices will actually integrate before making the jump.
I've also been impressed by the four integrated microphones, which reliably pick up my voice from across the room, even with music playing through a HomeView or the TV on in the background. That's particularly useful in my kitchen, where I can be making coffee or cooking dinner while asking Siri for information, controlling music, or making a FaceTime call without stopping what I'm doing.
FaceTime is another highlight. The 12-megapixel camera delivers good video quality, and Center Stage does a solid job keeping me in frame as I move around the kitchen, though it can only follow me within the camera's field of view.
On the wall-mounted HomeView in my entryway, I've also found myself asking Siri for directions, calendar updates, or simply what I've missed when getting home or starting the day. It's convenient to have that information available in a central location without pulling out my iPhone.
There's also a surprisingly useful Mirror feature, accessible through Control Center, which uses the built-in camera to show a live view of yourself. You can switch between 1x and 2x views, and while it's not something I'd necessarily buy a HomeView for, it's a neat addition for a device mounted near the front door. I've used it for a quick look before heading out.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Of course, the HomeView isn't an iPad, and Apple isn't trying to turn it into one. There's no App Store, and third-party app support is limited. Interestingly, Apple is leaning on CarPlay compatibility to bring select audio and video media apps to the HomeView.
I've been able to use Spotify, Nugs, Apple Music Classical, and SiriusXM, though what's available can change depending on whom HomeView recognizes, since it pulls from that person's profile and connected iPhone.
It's a curated experience, and I think that works well here. I get the sense it's meant to avoiding overwhelming you, or becoming another screen that's constantly demanding your attention. Instead, it's arguably Apple's first truly ambient device, designed to surface information when you need it and fade into the background when you don't. It doesn't even feature notifications except for Home alerts or when a call comes into your iPhone.
It's both touch- and voice-enabled, and Apple's mainstay apps are here, including Music, Podcasts, Safari, FaceTime, Calendar, Messages, Home, Intercom, Weather, Find My, Reminders, Alarms, Timers, World Clock, Audiobooks, Apple TV, and Settings. News is also part of the experience, though the selection is still more limited than what you'd find on an iPhone or iPad.
Although the HomeView has Apple TV built in, don't expect it to replace your television or even an iPad. There are no dedicated apps for YouTube, Disney+, Hulu, Peacock, or Netflix, though you can start a YouTube video on your iPhone and bring it close to your HomeView to hand off playback. And with a seven-inch display, substantial black bars, or a zoomed-in picture that crops the action, it's better suited to casual viewing while doing something else than settling in for a full TV episode or movie.
Audio is another major strength, particularly on the standard HomeView. For something so compact, the sound is seriously impressive, with a wide soundstage, remarkably strong bass, and enough volume to outdo the HomePod mini 2. It easily fills both my kitchen and adjoining living room with rich, robust audio, and I've actually found myself using it as my apartment's main speaker.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
At times, I've also grouped it with the wall-mounted HomeView for music playback across both spaces, and the experience works quite well. The tabletop model definitely has the advantage, though, with fuller sound and considerably more low-end punch. The wall-mounted version still sounds good for its size, but if music is a priority, the standard HomeView is absolutely the one I'd choose.
And while the HomeView is great for controlling my smart home, playing music, following recipes while cooking — especially with multiple pre-set timers — making FaceTime calls, and plenty more, I also appreciate that it doesn't constantly demand my attention. It doesn't make me want to reach for my iPhone, either. Sometimes, I just want to glance over to check the time, see the weather, or enjoy a photo of Rosie, and that's more than enough.
The HomeView is there when I need it and fades into the background when I don't, and I think that's a big part of its appeal.

Apple HomeView: Pricing and Availability
Apple’s HomeView is currently up for preorder at $299 in the US, £299 in the UK, and AU$449 in Australia, and will officially launch — and begin shipping — November 13, 2026. The standard HomeView, which has a base to stand on its own and comes with a wall plug, comes in four colors: Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink, and Space Gray.
There’s also the HomeView (Wall-Mounted) for the same price, available in Silver or Space Gray. With that, you’ll need to get a separate wall mount made by Schneider Electric, either one that ends with a USB-C port – a good option for renters – or an AC one, which requires proper installation.
Apple HomeView: Should I Buy?
Buy it if…
You've been waiting for Apple's smart display
It's been a long time coming, and the HomeView checks off many of the boxes you'd expect from a smart home hub. From music playback and quick access to Siri AI to smart home controls and a digital photo frame, Apple has delivered a strong first-generation product.
You want a communal screen for everyday tasks
The HomeView is excellent for those quick interactions throughout the day, whether that's checking messages, making a FaceTime call, controlling your lights, or glancing at the weather. And with personalized experiences for up to six users, it feels right at home in a shared space.
Apple HomeView: How I Tested
I spent eight days testing two Apple HomeViews in my apartment, with the standard model primarily living on my kitchen island and the wall-mounted version installed in my entryway. I also moved the standard HomeView into my office and bedroom to see how it worked in different spaces.
I used both devices throughout my daily routine, testing everything from Siri AI and Personal Context to smart home controls, music playback, FaceTime calls, messages, and customizable clock faces. I connected HomeView to my existing smart home devices, including Philips Hue lights, a Nest thermostat, and smart blinds, and tested how well it handled everyday requests and more complex tasks.
I also compared the HomeView to Amazon Echo Show and Google Nest Hub smart displays, along with several speakers, including the original HomePod mini, HomePod mini 2, second-generation HomePod, Sonos Move 2, and Sonos Era 100. I paid particular attention to audio quality, responsiveness, ease of use, and how naturally HomeView fit into my daily routine — including those moments when I wasn't actively interacting with it.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns as CEO in the wake of multiple affairs, Chinese spy allegations — Colette Kress appointed Interim CEO, board conducting search for permanent replacement
articles.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns in the wake of multiple affairs, Chinese spy allegations — Colette Kress appointed Interim CEO, board conducting search for permanent replacement
That didn’t take long
Nvidia’s board of directors has confirmed today that Jensen Huang has resigned as the company's CEO. The news follows revelations that Huang had been involved in not one but two extramarital affairs, one with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, and another with his direct report, Nvidia’s VP of health care, Kimberly Powell.
"NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately," the board stated. "Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates."
In recent weeks, stories have come to light alleging that Huang was involved in an overly familiar relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence agencies suspect may be a Chinese intelligence asset. It was reported that the AI GPU giant’s CEO may have been the target of a spy plot — Megaspeed is under investigation for its involvement in the smuggling of $2 billion worth of export-controlled AI GPUs into China.
Nvidia shares plunged more than 10 percent in early market trading following the news, and are now down more than 23% in the last month.
Over the weekend, Jensen Huang admitted that he had been unfaithful to his wife and issued a company-wide apology. Separately, Nvidia’s Board of Directors launched an independent investigation into reports that Huang’s entanglement may be a matter of national security, given his role in the global AI revolution.
Colette Kress has been Nvidia's Executive Vice President and CFO since September 2013; prior to that, she spent 25 years at Cisco and Microsoft, among others.
Just a couple of days later, a second bombshell report emerged claiming that Jensen Huang was also romantically involved with Powell, one of his direct reports at the company. Reports indicate the affair was known within the company, and that the two were even filmed being affectionate in a San Jose hotel at Nvidia GTC. Security allegedly sequestered a bystander who filmed the interaction on camera and made the person an offer to sign a nondisclosure agreement.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Nvidia also announced that Harvey C. Jones will serve as the company's first-ever Chair of the Board; he has previously served as CEO and Executive Chairman of Synopsys.

He has covered the world of consumer tech from nearly every angle, including supply chain rumors, patents, and litigation, and more. When he's not at work, he loves reading about history and playing video games.
