articles.title: Ottawa woman charged after sleeping in self-driving car on highway
articles.text:
Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) have charged an Ottawa woman after she was found sleeping behind the wheel of a self-driving Tesla on the highway.
On Instagram, the official OPP East account said an officer spotted the woman in the driver’s seat of a Tesla with her eyes closed and hands off the wheel while going down Highway 417 during morning rush hour on Tuesday.
View this post on Instagram
Under Ontario’s Highway Traffic Act, owners of autonomous vehicles must “remain at all times in the driver’s seat of the vehicle and shall monitor the vehicle’s operation,” which includes always having your hands on the wheel. The OPP notes that the woman received a Careless Driving charge, which carries a penalty of $490 and six demerit points upon conviction.
Notably, OPP told CityNews this was one of two incidents of people in self-driving cars not being attentive behind the wheel. The other incident also took place on a highway on Tuesday evening. We’ve also heard of similar examples of irresponsible autonomous vehicle owners in provinces like B.C.

articles.title: Neutronenstern oder Schwarzes Loch? Dieses Objekt dürfte es eigentlich nicht geben
articles.text:
Wissenschaftler entdecken unsichtbares Objekt im Weltall, das es eigentlich nicht geben dürfte
Ein Team von Wissenschaftler:innen hat im Sternbild Fische ein Doppelsternsystem mit einem Roten Riesen als Hauptstern entdeckt. So weit, so unspektakulär. Schließlich sind etwa 50 bis 70 Prozent aller Sterne der Milchstraße Teil eines Doppel- oder Mehrfachsystems.
Klein, unsichtbar und ungewöhnlich massereich
Doch der Begleiter des Roten Riesen gibt den Forschenden Rätsel auf. Er ist sehr klein und außergewöhnlich massereich.
Das mysteriöse Objekt ist außerdem unsichtbar. Es lässt sich also nicht direkt optisch wahrnehmen, sondern nur durch die Auswirkungen seiner Schwerkraft auf die Umlaufbahn des Roten Riesen.
Ist das unsichtbare Objekt ein Neutronenstern?
Um welche Art von Himmelskörper handelt es sich bei dem seltsamen Begleiter? Die Autor:innen der Studie, die in der Zeitschrift Science Advances erschienen ist, tippten zunächst auf einen Neutronenstern.
Da Neutronensterne sehr klein sind, ist ihr Licht mit gängigen Instrumenten meist nicht messbar. Diese extrem dichten Objekte entstehen, wenn ein massiver Stern als Supernova explodiert.
Neutronensterne besitzen typischerweise eine Sonnenmasse von 1,4. Sie sind also 1,4 Mal so massereich wie unsere Sonne.
Zu schwer für einen Neutronenstern – zu leicht für Schwarzes Loch
Der mutmaßliche Neutronenstern im neuentdeckten Doppelsystem weist laut den Forschenden jedoch eine Sonnenmasse zwischen 1,8 und 2,8 auf. Die wahrscheinlichste Schätzung liegt bei 2,2 Sonnenmassen.
Für einen Neutronenstern ist das Objekt also zu massiv. Für ein Schwarzes Loch ist es aber wiederum nicht massereich genug. Dieser Typ entsteht, wenn noch massereichere Sterne als bei den Neutronensternen explodieren.
Leichte Schwarze Löcher sind mindestens drei Mal so massig wie unsere Sonne. Supermassive Schwarze Löcher können bis zu mehreren Milliarden Sonnenmassen entsprechen. Schwarze Löcher sind unsichtbar, da das Licht ihrer starken Anziehungskraft nicht entkommen kann.
Gigantischer Neutronenstern oder schwaches Schwarzes Loch?
„Damit befindet sich der unsichtbare Begleiter potenziell in der Masselücke zwischen Neutronensternen und Schwarzen Löchern“, heißt es in der Studie. Es handelt sich also entweder um einen besonders massiven Neutronenstern oder ein extrem massearmes Schwarzes Loch.
Am wahrscheinlichsten ist es laut der Studie, dass der mysteriöse Kompagnon ein supermassiver Neutronenstern ist. Diese Objekte sind ziemlich selten, da sie sich von ihrer Masse her an der Grenze bewegen, an der ein Stern normalerweise zu einem Schwarzen Loch kollabiert.
So könnte der supermassive Neutronenstern entstanden sein
Auf die Frage, wie dieser mutmaßliche supermassive Neutronenstern entstanden ist, haben die Forschenden noch keine Antwort. Supermassive Neutronensterne können in Doppelsystemen entstehen, wenn Neutronensterne Materie vom anderen Stern absorbieren.
Doch in diesem Fall liegen die Umlaufbahnen des Roten Riesen und seines Begleiters so weit auseinander, dass ein direkter Austausch von Materie unmöglich scheint.
Entdeckung stellt Stand der Forschung infrage
Stattdessen könnte das System ursprünglich aus drei Sternen bestanden haben. Aus zwei Neutronensternen oder einem Neutronen- und einem normalen Stern könnte sich ein einziges, supermassives Exemplar geformt haben.
Die Forschenden schließen auch nicht die Möglichkeit aus, dass supermassive Neutronensterne aus ganz normalen Supernovae entstehen können. Und unser bisheriges Wissen über extrem massive Himmelskörper noch große Lücken aufweist.

articles.title: Revolut Pay débarque dans l’appli Uber, et vos courses peuvent rapporter jusqu’à 15 fois plus de RevPoints
articles.text:
Revolut Pay devient un moyen de paiement dans l’application Uber, en France et en Europe. Les courses et commandes Uber Eats peuvent désormais se régler depuis la néobanque, avec des RevPoints multipliés jusqu’à quinze fois d’ici au 6 janvier.
Payer sa course Uber avec Revolut Pay, sans sortir sa carte bancaire, c'est l'intrigante nouveauté que la néobanque et le géant du VTC viennent d'officialiser ce jeudi 12 novembre 2026. L'intégration repose sur un paiement de compte à compte validé en un instant depuis l'application Revolut, avec à la clé une vision plus nette de ce que l'on dépense en trajets comme en livraisons de repas. Pour séduire plus de 5 millions d'utilisateurs des deux services, Revolut sort aussi l'arrosoir à points de fidélité, et ses abonnés Premium pourront faire valoir leurs avantages Uber One en payant de cette façon.
Revolut Pay, ou l'art de régler Uber sans dégainer sa carte
Pour l'utilisateur, comment ça marche ? En fait, au moment de régler une course ou une commande Uber Eats, on sélectionne Revolut Pay, puis l'application Revolut prend le relais, et après une authentification biométrique, et le paiement est validé. La somme part directement du compte, sans numéro de carte à saisir. C'est le principe du paiement de compte à compte, ou A2A pour les intimes.
Dans le détail, chaque trajet ou repas payé de cette façon déclenche une notification instantanée et s'inscrit en temps réel dans le suivi des dépenses. On peut ainsi garder la main sur un budget VTC qui a la fâcheuse manie d'enfler, y compris en voyage, puisque les paiements en devises locales sont simplifiés. Alex Codina, le directeur général de l'acquisition marchande chez Revolut, explique que peu importe que l'on se fasse livrer un repas chez soi ou qu'on soit en vadrouille à l'étranger, tout se suit depuis l'application de la banque. La solution est taillée pour absorber les gros volumes de plateformes internationales comme Uber, et affiche selon Revolut un taux d'autorisation moyen de 98,5 %, un taux d'abandon inférieur à 5 % et plus de 33 devises prises en charge.
Le vice-président du commerce mondial chez Uber, Karl Uebert, évoque comme arguments davantage de choix, une meilleure visibilité sur les dépenses et des avantages exclusifs, pour essayer de convaincre les utilisateurs. Pour Revolut, c'est une vraie tribune, puisqu'Uber revendique plus de 215 millions d'utilisateurs actifs chaque mois, dans 75 pays. La néobanque, qui dépasse les 80 millions de clients particuliers, renforce un partenariat déjà existant, avec l'ambition évidente de faire de son bouton de paiement un réflexe.
Des RevPoints multipliés par quinze… mais pas partout
Pour l'occasion, Revolut annonce quintupler les RevPoints, son programme de fidélité paneuropéen, sur chaque course Uber ou commande Uber Eats réglée avec Revolut Pay, du 11 novembre au 6 janvier. Le « jusqu'à 15 fois plus » brandi en tête du communiqué suppose toutefois d'additionner ce bonus au multiplicateur par dix déjà proposé dans certains marchés éligibles, dont la liste n'est pas détaillée. Ailleurs, le gain devrait donc s'en tenir au ×5.
Ces points n'ont pas vocation à prendre la poussière, car on peut les dépenser au moment de payer, pour une réduction immédiate sur Uber ou Uber Eats, ou les échanger contre des miles si vous prenez l'avion, des séjours à l'hôtel ou des expériences proposées dans l'application Revolut. Les abonnés Revolut Premium, dont la formule est passée de 9,99 à 10,99 euros par mois cette année, peuvent par ailleurs profiter de leurs avantages Uber One, l'abonnement maison d'Uber, en réglant avec Revolut Pay, désormais reconnu comme moyen de paiement éligible.
Revolut vit une année 2026 faste, et mouvementée. L'incident électrique survenu chez Google Cloud le 20 octobre, qui avait privé des clients Revolut de paiements pendant de longues heures, semble bien oublié. Du 2 au 5 décembre, les quelque 8 millions de clients français revendiqués par la néobanque basculeront vers Revolut Bank S.A., sa banque hexagonale dotée cet été d'un agrément bancaire de plein exercice. Reste à voir, dans les prochaines semaines, si les utilisateurs d'Uber et de Revolut adopteront ce nouveau moyen de paiement.

articles.title: Who will succeed Jensen Huang? The race to find Nvidia's next chief begins
articles.text:
Who will succeed Jensen Huang? The race to find Nvidia's next chief begins
Jensen Huang’s departure ends a 33-year leadership era at Nvidia, triggering a search for his successor. Names including Lisa Su, Rene Haas and Tim Cook have entered the conversation, with Trump’s endorsement of Cook adding an unexpected twist.
Nvidia has begun its search for a permanent chief executive officer after co-founder Jensen Huang resigned on November 12, ending a 33-year run at the held. The company board has said it would consider candidates from inside and outside the company.
Meanwhile, the chief financial officer Colette Kress has been appointed the interim CEO.
The leadership crisis follows a week of mounting controversy at the chipmaking company, which is a key player in the global AI race. Nvidia faced scrutiny over reports of a possible foreign intelligence operation targeting Huang.
On November 8, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did,” he wrote.
The statement followed reports of his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, a company scrutinised by US authorities over suspected assistance to Chinese customers seeking advanced Nvidia chips subject to export restrictions.
The controversy deepened with reports of another relationship involving Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare.
On November 12, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter, that Huang also had an intimate relationship with another female Nvidia employee, whose identity it did not disclose.
Nvidia’s board had earlier launched an independent investigation into reports that Huang had been targeted in a foreign intelligence operation. It said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised."
The independent directors subsequently appointed former acting US attorney Joon H. Kim and law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct the inquiry. No findings have been published.
US Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Justice Department had reached no conclusion on whether Alice Huang was a spy, while confirming that the FBI was examining the reports.
These developments come amid the wider backdrop of a tightening contest over access to advanced AI chips.
US export controls restrict the sale of certain high-end Nvidia processors to China. Reuters reported on November 12 that Chinese AI firms were seeking to reserve Nvidia-powered computing capacity at overseas data centres, partly out of concern that Washington could tighten restrictions on remote access.
A proposed US Remote Access Security Act, which would give the Commerce Department authority over cloud-based access to restricted technology, has passed the House of Representatives but it still requires Senate approval.
The search for a successor
Meanwhile, Nvidia’s board has appointed longtime director Harvey C. Jones as its first chair and formally opened the search for a successor. The company has not announced a shortlist.
Reuters identified CFO Colette Kress and Ian Buck, a senior engineering executive who joined the company in 2004 and helped develop CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture), as prominent internal candidates being discussed by analysts and investors.
External names floated by media outlets include Arm chief executive Rene Haas, who is also a former Nvidia executive; and AMD chief Lisa Su. Axios mentioned former Intel chief Pat Gelsinger, Google Cloud head Thomas Kurian, and Apple executive chairman Tim Cook in a broader list of potential names.
None has been announced by Nvidia as a candidate, and there is no publicly confirmed official shortlist.
US President Donald Trump added a political twist to the proceedings by publicly suggesting Cook for the position. He posted a statement, “There is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!”
Beyond the leadership change
The succession race matters because Nvidia is seen as more than a company selling graphics processors.
Founded in 1993, the company initially focused on gaming graphics before expanding into accelerated computing, which uses specialised processors to handle large numbers of calculations simultaneously. Its CUDA software, data-centre systems, and networking technology now form a broad platform for training and running AI models.
The next CEO needs to maintain Nvidia's technological advantage while managing customers, regulators, and the company’s increasingly strategic role in US-China technology policy.
Competition is also intensifying. On November 12, AMD updated its Instinct MI400 accelerator range, announced the MI450X GPU, and shared new performance results for its MI455X GPU on its Helios rack-scale system. The announcements underline company's efforts to challenge Nvidia in AI data centres.
Nvidia, meanwhile, announced a partnership with South Korea’s Rebellions and SK Telecom to connect Korean-designed AI processors with its infrastructure for sovereign AI projects. The planned Rebellions R200 systems are expected to be ready in 2028.
Kress has sought to reassure customers and investors about continuity. In her statement following the appointment, she said, “We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead.”
Nvidia’s third-quarter fiscal 2027 results are scheduled for November 17, with Kress due to provide written financial commentary ahead of the investor call.
That will offer an early opportunity to assess operational continuity under the interim leadership. The bigger challenge, however, lies with the board.
Jensen Huang has been central to Nvidia's identity, strategy and influence for more than three decades. So his replacement has to be someone capable of managing not just a major semiconductor business but also an entire technology ecosystem.
Edited by Swetha Kannan

articles.title: Lunettes connectées Apple : un fournisseur chinois nous met sur la piste de plusieurs projets
articles.text:
Les rumeurs se font de plus en plus nombreuses autour des lunettes connectées d’Apple. Sans écran et voulant concurrencer les Ray-Ban Meta, elles arriveraient fin 2027. Désormais, ce sont des indices plus tangibles qui apparaissent : cette fois-ci, c’est un rapport financier d’un fournisseur d’Apple en Chine.
Ce fournisseur d’Apple a son carnet de commandes rempli
L’histoire nous vient du média chinois iFeng : l’entreprise TCB Devices, a indiqué dans son rapport financier du troisième trimestre 2026 participer aux projets d’« IA Glasses » et de « nouveaux écouteurs intelligents ». Son carnet de commandes est donc bien rempli, notamment pour l’année 2027 : ces deux projets devraient constituer une grande partie de son chiffre d’affaires. Et c’est là que tout se resserre : et si Apple était derrière ces grosses commandes ? L’industrialisation de lunettes connectées est en développement chez TCB Devices : cette collaboration porte sur de la soudure de précision et de l’inspection par vision machine.
Second produit évoqué, des AirPods dotés de caméras, qui pourraient eux aussi être lancés fin 2027. Les rumeurs à propos de ce produit vont déjà bon train : ces écouteurs auraient des capteurs photo basse résolution dans les tiges qui permettraient d’utiliser Siri avec Apple Intelligence. D’ailleurs, des informations sur ce produit auraient été repérées dans le code de macOS 26.7.
Ce qu’on sait des lunettes connectées d’Apple
Depuis des années, on sait qu’Apple travaille sur une première paire de lunettes connectées. Il ne s’agirait donc pas d’une nouvelle version du Vision Pro. Elles n’auraient pas d’écran et leur objectif serait de concurrencer les Ray-Ban Meta. Ces lunettes s’utiliseraient donc uniquement avec un micro et des haut-parleurs, pour communiquer avec Siri et Apple Intelligence. Elles également dotées de caméras pour prendre des photos et des vidéos, mais aussi pour que Siri/Apple Intelligence puisse analyser l’environnement : reconnaître des lieux, traduire du texte, aider à la navigation, etc.
Concernant le calendrier, il se serait décalé : d’abord prévues pour fin 2026, les lunettes auraient été repoussées pour le second semestre 2027, puis pour la fin de l’année 2027. Mais Apple pourrait décider de les présenter dans un premier temps lors de la WWDC 2027, sa conférence pour les développeurs prévue pour juin prochain. Face à la concurrence de Meta et à la myriade d’autres marques qui se lancent sur le secteur, Apple n’aurait plus le choix : il lui faut ses lunettes connectées. Et pour capter des parts de marché, Apple peut s’appuyer sur sa renommée, mais aussi son expérience utilisateur et logicielle et son intégration de Siri.

articles.title: Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock
Part 1 of this series built the operating model that controls Amazon Bedrock spend: attribution with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal tags and Cost and Usage Report 2.0, observability with model invocation logging, enforcement at three tiers, and a review cadence. That layer answers who spent it, and you can stop them. It can’t tell you whether the spend was well spent.
This post answers two questions that Part 1 deliberately left open. First: Why is this workflow expensive? The answer requires thinking in cost per task, not cost per token. Second: Is the agent better than the humans were? The answer requires baselines, controlled experiments, and a scorecard tied to decisions.
In this post, you learn a framework for calculating true model cost (including four hidden cost drivers that the pricing page doesn’t show), techniques for reducing cost per task through caching, routing, and output constraints, and a discipline for measuring agent ROI with human baselines, holdout experiments, and a five-dimension scorecard. This post is written for two audiences: the application and platform engineers who own the optimization levers, and the product owners and FinOps partners who need to justify agent spend to leadership.
Cost per task, not cost per token
Price per token invites quick comparison, but it doesn’t reflect what you actually pay. The published rate reflects the cost of a single token. Your bill reflects the cost of completing a task. A task is one complete unit of work your application asks a model to do: resolve one support email, extract fields from one invoice, or answer one user question. A task runs from the request through to a usable result, however many model calls it takes.
The lower-priced model might not be the cheaper one to run. A cheaper model might fragment your text into more tokens, pad responses with filler, misread your tool schema and loop through corrections, or burn thousands of reasoning tokens before answering. None of these costs appear on the Bedrock pricing page.
The four hidden cost drivers
Four model characteristics determine what that published rate actually costs you on your workload.
Tokenizer efficiency
A token isn’t a word, and it is not equal across models. Every model family uses a different tokenizer and vocabulary. The same text, code, or JSON payload splits into different token counts. If Model A’s list price is 15 percent lower but its tokenizer needs 40 percent more tokens for your data (common with structured schemas and numerical arrays), Model B is cheaper. The gap widens for non-English text: many tokenizers fragment non-Latin scripts into two to three times more tokens than the equivalent English.
Output alignment and verbosity
Output tokens commonly cost 3–5x more than input tokens (the ratio varies by family. Refer to the Bedrock pricing page). A model that ignores formatting constraints like “return only raw JSON” makes you pay that output premium for filler words. A model that follows formatting instructions closely saves money by generating fewer of these more expensive output tokens.
Agentic loop efficiency
Agentic workflows change the cost math entirely. Tool use (function calling) lets a model invoke external functions, requiring a multi-turn loop: analyze the prompt, decide to call a tool, wait for the observation, generate an answer. Each turn re-sends the full conversation history and tool results as input tokens. A model that takes four turns (each one re-sending a larger context payload) costs far more than one that finishes in a single pass.
Reasoning overhead
Many models support extended thinking, working through a chain of thought before the visible answer. Reasoning tokens bill as output tokens, so a model that thinks for 2,000 tokens before a 200-token answer bills you for 2,200. Some models redact the reasoning while still charging for it. Start with reasoning turned off and enable it only when benchmarks show a quality gap that justifies the cost.
Cost per task: A worked example
Consider an agentic workflow that reads a 750-word customer email, extracts entities, calls an API to verify account status, and outputs strict JSON. The following comparison uses illustrative prices (always benchmark against your own data and current Bedrock pricing):
| Metric | Model A (lower list price) | Model B (higher list price) | 
| Input list price | $0.50 / 1M tokens | $1.00 / 1M tokens | 
| Output list price | $1.50 / 1M tokens | $3.00 / 1M tokens | 
| Tokenizer efficiency (turn 1 input) | 1,500 tokens | 1,000 tokens | 
| Output verbosity (final response) | 450 tokens | 150 tokens | 
| Agentic loops required | 3 turns (error correction) | 1 turn (zero-shot) | 
| Cumulative input tokens, all turns | 6,150 | 1,000 | 
| Cumulative output tokens, all turns | 750 | 150 | 
| Total task cost | $0.0042 | $0.00145 | 
Model A: (6,150 x $0.50 + 750 x $1.50) / 1,000,000 = $0.0042
Model B: (1,000 x $1.00 + 150 x $3.00) / 1,000,000 = $0.00145
Why the 2x-priced model costs 65 percent less: three compounding factors. Model A’s tokenizer fragments the email into 50 percent more tokens, inflating every input payload. It pads its JSON with filler, tripling output tokens. And it misaligns with the tool schema, needing two correction turns that each re-send a growing history.
Cost per successful task
The preceding example assumes both models eventually succeed. In production they won’t, and a failure is rarely free. The formulas:
For retry-until-success workflows:
cost per successful task = cost per attempt / success rate
For escalate-on-failure workflows:
cost per successful task = cost per attempt + (1 - success rate) x escalation cost
Input further splits into three buckets when prompt caching is active: uncached input at base rate, cache reads below base rate, and cache writes above base rate.
Measuring it on your own workload
Which model is actually cheaper only shows up when you benchmark against your own data. Amazon Bedrock model evaluation is the managed feature for the quality half of that: define criteria, upload your prompt datasets, and get scored results with automatic metrics and optional human review, with no custom infrastructure required.
Quality scores alone don’t produce a bill, though. Three more Bedrock features supply the token and turn counts you price against them:
- CountTokens returns the input token count a given model would charge for a given payload without running inference. It’s the cheapest way to compare tokenizer efficiency (driver #1) across candidates before you spend anything on generation.
- Model invocation response carries a usage block with inputTokens, outputTokens, cacheReadInputTokens, and cacheWriteInputTokens. Accumulating those across the turns of a single task gives you the four terms of the preceding cost-per-attempt formula. One gotcha: when caching is enabled, inputTokens counts only the uncached tokens, so your total input volume is inputTokens + cacheReadInputTokens + cacheWriteInputTokens. Sum them to know the footprint, but price them separately, since the three bill at different rates. Evaluate this multiple times throughout your journey and set the cache checkpoints based on what is the active current load. The drift in cache checkpoints happens as the application progresses and the tools become stale. This means that you will be writing more to the cache in 3 months from now when the drift has happened. Evaluating your data constantly for optimal cache usage becomes a primary lever to reduce cost.
- Model invocation logging writes per-invocation token counts to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch Logs, so you can measure turns-to-completion against real production traffic instead of a sample. Tag calls with request metadata to slice those logged token counts by team, feature, or experiment. However, these are log fields, not cost allocation tags, and never appear in AWS Cost Explorer or your Cost and Usage Report. Application inference profiles do reach both, at a grain of one usage type per day. That grain is right for chargeback but too coarse for cost per task. Multiplying logged token counts by the published rates gives you a near real-time estimate rather than an invoice. It won’t reflect commitments, batch pricing, or provisioned throughput unless you model them. Reconcile against your Cost and Usage Report before you treat it as the bill.
Reducing cost per task: Four levers
Each of the four drivers has a lever, and each is documented in depth. Prompt caching cuts the re-sent context that made Model A expensive, which makes it the largest win on agentic paths. Intelligent prompt routing sends the easy requests to a cheaper model in the same family. A tool schema plus a maxTokens cap holds verbosity down more reliably than prose instructions do, and extended thinking stays off until a benchmark shows it earns its cost back. Batch inference halves the rate on bulk single-turn work, though it rules out tool calling and multi-turn exchange.
Proving agent ROI: Describe the human baseline
Efficient isn’t the same as valuable. An agent can be perfectly optimized and still not be worth running. The question that decides budgets is: is the agent better than the humans were?
Document the human process first
The biggest mistake in agent ROI is trying to prove value without first describing the human workflow. Before building or scaling an agent, write down the current process in operational terms: what triggers the work, which human roles are involved, where the handoffs sit, how completion is defined. This sounds like bureaucracy. It’s actually measurement design. Every instrumentation decision downstream (what counts as a run, what counts as success, where human time is spent) falls out of this description.
Measure the baseline before the agent ships
With the process described, measure the human baseline over a meaningful window: time to completion, queue time, active effort, reopen rate, escalation rate, cost per task, and outcome quality. Baselines must be measured before the agent goes live, not reconstructed from memory after the fact. Retrospective baselines are systematically flattering to the agent: people remember the average case and forget the fast ones.
Instrument the workflow as an experiment
After the baseline exists, instrument the agent workflow as an experiment from day one. Every run gets a trace ID, and every meaningful step is observable. A workflow-run record aggregates everything above the model call into a single analyzable unit:
Three fields deserve emphasis:
experiment block: Stamped at run creation and propagated into Bedrock request metadata, so model-level and workflow-level records join cleanly.
humanMinutes: What most teams omit and most need. Without it, “the agent did the work” silently excludes the 35 minutes a human spent reviewing it.
revenueEventId: The hook that makes revenue attribution possible later. It costs nothing to record and can’t be reconstructed afterward.
The rule: If the workflow telemetry can’t answer the business question, the instrumentation is incomplete.
Join cost to outcomes
With invocation logs landing in Amazon S3 (Part 1) and workflow-run records in your analytics store, one join produces the metrics that matter. Amazon Bedrock logs record tokens, not dollars, so first build a view that prices each invocation from token counts and your model rate sheet, aggregated by run ID. Then query with Amazon Athena:
        Note: Column names and join keys shown in the preceding query are illustrative. Verify against your invocation log schema and workflow telemetry store, which might vary by implementation.
Cost per successful outcome, retries per success, and human minutes per success are the three numbers that survive contact with a skeptical CFO. Cost per call flatters agents that loop. Cost per success doesn’t. Note the variant grouping: the same query, split by experiment arm, is the ROI comparison.
Compare agents and humans correctly
The most credible evaluation is an A/B or holdout test. Controlled treatment and control groups compare the agent-assisted workflow against the human baseline without confusing the result with market, seasonal, or organizational changes.
For customer-facing or revenue-linked workflows, randomize at the visitor, lead, account, or case level. For internal workflows (support operations, coding assistants), use matched cohorts: teams, repository groups, or pods.
The comparison covers four dimensions:
Efficiency: time to completion, hours recovered, queue-time reduction.
Quality: error rate, approval rate, reopen rate, escalation rate.
Cost: cost per task, cost per successful outcome, total cost to serve.
Business value: conversion lift, retention lift, expansion rate, revenue per rep or per workflow.
If the agent improves one dimension while meaningfully degrading another, the result is ambiguous and the deployment needs tuning.
Revenue: The hardest metric
Efficiency gains are the easiest part of the ROI story to prove. Revenue impact is harder, and it is the metric leadership funds against. In revenue-adjacent workflows, measure whether the agent improves conversion, time-to-response, deal progression, or revenue per rep. Holdout tests are the most reliable way to separate incremental revenue attributable to the agent from general business momentum.
When revenue lift is real, the conversation changes. The organization stops asking whether the Bedrock bill went up and starts asking whether the additional spend is buying a meaningful increase in business output.
The scorecard
Based on what we have observed working with customers, a strong operating model doesn’t require fifty metrics. What works is a small scorecard tied to decisions, reviewed on a regular cadence for every production agent.
The following thresholds are starting points, not prescriptions. Calibrate them against your own fleet data and organizational context.
| Dimension | Metric | Green | Yellow | Red | 
| Adoption | Active users / intended users | >70% | 40-70% | <40% | 
| Quality | Tasks completed without rework | >90% | 75-90% | <75% | 
| Efficiency | Hours recovered per week | >target | 50-100% of target | <50% of target | 
| Cost | Cost per successful outcome | ≤budget | 1-1.5x budget | >1.5x budget | 
| Business impact | KPI lift compared to baseline | Significant | Marginal | None or negative | 
Green means scale: the agent beats baseline while meeting cost and quality thresholds. Yellow means tune: promising but needs work. Red means retire or redesign: the agent consumes cost without enough measurable value. The willingness to actually retire a red agent is what makes the rest of the scorecard credible.
Conclusion
In this post, you learned how to calculate the true cost of a model by accounting for four hidden cost drivers (tokenizer efficiency, output alignment, agentic loop efficiency, and reasoning overhead), how to reduce cost per task through prompt caching, model routing, output constraints, and batch inference, and how to prove agent ROI by measuring human baselines, instrumenting workflows as experiments, joining cost to outcomes, and running holdout comparisons.
The cost optimization half answers “why is this expensive and how do I fix it.” The ROI half answers “is the agent better than the humans were.” Together with Part 1’s operating model (attribute, observe, enforce, optimize, operate), they form a complete framework: you can see who spent it, explain why, reduce the waste, and justify what remains.
To get started, benchmark your top model candidates against your own prompts using Amazon Bedrock model evaluation, capture tokens and turns from the usage block or your invocation logs, price them against current Bedrock pricing, and divide by success rate. For ROI measurement, consult the Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens for agent cost governance best practices.
If you have found other techniques for reducing cost per task or measuring agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock, let us know in the comments.

articles.title: Newly rebranded Signal Week unites major crypto players - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Paris Signal Week looks to bridge crypto and institutional finance
Paris Blockchain Week is now Signal Week, a reflection of cryptocurrency’s global expansion.
The newly rebranded event is joining forces with RAISE Summit, the annual AI and networking conference, and Machina Summit, Europe’s leading physical AI event. Event organizers expect approximately 2,500 attendees, highlighting the growing profile of blockchain technology.
“The industry has changed a lot,” said Michael Amar (pictured), chairman of RAISE Summit and co-founder of Signal Week. “We really want to be the place where we bridge traditional finance and digital assets. It’s where the market is finally, and we are embracing it completely. We have the desire to go abroad to launch other conferences. So it made sense that … we join everything under the same roof, but different flows, different marketing and different ticketing.”
Amar and Charlie Meraud (pictured), chairman of RAISE Summit and co-founder of Signal Week, spoke with theCUBE host Gemma Allen, during an exclusive interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed what to expect at the 2027 event and the evolution of cryptocurrency. (* Disclosure below.)
A signal of crypto’s growing presence
Signal Week is designed to cover the intersection between institutional finance and digital assets. Since its founding, the crypto market has grown to $40 billion in tokenized real-world assets, or RWA, according to Meraud. The week will also encompass the CXO Summit, a private gathering of C-suite executives.
“The CXO Summit is organizing a roundtable under Chatham House rules with these … crypto-native players discussing all sophisticated topics around what they are building and how they can partner all year long,” he said. “This is the kind of activation that makes people book a flight, buy a ticket and come to Signal Week. The industry needed a room for these players to connect and start actually doing business.”
Both founders see facilitating conversations between crypto leaders and traditional finance executives as one of the primary goals of the conference. The chief executive officers of Kaiko, Morpho and Fireblocks, all leading digital asset companies, are expected to attend. European Union regulators will also be present, Amar and Meraud emphasize, which will be critical for understanding the future of AI-powered finance.
“We’re creating those moments where people can get the most out of the conference,” Amar said. “If you talk about the C-suite, people coming from traditional finance and meeting the makers of the crypto industry, we’re creating the space where they will have talks in a very small room where actually we go very much into the details of the use cases of the implementation of a digital asset solution for a bank, for example.”
Another key topic at Signal Week and RAISE Summit will be custody, the safekeeping of private keys that allow a person to prove they control an address and the cryptocurrency it holds. Security has long been a divisive issue for cryptocurrency, spurring a variety of solutions.
“When we started … self-custody was one of the promised digital assets,” Meraud said. “A lot of players have been offering different ways of custodying digital assets. And having the most sophisticated solution coming to Signal Week, explaining all the new features, they’ve been building over the years is one of the reasons financial institutions are willing to connect and network with our audience.”

articles.title: Jensen Huang was having a third affair, Reuters reports | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang was having a separate affair with an employee that has not been previously reported, Reuters reported on Thursday.
Huang stepped down as CEO and board member for the company earlier today, in the wake of news of extramarital affairs with accused spy Alice Huang and Nvidia VP of Healthcare Kimberly Powell. CFO Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO, but no permanent successor has been named.
Reuters is withholding the name of the new employee linked to Huang but says she is an employee of Nvidia.
Huang has been called before Congress to testify about the national security implications of his relationship with Alice Huang in the coming weeks — but it’s unclear how much more will be revealed before the hearings take place. Already, his abrupt fall from grace is expected to have significant repercussions for the industry at large.

articles.title: AI could disrupt India's outsourcing model. It could also create millions of new exporters
articles.text:
AI could disrupt India's outsourcing model. It could also create millions of new exporters
AI is letting small Indian teams win global work that once needed a big company. As AI separates capability from headcount, it could shape India’s next export story.
I recently spoke to someone running a small creative agency from a Tier II Indian city, with most of his clients outside India. When AI came up, I expected him to talk about producing more content, faster. What he described was more interesting.
Rotoscoping, repetitive edits and parts of project management were now largely automated. His tiny team now takes on projects that once needed outside freelancers.
This is usually told as a productivity story. I think something more fundamental is happening: AI is changing how big a company must become before it can sell sophisticated services to the world.
For India, that is both an opportunity and an uncomfortable question.
The model that built India's services industry is changing
India’s services exports reached $421.3 billion in FY26, up from $387.5 billion a year earlier, with IT and business services the largest contributors. For three decades, the IT services industry ran on a simple equation: win more customers, hire more people.
AI challenges that. Coding, testing, research, documentation and customer support are the backbone of Indian outsourcing, and they are exactly where AI is improving fastest.
NASSCOM estimates that India’s tech industry earned $10-12 billion from AI services in FY26, while overall revenue grew 6.1% to $315 billion. Hiring continues, but total headcount rose just 2.3%. The link between revenue and people is loosening.
That threatens a model built on selling human capacity. Seen from a five-person company, the same shift looks very different.
AI reduces the minimum scale needed to compete
Small services firms have always faced a capacity problem: winning a large project meant building the organisation to deliver it. AI is beginning to separate capability from headcount.
I saw this first-hand when I spoke to the founder of a growth-marketing firm with 15 people and 22 AI agents, serving clients across more than seven countries. Its founder sorts every task into three buckets. Manual tasks, such as discovery calls, are deliberately kept away from AI. In AI-assisted tasks, AI does 85-95% of the work and a person checks the rest. Fully automated tasks, such as market research, run end to end and the only human step is sending the report to the client. About 40% of the firm’s budget goes to AI agents and software rather than headcount. The founder says it runs at 60-70% margins, against 20-25% for a typical agency.
Even discovery has changed. One UK client told the same growth-marketing founder that he found, evaluated and signed the firm within a single Perplexity chat.
We are beginning to see this from the payment layer
Building in cross-border payments, we see thousands of Indian businesses being paid from abroad, and what stands out is how small many of them are. Over the last 12 months, 347 solo professionals each collected more than $100,000 from overseas clients, and 117 teams of two to ten people each crossed $250,000.
The base is widening too. Exporters actively billing overseas customers each quarter grew roughly fivefold over seven quarters, from about 2,800 to 13,900. Some of that growth reflects more businesses coming onto our network, not just new exporters entering the market. But the median invoice stayed near $1,500 throughout, which suggests many more people are selling, rather than a few landing bigger deals. Eighty-two per cent of these exporters have ten or fewer people.
Exporters in AI, machine learning, data or automation grew about ninefold, and their median invoice is nearly double. They are roughly 2% of volume, so this is a direction, not yet a trend. One of them, a solo AI and machine-learning consultant, billed about $266,000 to US clients in 12 months from just four buyers. That is not typical, but a decade ago that work would have needed a firm.
Selling expertise, not capacity
If India’s response to AI is simply to perform the same outsourced work with fewer people and charge customers less, we may improve productivity without fundamentally improving our position in the global value chain.
The larger opportunity is to move from selling capacity to selling expertise and outcomes.
AI can analyse 500 customer conversations. It cannot independently decide which customer problem a business should build its future around. It can generate software. Someone still has to understand what should be built, how it fits into a customer’s organisation, and take responsibility when it doesn’t work.
The value increasingly lies in asking the right questions, applying domain knowledge, exercising judgement and owning the result.
This may actually make deep expertise more valuable, not less. Consider the Indian professional who has spent 15 years understanding insurance claims, semiconductor design, pharmaceutical regulation, supply chains or financial risk. That person can now combine their domain knowledge with tools that dramatically expand what one person can execute.
India has no shortage of such people. According to the Economic Survey 2024-25, the country accounts for 28% of the world’s STEM workforce and 23% of global software engineering talent. New kinds of work are already emerging. I find this example striking: a medical professional in Kochi spends her week marking organs and flagging anomalies in foetal ultrasound scans. She isn’t treating patients directly; she’s helping train AI systems being built for hospitals in the US.
A five-person global company cannot have a 50-person back office.
There is one problem.
India’s export framework was designed for firms with finance teams. Proof-of-export documentation, GST filings, foreign exchange conversion and bank reconciliation all assume someone in the back office is handling them.
A five-person firm billing clients in California and London, in multiple currencies, has no such person. Yet it may have hundreds of thousands of dollars moving across borders every year.
If AI shrinks the team needed to deliver the work, but the founder still loses hours each month to paperwork and compliance, the bottleneck has simply moved. Regulators, banks and the wider fintech ecosystem need to make cross-border compliance as lightweight as the businesses it now serves.
India’s next services giants may not look like giants
India’s first services-export era was built by assembling millions of skilled people into large organisations. That model isn’t disappearing. But the next phase may look much less concentrated: thousands, perhaps eventually many more, of specialist Indian businesses selling their expertise to the world.
The agency I spoke to is interesting not because AI helps it edit videos faster. It is interesting because a handful of people in an Indian city can now compete for work anywhere in the world.
Twenty-five years ago, India's services-export breakthrough was partly about proving that global work could be done from India.
The AI-era opportunity may be proving that you no longer need to build a large company to do a large amount of it.
Srivatsan Sridhar is Co-Founder and CEO of Skydo.

articles.title: Le PDG de Nvidia vient de démissionner, c’est officiel
articles.text:
C’est officiel, Jensen Huang n’est plus le PDG de Nvidia. L’homme a remis sa démission ce jeudi 12 novembre 2026, avec effet immédiat. Jensen Huang avait cofondé Nvidia en 1993. Une page se tourne dans le secteur de la tech.
Jensen Huang n’est plus le PDG de Nvidia
Ce jeudi 12 novembre 2026, le conseil d’administration de Nvidia a tenu une réunion pour décider du sort de Jensen Huang. C’est finalement Jensen Huang lui-même qui a présenté sa démission avec effet immédiat. Colette Kress, directrice financière de Nvidia depuis 2013, a accepté d’occuper temporairement le poste de CEO de Nvidia jusqu’à la nomination d’un successeur permanent.
Une décision inévitable
Pour rappel, Jensen Huang a avoué avoir entretenu une relation extraconjugale avec Alice Huang, dirigeante de l’entreprise singapourienne Megaspeed. Outre les problèmes d’ordre personnel, les autorités américaines soupçonnent Alice Huang d’être une espionne au service de la Chine. Par la suite, Donald Trump a défendu Jensen Huang et le FBI a ouvert une enquête. Mais cela n’est pas tout puisque nous avons appris que le désormais ex-dirigeant de Nvidia a également entretenu une relation avec une employée de l’entreprise. La situation étant trop sensible, Jensen Huang a donc remis sa démission. Il reste à voir si cela résulte d’un accord avec le conseil d’administration ou si Jensen Huang a tout simplement pris les devants avant que le conseil d’administration de Nvidia ne décide de l’évincer. Jensen Huang a cofondé Nvidia en 1993. Une page importante se tourne donc pour l’entreprise.
Le conseil d’administration de Nvidia va maintenant devoir élire un nouveau CEO. Selon Bloomberg, Nvidia a d’ores et déjà fait appel à une entreprise externe pour identifier des candidats au poste de PDG.

articles.title: Amazon brings agentic shopping to Canada
articles.text:
Amazon has announced the launch of Alexa for Shopping in Canada. This brings an agentic AI shopping experience that combines Rufus’ (Amazon’s AI shopping assistant) product expertise with Alexa+ conversational capabilities.
The AI is personalized for each user, as it studies their product knowledge, shopping history and conversational context to offer tailored recommendations. It’ll remember customer preferences and previous purchases and conversations.
Customers are able to ask questions directly in Amazon’s search bar, and use AI-generated product category overviews and make custom shopping guides, comparing features, prices and reviews.
And Alexa for Shopping can help customers automate routine shopping tasks, it can build carts and reorder essentials. It also offers 30-day, 60-day or 365-day product price history tracking.
Additionally, Alexa for Shopping in Canada is bringing the ability to set a target price for a product and get notified when the price gets to what you want. Further, Alexa is also going to add ongoing improvements to how Alexa for remembers your preferences and conversations across different devices.
Alexa for Shopping will roll out to Canadians over the coming week. To get it started update your Amazon Shopping app and tap the Alexa icon in the bottom navigation bar or it’s at the top of your screen on desktop. Anyone can use it no Echo device, Alexa app or Prime membership is needed.
Source: Amazon Alexa

articles.title: Building a self-service LLM gateway with Amazon Bedrock and LiteLLM | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Building a self-service LLM gateway with Amazon Bedrock and LiteLLM
Developers want AI coding assistants with minimal setup. With a large language model (LLM) gateway and LiteLLM, they can quickly access foundation models (FMs) available on Amazon Bedrock while you gain visibility and usage control. Platform teams need to monitor latency and errors, finance teams need to attribute inference costs to teams and projects, and security teams need consistent access controls. An LLM gateway can help address these needs by providing a centrally managed access point to the models that power coding assistants.
In this post, we show how to build a self-service LLM gateway using Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles with LiteLLM running on AWS Fargate to abstract Amazon Bedrock behind an OpenAI-compatible API. With this pattern, developers can access foundation models through a single API with a dedicated key while you gain per-user cost controls and model performance observability. By the end, you will understand the pattern well enough to build your own version from the illustrative snippets and AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) constructs. This post uses Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku models for example purposes. For a list of models and availability by AWS Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
This LLM gateway pattern follows a straightforward request flow from the developer, through the LiteLLM layer, to Amazon Bedrock and the underlying FM. The following diagram illustrates the production topology behind that flow. For simplicity, we don’t cover the addition of Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, such as content filtering and grounding, but you would normally include appropriate responsible AI controls before deploying to production.
A developer’s OpenAI-compatible client reaches the LLM gateway through Amazon Route 53, Amazon CloudFront, and an Application Load Balancer (ALB). It authenticates to LiteLLM on Fargate with a per-user API key. Behind that, the request draws on Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) (PostgreSQL) for virtual-key and spend state. It also interacts with Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey as a cache, and AWS Secrets Manager for secrets. LiteLLM then ultimately invokes Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles using a scoped AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) task role. Amazon CloudWatch captures requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM) metrics and the quota alarm.
The architecture consists of these core components:
- LiteLLM on AWS Fargate: LiteLLM provides a proxy that exposes an OpenAI-compatible API. We run it on an AWS Fargate task with target-tracking Auto Scaling on CPU utilization. Developers point their tools at this endpoint and don’t interact with Amazon Bedrock directly.
- Self-service portal: LiteLLM includes a lightweight portal for admin and developer self-service. This web app can integrate with your corporate single sign-on (SSO). Using the portal, operations engineers set the spend policy while developers self-provision API keys within those parameters.
- Persistent and cache storage: LiteLLM uses Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey for non-persistent response caching. It also coordinates rate-limiting across AWS Fargate tasks. A separate Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL) database is the database of record for persistent state such as API key metadata and spend tracking.
- Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles: Each model (such as Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku) gets its own inference profile, which you manage using the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). With this, you get per-model quota isolation and a clean abstraction layer between LiteLLM’s configuration and the model versioning of Amazon Bedrock.
- Langfuse: Open source LLM observability for prompt-level telemetry, latency tracking, and debugging. It complements the infrastructure-level metrics of Amazon CloudWatch with application-level insight.
By using an OpenAI-compatible protocol, developers can configure their tools, such as Claude Code, Continue, and Cursor, with a single base URL and API key. Developers then operate at a level above the Amazon Bedrock backend and can swap models, add fallbacks, or migrate model providers without touching developer configurations.
Prerequisites
You will need an AWS account, Amazon Bedrock model access, and appropriate IAM permissions to deploy this project. You will also need LiteLLM. The LiteLLM AI Gateway component is open source and suitable for a small pilot with some limitations. LiteLLM documents the AI Gateway as free for up to five users with a license required beyond that. LiteLLM Enterprise is a scalable, production-minded licensed version that includes the open source gateway plus single sign-on, audit logs, delegated admin roles, and support. While the free tier supports virtual keys, the self-service key issuance described in this post requires the Enterprise version.
End-to-end configuration: Left to right
We walk through each configuration layer from the developer’s machine to the foundation model.
Step 1: Developer IDE configuration (for example, Claude Code)
Developers configure their coding assistant to point to the LLM gateway. This is the only configuration a developer needs to make to their tool:
With that configuration, each developer gets their own API key from the self-service portal and drops it into their tool configuration.
Step 2: LiteLLM gateway configuration
Deploy LiteLLM to a container service following the LiteLLM documentation. In this example we are using AWS Fargate. This will include the portal, which you can open at http://localhost:4000/ui during local testing.
The LiteLLM gateway is where you will map and enforce model names to Amazon Bedrock inference profile ARNs with per-key spend limits:
Set on the Fargate task from AWS Secrets Manager:
Note: Don’t hardcode the master_key or database credentials in config.yaml. LiteLLM resolves os.environ/VAR_NAME references at load time, so set LITELLM_MASTER_KEY and DATABASE_URL as environment variables on the Fargate task, sourced from AWS Secrets Manager. Set the Langfuse credentials the same way in Step 5.
When a developer calls claude-sonnet-4-20250514, for example, LiteLLM resolves it to the inference profile ARN. It then authenticates to Amazon Bedrock using the AWS Fargate task’s IAM role and streams the response back in OpenAI format.
Step 3: Bedrock inference profiles (CDK)
With Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles you can create named endpoints for specific models, so you get quota isolation and fine-grained IAM control.
Choosing cross-Region inference (CRIS): Geographic or Global
Amazon Bedrock CRIS avoids the overhead of implementing cross-Region request routing yourself. Other benefits include:
- Access to a broader pool of Regional capacity.
- Automatic routing of requests to a supported Region with available capacity.
- Broader model selection, because some models are available only through an inference profile.
For this proxy pattern, we recommend Global cross-Region inference when the selected models support it and organizational policies permit inference processing across supported AWS commercial Regions worldwide. Geographic cross-Region inference keeps processing within a defined geography. For example, a US inference profile routes requests only to supported US Regions. Global cross-Region inference provides access to a broader pool of Regional capacity with potential pricing benefits compared with Geographic cross-Region inference. You can verify model availability, applicable service quotas, and model-specific pricing through current AWS documentation and AWS pricing pages.
CDK construct
Important: For Global CRIS, the copyFrom ARN must reference the system-defined inference profile prefixed with global., not the foundation-model ARN directly. Using a foundation-model ARN creates a single-Region profile without cross-Region routing. Additionally, the IAM policy must include the resource ARNs the invocation actually touches: the application inference profile and the underlying foundation model in any Region it might route to (Region-wildcarded). Scoping only to the application-inference-profile ARN returns not authorized to perform: bedrock:InvokeModel on resource: arn:aws:bedrock:us-east-1::foundation-model/... at invoke time. This is scoped least-privilege: it names the exact models in use, not bedrock:* or *.
Step 4: Bedrock invokes the foundation model
The inference profile handles model resolution and cross-Region routing transparently without additional configuration. When LiteLLM calls the inference profile ARN, Amazon Bedrock routes to available capacity across configured AWS Regions and returns the response.
Step 5: Langfuse observability
LiteLLM integrates with Langfuse through logging callbacks, providing visibility into model invocations without requiring changes to developer tool configurations. To enable the integration, merge the following entries into the existing litellm_settings block from the Step 2 configuration, preserving existing callback entries:
Configure the Langfuse public key, secret key, and deployment endpoint as environment variables on the Fargate task. Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager:
The endpoint must match the selected Langfuse Cloud region or self-hosted deployment. Choose the hosting option based on data governance and operational requirements. Before enabling prompt and response logging, review the content captured by the integration and configure appropriate redaction, retention, and access controls.
Langfuse traces can include prompts, responses, model parameters, token usage, and latency, depending on the integration and logging configuration. This information helps investigate unexpected model responses and complements the operational metrics collected in Amazon CloudWatch.
Implementing cost controls
Cost controls are an important dimension to a successful AI strategy. Without cost controls, heavy usage of extended thinking features can lead to unexpectedly high charges, which we observed in our early pilots.
The spend limits configured in Step 2 (max_budget: 250, budget_duration: 7d) enforce a rolling 7-day window per API key, provided per-model model_info costs are set (refer to the Step 2 note). When a user reaches their limit, LiteLLM returns an HTTP 429 code with a clear message explaining that their budget has been exceeded. There’s no silent degradation or surprise bill. Developers and engineering teams can check current spend and reset timing through any of the following:
- Daily spend: Query GET /user/daily/activity with a start_date and end_date range to get per-day metrics: spend, prompt tokens, completion tokens, and API requests, broken down by model, provider, and API key.
- Per user spend: Query GET /user/info?user_id=… for a summary of a user’s total spend and the spend on each of their associated API keys.
- Portal dashboard: The Admin UI (at https://<proxy-host>/ui) includes a Usage tab where developers and admins can browse spend by model, user, and tag without hitting the API directly.
These same endpoints are how your finance team gets per-user attribution without you building custom metering infrastructure. A scheduled job hitting /user/daily/activity or /global/spend/report is enough to feed a cost dashboard or chargeback report.
Developer self-service portal
The self-service portal also handles key lifecycle processes. Developers authenticate with your corporate SSO to generate a key bound to their identity, which they can later regenerate if the key is exposed or to match a rotation policy. Platform engineers configure the budget policy once for individual developers to autonomously operate within their constraints. Two things developers use the portal for directly:
- Key generation: On the Admin UI’s Virtual Keys page (https://<proxy-host>/ui), developers authenticated through SSO choose Generate Key to create their own key, bound to their identity.
- Rate limit visibility: Each /chat/completions response includes x-litellm-key-remaining-requests-{model} and x-litellm-key-remaining-tokens-{model} headers, so developers can see their remaining RPM and TPM headroom for that model directly in their tool’s response. This is distinct from the dollar-based spend tracking earlier in this post.
Monitoring and observability
For an LLM gateway, traditional metrics like latency percentiles can be misleading, especially with extended thinking models, where a single request can take several minutes. Instead, we focus on requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM) as primary signals. Here, Amazon CloudWatch can help you monitor and alarm for these signals with the following configuration.
Amazon CloudWatch alarms for quota management
Note that the alarm configuration alerts at 60–70 percent quota utilization rather than waiting for throttling. This provides lead time to scale Amazon Bedrock quotas before users experience degradation.
Emitting the metric: LiteLLM has no built-in callback that publishes a metric named TokensPerMinute to a LiteLLM/Gateway namespace, so the alarm needs a source. A small custom-logger callback that calls CloudWatch PutMetricData on each request does the job. Register it through litellm_settings.success_callback (which is additive), not callbacks. The callbacks list replaces LiteLLM’s internal logger list, which includes the built-in spend-tracking logger, and will silently disable budget enforcement.
Here’s a minimal version of that callback, using LiteLLM’s CustomLogger class:
For prompt-level debugging, we run Langfuse alongside CloudWatch. When a developer reports “the model gave a bad response,” you can use Langfuse to inspect the exact prompt, token counts, and model parameters. For compliance-sensitive environments, Amazon Bedrock’s native invocation logging to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) provides an immutable audit trail.
Lessons learned at scale
We deployed this pattern end-to-end on a fresh AWS account to confirm the sample snippets work. In our own deployment, we scaled this LLM gateway to several hundred developers and learned several lessons.
Operational lessons
The main findings from running at scale:
- Extended thinking changes everything about latency. Requests using Claude’s extended thinking can take several minutes or longer, depending on the thinking budget. If your load balancer has a 60-second idle timeout, those requests will fail silently. To address that, you can set load balancer idle timeouts to at least 900 seconds and configure LiteLLM’s request timeout accordingly (timeout: 900 in the Step 2 configuration earlier in this post).
- When throttled, back off and retry on the same model before initiating a fallback. Our initial instinct was to fall back from Sonnet to Haiku upon throttling. But this is suboptimal for coding assistants because changing models breaks the consistent behavior developers rely on. Instead, retry the same model with exponential backoff at the proxy level (max_retries: 3 in Step 2). When a request cannot be served after retries, surface the error clearly rather than returning an alternate model’s completions.
- Separate automation tool invocations from developer traffic. continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines and automated code review tools should call Amazon Bedrock directly with their own inference profiles and quotas. Mixing automation traffic with interactive developer traffic leads to unpredictable latency and hinders meaningful cost attribution.
- Start with Global CRIS from day one, if feasible. We initially used Geographic (US) CRIS but ultimately migrated our inference profiles when we reached Regional quota limits. For our use case, we didn’t have data residency constraints so we could use Global CRIS. Global CRIS routes requests across Regions to draw on a broader capacity pool, simplifying management at scale.
Deployment considerations
Two configuration mistakes are common and hard to notice until spend or connectivity breaks:
Configuring per-model costs is mandatory for enforcing budgets. The model_info block on each model isn’t optional if you want to track per-user cost controls. When model points at an Amazon Bedrock inference-profile ARN, LiteLLM can’t look up the ARN in its built-in pricing table. It instead records $0 per token, so the max_budget and 429 throttle enforcement silently don’t trigger. Spend remains at $0 no matter how many tokens flow. Fix this by setting input_cost_per_token and output_cost_per_token (or input_cost_per_million_tokens).
Database compared to cache: The database_url must be PostgreSQL. LiteLLM’s virtual keys (/key/generate), store_model_in_db, and spend tracking are Postgres-backed.
A handful of smaller deployment details rounded out our checklist:
- Global CRIS IAM needs the foundation-model resources, not only the app-inference-profile ARN. Otherwise, invocation is denied at runtime.
- Give the Fargate task enough memory. LiteLLM’s gateway image runs out of memory and is killed at 512 MB (exit 137) before it can pass a health check. About 2 GB is a safe floor.
- Override the container entryPoint. The official image’s entrypoint is litellm. If you render a config at startup with a shell script, set entryPoint: ['/bin/sh','-c'] or your script is passed as arguments to litellm.
- IAM role and security-group descriptions must be ASCII. Em-dashes and -> arrows are rejected by IAM and Amazon EC2.
- Confirm model availability in your account and Region. Model IDs and CRIS profiles change. Verify with aws bedrock list-inference-profiles (for example, we used claude-haiku-4-5 because claude-haiku-3-5 was not available).
Clean up
This post walks through the pattern with illustrative snippets rather than a single deployable stack, there’s no one-command teardown. But the architecture relies on several resources that continue to bill while they run. These include the AWS Fargate service, Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL), Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey, and the Application Load Balancer, along with supporting Secrets Manager secrets, CloudWatch alarms, and Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles. When you finish testing, remove them to avoid ongoing charges.
If you deployed the full solution using the Guidance for Multi-Provider Generative AI Gateway on AWS, follow that solution’s cleanup instructions to remove everything it created. For AWS CDK, run cdk destroy. For AWS CloudFormation, delete the stack.
If you built the pattern yourself from the snippets in this post, remove each resource:
- AWS Fargate service and cluster: Delete the Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) service to stop and drain the tasks, then delete the cluster.
- Application Load Balancer: Delete the ALB along with its listeners and target groups.
- Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL): Delete the database instance. Take a final snapshot first only if you need to retain API key and spend data.
- Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey: Delete the replication group or cluster. It holds only cache data, so no snapshot is needed.
- Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles: Delete the profiles created in Step 3, either by removing the AWS CDK construct or by running aws bedrock delete-inference-profile.
- AWS Secrets Manager secrets: Schedule deletion of the proxy’s secrets, such as the master key and database credentials.
- Amazon CloudWatch alarms and log groups: Delete the TPM alarm and any LiteLLM log groups.
Delete the AWS Fargate service and ALB before the Amazon RDS and ElastiCache endpoints they depend on, so running tasks don’t error against removed backends during teardown.
Conclusion
In this post, we detailed a pattern for an LLM gateway that abstracts the multi-model architecture of Amazon Bedrock to provide your teams with scalable and observable self-service access. Because Amazon Bedrock routes across models through a single interface without changing infrastructure, your developers get instant access to foundation models through familiar APIs. Cost governance, observability, and a single control plane go to your engineering and security teams while finance gets per-user attribution without you building a custom metering infrastructure.
Start by working through the pattern and snippets in this post to understand how the pieces fit together. The AWS CDK snippets cover the Amazon Bedrock application inference profile, its IAM policy, and the CloudWatch alarm. The surrounding AWS Fargate service, Amazon RDS, Amazon ElastiCache, ALB, and AWS Secrets Manager resources follow standard AWS CDK patterns and aren’t shown.
When you’re ready for a complete, deployable implementation, the Guidance for Multi-Provider Generative AI Gateway on AWS closely aligns with this pattern. You can find the guide on the AWS Solutions Library with the accompanying blog post and GitHub projects. While this post stepped through the same core pattern, it focused on Amazon Bedrock for developer coding assistants. The larger solution architecture adds multi-provider support, Amazon ECS or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon CloudFront and AWS WAF options, and an admin UI.
Explore the components of this architecture with additional documentation for Amazon Bedrock Inference Profiles, LiteLLM gateway, AWS Fargate, and Langfuse.
Try this pattern in your organization. Start with a pilot team, validate the cost controls, and scale from there.

articles.title: Wenn Chefs zu viel dürfen: Was Fehlverhalten an der Spitze mit einem Unternehmen macht
articles.text:
Wenn Chefs zu viel dürfen: Was Fehlverhalten an der Spitze mit einem Unternehmen macht
Der Fall von Jensen Huang ist tief: Am Sonntag hatte der Nvidia-Chef in einer Nachricht an seine Mitarbeitenden mitgeteilt, dass er seiner Frau untreu gewesen ist. Scheinbar hatte Huang eine Affäre mit einer mutmaßlichen chinesischen Spionin, mit der Nvidia auch in Geschäftsbeziehungen stand. Zunächst kündigte Nvidia die Einleitung einer Untersuchung an, auch das FBI wurde involviert. Dann der nächste Paukenschlag: Eine zweite Affäre wurde bekannt, diesmal mit einer Nvidia-Managerin. Etwas, das Jensen Huang nun wohl endgültig zu Fall gebracht hat. Der Nvidia-Boss ist mit sofortiger Wirkung von seinem Posten zurückgetreten.

articles.title: Black Friday Amazon: 5 climatiseurs réversibles de retour en stock, pour l’hiver comme pour l’été
articles.text:
Le prix repère du gaz augmente encore de 5,8 % au 1er décembre, et les climatiseurs réversibles, qui se faisaient rares pendant les canicules de l’été, reviennent en stock sur Amazon à l’approche du Black Friday. Nous en avons retenu 5, du modèle mobile pour une chambre à la console murale pour un séjour, en regardant de près ce que chacun annonce vraiment en mode chauffage.
Cet été, les climatiseurs mobiles ont disparu des rayons à chaque vague de chaleur, au point que nous suivions leurs retours en stock d’une canicule à l’autre. Ceux qui reviennent aujourd’hui sur Amazon sont réversibles : ils rafraîchissent en été et produisent de la chaleur en hiver. Les acheter maintenant, c’est s’éviter la course aux stocks de juin prochain, et disposer dès cet hiver d’un chauffage d’appoint pour une pièce.
Côté chauffage, le contexte s’y prête : la Commission de régulation de l’énergie a relevé son prix repère du gaz de 6,6 % au 1er novembre, puis de 5,8 % au 1er décembre, à 206,26 €/MWh TTC. Un climatiseur réversible ne remplace pas une chaudière, mais il permet de chauffer une seule pièce sans monter le thermostat de tout le logement. Les prix indiqués sont ceux affichés sur Amazon le 12 novembre : il s’agit d’une disponibilité retrouvée, pas encore de remises Black Friday, à une exception près, signalée dans la liste.
5 climatiseurs réversibles de nouveau disponibles sur Amazon
- Climatiseur mobile réversible CREATE Silkair Dual Connect 9000 à 270,95 €
- Climatiseur mobile réversible MovAIR MOV16-12-BC 3,5 kW à 499,90 €
- Climatiseur monobloc mural réversible Sannover Fresho 12 HP 2,5 kW à 890,99 €
- Climatiseur mobile chaud et froid ZJUNLI à 516,21 € (15 % de réduction appliqués au passage de la commande)
- Climatiseur mobile LIFEZEAL 14 000 BTU avec chauffage à 719,99 €
VPN, logiciels, abonnements : les promos à saisir en ce moment
Chambre, séjour, grand volume : à chacun son climatiseur réversible
Ces cinq appareils n’ont ni la même puissance, ni la même installation, et leurs fiches ne sont pas toutes aussi détaillées. Point commun : aucun n’est vendu par Amazon lui-même, mais par des vendeurs tiers de sa place de marché, qui assurent aussi l’expédition. Voici ce que chacun annonce, et ce qu’il faut vérifier avant de commander.
- CREATE Silkair Dual Connect 9000 : le moins cher de la sélection vise les pièces jusqu’à 20 m², une chambre ou un studio. Il annonce 9 000 BTU en froid, une pompe à chaleur de 7 000 BTU en chaud, une déshumidification jusqu’à 42 litres par jour et un pilotage depuis l’application Create. Il est livré avec un kit pour fenêtre coulissante ; pour une fenêtre battante, le fabricant renvoie vers une autre version. Sa note moyenne de 3,3 sur 5, sur 12 avis, invite à lire les retours avant de commander.
- MovAIR MOV16-12-BC : c’est le modèle mobile dont la fiche chauffage est la plus précise : 3,20 kW en chaud avec une classe énergétique A+, 3,50 kW en froid en classe A. Il ajoute le Wi-Fi, une déshumidification de 40,8 litres par jour et un niveau sonore annoncé entre 51 et 53 dB(A). Comptez 26 kg à déplacer d’une pièce à l’autre.
- Sannover Fresho 12 HP : ce n’est pas un climatiseur mobile, mais une console monobloc qui se fixe au mur, sans unité extérieure : il faut percer deux ouvertures pour l’entrée et la sortie d’air. En échange, c’est le seul de la liste à annoncer un coefficient de performance, un COP de 3,98, en classe A+, pour 2,5 kW (9 000 BTU) et 46 dB. Supports, grilles et tuyaux sont fournis, mais la pose demande des travaux. Avec 4 sur 5 sur 27 avis, c’est aussi le mieux noté des cinq.
- ZJUNLI : sa fiche est la moins claire de la sélection. Le titre annonce 18 000 BTU en froid et 9 000 BTU en chaud, mais le lien mène à une variante intitulée « 5000 BTU », et la page ne donne ni surface conseillée, ni classe énergétique. Une réduction de 15 % s’applique au passage de la commande, et l’expédition est annoncée sous 6 à 7 jours. À réserver à ceux qui prendront le temps de vérifier la variante avant de payer.
- LIFEZEAL 14 000 BTU : avec 14 000 BTU annoncés pour des pièces jusqu’à 40 m², une oscillation automatique sur 70° et l’application Smart Life, il vise les grands séjours. Il promet un mode chauffage, mais sans puissance chiffrée, et sa fiche technique ne mentionne que le refroidissement. Pour un usage d’abord estival, il a sa logique ; pour chauffer, les fiches du MovAIR et du Sannover sont plus complètes. Amazon n’en affichait plus que 11 exemplaires le 12 novembre.
Chauffer avec un climatiseur réversible, est-ce vraiment rentable ?
Un climatiseur réversible chauffe en pompe à chaleur : il prélève des calories dans l’air et restitue plus d’énergie qu’il ne consomme d’électricité. Avec le COP de 3,98 qu’annonce le Sannover, un kilowattheure d’électricité produit près de 4 kilowattheures de chaleur. À ce rendement, la chaleur revient bien moins cher qu’avec un radiateur électrique classique, et soutient la comparaison avec le gaz, dont le prix repère moyen atteindra 206,26 €/MWh TTC au 1er décembre.
Les modèles mobiles, eux, n’annoncent pas de COP, et leur rendement en chauffage reste plus modeste : comme le rappelle notre comparatif des meilleurs climatiseurs mobiles, la dépression d’air créée par l’évacuation pénalise les monoblocs. Ils conviennent pour tempérer une chambre ou un bureau quelques heures, pas pour chauffer un logement entier. Si vous pensez d’abord à l’été prochain, ce comparatif classe aussi les modèles par usage, du plus silencieux au plus adapté aux grands espaces.
Climatiseur réversible en hiver : vos questions
Un climatiseur mobile réversible peut-il remplacer un chauffage au gaz ou au fioul ?
Non, il sert de chauffage d’appoint pour une pièce. Les modèles mobiles de cette sélection annoncent de 20 à 40 m² quand leur fiche précise une surface, et leur rendement en chauffage reste en retrait d’une pompe à chaleur fixe.
Faut-il percer un mur pour installer ces climatiseurs ?
Pas pour les quatre modèles mobiles, livrés avec un kit pour fenêtre qui fait passer le tuyau d’évacuation. Le Sannover Fresho 12 HP fait exception : cette console murale demande deux ouvertures dans le mur.
Quelle puissance choisir selon la taille de la pièce ?
Les fiches donnent un repère : 9 000 BTU pour une pièce jusqu’à 20 m² sur le CREATE, 14 000 BTU jusqu’à 40 m² sur le LIFEZEAL. Le Sannover annonce 9 000 BTU et le MovAIR 3,5 kW, soit environ 12 000 BTU, sans préciser de surface.
