articles.title: « Ramenez LE patron » : chez Nvidia, des salariés se mobilisent pour le retour de Jensen Huang — Frandroid
articles.text:
Jensen Huang a quitté Nvidia ce jeudi 12 novembre, 33 ans après avoir cofondé l’entreprise, comme nous l’expliquions lors de l’annonce. Sa directrice financière, Colette Kress, assure l’intérim. Le soir même, une troisième liaison présumée, avec une autre salariée, est venue s’ajouter aux deux déjà connues.
Jusqu’ici, on entendait surtout des soutiens à Jensen Huang depuis l’extérieur de l’entreprise, de Tim Sweeney, le patron d’Epic Games, à Elon Musk, prêt à l’embaucher. Or, à l’intérieur de Nvidia aussi, des salariés refusent ce départ et demandent au conseil d’administration de faire revenir leur fondateur. Le magazine américain Wired l’a révélé dans la nuit de jeudi à vendredi, après avoir consulté des échanges internes.
Tout part d’un message déposé dans la « boîte à idées » interne de Nvidia, l’espace où les salariés adressent leurs propositions à la direction. Un ingénieur présent depuis longtemps dans l’entreprise l’a publié avant la démission : il y demandait au conseil de tenir compte de l’avis des employés avant toute décision sur Huang.
Jouez dans les meilleures conditions avec la TV TCL P89L : une expérience gaming fluide en 144 Hz et 4K , actuellement en promotion !
Le message a depuis recueilli plus de 1 600 commentaires, en majorité favorables à son retour selon Wired, et plusieurs demandent aux administrateurs de trouver un moyen de revenir sur la décision. « Si vous croyez en la mission, ramenez LE patron », écrit l’un d’eux, quand d’autres demandent une seconde chance pour ce qu’ils appellent une erreur humaine.
Nvidia comptait environ 42 000 salariés à la fin janvier 2026. Les 1 600 commentaires ne correspondent pas forcément à autant de personnes, puisqu’un même salarié peut réagir plusieurs fois.
« Je soutiens Jensen », écrit un salarié à toute l’entreprise
Un autre employé est allé plus loin, en envoyant un email à l’ensemble de l’entreprise pour exiger de la transparence sur les raisons du départ de Huang. « Je soutiens Jensen », y écrit-il, tout en précisant qu’il ne croit pas pour autant les gens infaillibles. Il va même jusqu’à affirmer que « si l’Amérique laisse tomber l’homme qui a aidé à construire son avenir, alors ce monde ne mérite pas Jensen Huang ».
Dans les heures qui ont suivi la démission, une vingtaine de salariés ont aussi affiché leur soutien à Huang sur LinkedIn. Sur la même période, Wired n’a trouvé aucun message d’employé qui approuve son départ. Mais ce relevé se limite à LinkedIn, où l’on publie sous son vrai nom et sous les yeux de son employeur.
Un salarié arrivé il y a quelques années, qui n’est pas autorisé à s’exprimer, affirme au magazine qu’une grande partie de l’entreprise espère son retour. Ces salariés craignent que Nvidia souffre sans un fondateur qui n’a jamais installé de numéro deux ou prévu de successeur.
Un conseil de fidèles, et aucune explication
Beaucoup d’employés pensaient que le conseil irait au bout de son enquête interne avant tout grand changement. L’une des suggestions demandait même d’en partager les conclusions avec le personnel. Or les administrateurs indépendants n’avaient engagé le cabinet d’avocats Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz pour la mener que ce mardi 10 novembre, deux jours avant le départ de Huang. D’après Wired, les salariés s’en étonnent d’autant plus que ce conseil compte surtout des investisseurs historiques et des proches de longue date de leur ancien patron. Contactés par Wired, Nvidia et Harvey C. Jones, le nouveau président du conseil, n’ont pas répondu.
Pourtant, le conseil a des raisons de ne pas traîner. Le dimanche 8 novembre, Huang a lui-même reconnu dans un email avoir été « infidèle » à sa femme. Le FBI enquête sur Alice Huang, la dirigeante de Megaspeed soupçonnée de travailler pour le renseignement chinois, et des parlementaires américains réclament des comptes, ce qui fait peser sur Nvidia des risques bien au-delà de la vie privée de son patron. L’entreprise, elle, a perdu environ 1 760 milliards de dollars de valeur boursière depuis son record du 6 octobre, dont près de 500 milliards de dollars sur la seule semaine du scandale.
De son côté, Huang a accepté d’être entendu à huis clos par trois commissions de la Chambre des représentants d’ici Thanksgiving, le 26 novembre, mais aucune date n’est encore fixée. Le conseil d’administration cherche toujours un successeur permanent, sans avoir donné de calendrier.

articles.title: Fracasa la segunda negociación sobre vivienda en Valencia y provoca la retirada de la acampada
articles.text:
La acampada por la vivienda de Valencia termina hoy. Después de 40 días, sus integrantes ya están retirando las tiendas de la plaza del Ayuntamiento. El motivo inmediato es que la segunda mesa con las administraciones, que exigían como condición para irse, no salió adelante. Entre tanto dime y direte, esta es la secuencia completa de hechos y las versiones enfrentadas.
Cómo empezó. Como ya documentamos, el 3 de octubre hubo manifestaciones por la vivienda en unas 50 ciudades. En Valencia la marcha acabó con cargas policiales ante el Palau de les Arts, donde se celebraba un congreso inmobiliario. Esa misma tarde, parte de los manifestantes montó tiendas en la plaza del Ayuntamiento. La idea copiaba la acampada de Sol, activa desde el 26 de septiembre y que finalizó el 3 de noviembre.
Cuántos eran. Depende de quién cuente y de qué día, como pasa siempre: en Puerta del Sol algunos decían que había 200 personas y otros que 2000. Según se estima, el 12 de octubre había más de 400 tiendas. Cuatro días después, el portavoz municipal hablaba de más de 700. El 3 de noviembre, otra cuenta daba más de 600. En este particular no existe un censo común y conviene recordar que una tienda no equivale a una persona. Puede ser una pareja y hasta un grupo de amigos o familiares.
Qué pedían. Dos cosas: que Valencia se declare zona tensionada, para poder limitar los alquileres de una vez por todas. Por otro otro lado, una mesa para que se sentaran los portavoces de Ayuntamiento, Generalitat y Delegación del Gobierno. La alcaldesa, María José Catalá, remitió lo primero al Pleno municipal. La Delegación, con Pilar Bernabé y después con Roger Llanes, descartó desalojar. Llanes justificó que en Valencia las “dinámicas” eran distintas a las de Sol.
Cinco fechas clave:
- 5 de noviembre: primera mesa, de carácter técnico. Duró más de tres horas. Los acampados habían citado a la alcaldesa, al delegado y a la consellera de Vivienda. Acudieron perfiles técnicos.
- 9 de noviembre: la acampada anunció una desescalada progresiva: menos espacio y fuera las tiendas vacías. Quería dejar sitio a la pista de hielo, el tiovivo y el árbol de Navidad. Ese mismo día, Ayuntamiento y Subdelegación del Gobierno mantuvieron una reunión técnica en la que concluyeron que la continuidad de la protesta era incompatible con la seguridad ciudadana y con el montaje de las instalaciones navideñas. La conclusión se apoyaba en informes de la Policía Local.
- 10 de noviembre: los acampados dijeron haber cumplido su parte y exigieron una segunda mesa para el jueves. Catalá respondió que “ya es momento de darle fin”. Llanes no fijó fecha límite para marcharse, aunque aseguró que las condiciones para la retirada avanzaban “a pasos agigantados”, si bien sonó especialmente jactancioso.
- 11 de noviembre: y llegamos a la huelga general por la vivienda. En la Comunitat Valenciana, el seguimiento fue aproximadamente del 60% según los sindicatos y del 2,5% según la patronal. Esa tarde, la policía cargó junto a la plaza contra varios viandantes, al final de una marcha de la CGT, si bien no hubo incidentes graves.
- 12 de noviembre. La segunda mesa no se celebró, así que la acampada anunció la retirada y comenzó a desmontar las tiendas durante la mañana.
Dos versiones del mismo final. Los acampados dicen que Delegación les trasladó el miércoles que no podía reunirse con ellos y que debían irse “inmediatamente”. Lograron retrasarlo un día para recoger de forma ordenada. Según su portavoz, la alternativa era la fuerza: “o desacampamos o nos enfrentamos a un desalojo forzoso”. La Delegación niega haber dado plazo alguno.
Catalá lo ve de otro modo: recuperar la plaza es, dijo, una buena noticia, y no hay negociación con quien presiona por la fuerza. El Ayuntamiento ya programó la limpieza y la retirada del vallado (están ahora en ello, de hecho). Ayer se escuchaba a más de un manifestante preguntar que desde cuándo la campaña de Navidad es más relevante que escuchar los derechos de la ciudadanía.
Limpieza responsable. Además, los acampados quieren dejar la plaza como la encontraron y donar los materiales que todavía puedan aprovechar otras personas. Hoy terminarán de desalojar, limpiar el espacio y devolverlo a su estado anterior. En su comunicado insisten en que la seguridad de quienes han participado y la no violencia han sido prioridades durante los 40 días de protesta. Su mensaje de despedida, según elDiario.es, es: “Nos levantamos, pero no renunciamos a nada”.
¿Y ahora? Es obvio que Valencia se desmarcó de Madrid a principios de noviembre. Allí, Sol acabó con el desalojo de 334 personas y el traslado de la protesta a los barrios. Valencia aguantó otra semana y termina sin bomberos, pero también sin la mesa que pedía. Serán en las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre donde se hablará mediante el voto. Entretanto, el Gobierno ya ha sacado adelante su decreto de vivienda a través de la Diputación Permanente.

articles.title: Chicago schools tell Google they'd rather lose Search than be forced to accept AI
articles.text:
Ripple effect: Not long after Google announced its definitely-not-petulant response to schools banning its AI services by threatening to remove its search engine completely, Chicago Public Schools has said it will simply use a different search solution. Google's actions have also led to protests against the company, with demonstrators chanting the catchy slogan, "Hey Google, nice try. We don't want your Gemini."
At the start of November, Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager for education, said K-12 schools will soon have to accept the company's AI services to retain student access to its search engine. The reason, he claimed, was that Search and AI are now deeply integrated services. Instead of the usual results, students will see a message from their school stating that the services are not available.
A lot of people didn't take this well, claiming Google was essentially blackmailing schools into using a service they didn't want. Chalkbeat Chicago reports that it led to protests in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and in Chicago, where the city's school district recently blocked student access to generative AI tools such as Gemini.
Chicago Public Schools (CPS) has yet to respond to Google's announcement, but a CPS spokesperson said in a statement that the district was "actively exploring all options to independently suppress" the AI Overviews that appears at the top of Google searches. The spokesperson added that if CPS cannot provide students access to Google's search engine without its AI feature, the district will "look to other search solutions."
It's not just CPS that's unhappy about Google's behavior. About 30 protesters, including parents, educators, and students, demonstrated outside Google's office in Chicago's West Loop.
"We are owed lessons and feedback from the people CPS hired, people who are passionate and dedicated to making learning fun," said Reese Mackey, a junior at Kenwood Academy High School. "Not by a bot whose only job is to be a yes man and compile random sources from the internet for a nonsensical answer."
A Google spokesperson said the company was working to improve Search for classroom use, including testing its "Guided Learning" feature, which uses AI to guide students through problems one step at a time instead of simply giving them answers.
Chicago is far from alone in pushing back. In October, Frederick County's school board voted 6 – 1 to restrict student AI use from pre-K through 12th grade, just weeks after allowing older students to try Gemini with teacher permission. Board members raised concerns about the lack of warning to parents and teachers' inability to disable the tool on student devices. Exceptions remain for lessons about AI and accommodations for students with disabilities.
New York City also introduced a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI from preschool through eighth grade for the 2026 – 2027 school year. High school use is limited to approved tools in supervised pilot or career-readiness programs, while Los Angeles has temporarily blocked generative AI tools on student devices across all grades.
Google faces an uphill battle to convince schools that using AI is the way forward for students, but threatening to remove search from those who say no is hardly going to help convince them otherwise.

articles.title: Google's Gemini 4 coding agent now switches models mid-task — and finishes 19% faster
articles.text:
Google’s Gemini 4 coding agent now switches models mid-task — and finishes 19% faster
Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen on Thursday alongside a new system that changes how coding agents use AI models. Rather than keeping its most capable model running across an entire session, Google is pairing Hydrogen with the more powerful Gemini 4 Carbon and switching between the two as the work progresses.
The company says the combination gets nearly the same results as running Carbon on its own while using 24% less quota and finishing tasks 19% faster.
How Orchestrator handles the work
The switching runs through Orchestrator, a new feature in Google’s Antigravity development environment, where Carbon takes on the more demanding reasoning, including architecture and debugging, while Hydrogen handles code changes and testing.
Carbon might work through a repository to figure out how to implement a feature and then hand the actual coding to Hydrogen, stepping back in when a failing test calls for rethinking the approach before passing execution back.
Clement Farabet, VP, AI engineering at Google DeepMind, calls the combination “a huge unlock for agentic coding” in a post on X. 
Varun Mohan, who leads Google’s Antigravity team, says in a separate post that pairing Hydrogen with Orchestrator and swarms has become “very popular internally.”
Where Google’s numbers don’t match
Google’s own benchmark reporting doesn’t quite line up, since the main Gemini announcement cites Terminal-Bench 4.0 while the Antigravity announcement references version 4.1.
The company also hasn’t published Carbon’s standalone success rate, a per-task breakdown or enough detail about Orchestrator’s routing decisions to show where the reported efficiency gains actually come from.
…hasn’t published Carbon’s standalone success rate… or enough detail about Orchestrator’s routing decisions to show where the reported efficiency gains actually come from.
Hydrogen outscores a pricier model
Google describes Hydrogen as a “daily driver for agentic workflows,” and it costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, with those rates holding across its full million-token context window.
The model is available through Google AI Studio and the Gemini API, as well as the Gemini app and Google Search.
On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Hydrogen scores 51 at its default high thinking level, just ahead of the more expensive Gemini 4 Argon at 50. Turning the reasoning effort up to Google’s new xhigh setting brings Hydrogen’s score to 54, although the additional reasoning can increase token consumption and processing time.
Argon was Google’s flagship when it launched on September 30, but Gemini 4 Carbon surpassed it on most published benchmarks following its October 28 release. Hydrogen’s one-point lead is modest, but it’s another sign of how quickly Google’s lower-cost models are catching up with what passed for frontier performance just weeks ago.
Google also claims Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash at the default setting, with its Terminal-Bench 4.1 score reaching 57% against Flash’s 18.2%. The company reports more than a fivefold reduction in fabricated claims.
Hydrogen’s one-point lead is modest, but it’s another sign of how quickly Google’s lower-cost models are catching up…
The cost of switching models
Google hasn’t disclosed how Orchestrator decides when to switch models or what those handoffs cost in additional tokens and latency.
For now, Orchestrator is limited to Google AI Ultra subscribers, with support for more models and subscription tiers planned. Hydrogen is rolling out to paid Antigravity users, with broader availability expected.

articles.title: Netflix releases new trailer for Ray Gunn
articles.text:
We caught the first trailer for the upcoming Netflix animated film Ray Gunn in September and were charmed by director Brad Bird’s blend of a Jetsons-like future with classic 1930s noir detective thrillers. Bird has described it as a mashup of The Maltese Falcon and Buck Rogers, and the latest trailer definitely gives off that energy.
As previously reported, Bird has directed some of our all-time favorite animated films: The Iron Giant (1999), The Incredibles (2004), and Ratatouille (2007), with the latter two snagging well-deserved Oscar wins. He’s been kicking around the idea for Ray Gunn for the last 30 years, working on his many other film projects while the Ray Gunn script—co-written by Matthew Robbins, who also co-wrote 1987’s Batteries Not Included with Bird—“stayed in a filing cabinet at Warner Brothers,” the director said earlier this year.
The film’s inspiration came when Bird heard the opening of the B-52s’ “Planet Claire” (a personal favorite that also provides the soundtrack to the new trailer) and initially thought it was a cover of Henry Mancini’s theme music from the classic TV show Peter Gunn. Bird is a longtime fan of film noir and hard-boiled detectives, and he came up with the idea of a futuristic detective named Ray Gunn (a play on “raygun,” of course). “It’s film noir and a hard-boiled detective story, but it’s got a lot more comedy and a lot more action than the average film noir,” said Bird.

articles.title: Trump pide a Tim Cook como CEO de NVIDIA tras la renuncia de Jensen Huang: "Una leyenda por otra leyenda"
articles.text:
La renuncia de Jensen Huang como CEO de NVIDIA es, sin dudas, el tema del día. El escándalo por infidelidades le ha costado al empresario el puesto que ostentó durante los últimos 33 años, y el asunto promete seguir dando que hablar por bastante tiempo. Lo más curioso es que todos tienen una opinión sobre el tema y hasta Donald Trump ha propuesto a un reemplazante de alto perfil: Tim Cook.
En las horas posteriores a la salida de Jensen Huang, Trump usó su perfil en Truth Social para postular a Cook como próximo CEO de NVIDIA. De acuerdo con el presidente de Estados Unidos, el exCEO de Apple es la única persona que tiene lo necesario para hacerse cargo de un rol tan complejo.
A sabiendas de cómo piensa y actúa Donald Trump, no quedan dudas de que el mandatario estadounidense habla en serio. Claro que hoy parece improbable que Tim Cook esté dispuesto a asumir un rol tan notorio fuera de Apple, en especial por lo repentino y desastroso del desenlace de Jensen Huang.
"Ahora que el CEO de NVIDIA, Jensen Huang, quien ha hecho un trabajo fantástico, ha renunciado, solo hay un hombre capaz de tomar su lugar: Tim Cook, de Apple. ¡Una leyenda reemplaza a otra leyenda! Presidente Donald J. Trump", publicó el presidente de Estados Unidos.
Donald Trump quiere a Tim Cook como reemplazante de Jensen Huang en NVIDIA
Más allá de las virtudes de Jensen Huang y Tim Cook para conducir durante gran cantidad de años (y con gran éxito) a sus respectivas empresas, Trump no ofrece detalles de por qué el exjefe de Apple debería reemplazar a su antiguo colega en NVIDIA. Tal vez solo sea porque Cook ha sabido congraciarse con el presidente estadounidense durante sus mandatos, tal y como lo hizo Huang en su momento.
Sea como sea, todavía no se sabe quién reemplazará definitivamente a Jensen Huang. Colette Kress, la jefa de finanzas de NVIDIA, fungirá de CEO interina hasta que se designe a un nuevo responsable del cargo. La junta del gigante verde anunció la puesta en marcha de un proceso de búsqueda de nuevo consejero delegado, para la cual analizará a candidatos internos y externos. Asimismo, se ha designado a Harvey C. Jones como presidente del board, el primero en ocupar ese rol en la historia de la compañía.
¿Tiene posibilidades Tim Cook de ser el próximo CEO de NVIDIA? Hasta hace menos de 15 días, era inaudito pensar en dicha empresa sin Jensen Huang como jefe, pero ya hemos visto que los imposibles no existen y que no se puede descartar nada. Dicho esto, Cook se encuentra extremadamente cómodo en su nuevo rol como presidente ejecutivo de Apple.
Además, no es un directivo enfocado en producto como sí lo fue Jensen Huang; algo que podría no importar en cualquier otra empresa, pero que ha sido crucial para el crecimiento de NVIDIA bajo el comando de un único CEO en sus 33 años de vida. Ya veremos qué novedades surgen en tal sentido.

articles.title: I reviewed the new Apple TV 4K (4th Gen) as a long-time Apple TV fan — and Siri AI is very, very far from justifying this new high price
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Apple TV 4K (4th Gen) has very little meaningful improvement over the model from four years ago, yet the minimum price has doubled. It remains the best streaming device for those with lots of Apple devices, or those who care about data privacy — but its price now feels less proportionate to its advantages, and it hasn't kept up with the rest of the world in areas such as game streaming. The new remote that emits a noise is genuinely useful, but Siri AI is far too inconsistent to be useful upgrade.
- 
Features Excellent format support and great Apple integration, but no game streaming and half-baked Siri AI are disappointing.
- 
Performance Best-in-class video quality, and general performance in the OS is as slick as it gets for streaming boxes.
- 
Design A nice small box and hardy aluminum remote, though the latter is maybe too simple in places. Not everyone will love the built-in mics.
- 
Value The difference in quality and features between this and a cheaper streaming stick is not easy to justify, even it does bring better privacy.
Reasons to buy
- + Excellent picture quality and format support
- + Features such as instantly entering passwords from your phone are great
- + New findable remote is useful
Reasons to avoid
- - The new price is hard to justify
- - Siri AI is inconsistent and not smart enough even at its best
- - Integrated mics will put off some people
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Apple TV 4K (4th Gen) review
The Apple TV 4K (2026) has been a strange product to review. I’ve been an Apple TV user since the Apple TV 3rd Gen, released in 2012 — in over a decade of sticking with it, I upgraded to the first 4K version, and the 2021 4K version with the better remote. I skipped the Apple TV 4K 2022 version, since the upgrades were minimal.
Despite this, I still recommended that version wholeheartedly to people buying for the first time, for the same reason that home theater enthusiasts online have recommended it. Its picture quality is best-in-class, its format support is excellent, and it offers more privacy protection (and an ad-free home screen) than its rivals from the likes of Roku, Amazon and Google — even though it’s more expensive than those models. The premium was worth paying.
But the premium has changed. The 2022 model launched at $129 / £149 / AU$219 as the starting price. In the middle of 2026, the price rose to $199 / £249 / AU$399. Now the new model is $299 / £299 / AU$449.
This is compared to $84.99 / £99.99 / AU$149 for the Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Max, which has also had a price rise this year. The two products have basically the same format support, too.
I should mention here that the Nvidia Shield Pro is also now $299, but has much older tech in it than that this new Apple TV 4K. So the new model isn't bad value compared to the most direct competitor, the question is whether anyone really wants to pay this much for what's on offer from either of these compared to the cheaper equivalents.
Let's address it bluntly. Is the Apple TV 4K worth its higher price for upgraders from previous 4K models? Short answer: no.
Is it worth its higher price if you’re new to Apple TV boxes? Only if you care a lot about image quality and privacy.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Let’s start with the basics. The box runs tvOS, which is software specific to these devices, and is a spin-off from the iOS software used on iPhones. As a result, the Apple TV 4K is more versatile than most other streaming boxes. Yes, you have all the big streaming apps, but you also have practical apps that might be useful for some people — though obviously 99% of people will be focused on streaming.
The Apple TV 4K (2026) also supports games, in the sense that it works like a mini console, and you can connect games controllers to it (including the official PlayStation and Xbox controllers). This all works well enough, and there are some pretty decent games on there… though there are no game streaming services, due to restrictions in Apple’s policies, and I think this is a huge miss here in 2026.
We didn’t mind this too much when Apple released the last version, but cloud gaming has only grown in that time — and with the price of consoles and PCs spiking too, it’s becoming an increasingly tempting option.
It’s one of the slicker bits of streaming software in terms of performance, opening apps super-quickly and generally feeling perfectly smooth to move around. It does have its foibles — rearranging apps is theoretically an intuitive process, and yet suddenly this is where performance became less predictable. But I would say it’s generally the least annoying of the streaming systems.
That’s partly because it doesn’t have the same aggressive advertising right on the home screen that all the other platforms do. When you highlight a particular app, it might show recommendations from the app at the top of the screen, but you never have shows pushed on the home screen unless you’re already hovering over the app.
Apple also has, predictably, included some excellent integrations with its own products. The most useful is easily the ability to share passwords saved on your iPhone's Passwords app instantly with the Apple TV when you try to log into a service or app, though the ability to your iPhone's on-screen keyboard to search or type information in is also excellent.
There are lots of other integrations as well, some of which will be more useful than others to individuals. You can see your iCloud photos and use them as a screensaver (though the Apple TV's beautiful built-in screensavers are one of its highlights). You can use your iPhone for FaceTime calls, where you see other people on the big screen, and your iPhone camera beams your image over to the TV and then to the person you're calling. You can beam audio or video over to the box from your phone using AirPlay.
The remote that comes with the latest Apple TV is relatively easy to use. You don’t have lots of buttons for directly launching streaming services, for better or worse — this is, let’s be clear, a form of advertising of its own, but it’s one that can be pretty useful. That said, there is a button that looks like a TV, and pressing this once launches the Apple TV app, which includes the Apple TV streaming service’s wares — but it’s also a hub for things you’ve been watching in other services, so it’s not purely a play to get you to watch Apple’s own stuff.
Unfortunately, the Apple TV hub doesn’t work with every major streaming app, with Netflix being the most egregious omission. Netflix also doesn’t work with Siri’s ability to play movies or the universal search function. So it’s possible to ask Siri to find a particular movie, the system will tell you which of your apps have it so you can watch it right away… except you have to check Netflix separately.
There’s a button on the side of the remote to invoke Siri if you want to use your voice to find and control things, but Apple has now also added microphones to the Apple TV box itself, so you can — in theory — use the device hands-free. Just say ‘Siri’ and ask what you want to ask.
And the reason Apple has included these new mics is because Siri has now been upgraded to Siri AI, and the company is surely hoping you’ll want to use Siri way more now that it’s smart. The problem is that while Siri itself may have become smart, its implementation often still isn’t.
The most obvious gripe for me was the information presentation, and the density of that information. Sometimes it’s too crowded, packing paragraphs of information with no formatting to aid readability into a small window on the side of the screen. At other times, it’s too simple, taking over the full screen yet displaying text so large that only a few words fit in before the cut off (and if you click the remote hoping it will open the rest of the text, it doesn’t — a different part of the screen is selected by default). It’s always too much or not enough, and it’s somehow never just right.
How smart Siri is at recognizing things within a movie/show is really variable. This might be tied to whether the default tvOS player is used by the app, because in some of them I’d ask Siri a question about what I’m looking at, and it would claim there’s a blank screen.
Watching Netflix, it told me it couldn’t see what I was viewing, and asked me to just tell it the name of the movie — but if I paused it, causing the name to appear on screen, and asked the same question, it was now able to see the title. A system that responds so differently per-app is not really a reliable system.
I asked it to identify the music playing in the background of a scene of Tony on Prime Video, and it claimed the song was… the movie Tony on Prime Video. I asked it who the guy on the screen was, and it recognized Dominic Sessa, bringing up info about his work. Then I asked the same question when Stavros Halkia was on screen, and it brought up info about Dominic Sessa again.
It worked better when I watched a documentary about chefs, and the system was able to identify Marco Pierre White instantly when I asked — but that was on a service that used the native player, so I don’t know if that helps Siri have better visibility of what’s on-screen.
Later, I asked the system to show me some good Jason Statham movies available on the streaming services I have. It was able to suggest some movies on the services I have, but there was no visible info on how they were rated, even though the results took up the whole screen. So I asked a follow up question about whether any of them were actually worth watching, and then it showed movies it considered to be good, but not whether they’re available on my services. So I asked a third time if any of these good movies were available on my services, and it finally narrowed down to a list of what I originally asked… except the first movie on the list wasn’t accessible on any of my streaming apps.
I browsed to The Pelican Brief’s page on Netflix, and I asked if I would like this movie. I thought maybe it would use the fact that I own a lot of ’90s thrillers — including Grisham thrillers The Firm and The Rainmaker — in my Apple TV Store library to make a recommendation.
Instead, it gave me an OK text-based answer about what people generally think of the movie, presented in the dullest way possible as just a column of text. I really hoped it might do something clever here, because not only do I own movies like the ones mentioned above, but I also own The Pelican Brief. So it was a trick question, but I really thought a smarter system would be able to spot that I might like a movie that I went to the trouble to buy already.
One thing it pointed out in its description of whether I might like it is that some people think the movie is overlong. So I asked for similar but shorter movies available on all my services, and it gave me exactly two middlingly reviewed options. I own Witness in my Apple TV library, so couldn’t it pull that recommendation out for someone looking at an on-the-run potboiler thriller lasting under two hours?
Incidentally, it offers source citations for answers, but you can’t open them to check if it’s actually pulled correct information from the pages. It’s an attempt at being reassuring, but I have witnessed LLM answers cite a source where the source says something totally different to the answer, so I personally see little use in citing a source I can’t click to verify.
Another challenge: I asked Siri which episode of Taskmaster has Ed Gamble melting down over transporting some ducks in the garden. It identified the episode. It didn’t offer to play it, so I prostrated myself and asked if we could watch it, please. It fired up the relevant app and played… the most recent episode, not the correct one. That could be an issue with the app rather than Siri AI, but the result is a failure either way.
I tried the same thing with another show I thought might work better, because I owned it in my Apple TV library. I asked which episode of 30 Rock had a particular quote from Alec Baldwin (which I got slightly wrong). While it identified the episode correctly, yet again it didn’t consider whether maybe I’d like to watch it. So again I asked to play it, and this time it took me to the correct episode, presumably because it has better access to individual episode data, given I own them within the Apple TV app. But also, it didn’t automatically play it even though that's what I'd asked; I still needed to click to play it. So if I’m trying to do all of this hands-free with the new mics on the box, without touching the remote, it was a failure.
Ultimately, Siri still feels half-baked on Apple TV. It’s just that now it’s a much more elaborate type of bread that’s been half-baked. And sure, it’s technically in beta still, so Apple might say it should be no surprise that it’s been half-baked — but what are we paying so much more for the elaborate chip inside the new Apple TV 4K for, if not the AI powers? It’s not like the movies play any differently.
I know that the mics that are always listening will be contentious with people. And while it’s possible to turn this functionality off in the settings, there’s nothing like the switch Sonos has on its products that electronically disconnects the mics so they literally cannot hear any more — it’s just a software change, which won’t reassure everyone.
However, the built-in mics are useful for one of the few truly notable new tricks of this Apple TV, which is that you can now use these hands-free mics to ask Siri to find your remote when it’s lost. The remote will make a noise, saving you from hunting in vain.
Crucially, this even works while the Apple TV 4K is in standby mode — you don’t get any sign from the box itself that it’s heard you (I thought maybe its little white light might flash). But sure enough I asked “Siri, where’s the remote” while my whole system was off, and it started chirping from under a cushion.
I mentioned early on that image quality is one of the most important elements that draws enthusiasts to the Apple TV, and that’s for a few reasons. One is its support for both Dolby Vision and HDR10+ advanced HDR formats, not to mention the HDR10 and HLG standard formats.
It can also change formats on the fly, including switching to 24fps output for movies, so that you get more natural movie motion, especially if you have a 120Hz TV.
But it also has excellent upscaling of lower-resolution content, better than the vast majority of TVs people own at home. The latest flagship TVs with good neural-network-based upscaling might beat it, but there’s also a lot more mediocre ‘AI upscaling’ in TVs — the Apple TV takes non-4K content and makes it look naturally sharp, consistently, without looking like it’s been messed with.
On top of this, the other factor is that the Apple TV movie store offers basically the highest-quality streaming you can get outside of expensive specialist services such as Kaleidescape. These moves come at a higher bitrate (meaning the amount of data transferred per second) than anything like Netflix or Disney+ offers, so they look cleaner and more detailed, especially in scenes with lots of motion.
And while you can buy movies from the Apple TV store on other devices, the highest bitrate quality is reserved for Apple TV 4K boxes only — and the movies look fantastic. It’s a big part of why I use them to this day. The problem is that these movies look exactly the same as they do on the previous 4K model, which was less than half the price at launch.
So let’s talk about whether there’s really anything here for upgraders. I already said I think there basically isn’t, but I should at least show my working. When it comes to picture and sound performance, there are no meaningful changes.
Even if I thought Siri AI was a great upgrade, it is coming to the last two generations of Apple TV 4K too, so that isn't a reason in itself. Some people obviously might like the hands-free mics, and the remote that can play a noise so you can find it. The latter is a truly useful upgrade; it just isn’t worth the price if you have one of the previous models.
The new model does have faster Wi-Fi. Again that doesn’t mean much in itself, but it appears to have enabled this version to support a full surround system using HomePods for the first time (seemingly due to lower latency in the wireless tech, based on what Apple's said about it).
You can have four HomePod or HomePod Mini 2nd Gen speakers (two at the front, two at the back), or two HomePod 2nd Gen (at the front) and two HomePod mini 2nd Gen (at the rear). Because these are separate products, I’m not going to factor them into reviewing the Apple TV 4K — however, I have been very impressed with the HomePod 2nd Gen as TV speakers with Apple TV in the past.
The price of getting a setup like these used to be highly competitive too, though after HomePod price rises they’re a little more middle of the pack compared to wireless home theater speaker options from the likes of Hisense and Sonos.
Ultimately, I'm dropping our score for this model to 3.5 stars from 4.5 stars for its predecessor, and it all comes down to value. Yes, prices are rising everywhere, but I think this Apple TV box has simply fallen outside of the point where I can argue that it's good value despite being more expensive than the competition.
If the money is no problem to you, I strong recommend it. But compared to the Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Max, is the extra privacy and slick Apple integration worth an extra

articles.title: Suspected Chinese spy at center of Jensen Huang affair surfaces in Beijing — Alice Huang last spotted heading to Shanghai after being detained, questioned in Singapore in 2025, allegedly helped China smuggle hundreds of thousands of banned H100 and H200 chips
articles.text:
Suspected Chinese spy at center of Jensen Huang affair surfaces in Beijing — Alice Huang last spotted heading to Shanghai after being detained, questioned in Singapore in 2025, allegedly helped China smuggle hundreds of thousands of banned chips
It's still unclear why Alice Huang is in Beijing.
Alice Huang, the person allegedly involved in an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, has reportedly surfaced in Beijing, marking the first sighting of the Megaspeed executive since the scandal broke out. According to Bloomberg, it’s unclear when the suspected Chinese spy arrived in the capital or why she’s in the area, but she was last spotted leaving Singapore for Shanghai in 2025 after she was detained and questioned during the city-state’s investigation into the $2-billion smuggling case involving Megaspeed.
The Nvidia CEO is now under intense scrutiny after the revelation of his indiscretion with the Megaspeed executive, with Congress threatening to issue a subpoena if he does not respond to their invitation to “a joint, closed-door briefing” with the heads of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence. The FBI is also looking into the relationship between the head of the largest AI hardware company in the world and a person suspected of helping sanctioned Chinese companies secure hundreds of thousands of banned H100 and H200 chips. Overnight, a second bombshell report claims that Jensen Huang was also involved in an extramarital affair with Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell.
Although the Chinese embassy in Washington has denied any links to Alice Huang, calling it nothing but “groundless smears and slanders” against Beijing, there is speculation that she’s under the control of the Ministry of State Security (MSS), which is the primary agency that handles China’s foreign intelligence and counterintelligence operations. The U.S. intelligence community suggests that she may be passing on information to the MSS, but it remains unclear if she was specifically tasked by Chinese intelligence to target Jensen Huang or if they were only leveraging her relationship with the Nvidia chief to get insights into the U.S. AI industry.
A deeper investigation into Alice Huang, known by her Chinese name as Huang Le, revealed that she supposedly worked in media before jumping into banking and finance. The Wall Street Journal reports that it’s unclear when she met her husband, Kang Wei, but the couple ran a private equity and investment management firm called Shanghai Hexi in 2016. This allowed the couple to invest in companies across industries, including gaming, pharmaceuticals, and, eventually, data centers and cloud computing.
The couple is known for riding trends and isn’t a stranger to scandals. Their firm, Shanghai Hexi, invested in gaming companies in the 2010s, especially when mobile gaming started to boom across the world, while Chinese regulators fined Kang and the company in 2018 for disclosure failures and other violations while it was in the midst of a takeover battle for a corporation. Kang’s moves in the gaming industry are what allowed him to meet Jensen Huang, which eventually led to a close relationship between the couple and the Nvidia chief. Sources told the WSJ that Kang apparently accepted Alice and Jensen’s extra-marital relationship, even sometimes jokingly telling people that she was Jensen’s “personal assistant.”
It seems that the couple is used to leveraging their relationships to gain business advantage, and with investments in AI data centers expected to hit $32 trillion by 2050, Alice Huang’s “close” relationship with Jensen Huang put Shanghai Hexi in an excellent position to take advantage of the trend through Megaspeed and make big money. And with U.S. sanctions making it harder for competitors to acquire Nvidia chips, it appears that their access has turned into a gold mine for the company. But whether Alice Huang acted solely out of business interest with the supposed procurement of Nvidia chips or was leveraged by Chinese authorities to import these chips, the fact remains that $7.5 billion worth of banned chips reportedly made their way into China despite Washington’s efforts.

articles.title: Widespread Microsoft outage takes down Outlook, Teams and more
articles.text:
A major Microsoft outage has left several of the company’s apps out of service.
On Downdetector, more than 140,000 North American users have reported issues with Outlook alone, with many other users noting difficulties with other Microsoft services like Teams and Copilot.
In a thread on X (Twitter), Microsoft’s official support page confirmed Microsoft 365 service may be disrupted “in any region” and said it’s “aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact.” The company didn’t provide a timeline for when the outages may be resolved, but in a subsequent post in the thread, it noted that the “elevated load isn’t driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure.”
We’ll update this story once we get further updates from Microsoft. For now, though, just know that you’re far from alone in having any issues with with Microsoft services right now.
Update: 12/11/2026 at 8:56 p.m. ET — Microsoft has said service has been returning for some users but issues persist for many others.

articles.title: Google erweitert Android Auto mit Gemini – doch die meisten Smartphones gehen leer aus
articles.text:
Android Auto: Warum Googles neue Gemini-Funktion die meisten Smartphones ausschließt
Google erweitert sein System Android Auto, das Inhalte eines gekoppelten Smartphones auf dem eingebauten Bildschirm im Fahrzeug darstellt, um sogenannte proaktive Vorschläge. Wie Karthik Thirumalai, Product Director für Android-KI, im Firmenblog mitteilt, basiert die Erweiterung auf der Programmsammlung Gemini Intelligence und setzt ein kompatibles Pixel-Smartphone voraus.
Im Unterschied zur bisherigen Sprachsteuerung wartet die Software im Fahrzeug dabei nicht mehr darauf, dass Autofahrer:innen einen Befehl einsprechen, sondern verknüpft im Hintergrund selbstständig Daten aus verschiedenen Anwendungen. Fragt beispielsweise ein Kontakt per Textnachricht nach dem Treffpunkt für einen Pilates-Kurs, sucht das System die Adresse aus der zugehörigen Bestätigungs-E-Mail in Gmail heraus und blendet auf dem Autodisplay eine Schaltfläche ein, um die Ortsangabe mit einem Fingertipp zu versenden.
Gemini Intelligence in Android Auto: Exklusivität für Pixel 10 und Pixel 11
Mit dem aktuellen November-Update schaltet der Hersteller die Programmsammlung Gemini Intelligence, die lokale Berechnungen der künstlichen Intelligenz (KI) auf dem Gerät mit Cloud-Verarbeitung kombiniert, erstmals für die Hauptmodelle der Pixel-10-Reihe frei. Damit beschränkt sich die angekündigte Funktion für Android Auto laut Googles Support-Dokumentation auf diese Smartphones sowie auf die bereits im Sommer eingeführte Pixel-11-Generation.
Ausgenommen davon sind das Mittelklasse-Modell Pixel 10a sowie ältere Baureihen wie das Pixel 9, die aufgrund der Hardware-Anforderungen von mindestens zwölf Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher und einem entsprechenden Hauptprozessor außen vor bleiben.
Wie Android Authority berichtet, seien zudem Smartphones anderer Hersteller von der Funktion in Android Auto ausgeschlossen, obwohl Gemini Intelligence grundsätzlich auch auf Samsungs Galaxy-S26-Reihe, dem Galaxy Z Fold8 und Z Flip8 sowie künftig auf dem Modell Signature 27 von Motorola laufe.
Unterschied zu Personal Intelligence und Zugriff auf persönliche Daten
Die nun angekündigte „Proaktive Unterstützung“ geht über die im Oktober für Android Auto eingeführte Funktion „Personal Intelligence“ hinaus, über die wir bereits berichteten. Während „Personal Intelligence“ eine Schnittstelle bildet, über die der Assistent auf ausdrückliche Sprachabfrage hin Informationen aus Diensten wie Google Kalender, Google Maps oder Google Fotos abruft, analysiert die proaktive Variante laufend eingehende Benachrichtigungen und Bildschirminhalte ohne vorherige Aufforderung.
Für diesen automatisierten Abgleich benötigt die Software weitreichende Zugriffsrechte auf private Kommunikationsdaten wie E-Mails, Standortinformationen und Kurznachrichten in Google Messages. Google stuft die Funktion daher als Opt-in-Verfahren ein, das volljährige Kontoinhaber:innen erst manuell in den Einstellungen der Gemini-App aktivieren müssen, und gibt an, die Daten in isolierten Bereichen zu verarbeiten, auf die weder das Unternehmen selbst noch Drittanbieter-Apps Zugriff hätten, solange ein Vorschlag nicht angetippt wird.
Verfügbarkeit in Deutschland und Neuerungen im November-Update
Einen konkreten Termin für die Auslieferung der proaktiven Vorschläge in Android Auto nennt Google bislang nicht, zudem greifen geografische und sprachliche Einschränkungen. Laut der Support-Dokumentation steht die zugrunde liegende „Proaktive Unterstützung“ derzeit ausschließlich in den USA, Kanada, Australien, Indien, Malaysia und Singapur auf Englisch sowie in Japan auf Japanisch zur Verfügung, während Europa insgesamt und die deutsche Sprache noch nicht unterstützt werden.
Unabhängig davon bringt das aktuelle November-Update in Verbindung mit der Betriebssystemversion Android 17 QPR2 – einem vierteljährlichen Wartungs- und Funktionsupdate – andere KI-Erweiterungen nach Deutschland. Wie 9to5Google berichtet, sind die KI-gestützten Benachrichtigungszusammenfassungen ab dem Pixel 9 nun auch in Deutschland freigeschaltet, während der automatische Benachrichtigungs-Organizer ab sofort die deutsche Sprache unterstützt.

articles.title: Microsoft's Outlook email hit by new outage | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Microsoft said its Outlook email service is currently experiencing an outage, preventing both business and consumer users from accessing their inboxes.
The issue was initially flagged as affecting the U.S. and the Americas, and later expanded to affect “any region.”
Microsoft hasn’t given a specific cause, but said that it was providing updates in its admin center, which wasn’t reachable at the time of publication. In a post on X for users who can’t access the admin center, Microsoft said some of its infrastructure was experiencing “elevated load,” and that it was “redistributing connection traffic across our broader worldwide infrastructure to help balance the load.”
In its latest update, Microsoft attributed this incident to “a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable,” for reasons it did not explain. Microsoft said it continues to investigate the outage.
Microsoft says its video conferencing tool Teams, file sharing platform SharePoint, and its AI tool Copilot are also unavailable. The company says its Defender XDR security system is also affected by the outage.
Consumers are also unable to access their OneDrive storage, Office (for the web), and several other Microsoft services during the ongoing outage.
TechCrunch will reach out to Microsoft for comment, as soon as our own email service has resumed.
The company’s last major incident was in September, when a days-long outage hit Microsoft 365, its online productivity suite that includes Outlook. During that outage, Microsoft blamed a “core authentication configuration” issue that prevented users from accessing the service.

articles.title: IBM Quantum and the race to make scientific advantage useful to industry - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
IBM Quantum and the race to make scientific advantage useful to industry
QDC26 shows progress in the hardware, software and tooling around quantum computing as customers look for evidence of better outcomes.
IBM Corp.’s Quantum Developer Conference in Chicago this week marked a change in emphasis. IBM claims that researchers have demonstrated quantum advantage in 2026 by working with the classical computing community. Its public presentations showed progress in processors, error correction, scientific software and the integration of quantum with conventional computing.
The company’s quantum leader, Jay Gambetta (pictured), also set a new target. The next big milestone comes by demonstrating industry impact by 2028, conditional on collaboration across enterprise application researchers and the classical and quantum communities.
Our key takeaway is that IBM is assembling more of the full system required to turn a quantum experiment into useful scientific work. Hardware is important, but the real innovation will come from software. Importantly, the tools that help a scientist formulate a problem, run it across different computing resources, check the result and understand the economics are where much of the innovation is headed. These capabilities address several of the barriers customers described to us in our spring quantum tour of major scientific research labs; and the issues discussed with technologists on our Quantum 101 Series at theCUBE’s NYSE studio.
Despite the progress being made, the remaining gaps and challenges are many. Quantum science is advancing but impact on industries is still years away. Better software is the key to making dramatic improvements in quantum performance and a new service capability can attract researchers. But if a chemist needs to understand the deep nuances of quantum computing, it limits adoption. We believe the next phase of innovation will focus on abstracting quantum complexities and making measurable improvements in simplicity to drive further usage.
In this Special Breaking Analysis, we examine IBM’s public QDC proclamations through the prism of our spring interviews with six quantum and supercomputing experts. We add customer perspectives from our partner Qualitate, assess the implications of IBM’s foundry investments and consider what evidence would signal that progress is moving from scientific advantage to industry impact.
Three milestones with different proof points
IBM’s progress comes into better focus when evaluating its milestones separately. IBM’s goal of demonstrating Quantum Advantage by 2026 is generally accepted as met, based on achieving particular computation superiority relative to today’s classical methods. But to truly show industry impact, IBM needs to show results make a difference to an organization. Milestones around fault-tolerant architectures will increasingly focus on the ability to sustain reliable computation in the face of errors. Progress in one category will definitely support another but it’s useful to look at milestones and proof points separately as shown below.
IBM deserves high marks for achieving that advantage but is subject to scrutiny. Gambetta’s keynote described classical researchers overtaking quantum results, claims being withdrawn as classical makes improvements, and subsequent quantum work moving the needle in favor of quantum again. This of course is how a competitive scientific ecosystem should operate. We’re eager to see the leapfrogging end and await a day where a quantum advantage becomes sustainable with clear evidence that classical computing has no chance of catching up for specified use cases.
Observers can rightly be concerned that incorrect inferences may be drawn from the term “advantage.” The phrase can sound like a statement of superiority. But if that advantage is not consistently held, then the broader industry might remain skeptical. The same applies to verifying that a customer outcome is attributable an underlying scientific model powered by quantum.
A public Allstate example is useful and illustrates the difference. IBM described underwriting-optimization results as comparable to classical optimization schemes. That can represent progress, but it does not show that quantum has delivered a superior underwriting outcome. Customers need to decide how much they are prepared to invest in learning before a measurable benefit appears. IBM, in our view, is working hard to simplify the heavy lift and broaden adoption.
Our 2026 spring interviews provide practical research lab data points
The researchers we interviewed in spring 2026 for World Quantum Day were already thinking beyond the hardware. Their concerns included application selection, reliability, integration, software complexity and the ability to preserve optionality as hardware evolves. These were six independent editorial interviews conducted on theCUBE, made possible by Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., across five institutions, offering a view of the work required to make quantum useful. The discussions were hosted by this author and Paul Gillin, managing editor at SiliconANGLE.
The following table highlights the to priority stated by each researcher at the time and our take on how IBM has responded in the past 6-9 months.
| Expert and affiliation | Priority in Q1 | How the public QDC material responds | 
| Laura Schulz Argonne National Laboratory | Let scientists work without mastering every hardware detail. | AI skills and application tools reduce some assembly work; independent use still needs more proof. | 
| Amir Shehata Oak Ridge National Laboratory | Coordinate quantum and conventional resources efficiently. | Managed workflows expose execution stages and combined resource usage. | 
| Dr. Pascal Elahi Pawsey Supercomputing Centre | Identify the quantum portion of a larger scientific problem and supply expertise. | Problem-mapping tools and hybrid workflows support that approach. | 
| Dr. Mikael Johansson CSC, Finnish IT Center for Science | Find useful applications and build skills across diverse technologies. | Chemistry, materials and optimization tools create more ways to experiment. | 
| Tom Beck Oak Ridge National Laboratory | Connect promising science to reliable computation while preserving hardware options. | Materials workflows and error-correction work address parts of that requirement. | 
| Dieter Kranzlmüller Leibniz Supercomputing Centre | Judge application performance and economics while retaining technological independence. | Usage visibility helps assess economics; portability remains a customer requirement. | 
IBM is directing effort toward problems that these practitioners identified months earlier. We believe that is a strong indicator of product relevance, an even more important than hardware milestones.
It also gives us a more reasonable test of true progress. A scientist must be able to attack a meaningful problem with less setup effort, run it more reliably and compare the result with a credible classical alternative. IBM’s public announcements show capabilities intended to support that progression and the gaps identified this spring by our researcher friends. Thus far, however, they don’t show how broadly researchers can complete their tasks without specialist assistance. IBM shared additional capabilities to a small group of industry analysts under NDA, which look encouraging.
The practical measure is in running the experiment end-to-end
Some of the most interesting material in Chicago concerned ordinary operational friction. In the public developer sessions, IBM described experiments interrupted by sleeping laptops, dead notebook sessions, running out of memory or tokens, and lost work in process. In quantum research, as with AI YOLO training runs, they add expense and blockers to work that already requires specialized expertise.
Managed workflows address this through simplification by moving execution into a hosted environment with conventional computing resources and tools to capture and save work in process. Researchers can associate quantum jobs with the workflow and monitor consumption across both quantum and classical support infrastructure. That creates a basis for repeating experiments and understanding where resources are consumed and how to optimize the complete process.
Take the chemistry approaches discussed at the event. Researchers can divide a larger molecular problem into smaller parts, use quantum or classical computing methods for appropriate parts and combine the results. At QDC26, IBM described improvements in classical algorithms that support the processing of quantum jobs. Classical solving steps can become a major bottlenecks and represent opportunities for optimization.
The relevant focus is increasingly the complete research workflow. Here we’re referring to the preparation, the quantum work, the classical processing and the validation. This expands the opportunity for IBM and its partners because more of the work can be supported through its software and services. It also shines a light on how the economic case needs to evolve, with a focus on the cost of an outcome.
Faster quantum hardware alone is not the answer. Conversely, better classical software can make quantum experiments much more productive. Both are developments that came into focus at QDC26. Customers need enough visibility to identify the bottlenecks and implement improvements.
AI’s role in reducing the cost of quantum
IBM’s pronouncements about AI are expected to address barriers raised in our spring interviews – the complexity of translating domain knowledge into a working quantum experiment. IBM must provide skills that assist with choosing methods, workflows, applying classical algorithms and the like. And validating implementations before longer, more expensive runs take place. Our developer conversations at the event underscore demand for AI assistance with calls for simpler packaging and managed services.
We believe this marks is an important near-term relationship between AI and quantum. AI can help scientists use quantum computing more effectively before quantum delivers a broadly demonstrated improvement in AI itself. The immediate opportunity is to simplify – reducing the effort required to apply specialized software and infrastructure.
This requirement has implications for how scientific software is packaged. A library contains reusable code. Increasingly, skills will supply context and guidelines for selecting and applying that code. As skills improve, we expect more of the integration work to be assisted by software. The value of a mature library will still depend on its performance and suitability for the task at hand. The public QDC releases include libraries, mapping tools and AI skills together; they hint toward an evolution in how software will be used in the future.
Another gap is accountability. For example, what happens if a workflow executes but uses invalid scientific assumptions. An AI-generated configuration can appear valid while making a poor trade-off between accuracy and cost, for example. In our view, a useful abstraction must maintain the ability to understand those AI decisions and validate them in terms that a domain expert/scientist comprehends.
This is where customer evidence must become more specific in our view. For example, can a chemist repeat useful work without a vendor team guiding them every step? Can another scientist reproduce the result? Can the organization see what exactly changed between runs? We would place considerable weight on those conditions when judging whether easier programming translates into broader scientific adoption.
Chemistry offers a clear fit but still requires more proof
Chemistry and materials are fields that provide a strong connection between our spring interviews and the public QDC discussions. Johansson at CSC emphasized the challenge of modeling interacting electrons. Beck at Oak Ridge described materials and chemistry research with potential relevance to fusion and biology. IBM’s sessions discussed tools for decomposing problems and processing results across quantum and conventional systems working in tandem.
We view these fields as particularly credible places to look for early useful applications because the scientific problems involve quantum behavior. That is a reason to prioritize research that benefits from quantum. Problem scope, accuracy and economics (or feasibility) relative to conventional methods will determine the ultimate usefulness of quantum.
The economics must include the full result
IBM’s performance progress is notable, but its points of comparison are instructive. Its headline 25-fold improvement in maximum circuit throughput compares Nighthawk r2 with Heron. Several application improvements also compare newer IBM quantum systems with earlier ones. Those figures demonstrate progress within IBM’s generations but a customer still needs a comparison with the best practical classical approach to the same problem.
The mot useful metric in our view is the cost and time required to obtain a validated outcome. The calculation should include all aspects of conventional preprocessing and post-processing, the quantum work done, job completion times and the intensity of the technical skills required perform and validate the result. Importantly, an important future measure is whether the process can be consistently repeated at scale.
Customers should absolutely invest before quantum consistently wins. The key is to identify those investments as a learning experience.
Qualitate customer data reveals little enterprise focus outside of PQC
Post-quantum cryptography or PQC is a topic we unpacked at theCUBE’s Quantum Readiness Day this past September. Qualitate customer survey findings add another dimension to our PQC analysis. But don’t confuse PQC spend with quantum application adoption.
A query of Qualitate’s interview data on quantum adoption focuses heavily on PQC, a tactical topic that is top of mind for enterprises today. Organizations are spending to prepare existing information systems to resist future quantum-enabled attacks. The data include customers already taking action, as well as those evaluating.
“Now is the time we’re really starting to go all in on post quantum cryptography.”
The same participant, a technology lead at a professional services company, explains the rationale in terms of future loss avoidance:
“We anticipate that this will significantly save us on dealing with enormous crises in the future.”
Today’s enterprise focus as it relates to quantum is on modernizing cryptography. This is far ahead of investing to find useful applications for a quantum computer. Today’s practitioners are consumed with deploying and securing agents and making AI trustworthy. Quantum applications, other than PQC, are not top-of-mind for most enterprise customers. Security work to protect conventional systems is tactical and there’s little evidence of interest in running workloads on quantum hardware within organizations today.
NIST released its first three finalized post-quantum cryptography standards in 2024 and encourages organizations to begin transitioning. Its guidance also explains the risk that adversaries collect encrypted information today for possible decryption later. Unlike Y2K, which had a definitive date associated wth the risk, the timing of a capable quantum attack remains uncertain. As such, migration planning is sensible now, independent of IBM’s application and hardware milestones.
The following competitive signals are seen in the Qualitate data and are almost exclusively security-related:
| Vendor | Perception reported in the Qualitate surveys | 
| IBM | Quantum-safe cryptography breadth and hybrid solutions, with existing relationships and executive sponsorship influencing interest. | 
|  | Some participants associate quantum hardware expertise with credibility in defending against the future threat. | 
| Microsoft | An existing Azure environment makes Microsoft a natural extension of the customer’s current platform relationship. | 
The opportunity for specialists also remains open. One participant states:
“The field is still not crystallized. And probably we will not necessarily rely on the hyperscalers. Probably will rely on specialists.” – Global head of analytics, financial services and insurance, large U.S. corporation (Source: Qualitate)
Our take is that technical credibility and existing relationships, combined with the ability to affect a successful migration, may all influence these purchases. IBM has many assets, but customers are still evaluating alternatives. Success in quantum-safe security strengthens its commercial position without, by itself, resolving which quantum computing architecture or application platform will prevail when quantum goes mainstream.
Quantum chip manufacturing adds another dimension to the competition
Quantum computing also needs to progress from building exceptional devices to producing dependable systems repeatedly. The manufacturing announcements around IBM’s roadmap deserve scrutiny in that context.
In September, IBM acquired, Anderon, finalizing a $1 billion CHIPS award supported by an additional $1 billion IBM investment. IBM has reported it has an Albany, New York-based, 300-millimeter quantum wafer foundry serving customers across the ecosystem, with initial wafers already running through the facility.
Our view is that the learning curve will be as important as any single milestone. More repeatable production can confer experience advantages to IBM (Wright’s Law), much in the same way Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. has demonstrated its leadership in semiconductor manufacturing. Serving multiple customers could help support volume across shared infrastructure. Whether those benefits emerge depends on demand, process stability, yields and the ability to protect each customer’s intellectual property. In addition, IBM can learn from Intel’s missteps and its own foundry challenges.
The industry needs to watch for manufacturing progress alongside qubit performance. Capital investments are followed by innovation. IBM’s August acquisition of HRL Laboratories adds a related strategic chess move. The rationale explained by IBM is to acquire expertise in silicon-spin qubits, sensing, materials, cryogenics, controls, packaging and interconnects. IBM describes that expertise as complementary to its superconducting work and identifies opportunities to collaborate with Anderon.
We interpret the acquisition as a way for IBM to control its destiny in a return to its vertically integrated mainframe past. At the same time, it doesn’t have the volume economics to achieve its objectives purely as a captive/integrated systems player. So it must open up its manufacturing capability to other parties, including its competitors.
IBM is competing to organize the work around quantum
Taken together, the public announcements at QDC26 suggest a broader platform ambition. IBM is connecting access to quantum hardware and software with classical computing, application functions, development tools and the like. We believe this could increase its role in the customer’s research process and create more opportunities for ecosystem partners to package specialized capabilities.
The competitive advantage will come from making useful work easier to perform and repeat. A customer that can move from a scientific experiment to a reliable result at scale, with less effort, has a reason to stay with a vendor and invest more. That advantage still has to be earned through application quality, performance, service reliability and superior economics.
There is also a customer tradeoff – the classic lock-in risk. An integrated service can reduce operational complexity while increasing dependence on the provider’s tooling and ecosystem. Open-source tools help minimize the risk, but portability also depends on whether models, workflows, validation and operational models transfer to another platform. Our spring conversations with Kranzlmüller – and his emphasis on technological independence – along with Shehata’s interest in interoperable specifications – make that point clear.
We would not declare IBM as a decisive winner from this conference. But the company has presented an impressive combination of hardware, software and infrastructure progress. Customers will determine its value through repeated use and outcomes. Competing systems from specialists and hyperscalers – as well as progress from classical methods – will continue to shape the narrative.
Gambetta’s 2028 gambit
If Jay Gambetta’s prediction holds true, the next two years will produce a more tangible conversation around industry impact. Look for significantly more quantum POCs, more named customers solving consequential problems and a measurable change in a scientific or business decision. We would also want enough evidence for an independent team to assess the contribution; and for the customer to explain the full cost of achieving an outcome.
Some additional items to watch:
- We believe chemistry and materials deserve close attention;
- Research workflows must be easier to use;
- Track whether more domain scientists can work independent of highly skilled quantum experts;
- Whether quantum advantage survives a sustainable lead vis a vis classical;
- Whether chip manufacturing shows up as reliable, consistent and independent.
For enterprise leaders, the sensible approach is to separate cryptographic readiness from quantum application programs tied to specific problems and economics.
IBM has made a stronger case that the surrounding machinery for useful quantum computing is coming together. The future test is whether customers can show what changed because of quantum. A demonstrably improved scientific result or an economically superior workflow would make the 2028 ambition impressive.
That is the evidence we will be watching.
What’s on your quantum radar? Let us know.
