articles.title: Los lentes con Gemini de Google costarán desde USD 395 y llegarán a las tiendas el 10 de diciembre de 2026
articles.text:
Google y Samsung abrieron este jueves las reservas de sus primeros lentes inteligentes con el asistente Gemini. Los modelos de la marca Warby Parker cuestan desde USD 395 y los de Gentle Monster desde USD 449. Se venderán en tiendas y por internet a partir del 10 de diciembre.
Los dos fabricantes de lentes diseñaron los marcos, pero el equipo es idéntico: pesa unos 41 gramos, tiene una batería de hasta nueve horas y un estuche que la recarga hasta siete veces, según Google. Incluye una cámara de 12 megapíxeles, parlante y micrófonos, pero no tiene pantalla.
Gemini responde a lo que el usuario ve y escucha. Según Google, ofrece indicaciones para llegar a un lugar, traducciones en vivo y descripciones de lo que hay frente a la cámara. También permite sacar fotos, escuchar música y revisar la agenda sin sacar el teléfono del bolsillo.
Por ahora el mercado es acotado. Los lentes solo funcionan con cuentas de Google de Estados Unidos y Corea del Sur, y exigen que el titular sea mayor de 18 años. Ni Google ni Samsung han dicho cuándo llegarán a otros países.
Qué teléfonos son compatibles
Los lentes se conectan con los iPhone desde el 13 Pro, con los Pixel desde el 7 y con los Samsung Galaxy S y Z que tengan One UI 9.0 o una versión posterior. Quedan afuera los Galaxy más baratos y los equipos de otras marcas, según las condiciones publicadas por Google.
Wired comparó el producto con las gafas de Meta, que lideran este mercado y cuentan con el diseño de Ray-Ban. Los de Google pesan unos 10 gramos menos que la tercera generación de Meta. Las de Warby Parker se pueden probar en más de 360 tiendas de esa cadena.
Cómo intentan evitar que graben a escondidas
Google presentó junto con el producto un conjunto de reglas de privacidad, porque una cámara en el rostro preocupa a quienes quedan frente a ella. Una luz blanca se enciende cuando el usuario toma una foto o graba un video. Si alguien la tapa, los lentes dejan de grabar.
Asimismo, la cámara se bloquea si detecta que la luz fue alterada. 9to5Google precisó que el sistema verifica el funcionamiento de la luz cada vez que los lentes se cargan. Sumado a esto, cada par tiene un interruptor que los apaga por completo.
Los videos duran como máximo 90 segundos, frente a los cinco minutos que permiten las gafas de Meta. Google prohíbe que las aplicaciones de su tienda transmitan en vivo desde los lentes o identifiquen rostros en tiempo real.
Cuando el usuario pide a Gemini que mire algo, el teléfono oculta antes los rostros de las personas cercanas. Google afirmó que esas imágenes no se guardan en el historial de Gemini y que no se usan para entrenar modelos de IA ni para dirigir anuncios.
Juston Payne, director de gestión de producto de realidad extendida de Google, dijo a The Verge que alguien podría inventar una forma de burlar la luz que los algoritmos no detecten. Por eso, explicó, la empresa borra rostros y ruido ambiente: “No vamos a entrenar a Gemini con eso”.
Las promesas tienen límites. Expertos señalan que las conversaciones de voz con Gemini no gozan de la misma protección que las imágenes y que los datos no están cifrados en los servidores de Google. La empresa dijo que trabaja para llevar a los lentes su sistema de procesamiento privado de IA, que impediría el acceso incluso a sus empleados.
Quien use los lentes debe aceptar no grabar a otras personas sin permiso ni en lugares sensibles, y no tapar la luz. Si incumple, Google puede desactivar los lentes. Las pruebas en tiendas ya están disponibles y las ventas comienzan el 10 de diciembre.

articles.title: Dropbox Shares How Its In-House Cookie Auditor Tests Consent Behaviour Across 200+ Web Surfaces
articles.text:
Dropbox engineering has published a detailed account of how its in-house cookie auditor validates consent behaviour across more than 200 web surfaces, offering a glimpse into the practical challenges of maintaining privacy compliance at scale. The post, authored by Yasmin McDowell and Lawrence Good, outlines a Playwright-based system that behaves like a privacy-conscious visitor and checks that pages only load cookies consistent with a user's stated preferences.
The auditor runs three separate tests against every page in scope, one simulating a standard US visitor, one simulating an EU visitor, and a third that sends a Global Privacy Control (GPC) signal. Each test begins in a fresh, isolated browser context with no existing cookies, mirroring what a new visitor would see. Before any interaction, the auditor records which cookies have already loaded and verifies they match the expected baseline for that scenario, then locates the page's consent controls, declines non-essential cookies, reloads the page and checks that the preference still applies.
The controls are not identified by text. Dropbox supports 22 languages and the banner may appear as a floating element, a preferences window, or a footer link, so the auditor interacts with the underlying consent elements rather than button labels. A pragmatic design choice is keeping cookie classifications outside the auditor's source code, which allows the Privacy team to update the approved cookie list and known exceptions without waiting for an engineering release. Because the consent banner itself was also built in-house, the auditor plugs directly into existing infrastructure rather than wrapping an off-the-shelf product.
Dropbox built what it calls "an auditor for our auditor," a companion URL detector that uses traffic data to find every live Dropbox web surface. Billions of visit records are filtered down to a manageable list of unique paths, then grouped by consent logic so that representative URLs can stand in for large families of similar pages.
Projects such as @slashgear/gdpr-cookie-scanner ship an open-source CLI that scores GDPR behaviour from 0 to 100 and integrates with GitHub Actions, while ConsentCrawl targets over 25 consent manager platforms including OneTrust, CookieBot and TrustArc Truste. A Dutch study recently used Playwright to analyse 6,168 political party URLs for unconsented tracking, suggesting the same browser automation approach is becoming standard in academic privacy research.
Platform engineers interested in building similar tooling can see the shape of a minimal Playwright assertion in a recent qaskills.sh guide.
Today the auditor produces a weekly report for Privacy and Engineering teams, separating likely violations from known false positives and tracking historical trends. Dropbox's next planned iteration is routing findings directly to the teams that own each page, shortening the loop between detection and fix. The team notes that the browser automation itself may be the simplest part of such a project, with the harder work sitting around it: defining correct behaviour, maintaining an accurate inventory and separating real issues from noise.
Dropbox is a cloud-based file hosting and collaboration platform founded in 2007 by Drew Houston and Arash Ferdowsi and headquartered in San Francisco. The company operates more than 200 web surfaces across its product lineup, which includes Dropbox, Dropbox Sign, DocSend and FormSwift, and has invested heavily in privacy and compliance programmes covering GDPR, CCPA and ISO 27018.
Playwright is an open-source browser automation library developed and maintained by Microsoft. It drives Chromium, WebKit and Firefox through a single API across JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java and .NET, and has become a widely used tool for end-to-end testing, web scraping and, increasingly, automated privacy and compliance audits of the kind Dropbox describes.

articles.title: PHP2Shell Exploited in Destructive Check Point Gateway Attacks
articles.text:
Threat actors have been exploiting PHP2Shell vulnerabilities to hack Check Point Gateway appliances and deploy a wiper against victim organizations, Check Point reports.
The attacks unfolded in two waves. An initial, destructive round started on October 30 and targeted Israeli organizations, and a second one started on November 2, targeting organizations across multiple countries.
PHP2Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, refers to two critical vulnerabilities leading to remote code execution (RCE) and affecting all PHP versions from PHP 5 onwards. They were patched on October 21, but exploitation started days before patches and mass exploitation shortly after.
Dream has linked attacks targeting PHP2Shell to root Palo Alto Networks firewalls to Chinese hackers, and the hackers targeting Check Point gateways have left a note mentioning the cybersecurity firm.
As part of the Check Point campaign, the attackers exploited PHP2Shell for initial access, then targeted CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege escalation in the DynamicCLI process, to gain root access and deploy PHP webshells and establish persistence.
In late October, the attackers targeted Check Point Mobile Access gateways across multiple Israeli organizations. They placed PHP webshells in a directory the Mobile Access portal uses to construct login pages, allowing them to send commands and establish a stronger foothold on the environment.
Next, they deployed TSGA and TSProxy, variants of the malware framework PhiliKit previously seen (PDF) in China-linked UNC5221’s hacking into Ivanti products, for backdoor access and network function interception.
The attackers followed up with internal asset discovery, then moved laterally to a VMware ESXi host where they deployed and executed a wiper, and then deployed a note mentioning Dream Security.
According to Check Point, the hackers operated during typical Chinese working hours. Despite this and the use of China-linked malware and infrastructure, the use of a wiper and the destructive nature of the attacks do not align with known Chinese cyber operations.
“Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation. Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen,” Check Point says.
The second wave targeted Check Point Security Gateways across organizations worldwide, including some Israeli entities targeted in the first wave. No destructive activity was observed during this second wave.
“Neither wave showed a clear sector preference, suggesting opportunistic initial-access attempts rather than sector-specific targeting,” Check Point notes.

articles.title: Building a rocket is hard. AST SpaceMobile thinks it's "simple."
articles.text:
During an hour-long event on Thursday, Abel Avellan, the founder and chief executive of the telecommunications company AST SpaceMobile, laid out his vision for developing a large rocket to launch his Bluebird satellites into orbit.
Avellan emphasized, over and over again, that AST plans to build a “simple” rocket. He paraphrased SpaceX founder Elon Musk several times, saying, “the best part is no part.” Avellan emphasized that AST has already procured engines for its proposed Blacklift rocket, asserting that engine development accounts for 80 percent of a typical rocket’s development cycle.
“Of course rocket engineers are going to get mad with me, but you can simplify it as a big tank feeding engines,” he said of the rocket. “So big tanks—we know how to do them. We know how to do them. We know how to do them in composite.”
I am not a rocket engineer, and I am not mad at Avellan. But he sure seems to be substantially underestimating the challenge of building rockets.
AST feels its hand is forced
Avellan also has a problem. AST SpaceMobile appears to be successful in building very large satellites, Bluebirds, that are capable of providing direct-to-cell capability from an orbit about 550km above Earth. The problem is there is a commercial launch crunch, and the company is struggling to get its satellites on orbit today, and projects to do so into the future.
“We’re not doing this thing because we like rockets,” he said during the presentation. “We’re not doing this thing because we want to be in the launch business. We want this because we have so much demand of our satellites, and as you have seen it, we cannot get enough launches.”

articles.title: Build composable, interoperable multi-agent systems with A2A on AWS | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Build composable, interoperable multi-agent systems with A2A on AWS
Agents in multi-agent systems that span organizational boundaries often need to collaborate in a composable, interoperable way, with agents that other organizations build and run. They need a way to discover each other, communicate, and exchange tasks without exposing internals or requiring the same framework on both sides.
The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol addresses this constraint. Without A2A, building composable multi-agent systems across organizational boundaries requires custom integration code for each customer and framework. Independent software vendors (ISVs) can instead build composable, interoperable agents that work with the A2A-compatible frameworks their customers already use.
While we frame this post around the ISV use case, the pattern also applies to organizations that expose agents across boundaries, whether to partners, customers, or internal teams that use different frameworks. As your system grows, you add skills by registering Agent Cards with the orchestrator, without changing the agents already running.
In this post, we walk through a deployed reference architecture on AWS. A LangChain-based enterprise orchestrator communicates with a Strands Agents-based software as a service (SaaS) agent across organizational boundaries using A2A, with the enterprise and the SaaS provider in separate AWS accounts. Neither side depends on the other’s framework or SDK, and the two sides share no secrets. We cover the architecture and implementation patterns, then deploy the system from three Jupyter notebooks and run an end-to-end test.
The A2A protocol is now a Linux Foundation project, and AWS is among the organizations that support it. With A2A, agents can discover each other, negotiate tasks, and collaborate across organizational boundaries through a standardized protocol. The protocol uses existing authentication standards such as OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC) for cross-boundary security, and is designed to work across A2A-compatible frameworks.
In Open Protocols for Agent Interoperability Part 4: Inter-Agent Communication on A2A, we introduced A2A concepts and demonstrated two Strands agents communicating using the protocol on AWS. That post established the foundation with Agent Card discovery, structured task execution, and the A2A server pattern. This post builds on that foundation with cross-framework interoperability, cross-organizational trust boundaries, and OAuth in both directions.
Solution overview
Three agents run in two AWS accounts, one for the enterprise and one for the SaaS provider. The A2A protocol connects them, with OAuth authentication in both directions. Each account has its own Amazon Cognito user pool, so each side authenticates with its own identity provider.
During onboarding, the enterprise and the SaaS provider exchange only public values, such as identity provider URLs, client IDs, scopes, and endpoint URLs. Each side then trusts tokens from the other side’s user pool, and no secrets are shared.
After onboarding, each request follows these steps:
- The enterprise app gets an access token from the enterprise’s Amazon Cognito user pool.
- The app sends a question over HTTPS to the user API in Amazon API Gateway, then polls for the answer.
- Amazon API Gateway forwards the request privately, through a VPC link and an internal Network Load Balancer, to the Enterprise Orchestrator, a LangChain agent.
- When its model decides that the question needs a compliance scan, the orchestrator gets its own token from the enterprise user pool, using a client secret stored in AWS Secrets Manager.
- The orchestrator sends an A2A request to the compliance SaaS agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, using the skill it read from the agent’s Agent Card at startup.
- The compliance agent checks the enterprise context agent’s Agent Card at the callback URL registered at onboarding, then gets a token from the SaaS provider’s own pool.
- The compliance agent calls back to the enterprise context agent for account metadata, finishes its scan, and returns the answer to the orchestrator and then to the app.
On the enterprise side, two agents run on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate. The Enterprise Orchestrator is the entry point for users. LangChain provides the agent framework and tool-calling abstractions, and Amazon Bedrock provides the foundation models (FMs) that power each agent’s reasoning. The orchestrator uses LangChain and Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6). At startup, the orchestrator fetches the SaaS agent’s Agent Card from its well-known URL and creates a LangChain tool for each skill described on the card. The model then decides which tool to call based on the user’s question, so the orchestrator needs no hardcoded routing logic. It sends compliance scan requests over A2A with OAuth bearer tokens and summarizes the results for leadership. Users reach the orchestrator through an Amazon API Gateway HTTPS endpoint that accepts only tokens from the enterprise’s own pool.
The second enterprise agent provides internal context. The Enterprise Context Agent is built with LangChain and Amazon Bedrock (Amazon Nova Lite). It provides internal account metadata such as internal policy rules, data classification, business criticality, and escalation contacts (team on-call rotations). The deployed agent uses the official a2a-sdk (AgentCard, AgentExecutor, and spec-conformant JSON-RPC routes), pinned to a2a-sdk[http-server]==1.2.2. The SaaS agent reaches the context agent through an API Gateway partner API that accepts only the SaaS provider’s callback token.
Both enterprise agents run in private subnets of an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), with no public IP addresses.
On the SaaS provider side, the Compliance SaaS Agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in the SaaS provider’s own AWS account. Built with the Strands Agents SDK, it checks AWS accounts against the enterprise’s own internal policies, such as no public storage in production and encryption at rest for confidential data. In production, the scanning tools would connect to services such as AWS Config, AWS Security Hub, or Amazon GuardDuty. For this demo, the agent uses synthetic data that simulates compliance findings across multiple accounts.
Before it scans, the SaaS agent calls back to the Enterprise Context Agent for enterprise context, such as which accounts are production, which internal policies apply, and who to escalate to. This bidirectional pattern makes the agents true peers instead of a client and a server. The callback goes only to the address the customer registered at onboarding.
The key design decision is to use A2A for all cross-boundary communication. The enterprise has no access to the SaaS agent’s internal tools, system prompt, or model choice. This separation means the ISV can change its internal architecture without changing customer integrations, as long as its Agent Card and A2A interface stay compatible. The SaaS card publishes one curated skill, not its internal tool names.
Amazon Bedrock provides API access to multiple foundation models, so each agent can use the model that fits its workload. In this solution, the orchestrator and SaaS agent use Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 for complex reasoning, while the context agent uses Amazon Nova Lite for metadata lookups. You can choose different models based on your own requirements.
A2A and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) solve different problems in this architecture. MCP connects an agent to its own tools and data sources in a client-server model. A2A connects agents to other agents as peers, where neither side exposes its internals. In production, the SaaS agent could use MCP internally to connect to its compliance scanning tools while exposing itself externally through A2A. The external interface stays the same regardless of how the agent connects to its internal tools.
Prerequisites
The notebooks contain the complete deployment procedure. Before you run them, you need the following:
- Two AWS accounts, one for the enterprise and one for the SaaS provider, in the same AWS Region: us-east-1, us-east-2, or us-west-2. In both accounts, access to Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 in Amazon Bedrock, and in the enterprise account, access to Amazon Nova Lite. Before the first run, submit the Anthropic first-time use form in each account, and give the identity you run the notebooks with the AWS Marketplace permissions listed in the Amazon Bedrock model access documentation. Model availability varies by Region. Check the Amazon Bedrock model availability documentation for the current list.
- A Jupyter environment with Python 3.10 or later, either: 
         
  - On your computer: JupyterLab, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) version 2, and an AWS IAM Identity Center profile for each account, set up with aws configure sso. You don’t need Docker: AWS CodeBuild builds the container images.
  - Or an Amazon SageMaker AI notebook instance in each account (ml.t3.medium is enough). See the Guide to getting set up with Amazon SageMaker AI.
- In each account, an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role with permissions to create AWS CloudFormation stacks and the resources in them. Each notebook lists the exact permissions in its Reference section. See the IAM User Guide.
Notebook 3 also runs the end-to-end test described later in this post, so you can verify the deployment.
Running this solution incurs charges for the resources it creates. In the enterprise account, the main always-on resources are a NAT gateway, two AWS Fargate tasks, the internal Network Load Balancer, and two interface VPC endpoints. Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore charge for what you use. Prices vary by AWS Region. See the pricing pages for Amazon VPC, AWS Fargate, Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Elastic Load Balancing. Run the Clean up sections when you finish.
Implement the solution
Deploy the system with three notebooks, run in order with Jupyter, one cell at a time. Notebook 1 (enterprise account, about 3 minutes) creates the enterprise identity and writes an onboarding request. Notebook 2 (SaaS provider account, about 5 minutes) deploys the compliance agent and writes an onboarding response. Notebook 3 (enterprise account, about 20 minutes) deploys the enterprise agents and runs the tests. The onboarding files hold only public values.
- Clone the GitHub repository, and set up two AWS profiles for local runs, or one notebook instance per account with the repository cloned to each.
- Run notebook 1 in the enterprise account.
- Give onboarding-request.json to the SaaS provider.
- Run notebook 2 in the SaaS provider account.
- Give onboarding-response.json back to the enterprise.
- Run notebook 3 in the enterprise account.
- After testing, run notebook 3’s Clean up, then notebook 2’s.
The following sections explain the key implementation patterns behind the deployment. Together, they demonstrate three capabilities:
- Interoperability across frameworks – A LangChain orchestrator calls a Strands agent using A2A, with neither side depending on the other’s SDK.
- Composability across organizational boundaries – An ISV’s compliance agent and an enterprise’s context agent compose into a workflow that neither team built alone.
- Bidirectional collaboration with OAuth – Agents act as peers, calling each other across trust boundaries with token-based authentication.
With A2A, the ISV in this scenario replaces multiple custom integration paths with a single protocol-based interface.
Build the SaaS compliance agent
Build the ISV’s compliance agent with the Strands Agents SDK and deploy it to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. For this demo, the scanning tools return synthetic compliance findings.
The agent exposes three compliance tools using the Strands @tool decorator (listing available accounts, running compliance scans, and retrieving remediation steps), plus a fourth that calls back to the enterprise, covered in the next section. The Agent Card doesn’t list these tools. It publishes one curated skill, so callers’ models see what the product does, not how it’s built. This simplified example shows the scanning tool:
Enable the bidirectional callback
This is where the solution goes beyond typical agent integrations. Most agent-to-agent demos show one-way request and response, where a client agent calls a server agent and waits for the result. That pattern breaks down when the called agent needs information that only the caller has. In production, agents need to be peers that can call each other.
The SaaS compliance agent needs enterprise context. Examples include which accounts are production, which internal policies apply, and who to escalate to. This is information that only the enterprise has.
The SaaS agent calls back over A2A, but only to the callback URL the customer registered at onboarding. It first verifies the customer’s public context card there, then gets a token from the SaaS provider’s own Cognito pool, and sends message/send to the enterprise partner API:
Every failure, from an unverified card to a rejected token, gives the model one message, “Enterprise context unavailable”, and the details stay in the SaaS provider’s logs.
Expose the agent over A2A on AgentCore
The A2AServer class from the Strands SDK handles the A2A protocol, Agent Card generation, and JSON-RPC message handling. The server publishes one curated skill and declares on the card how a caller gets a token:
When deployed to AgentCore, this automatically generates an Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json. The Agent Card is a JSON document that describes the agent’s name, capabilities, and skills. A2A-compatible clients can fetch this card and understand what the agent can do without documentation or SDK integration.
Build the enterprise orchestrator with LangChain
This is the interoperability proof. The enterprise orchestrator uses LangChain, deliberately different from the Strands-based SaaS agent. It uses raw httpx HTTP calls with A2A JSON-RPC and doesn’t depend on the Strands SDK. If the ISV switched from Strands to another A2A-compatible framework, the enterprise orchestrator would keep working without changes, as long as the SaaS agent still speaks A2A and publishes a compatible Agent Card. That is what protocol-level interoperability means in practice.
The orchestrator gets a token from the enterprise’s own Cognito pool and sends the JSON-RPC payload over HTTPS only to the agent URL pinned to the address it fetched the Agent Card from. This abridged code shows the core A2A client:
Discover agents and route requests with the LLM
At startup, the orchestrator fetches Agent Cards from configured ISV URLs. It reads the skill descriptions from each card and creates a LangChain tool for each skill. The orchestrator’s large language model (LLM), Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, then decides which tool to call based on the user’s question. This simplified code shows the pattern:
As a result, when the ISV adds or changes a capability, its Agent Card changes with it, and the orchestrator picks up the new skills the next time it restarts. The two teams don’t need to coordinate the change.
Build the enterprise context agent
The enterprise context agent uses LangChain and Amazon Nova Lite for enterprise metadata lookups, and exposes its capabilities over A2A using the official a2a-sdk. The SDK handles Agent Card serving, JSON-RPC routing, and protocol conformance. Because A2A is JSON-RPC over HTTP, a standard web framework can serve it. The orchestrator shows the client side: it sends A2A requests with plain httpx and no A2A SDK.
The agent also publishes its own Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json, which the SaaS agent checks before it calls back. This is the same discovery mechanism used in the other direction. The A2A specification defines Agent Cards, so they don’t depend on the framework that builds the agent.
Set up cross-boundary OAuth with Amazon Cognito
Agent-to-agent communication across organizational boundaries without authentication isn’t acceptable to most enterprises. Every A2A task request (message/send) in this solution carries a JSON Web Token (JWT). Each side authenticates with a token from its own identity provider, and the receiving side accepts only that provider, one client, and one scope. The only unauthenticated endpoint is the enterprise context agent’s Agent Card, which publishes descriptive metadata so callers can discover the agent.
The solution uses Amazon Cognito as the OAuth provider. The same pattern can use another OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider that issues signed JWT access tokens, after you update the sample’s Cognito-specific checks.
The authentication flow involves four components:
Amazon Cognito: one user pool per account. The enterprise pool issues tokens to the orchestrator and to the enterprise app, and the SaaS pool issues tokens to the SaaS agent for its callback. You can view them in the Amazon Cognito console.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is configured with the enterprise pool’s discovery URL, the orchestrator’s client ID, and one scope. It validates the JWT on every incoming A2A request:
Amazon API Gateway uses JWT authorizers. The partner API accepts only the SaaS provider’s callback token, and the user API accepts only the enterprise app’s token. View the configuration in the Amazon API Gateway console.
AWS Secrets Manager in each account stores that account’s client secret, and an IAM grant and a resource policy that denies every other principal limit each secret to the one workload that uses it. No secret is hardcoded or shared with the other account. You can manage secrets in the AWS Secrets Manager console.
This AWS CloudFormation snippet shows the partner API’s JWT authorizer:
One detail of machine-to-machine authentication is a common source of errors when you wire OAuth between API Gateway and AgentCore. An Amazon Cognito client-credentials access token carries client_id and scope, but no aud claim. When aud is absent, the API Gateway JWT authorizer checks client_id against the audience list. On the AgentCore side, configure allowedClients and leave allowedAudience unset.
Deploy the system with notebooks
The notebooks run the whole deployment from Jupyter. They deploy five AWS CloudFormation stacks, three in the enterprise account and two in the SaaS provider account. The enterprise infrastructure and services stacks are separate because of a chicken-and-egg problem: the ECS services need Docker images, but CloudFormation creates the Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repositories that hold those images. You can monitor the stacks in the AWS CloudFormation console.
The notebooks surface failures early. Each notebook first checks Amazon Bedrock model access with a short test call, before anything is deployed, and each step stops at the first error with clear output. The Clean up sections sit at the bottom of notebooks 2 and 3, after a stop cell, so Run All never reaches them.
Understand Agent Cards and discovery
Agent Cards make discovery possible without agreeing on tool definitions in advance. Without them, the enterprise would need documentation, an SDK, or a meeting with the ISV’s engineering team to understand what the compliance agent can do. With Agent Cards, the enterprise orchestrator fetches a single JSON document. It immediately knows the agent’s name, capabilities, and skills, programmatically, at runtime. This is the card the compliance agent publishes for one customer, abridged:
Each skill’s description becomes a tool docstring, so the orchestrator’s model routes each request to the right agent. The two teams never had to agree on tool definitions or share an SDK. The card also declares how a caller authenticates. The orchestrator checks that declaration rather than following it: it keeps the card only if it names the token endpoint and scope registered at onboarding.
Test end-to-end
Notebook 3 runs one end-to-end test through both accounts. It gets a token for the enterprise app, submits a question, and polls for the result:
The orchestrator discovers the SaaS agent through its Agent Card and routes the request over A2A. The SaaS agent calls back to the enterprise context agent for account metadata (bidirectional A2A), runs compliance scans with its internal tools, combines everything into an enriched report, and sends it back. The response contains data from both agents. This shows that two independently built agents, on different frameworks and different infrastructure, can compose into a workflow that neither produces alone.
The test passes only if the reply has compliance findings, includes an on-call rotation code that only the enterprise context agent knows, and the partner API’s access log shows a 200 from the SaaS callback client. Together they show that the callback worked. Notebook 3 then runs seven trust boundary checks that send a wrong, missing, or forged token to each gate, and every call must be rejected. This is abridged output from a test run (IDs are placeholders):
In that run, the report covered two production accounts and six findings, with the escalation contacts for each account. You can send the same request from any HTTP client, without an A2A SDK.
Production considerations
This demo simplifies several areas for clarity. For production, consider these changes:
- One runtime per customer, or a front door that accepts several customer identity providers, with per-customer callback clients.
- Key-based client authentication (private_key_jwt or mutual TLS) instead of client secrets.
- AWS PrivateLink for private connectivity, and TLS inside the VPC for end-to-end encryption.
- Customer managed AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys for Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon ECR, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.
- VPC Flow Logs and Network Load Balancer access logs. Both API Gateway stages already write access logs.
- A Secrets Manager rotation function for the Cognito client credentials.
- An authenticated onboarding portal or API instead of files.
If calls through API Gateway intermittently return HTTP 503, check that cross-zone load balancing is on for the internal Network Load Balancer. Each ECS service runs a single task that can start in either Availability Zone.
The repository’s README covers the full list in Security controls and Considerations for production.
Security considerations
Deploy this solution only in sandbox accounts with no customer or business data, and delete the stacks after testing. The sample uses synthetic data only, with no personal data. Its compliance agent checks example internal policies. It doesn’t assess or certify compliance with any law, regulation, or standard. The sample includes the following controls. You’re responsible for reviewing and adapting them before you use this pattern in production:
- Transport encryption. Every cross-account call uses HTTPS to Amazon API Gateway or Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and every route except the context agent’s public Agent Card requires a Cognito JWT.
- Guardrails. In this sample, each model call uses an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with prompt-attack and harmful-content filters, and text from the other organization is checked against the same guardrail before a model uses it.
- Least-privilege IAM. Each workload has its own role that names exact ARNs. Only the orchestrator and the compliance agent can read a secret, each only its own.
- Container hardening. ECS containers run with a read-only root filesystem and all Linux capabilities dropped. The base image is pinned by digest.
- Account isolation. The two accounts share no secret, key, or IAM permission. They exchange only public values.
Clean up resources
To avoid ongoing charges, delete all resources when you have finished testing. Run the Clean up section at the bottom of notebook 3, then notebook 2, one cell at a time. The last cell in each section confirms that nothing is left. After cleanup, check the AWS CloudFormation, Amazon ECR, and Amazon Cognito consoles in both accounts, and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console in the SaaS provider account, to confirm that no resources remain.
Conclusion
This post showed how to build a multi-agent system where agents from different organizations, built on different frameworks, collaborate through A2A on AWS.
A LangChain orchestrator on Amazon ECS communicates with a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Neither side needs the other’s framework or SDK. The SaaS agent calls back to the enterprise context agent for account metadata, and each side authenticates with its own identity provider. A new skill from the same ISV requires no changes to the code. Adding a second ISV takes one extension, because the orchestrator holds a single OAuth client today: give it one client and scope per ISV, as the README’s Considerations for production describes. Then run the same onboarding exchange, add its Agent Card URL, and restart the orchestrator.
To get started, clone the GitHub repository and run the three notebooks, in two accounts, with Jupyter on your computer or on Amazon SageMaker AI notebook instances. They handle infrastructure provisioning, agent deployment, and end-to-end testing.
To learn more about the services and protocol in this post, see the following resources:
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide
- Amazon Bedrock User Guide
- Strands Agents SDK documentation
- Open Protocols for Agent Interoperability Part 4: Inter-Agent Communication on A2A
If you have questions or feedback, leave them in the comments section.

articles.title: Agile Robots raises $500M funding led by SoftBank at $8.5B valuation - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Agile Robots raises $500M funding led by SoftBank at $8.5B valuation
German artificial intelligence robotics startup Agile Robots SE announced today that it has raised $500 million in new late-stage funding at an $8.5 billion valuation.
Japanese multinational investment holding company SoftBank led the Series F funding round. Other participants included AI chip leader Nvidia Corp., Japanese group Hitachi Ltd. and T Capital. The financing brings the total capital invested to $2 billion.
Founded in 2018 as a spinoff from the German Aerospace Center, Agile is one of Europe’s leaders in humanoid and mobile robots, robotic arms and dexterous robotic hands, along with the AI models needed to control them. The company combines robotic hardware with sensing, computer vision and AI software to automate physical work.
At the center of its hardware and software is force-sensitive manipulation. It allows robots to control how much force they use to handle delicate parts, perform precision assembly, and adapt to changing situations.
“Physical AI will fundamentally change how the world builds, moves and makes things,” said founder and Chief Executive Dr. Zhaopeng Chen. “Our vision is intelligent robots working alongside people in factories and warehouses everywhere, and Agile Robots is determined to lead that shift.”
Agile’s established flagship arm Diana 7 allows for precise manipulation and assembly; it includes torque sensors in all seven axes of movement that can detect and respond to the amount of force required to grab, lift and manipulate objects.
Agile One, the company’s humanoid robot, was publicly unveiled in November 2025 as an industrial-first platform. The launch extended the company’s approach into human-shaped platforms intended to carry out tasks across a production floor. It includes dexterous hands, advanced perception and human collaborative capabilities, allowing it to operate readily alongside personnel in manufacturing and logistics settings.
The company now offers an entire family of Agile One human-shaped robots, including the Agile One S, a compact humanoid reference platform built for research labs, universities, and developers. The company also offers Agile One SN, equipped with Dual Wuji five-finger hands and preconfigured for Nvidia Corp.’s Isaac GR00T AI models that act as robot “brains,” designed to let industry developers rapidly train, evaluate, deploy and test new robotic skills.
“We bring Physical AI out of the lab and into industrial production, across logistics, automotive, electronics and manufacturing,” added Chen.
The funding will support expansion into the United States, hiring more engineers and accelerating development of intelligent robotics applications. Additionally, the company said it intends to expand production, including in Germany, where it opened a facility in Fürstenfeldbruck, near Munich, in early 2026 to meet rising demand. Agile said the site can produce up to 10,000 legged and wheeled humanoid robots annually.
Agile has deployed around 20,000 industrial robotic solutions for customers across the automotive, consumer electronics, logistics and other industries. It boasts a growing portfolio of subsidiaries, including BÄR Automation, Franka Robotics, Idealworks and Krause Automation. Franka supplies manipulation technology, Idealworks develops mobile robots and coordination software, whereas BÄR and Krause build and integrate interaction capabilities.
In robotics, Agile faces stiff international competition from established automation suppliers such as Universal Robots A/S, ABB Ltd., FANUC Corp. and Yaskawa Electric Corp. Its Agile One humanoid faces rivals that include Figure AI Inc., Apptronik Inc. and Agility Robotics Inc.

articles.title: Starship : suivez en direct la tentative inédite de la double capture de la fusée géante en plein vol
articles.text:
Le 15e vol d’essai de Starship en résumé
- Quoi : le 15e vol d’essai (baptisé IFT-15) du Starship, dans sa version 3, la plus récente.
- Quand : pas avant ce vendredi 13 novembre, dans une fenêtre qui s’ouvre à 23 h 45, heure de Paris.
- Où : depuis Starbase, la base de l’entreprise à Boca Chica, au Texas.
- La charge utile : 26 satellites Starlink V3 opérationnels, comme lors du vol 14.
- L’enjeu : réussir un vol orbital, déployer les satellites, puis ramener le vaisseau de façon contrôlée jusqu’à la tour, pour une capture en plein vol. Le premier étage doit lui aussi être rattrapé par la tour, quelques minutes seulement après le décollage.
Où voir en direct le départ de la fusée géante de SpaceX ?
SpaceX retransmettra le vol en direct sur son compte X et sur la page de la mission de son site, comme à chaque tir. Le direct devrait débuter une trentaine de minutes avant l’allumage des moteurs. On y suivra le compte à rebours, le décollage depuis le pas de tir à Starbase, puis la séparation des deux étages.
Les liens seront ajoutés dès qu’ils seront disponibles.
Le vol doit durer un peu plus de 22 heures et demie, le temps de faire environ 14 fois le tour de la Terre, à quelque 275 kilomètres d’altitude. Si la fusée décolle à l’ouverture de la fenêtre, le propulseur devrait être rattrapé vers 23 h 51, environ six minutes et demie après le décollage. Le vaisseau, lui, doit revenir sur la tour dans la soirée de ce samedi 14 novembre.
Que doit accomplir Starship lors de ce vol ?
Le premier vol orbital de Starship, le 28 septembre, n’a pas duré aussi longtemps que prévu. Après la coupure trop précoce d’un moteur Raptor pendant la montée, SpaceX a fait redescendre le Ship (l’étage supérieur de la fusée) dans le Pacifique au bout de trois heures, au lieu des dix prévues.
Le vol suivant, que l’entreprise d’Elon Musk vise ce vendredi 13 novembre depuis sa base de Starbase, au Texas, place la barre bien plus haut : plus de 22 heures en orbite, puis un retour du Ship jusqu’à la tour de lancement, qui doit l’attraper au vol avec ses deux bras mécaniques. Or, dans la page de mission publiée le 7 novembre, SpaceX détaille presque autant les façons d’interrompre le vol que celles de le réussir.
Autrement dit, un retour anticipé du Ship, comme en septembre, fait partie des scénarios écrits à l’avance.
Sur le papier, le déroulé du vol commence par la partie que SpaceX maîtrise le mieux. Le Super Heavy, le premier étage (ici le Booster 22, dont les 33 moteurs ont été allumés au sol le 25 octobre), doit revenir se faire attraper par la tour environ six minutes et demie après le décollage, une manœuvre que SpaceX a déjà réussie trois fois, mais jamais depuis mars 2025, jamais avec un booster de cette version 3 et jamais depuis ce second pas de tir de Starbase.
Le Ship 42, qui a bouclé ses essais au sol fin octobre, doit ensuite libérer 26 satellites Starlink V3 vers 275 kilomètres d’altitude, puis faire environ 14 tours de la Terre, à peu près un toutes les heures et demie. Le décollage doit avoir lieu dans une fenêtre de 75 minutes, sous réserve du feu vert des autorités américaines.
Comme lors du vol 14, le Ship ne part pas directement en orbite. Il est d’abord placé sur une trajectoire suborbitale dite « passivement sûre », qui le ferait retomber de lui-même dans l’océan si ses moteurs ne se rallumaient pas, et les contrôleurs ne l’autorisent à passer en orbite qu’après avoir vérifié son état.
Une fois là-haut, SpaceX prévoit trois occasions de le faire redescendre plus tôt au-dessus de l’océan, deux près d’Hawaï et une au large du Chili, avec un point de contrôle calé un peu plus de sept heures après le décollage pour cette dernière. Le Super Heavy a lui aussi son plan B, un amerrissage dans le golfe du Mexique si la tour ou le booster ne sont pas en état.
Le vol 14 avait d’ailleurs montré l’utilité de ces garde-fous : le moteur coupé trop tôt aurait été victime d’un simple bug logiciel, selon Elon Musk, mais SpaceX avait préféré ne prendre aucun risque.
Jusqu’ici, tous les vaisseaux Starship (l’étage supérieur) ont fini leur course dans l’océan, loin de toute habitation. Pour rejoindre Starbase, le Ship doit cette fois allumer un seul moteur Raptor 3 environ 21 heures et 35 minutes après le décollage et rentrer dans l’atmosphère au-dessus du Pacifique. Il doit ensuite survoler le nord du Mexique et le sud du Texas, en enchaînant de petits virages pour passer au-dessus des zones les moins peuplées.
Ce survol a exigé une modification de la licence de lancement accordée par la FAA, l’autorité américaine de l’aviation civile, comme l’a détaillé NASASpaceflight le 6 novembre. SpaceX précise donc que le retour n’aura lieu que si le vaisseau remplit des conditions fixées en interne. Sinon, il terminera dans l’océan.
Le final reprend la manœuvre que SpaceX avait montrée en vidéo en octobre. Le Ship arrive par l’ouest en descendant à plat, rallume trois moteurs pour se redresser, puis se glisse entre les bras de la tour, qui se referment sur deux points d’accroche situés sous ses ailerons avant. Elon Musk, CEO de SpaceX, jugeait ce rattrapage « plus probable qu’improbable » fin octobre.
Quand décolle la fusée Starship ?
La fenêtre de lancement s’ouvre ce vendredi 13 novembre à 23 h 45, heure de Paris, et se referme 75 minutes plus tard. Si la fusée part à l’heure et que tout se passe comme prévu, le rattrapage du Ship aura lieu environ 22 heures et 32 minutes plus tard, soit ce samedi 14 novembre vers 22 h 17, heure de Paris. Si elle ne décolle qu’en fin de fenêtre, ce rattrapage glissera vers 23 h 32.

articles.title: L'IA de Gemini s'invite sur Apple Car Play
articles.text:
Google déploie depuis quelques jours l’application Gemini sur Apple CarPlay. Les utilisateurs d’iPhone peuvent y discuter à voix haute avec Gemini Live pendant qu’ils conduisent.
Gemini manquait encore à l’appel sur CarPlay, là où ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Copilot, Meta AI et Grok sont déjà installés. Google rattrape ce retard avec un lancement global, pour tous les utilisateurs iOS.
Une onde sonore, deux boutons et un historique synchronisé
Gemini Live, c’est le mode conversation de Gemini. Le conducteur peut parler, l’IA répond à voix haute, et il est possible de la couper pour ajouter un détail, de changer de sujet ou de faire une pause. Sur CarPlay, l’écran se limite à une onde sonore qui indique si Gemini écoute, réfléchit ou répond. Deux boutons, en haut à gauche, permettent de couper le micro ou de mettre fin à l’échange. En ouvrant l’app, on reprend un chat récent ou on en démarre un nouveau.
A l’arrivée de ChatGPT sur CarPlay, nous apprenions que les assistants de cette catégorie n’ont droit qu’à des interactions vocales, sans texte ni image à l’écran. Gemini arrive plus de sept mois après l’IA d’OpenAI. Jusqu’ici, il n’était présent sur CarPlay qu’à travers Google Maps, sans conversation Live ni application dédiée.
Google met l’accent sur la connexion à sa suite Google Workspace. Gemini peut ainsi lire votre agenda, vous dire à quelle heure partir pour votre prochain rendez-vous, vous donner votre résumé du jour, faire le point sur vos mails non lus ou résumer un long fil d’e-mails, puis vous aider à dicter une réponse. Il peut aussi recommander un lieu à proximité, raconter l’histoire d’un monument ou servir de partenaire pour répéter une présentation ou préparer une conversation difficile. Tout se synchronise avec l’app Gemini de l’iPhone et une fois garé, les résumés et les notes sont déjà dans l’historique.
Pour en profiter, il faut avoir mis à jour l’app Gemini sur l’iPhone, autorisé le micro et utilisé Gemini Live au moins une fois sur le téléphone. Précédemment, Gemini Live avait été déployée sur Android Auto. Siri dispose de son côté d’une app autonome dans iOS 27, elle aussi compatible CarPlay.

articles.title: Ascenso y caída de Jensen Huang: de llevar a NVIDIA a la cima a renunciar entre infidelidades y una presunta espía
articles.text:
La renuncia de Jensen Huang como presidente, CEO y miembro del Consejo de Administración de NVIDIA ha sacudido al mundo entero. La principal cara visible de una de las empresas más importantes del mundo acaba de irse por la puerta trasera, tras más de tres décadas conduciéndola. Esto, por dos grandes escándalos de relaciones extramatrimoniales: uno con una supuesta espía china; el otro, con una empleada de la compañía.
Como ya hemos mencionado, hasta hace pocas semanas era imposible pensar en NVIDIA sin Jensen Huang como CEO. El empresario no solo fue cofundador, sino que la lideró desde el primer día para convertirla en una de las empresas más importantes del mundo. En ese camino logró posicionarla en primera instancia como la referencia más importante del mundo gaming, gracias a su línea de tarjetas gráficas.
Con el tiempo, la apuesta paralela por el hardware especializado para IA pagó con creces, pues la explosión de los modelos generativos convirtió a NVIDIA en la empresa más importante del mundo, no solo del sector tecnológico. Huang fue el principal responsable de tamaño éxito, aunque su coqueteo con el poder tal vez haya sido lo que terminó marcando su caída.
Jensen Huang y NVIDIA: de un restaurante a una mole de 5 billones de dólares
Jensen Huang nació en Taiwán el 17 de febrero de 1963 y se mudó a Estados Unidos cuando todavía era un niño. Se graduó de la universidad como ingeniero electrónico e inició su carrera en el mundo de la tecnología en la década de 1980, primero en AMD y luego en LSI Logic.
En 1992, se produjo el punto de quiebre tanto para Jensen Huang como para el mundo tecnológico tal y como lo conocemos en la actualidad. Reunidos en Denny's, un restaurante de comida rápida, Huang y dos ingenieros de Sun Microsystems llamados Curis Priem y Chris Malachowsky tomaron la decisión de iniciar su propia empresa de tarjetas gráficas. Así nació NVIDIA, cuya fundación oficial se produjo en abril de 1993.
Con solo 30 años, Jensen Huang se convirtió en el CEO de NVIDIA y se encargó de llevar las riendas de la empresa hasta hoy. Así las cosas, el empresario fungió como consejero delegado de la compañía durante más de 33 años ininterrumpidos, abandonando su cargo tras un doble escándalo por infidelidades y un posible caso de espionaje.
El correr de los años le permitió a NVIDIA convertirse en la referencia máxima del hardware para ordenadores enfocados en gaming. Las GPU de la empresa se posicionaron como la opción más buscada debido a sus capacidades y rendimiento, logrando exposición mundial de la mano de amplios acuerdos con múltiples socios fabricantes.
NVIDIA salió a bolsa en 1999 y se mantuvo durante varios años como una tecnológica interesante, pero que los inversores miraban mayormente de reojo. Recién a partir de 2013 comenzó a mostrar números de crecimiento interanual más consistentes, aunque su explosión máxima se dio desde finales de 2022 gracias a la IA.
En paralelo con su apuesta por las tarjetas gráficas para gaming, Jensen Huang impulsó el abordaje del segmento dedicado a la infraestructura para empresas. Puntualmente, al desarrollo de chips avanzados para servidores de inteligencia artificial. Esto le permitió dar un salto bestial tras la popularización de los modelos y las aplicaciones generativas, que se inició con el debut de ChatGPT.
Hasta principios de noviembre de 2022, la capitalización bursátil de NVIDIA rondaba unos nada despreciables 350.000 millones de dólares. Pero la entrada en escena de OpenAI, Anthropic y un sinfín de otras startups de IA generativa llevó al gigante verde a un ascenso meteórico. En junio de 2023, superó 1 billón de dólares de valor de mercado, y en abril de 2024 pasó la barrera de los 2 billones. Apenas unos pocos meses después, en julio, ya valía 3 billones de dólares. La historia se mantuvo bajo la misma tónica en 2025, cuando los por entonces dirigidos por Jensen Huang se convirtieron en los primeros de la historia en superar los 5 billones de dólares de marketcap.
Desde entonces, solo Apple ha logrado superar esa barrera. El pico de capitalización bursátil de NVIDIA llegó a comienzos de octubre de este año, cuando marcó más de 5,6 billones de dólares. Claro que el panorama ha cambiado drásticamente en los últimos días, pues los escándalos de Jensen Huang han impactado sobre la acción de la empresa, borrando varios cientos de miles de millones de dólares.
De hecho, en los minutos posteriores a conocerse la renuncia de Jensen Huang, la acción de NVIDIA cayó hasta un 15 %. Esto llevó a que la empresa quedara por debajo de los 4 billones de dólares, siendo temporalmente tercera detrás de Apple y Microsoft. Al momento de redacción de este artículo, logró reponerse parcialmente para volver a ser segunda en capitalización bursátil.
El coqueteo con el poder, la caída y el futuro
El éxito de NVIDIA de la mano del boom de la IA generativa convirtió a Jensen Huang en una de las figuras más poderosas de Silicon Valley, con llegada directa a la Casa Blanca. Así, el empresario cultivó una relación muy cercana con Donald Trump tras el inicio del segundo mandato del republicano. De hecho, en la más reciente cena entre el presidente de EE. UU. y los principales referentes del sector tecnológico, Huang se sentó a la derecha del mandatario.
Jensen Huang era la personificación del too big to fail ("demasiado grande para fracasar"), pero la cosa cambió solo en un puñado de semanas. A finales de octubre, The New York Times publicó que el CEO de NVIDIA tenía una "relación cercana" con una presunta espía china. Alice Huang, ejecutiva de Megaspeed, una empresa con sede en Singapur dedicada a los centros de datos para IA, estaba bajo sospecha de Estados Unidos de colaborar con la inteligencia del gigante asiático. Incluso se reportó que Trump conocía sobre el asunto pero que evitó involucrarse.
NVIDIA negó de inmediato que el vínculo entre ambos tuviese algo raro, aunque el tono del discurso cambió poco después. El domingo pasado, con una pesquisa del FBI ya en marcha, la compañía anunció que también haría una investigación interna que contaba con el aval de Jensen Huang. En simultáneo, el CEO de la compañía reconoció haber mantenido una relación extramatrimonial con la sospechada de ser una espía.
El panorama no era prometedor, pero nada hacía pensar que el futuro de Jensen Huang al frente de NVIDIA pendiera de un hilo. De hecho, se ha reportado que la mayoría de los integrantes de la junta directiva de la firma eran muy cercanos a él. También, que durante los últimos 10 años el ejecutivo se negó a discutir sobre un posible plan de sucesión.
El vuelco definitivo se dio ayer, 11 de noviembre, cuando un nuevo reporte echó luz a una segunda aventura extramarital de Huang. El jefe del gigante verde mantuvo una relación a escondidas con una empleada de NVIDIA, lo que representaría una violación a las políticas de la compañía respecto de los vínculos entre ejecutivos y subordinados. Esto disparó titulares sobre un Consejo de Administración que analizaba destituir a la principal cara visible de la empresa.
Esta mañana, Jensen Huang finalmente renunció a la conducción de NVIDIA tras 33 años. Colette Kress, jefa de finanzas y vicepresidenta ejecutiva de la compañía, será la CEO interina hasta que se designe un reemplazo permanente. Huang se fue por la puerta trasera, sin un comentario de despedida, 4 días después de pedir disculpas públicas a su esposa por una infidelidad.
Por estas horas hay demasiadas especulaciones sobre el futuro de la firma californiana. Kress se ha comprometido a "seguir construyendo sobre la base extraordinaria que Jensen ha forjado a lo largo de los últimos 33 años". Es lógico pensar que NVIDIA no dejará de ser la principal referente del mundo del hardware para IA, las GPU avanzadas y los chips superpotentes como RTX Spark de la noche a la mañana. No obstante, son lógicas las dudas sobre quién podría tomar las riendas de una compañía hecha a imagen y semejanza de su líder saliente.
No todos en el mundo tecnológico han salido a patear a Jensen Huang mientras yace en el piso. Elon Musk dijo que sería "un honor" contratarlo, mientras que Tim Sweeney manifestó que despedirlo como CEO sería de "un nivel de idiotez" similar al de cuando Apple echó a Steve Jobs. Consumada la renuncia, el jefe de Epic Games expresó que era un "día triste para NVIDIA, los desarrolladores, Estados Unidos y toda la humanidad".

articles.title: Jensen Huang resigns after 33 years at Nvidia
articles.text:
Jensen Huang resigns after 33 years at Nvidia
Nvidia has appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive officer. The board will consider internal and external candidates for a permanent successor.
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has stepped down as president, chief executive officer and board member with immediate effect, ending his 33-year tenure as the company’s chief executive, following a turbulent week.
Nvidia has appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive officer. The board will consider internal and external candidates for a permanent successor.
Kress said, “Nvidia’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.”
Kress will retain the finance role while serving as interim CEO. She joined Nvidia in 2013 after nearly 25 years in finance roles at technology companies including Cisco and Microsoft.
The board appointed former Synopsys chief executive and executive chairman Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever chair.
Jones said Kress understood the business and its customers. He added, “The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”
On November 8, Huang apologised in a company-published message for being unfaithful to his wife and pledged to co-operate with an independent board inquiry into reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.
Reports say Huang had another extramarital affair with a senior executive of Nvidia, in addition to the relationship with a Chinese national Alice Huang, who was allegedly recruited as an intelligence asset by the Chinese government.
On November 10, independent directors appointed former acting US attorney Joon H. Kim and law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead the inquiry. The board said it had no reason to believe national security or company information had been compromised.
Nvidia faces a fast-growing, increasingly competitive AI-chip market. Founded in 1993 as a graphics-chip maker, it later adapted GPUs for parallel computing through software such as CUDA.
In its latest reported quarter, ended on July 26, it recorded revenue of $96.2 billion, including $89 billion from data centres. Its next results are due on November 17.

articles.title: Après les frigos des supermarchés, l’Europe s'inquiète des cyberattaques contre « les appareils ménagers »
articles.text:
En réaction aux cyberattaques visant les frigos de supermarchés en Europe, Juhan Lepassaar, directeur exécutif de l’Enisa, l’agence européenne de cybersécurité, tire la sonnette d’alarme. Selon lui, les appareils ménagers qu’on trouve dans les foyers risquent de se retrouver dans le viseur des cybercriminels.
« Aujourd’hui c’étaient les frigos, demain ce pourrait être les routeurs, et après-demain les appareils ménagers domestiques, et ainsi de suite », explique Juhan Lepassaar dans un entretien accordé à l’AFP.
Désormais connectés à Internet, les lave-linges, les fours, les aspirateurs robots ou les thermostats sont potentiellement exposés à des tentatives de prise de contrôle. Chaque service dont « vous dépendez en tant que citoyen, en tant qu’être humain, comporte une couche dans laquelle intervient un élément numérique, un morceau de code qui, s’il n’est pas protégé, peut être piraté », analyse le directeur exécutif de l’Enisa.
Quelques jours plus tôt, Christophe Bianco, responsable cyber chez Thales, abondait dans le même sens lors d’un point presse. Comme nous l’expliquions déjà en octobre en marge de la cyberattaque nationale, les frigos ne sont que « la partie émergée d’un iceberg ».
« Chez moi, j’ai un robot tondeur qui est connecté. Tous ces équipements qui peuplent de plus en plus nos environnements, dès qu’ils sont connectés, représentent une extension du périmètre à surveiller. Malheureusement, tous ne sont pas passés à travers une activité qui a permis de vérifier leur niveau de sécurité », souligne l’expert de Thales.
Des services essentiels en danger
Pour le responsable de l’Enisa, des cyberattaques pourraient un jour paralyser des services essentiels, comme « l’arrivée des policiers, l’intervention des pompiers, le fonctionnement de l’hôpital, le transport qui vous emmène du point A au point B […] ». Si ces services clés « ne fonctionnent pas, nous subirons un impact immédiat ».
En France, les autorités attribuent officiellement les cyberattaques à Shahid Kaveh, une unité cyber des Gardiens de la Révolution iraniens. Interrogé par l’AFP, Juhan Lepassaar s’est refusé à commenter cette attribution. Le patron de l’Enisa souligne toutefois que l’Europe est dans le viseur de plusieurs puissances étrangères.
« Que ce soit sur la Chine, l’Iran, la République populaire de Corée du Nord, il existe de nombreux acteurs alignés sur des États qui ciblent l’Europe, les entreprises européennes et les intérêts européens », estime le dirigeant.
Outre-Atlantique, le FBI alerte sur des « systèmes ciblés dans le monde entier ». Selon la police fédérale américaine, les cyberattaques ne se limitent pas aux frontières de l’Europe, et visent « les systèmes de réfrigération industrielle et de surveillance de la chaîne du froid » à travers le globe.
À lire aussi : « Une partie » de l’argent récupérée – le Crédit Mutuel Arkéa limite la casse après la cyberattaque
La « cybersécurité n’est pas bon marché »
Pour limiter les risques d’attaque, l’Europe mise sur le Cyber Resilience Act, un cadre qui impose des obligations de sécurité aux fabricants d’objets connectés, en vigueur dès l’année prochaine. Pour Juhan Lepassaar, « tous les incidents peuvent être évités », mais « la question est de savoir si nous sommes prêts à investir pour cela ». La « cybersécurité n’est pas bon marché », résume le responsable.

articles.title: Hugging Face CEO vows to keep fighting for open source AI after Jensen Huang's exit | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue briefly commented on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s departure on Thursday, calling it a “really sad day.” Nvidia had announced its plan to acquire the platform for open source AI models in September for $12.9 billion, making it the second-largest acquisition in the company’s history, just behind that of chipmaker Groq’s assets for $20 billion in December 2025.
“This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!,” Delangue wrote on X.
The post is interesting as it implies that Huang’s departure is potentially worrying to open source advocates, and he’s attempting to offer reassurance.
As Nvidia’s CEO, Huang was known as a strong advocate for open source AI and open-weight models, which is why there could be concerns about how a company that’s no longer under his leadership will now approach this space.
After Nvidia announced its plans to acquire Hugging Face, the U.S. Department of Justice began making inquiries about how the deal would impact competition in the AI market, Reuters reported in October. While Nvidia pledged that the platform would preserve open support, it would also allow the company to control a major distribution channel for AI models.
The Hugging Face deal is still scheduled to close in the first half of 2027. Requests for further comment on the deal status and whether Hugging Face has spoken yet with Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress were not returned.
Huang’s advocacy for open source and open-weight AI has long extended beyond Hugging Face. In July, the CEO published an AI policy letter as his first-ever post on the social network X. The letter, which was signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, Hugging Face, IBM, Palantir, and others, urged the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models. It said models that “anyone can download, inspect, modify, and run on their own infrastructure” are an important part of the AI ecosystem because they make AI “more accessible, adaptable, and widely available.”
Huang also wrote that open-weight models expand access to the AI economy, strengthen competition, and give customers greater control, as they know they won’t become locked into a single provider. “Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” his post on X stated.
In August, Nvidia also announced a $6 billion deal with the coding startup Poolside to help build out an open AI ecosystem in the U.S. to help the country compete against Chinese companies like DeepSeek and Kimi K3, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time. Last month, Nvidia expanded its Nemotron family of open-weight models with a large 120-billion-parameter model for agents used by the enterprise as well as with two new lightweight Bolt models that run on PCs.
Earlier this year, Huang promoted open source AI during his January keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas, noting that open source models have “really revolutionized artificial intelligence.”

As the industry approaches the singularity, embedding trust becomes as vital as technical advancement, ensuring sustainable, scalable semiconductor progress.

articles.title: 8 Nigerian startups bag $4k each at FMYD, Cascador youth founders pitch day - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Eight Nigerian startups have each won NGN5 million (US$4,000) in non-dilutive funding at the pitch day of the Founders Programme run by the Federal Ministry of Youth Development (FMYD), through the Nigerian Youth Academy (NiYA), and Cascador.
The pilot programme drew more than 19,000 applications after launching on International Youth Day in August, with 17 founders from 13 states selected for a four-week accelerator. Participating startups are tackling challenges such as post-harvest losses, malnutrition, waste, vaccine cold chains, clean energy and digital education.
Implemented by technical partner Sapphital, the programme offered training in sales, customer service and investment readiness, as well as regulatory sessions with agencies including NEXIM Bank, SEC, NITDA, NAFDAC and the Nigeria Data Protection Commission.
The eight pitch day winners are SewPro, Biuda, Sparklean Station Nigeria, Backel Food Services, Shellify, Rèkool Access Technology, Agrosavvy Consult and Craft Planet. The remaining nine founders will each receive NGN1 million (US$750), and all 17 get access to Sapphital’s SMECore ERP platform.
“We share NiYA and FMYD’s commitment to giving Nigeria’s ambitious young founders the capital and practical support they need to build stronger businesses,” said Trish Thomas, CEO of Cascador. “Seeing eight deserving founders secure funding at Pitch Day is an encouraging outcome for the pilot.”
All graduates keep NiYA alumni status and priority for future opportunities. The academy aims to train 7 million young Nigerians within two years.

articles.title: Kutlerri.ai raises $4M to help US restaurants grow revenue and cut costs using AI agents
articles.text:
Kutlerri.ai
View Brand Publisher
Kutlerri.ai raises $4M to help US restaurants grow revenue and cut costs using AI agents
Founded by former HighRadius executives Kiran Rana and Payal Tripathy, Kutlerri.ai charges restaurants a percentage of the revenue its AI agents generate or the costs they save.
Houston and Bhubaneswar-based Kutlerri.ai has raised $4 million from Houston-based Narahari Investments to scale its AI agents that help restaurants increase revenue and reduce operating costs.
Founded in December 2025 by former HighRadius executives Kiran Rana and Payal Tripathy, the startup develops AI agents that handle specific revenue and cost-related tasks for restaurants. Unlike conventional software subscriptions, Kutlerri.ai charges operators based on the revenue generated or costs saved by its agents.
The company currently serves restaurants in the US and has more than 10 signed customers. Its product and engineering team is based in Bhubaneswar, Odisha; it also has an office in Houston, Texas. The core founding team includes Ankit Narain and Rishabh Srivastav.
The funding will help scale its first commercial product, the AI Catering Sales Agent, bring three agents currently in beta to market, and develop a mobile-first self-service app.
Addressing restaurant profitability
According to the National Restaurant Association's 2026 State of the Restaurant Industry report, US restaurant and foodservice sales are projected to reach $1.55 trillion in 2026, although 42% of operators surveyed reported that they did not make a profit in 2025.
The association also noted in July 2026 that rising costs continued to put pressure on restaurant profitability. Even before the post-pandemic increase in costs, a typical restaurant retained only about five cents of every dollar earned.
With margins this narrow, even small improvements can make a difference. Kutlerri.ai focuses on increasing revenue and reducing costs through AI agents that take on tasks restaurants may not have dedicated staff to manage.
Restaurants already use software for point-of-sale operations, kitchen displays, inventory, online ordering, payroll, and accounting. However, these systems primarily record information rather than act on it.
For instance, catering enquiries may go unanswered, or delivery advertisements may continue running without producing results. Addressing such problems generally requires dedicated staff, which many independent restaurants cannot afford.
Kutlerri.ai’s agents are designed to handle these tasks. Its revenue agents work on catering, third-party delivery, and online ordering, while its cost agents focus on delivery advertising, food and labour costs, daily preparation, and waste.
Restaurants can use the agents through a fully managed service or, once launched, a mobile-first self-service app. In both models, Kutlerri.ai charges a percentage of the additional revenue generated or costs saved. If an agent does not deliver measurable results, the restaurant does not pay.
Catering agent generates $450,000 for RASA
Kutlerri.ai's first commercial product focuses on catering sales.
According to MONKEY's State of Catering 2026 report, 60% of catering orders came from just 5% of customers. The findings were based on transactional data from more than 8,000 restaurant locations and two million catering orders.
The figures highlight the importance of attracting new catering customers and reconnecting with previous ones, particularly for restaurants without dedicated sales teams.
The AI Catering Sales Agent identifies potential catering customers within a 30-mile radius of a restaurant. It contacts businesses through email, text messages, and phone calls, reconnects with inactive customers, responds to incoming calls, chats, and emails, and closes orders. Restaurant operators approve decisions and retain their customer relationships.
Kutlerri.ai developed the agent with RASA, a five-location fast-casual restaurant group in the Washington, DC, area. The two companies worked together to develop the product around RASA’s catering sales requirements, with the restaurant group paying for the service throughout the development period.
According to Kutlerri.ai, the agent generated $450,000 in new catering revenue for RASA over 10 months, more than 10X the amount the restaurant group paid for the service, without requiring additional hires.
The catering agent is now live with operators in most major US cities, the company said.
From HighRadius to restaurant operations
Rana, CEO, and Tripathy, COO, previously worked at HighRadius, where business functions had clear ownership of financial performance.
Their interest in the restaurant sector began after observing the operations of a restaurant run by someone close to them. While the restaurant used several systems to track performance, there was no dedicated person to act on the information.
The founders subsequently spoke with other operators, including fast-casual restaurants and multi-location groups generating around $3 million annually.
They found similar challenges: scattered data, delayed identification of problems, decisions based on judgement rather than data, and margins that had remained unchanged for years.
These observations led them to build Kutlerri.ai around AI agents that could take responsibility for specific revenue and cost-related functions.
Expansion plans
Kutlerri.ai’s product & engineering, marketing, business development and customer success teams operate from India, with each function responsible for outcomes linked to restaurant profitability.
The company currently has one commercially available agent, three agents in beta testing inside restaurants, and two more under development.
It plans to expand its strategy, marketing, customer success and engineering teams as it develops and launches these products.
While Kutlerri.ai currently focuses on US restaurants, it is open to expanding into India and other markets in the future. As the company continues to grow, explore career opportunities with the team [email protected].
