articles.title: Technical Debt is Social; it is the Price of Learning by Doing
articles.text:
Technical debt is not necessarily a sign of poor engineering. It can be the price of learning through software in use. As AI accelerates code production beyond our capacity to understand code and context, technical debt increasingly becomes a sociotechnical challenge, Xin Yao noted in her talk "What If Your Biggest Technical Debt Is Social", at GOTO Copenhagen.
Yao quoted Ward Cunningham, who defined debt as "not-quite-right code". Debt sounds like a negative thing, but it can be a deliberate business strategy, she explained:
If we release the code now, well knowing it’s not perfect for the future yet, we’ll get some business feedback, we’ll get some user feedback, we’ll probably get paid for something, and that’s good as a business strategy.
Debt isn’t about poorly written code; it arises when we design software with incomplete knowledge. Hence, debt is the price of learning by doing, Yao argued. Releasing software allows us to test our assumptions against reality. Once we’ve got a learning experience, we have to put that experience back into our code and pay off the debt, she added. The debt becomes problematic when our software doesn’t catch up with our new learning.
Debt can be a good communication strategy toward management. It provides an economic argument for the cost of postponing architectural improvements. However, framing technical debt solely as something to eliminate misses its strategic value. The question is not whether to incur debt, but whether the learning it enables justifies the cost, and whether we actually repay it.
Yao referred to Kent Beck’s article "Earn and Learn," which explores features vs. futures. Features deliver value today, while the future is actually the optionality to adapt those features, Yao explained:
Every bit of code already coded is complexity and a constraint. Every feature removes some future. If you go on producing features, maybe using your LLMs, then at a certain point, all you can do is use your capacity to pay the interest, to fix the code, and you can no longer release features.
The challenge is to balance delivering features with preserving future options, Yao said. Sometimes, delaying a design commitment preserves options until we know more, and this includes postponing some upfront architecture decisions to the last responsible moment as well. As Beck argues, waiting is not laziness; waiting is holding an asset.
Technical debt can therefore be understood as learning made visible in software. We design based on what we know, observe software’s impact, modularity, and its architecture’s implications, and we update our understanding, Yao explained:
The software no longer fits what we now understand, and yesterday’s good understanding becomes today’s debt.
AI introduces a new challenge: software can now be produced faster than teams can develop a shared understanding of its behavior, design decisions and consequences, Yao argued.
Agentic coding makes debt repayment more complex; beyond addressing poorly written AI-generated code, teams must close the gap between what the software actually does and what they understand it to do, while ensuring the code keeps pace with their evolving domain and architectural understanding. Paying off debt is no longer just a technical task, but a sociotechnical one, Yao concluded.
InfoQ interviewed Xin Yao after her talk.
InfoQ: What does learning from technical debt look like, and what benefit does it bring?
Xin Yao: We design and release software based on our best current understanding, then test our assumptions against business and user reality. Paying off debt means incorporating that learning back into the software and closing the gap between what we knew when we released the first iteration and what we know now.
Each iteration creates new debt and new learning. Small batches and tight feedback loops help teams retain the memory of their initial design decisions and continuously repay the old debt with new learning.
InfoQ: What does technical debt look like now that developers are using artificial intelligence?
Yao: With agentic coding, software production can outpace human understanding. Code increasingly becomes a fossil record of agents’ decisions, while humans remain accountable for its consequences. Local productivity gains can create collective costs: more code, weaker ownership and growing gaps in shared understanding.
A study on How Developers Discuss the Burden of AI-Assisted Software Development describes this as "a tragedy of the commons". The danger is not merely more poorly written agentic code, but accelerated learning debt across the sociotechnical system.

articles.title: Fine-grained access control for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base tools | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Fine-grained access control for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base tools
More enterprises are building AI agents into their daily work, and a common pattern is an agent that searches internal documents to compose its answers. A single organization might soon run hundreds of agents, each connected to many data sources and tools. This raises a question. When an agent searches on behalf of a user, can you make sure that it uses only the information that user is allowed to see?
Consider AnyCompany, a fictional company that builds an internal assistant shared by all employees. An employee in department A asks, “Compare my department’s business plan with the notice to all departments, and list the initiatives that are behind schedule.” The agent writes its own search queries and keeps searching internal documents until it has enough information. Employees in department B ask the same assistant the same question. If the application doesn’t scope searches to each user, the department B business plan can end up in an answer to an employee in department A. If you replace the departments with customer companies, the same problem occurs in a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) architecture where multiple customers share one assistant and knowledge base.
Controlling access to multi-tenant data through this agent is harder than in traditional applications. In a traditional application, the application code determines who the signed-in user is and searches with that user’s permissions. In an agent, a large language model (LLM) decides at runtime which tool to call and with which arguments. If a search tool takes “who to search as” as an argument, the LLM decides that value too. A prompt injection or an LLM error might then make the agent search as a different employee.
In this post, we build an internal assistant for AnyCompany. All employees share the same agent and knowledge base, yet each employee can search only the documents they’re allowed to view. We use Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base as the search backend and expose it to the agent as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The design principle is to not let the LLM decide who the user is. Instead, trusted code decides, based on information that your identity provider has verified. On top of that, we add independent layers of defense in case that mechanism has a bug or is bypassed.
Solution overview
Managed Knowledge Base has a feature called ACL awareness. When a search request includes a user context (userContext) with the user’s email in userId, the knowledge base returns only the documents that user is allowed to view. If your application calls the search API directly, the application code sets the search scope from the authentication result. Build multi-tenant agentic chat applications on enterprise data with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base shows this pattern. When you expose the knowledge base as an MCP tool through AgentCore Gateway, however, userContext becomes a tool argument, and the LLM constructs its value. Neither the gateway nor the knowledge base verifies that this value belongs to the authenticated user.
This solution injects verified user attributes into tool calls at the tool layer (AgentCore Gateway). It then scopes the search by those attributes at the resource layer (Managed Knowledge Base). The sample stores three documents in a single knowledge base: business plans for department A and department B, and a notice shared with all departments. Two users, user-a in department A and user-b in department B, search through the same agent. The following diagram shows the architecture.
The request flow is as follows. The step numbers correspond to the numbers in Figure 1. Figure 1 omits the call from the web app to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, so its step numbers differ from the diagram in the repository README.
- The user signs in with Amazon Cognito and receives an access token, a JSON Web Token (JWT). A pre token generation AWS Lambda trigger adds an email claim to it. The agent forwards this token in the Authorization header when it sends MCP requests to the gateway.
- The JWT authorizer of the gateway validates the signature, expiration, and client ID of the token.
- A request interceptor (an AWS Lambda function) on the gateway resolves the email from the validated token and overwrites the userContext argument of tools/call.
- Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (Policy in AgentCore) evaluates the modified request against a Cedar policy. It denies the request if userContext.userId doesn’t match the email claim in the JWT.
- The connector target calls the Managed Knowledge Base search API with the execution role of the gateway. The resource-based policy of the knowledge base denies searches from principals other than this role.
- With ACL awareness, the knowledge base returns only chunks from documents that the userContext user is allowed to view.
The four mechanisms map to layers and lines of defense as follows.
|  | Tool layer (AgentCore Gateway) | Resource layer (Managed Knowledge Base) | 
| Primary defense | Request interceptor: injects userContext deterministically from the verified token, which helps prevent the LLM or the client from spoofing it | ACL awareness: returns only the documents that the userContext user is allowed to view | 
| Secondary defense | Policy in AgentCore: checks the injected userContext against the token and denies requests that don’t match | Resource-based policy: denies search requests from principals other than the gateway execution role | 
For requests that go through the gateway, the two primary defenses are enough to achieve fine-grained access control, as long as no other principal can call the knowledge base. ACL awareness filters results based on the userContext that it receives and isn’t an authorization mechanism by itself. The two secondary defenses cover cases where an assumption behind the primary defenses fails, such as an interceptor bug or a principal that calls the knowledge base without going through the gateway. Add them based on your requirements. If other principals in the account have bedrock:Retrieve permissions, add the resource-based policy. The rest of this post covers ACL awareness, the MCP tools for Managed Knowledge Base, the request interceptor, Policy in AgentCore, and the resource-based policy, in that order.
Prerequisites
- An AWS account and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to create the resources in this post.
- An AWS Region where Managed Knowledge Base, AgentCore Gateway, Policy in AgentCore, and AgentCore runtime are available.
- Access to the Amazon Bedrock model that the agent uses.
- Node.js 22 or later and npm.
- uv, to package the agent and run the verification script.
- If you adapt the pattern to an existing Amazon Cognito user pool, the user pool must be on the Essentials or Plus feature plan, which access token customization requires. The stack in this post creates a user pool on the Essentials plan.
You can deploy the architecture in Figure 1 with a single AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) stack from the agentcore-access-control directory of the sample-managed-knowledge-base-patterns repository. Run the commands in this post from that directory. The repository installs the AWS CDK CLI and aws-cdk-lib (2.274.0 or later) as npm dependencies. The stack also deploys a web app on Amazon CloudFront and runs the agent, built with Strands Agents, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime. By default, the agent uses Claude Sonnet 5.5 through the global cross-Region inference profile global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5. The agent forwards the access token of the signed-in user to the gateway and contains no access control logic. For deployment steps, including how to fetch only this directory, see the README.
Scope searches per user with ACL awareness
Managed Knowledge Base is a new type of Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base. You connect a data source, and it runs parsing, chunking, embedding, indexing, search, and reranking as a fully managed service. It provides two search APIs. Retrieve runs a hybrid search. AgenticRetrieveStream breaks a query into subqueries and searches multiple knowledge bases iteratively.
ACL awareness keeps the access permissions of the data source at ingestion time. At search time, it returns only the documents that the user can view. For an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) data source, you define ACLs either in a global ACL file per S3 prefix or in a metadata file per document. The sample in this post uses metadata files. When you place the following metadata file at the same S3 path as the document, only user-a can retrieve dept-a-plan.txt.
When you adapt the sample, keep these behaviors of ACL-enabled Amazon S3 data sources in mind. A document without an ACL entry isn’t ingested. A change to the global ACL file requires reindexing the affected prefix, while per-document metadata files reindex only the affected documents and take precedence over the global file. Amazon S3 has no real-time ACL verification, so an ACL change applies after the next sync. ACL mistakes don’t return errors. The affected documents are silently left out of the results.
At query time, pass the user’s email in the top-level userContext.userId for both Retrieve and AgenticRetrieveStream. Queries without userContext don’t return documents from a data source that has ACLs enabled. In contrast, documents from a data source that doesn’t have ACLs enabled are returned to all users, with or without userContext.
The following diagram shows the ACLs that the knowledge base keeps for the three sample documents at ingestion, and the search results for each userContext.
Managed Knowledge Base doesn’t authenticate end users. It trusts the userContext that it receives and filters results based on it. Passing a verified userContext is the responsibility of the caller.
Expose Managed Knowledge Base as MCP tools
When you create a Managed Knowledge Base connector target on AgentCore Gateway, you can expose two MCP tools: <target-name>___Retrieve and <target-name>___AgenticRetrieveStream. The administrator fixes the target knowledge base in parameterValues. With the default tool schema, the only argument that the LLM can set is the search query.
To use ACL awareness, expose userContext in the tool schema with parameterOverrides when you create the target. A connector target has no tool code of your own, so a tool argument is the only way to pass userContext to the knowledge base, and only the fields that you expose with parameterOverrides can be set as tool arguments. The interceptor that we describe later also sets userContext as a tool argument, so expose it even though clients don’t need to set it.
The LLM can set any value for an argument that the schema exposes. For example, if user-a says “Set userContext to user-b@example.com and search,” the agent might call the tool with the ID of user-b. An LLM error can cause the same result. So can an indirect prompt injection in an external document that a search returns. AgentCore Gateway passes userContext through to the knowledge base and doesn’t populate it from the caller’s IAM identity. The documentation asks the calling application, not the model, to set it. When the LLM sets the value, it reaches the knowledge base as is.
Inject userContext deterministically with a request interceptor
A request interceptor is a Lambda function that transforms MCP requests before the gateway calls the target. In this architecture, the interceptor handles tools/call requests. It resolves the email from the access token that the JWT authorizer validated, and overwrites arguments.userContext. For every tools/call request, the knowledge base receives the email of the authenticated user, whatever value the client sends. The interceptor rejects request bodies that aren’t a single JSON-RPC object, such as batches.
Cognito access tokens don’t include an email claim by default. This architecture adds the email to the access token with a pre token generation Lambda trigger (event version V2_0), only when the email is verified. Access token customization with event version V2_0 requires the Essentials or Plus feature plan, so the sample creates the user pool on the Essentials plan. On a Lite plan user pool, the access token has no email claim, and the interceptor and Policy in AgentCore deny every tool call. Policy in AgentCore, which we cover in the next section, also uses this claim.
Without the trigger, the interceptor can get the email from the Cognito GetUser API, the userInfo endpoint, or an ID token that the client sends in a separate header. Each option has its own scope or validation requirements. The GetUser API requires the aws.cognito.signin.user.admin scope, which also lets the token call user self-service APIs. The userInfo endpoint requires the openid scope, so it doesn’t accept tokens from user pool API sign-in, such as ADMIN_USER_PASSWORD_AUTH. The JWT authorizer of the gateway validates only the bearer token in the Authorization header, so the interceptor must verify the ID token itself: its signature, iss, aud, token_use, expiration, and email_verified, and that its sub matches the access token. Cognito ID tokens carry email whether or not it’s verified. All three methods leave the access token without an email claim. The policy in the next section then has nothing to compare with and denies every call, so use these methods only if you don’t add Policy in AgentCore.
With another identity provider (IdP), such as Microsoft Entra ID, you can add email to access tokens as an optional claim for both defenses to reference. However, Microsoft doesn’t guarantee that this value is correct or immutable and advises against using it for authorization. For ACL matching, your IdP or application must verify the association between the authenticated user and their email within trusted tenants. Update ACLs and sync the data source when email addresses change or are reassigned.
ACL matching uses an exact email match, so your identity provider must keep each email unique and unchanged. For this reason, the sample user pool disables self sign-up and makes the email attribute immutable.
You attach the interceptor in interceptorConfigurations of the gateway. With passRequestHeaders: true, the gateway passes the Authorization header that the JWT authorizer validated to the interceptor. The headers that the gateway passes include the bearer token, so make sure that the interceptor doesn’t log them. The sample logs only the tool name, whether the client supplied userContext, and whether the interceptor replaced it, not the event, the headers, or the token.
Cognito access tokens carry the app client ID in client_id and include aud only when the client requests resource binding. The JWT authorizer checks allowedClients against client_id and allowedAudience against aud, and verifies both when you set both. So set only allowedClients to the app client ID. With resource binding, you can also set allowedAudience to the resource URI in aud.
The MCP client only attaches the access token to the Authorization header. It doesn’t need code that handles userContext. In the sample, the agent on AgentCore runtime forwards the access token that it received from the web app.
In the sample, AgentCore runtime and the gateway accept the same access token, and the agent forwards it. If your requirements call for tokens that only one resource accepts, request them with resource binding and set allowedAudience on each authorizer. Resource binding is available only with managed login.
Validate the injected request with Policy in AgentCore
With only the interceptor, access control depends on a single component. In the following cases, the gateway accepts a request with an invalid userContext as is:
- A bug in the interceptor injects a wrong value or skips the overwrite.
- An unauthorized code change injects the value of another user.
- A configuration change detaches the interceptor from the gateway.
Policy in AgentCore evaluates tool calls to the gateway with Cedar policies. It runs after the request interceptor. It can reference the claims of the token that the JWT authorizer validated as tags on the principal. The following policy permits a call only when the injected userContext.userId matches the email claim in the JWT. The policy engine denies calls that don’t meet this condition.
In this policy, principal represents the authenticated user, and resource specifies the gateway ARN. The action kb___Retrieve refers to the Retrieve tool on the gateway target named kb. The when clause requires the tool argument userContext.userId to match the JWT’s email claim. The snippet shows the policy for kb___Retrieve. The sample creates a second policy with the same condition for kb___AgenticRetrieveStream, because each policy names a single action and the policy engine denies any request that no permit policy matches.
The following figure shows how Policy in AgentCore denies a tool call when the interceptor doesn’t overwrite userContext correctly.
The interceptor and the policy both use the email from the same token, but they read it from different sources. The policy takes the expected value from the signature-verified token, and the actual value from the request body that the interceptor built. This lets it detect a missing interceptor or a wrong injection. The IdP, the pre token generation trigger, and the policy configuration itself remain shared dependencies of both. With the policy alone, the LLM goes back to constructing userContext, so we recommend that you combine injection and validation.
You attach the policy engine that holds the Cedar policy in policyEngineConfiguration of the gateway. When you set mode to ENFORCE, the gateway denies requests based on the evaluation result. When you add policies to a gateway that’s already in use, you can start with LOG_ONLY, check the decisions in the traces, and then switch to ENFORCE.
Create the gateway target before creating the Cedar policies. Creating the target registers its tool schema with the policy engine. Policy creation fails if a policy references a tool that has not yet been registered, whatever the validationMode.
Restrict access to the knowledge base with a resource-based policy
Policy in AgentCore evaluates only requests that go through a gateway with the policy engine attached. Two paths bypass the tool-layer controls. One is another gateway without the interceptor and the policy that points to the same knowledge base. The other is a direct call to the Retrieve API from an SDK or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI).
Managed Knowledge Base supports resource-based policies. When you attach the following policy to the knowledge base, it explicitly denies Retrieve and GetDocumentContent to principals other than the gateway execution role. Agentic retrieval can call GetDocumentContent to expand results to full documents. An explicit deny takes precedence over an allow in an identity-based policy in the same account, so the deny also applies to administrators and to other consumers of the knowledge base, such as the test window on the console. If other roles need to search the knowledge base, add their Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) to ArnNotEquals.
With AWS CDK, you can attach this policy document with CfnKnowledgeBasePolicy, which maps to the AWS::Bedrock::KnowledgeBasePolicy resource type. Set aws:PrincipalArn to the ARN of the gateway execution role, for example gwRole.roleArn.
You can’t list bedrock:AgenticRetrieveStream in the Action element of the policy. However, the searches inside AgenticRetrieveStream authorize bedrock:Retrieve for the caller on each knowledge base. As a result, the deny in this policy also blocks searches through AgenticRetrieveStream.
A resource-based policy limits which IAM principals can search the knowledge base. It can’t deny another gateway that reuses the same execution role. Don’t share the execution role with other workloads. Restrict which users can pass the role (iam:PassRole) and manage the resource-based policy (bedrock:PutResourcePolicy, bedrock:GetResourcePolicy, and bedrock:DeleteResourcePolicy), because anyone who can change or delete the policy can remove this control. The policy also doesn’t cover control plane operations such as GetKnowledgeBase, so protect the knowledge base configuration with identity-based policies.
Test the solution
The scripts/verify_defenses.py script in the repository signs in as both users and confirms that each mechanism blocks the path that it targets. Each sample document contains a unique code, so the script can tell from a response whether a document was inadvertently disclosed. The script signs in as the demo users with ADMIN_USER_PASSWORD_AUTH. For the AWS permissions that it needs, see docs/verification.md. The agent scenario depends on the model, so the script reports it as inconclusive (SKIP) if the agent doesn’t send the spoofed userContext in three turns.
To check Policy in AgentCore and the resource-based policy on their own, deploy the stack with -c enableBypassSimulation=true. This flag adds two test gateways for the same knowledge base. One has no interceptor, and the other has neither an interceptor nor a policy engine. Both run as a test role that the resource-based policy doesn’t exempt. Redeploy without the flag after testing to remove them. The following table shows the results.
| Scenario | Result | Blocked by | 
| user-a and user-b send the same query | Each user gets only the documents in their ACL | ACL awareness | 
| user-a calls kb___Retrieve or kb___AgenticRetrieveStream with the userContext of user-b | Only the documents user-a can view return | Request interceptor | 
| user-a prompts the agent to set the userContext of user-b | The agent might set it. If it does, only the documents user-a can view return | Request interceptor | 
| A client sends the userContext of another user to a gateway without an interceptor | The gateway denies the tool call with a Tool Execution Denied error | Policy in AgentCore | 
| A separate gateway with no interceptor, no policy, and its own execution role searches the knowledge base | The tool returns an error because the knowledge base denies the search | Resource-based policy | 
| A user with administrator permissions calls Retrieve directly from an SDK | AccessDeniedException with an explicit deny in a resource-based policy | Resource-based policy | 
| A user with administrator permissions calls AgenticRetrieveStream directly from an SDK | The stream fails with a dependencyFailedException that wraps the explicit deny on bedrock:Retrieve | Resource-based policy | 
When user-a and user-b send the opening question, the answer for user-a draws on the department A business plan and the notice, and the answer for user-b draws on the department B business plan and the notice.
The web app shows the tool arguments that the LLM generated next to the documents that came back. When user-a asks the agent to search as user-b, the app shows the spoofed userContext, but only the documents of user-a appear.
The following screenshot shows the web app after user-a asks the agent to search as user-b.
Clean up
To avoid future charges, delete the stack when you finish testing. Run npx cdk destroy in the infra directory of the pattern. This deletes the knowledge base, the S3 buckets and their objects, the user pool, the demo user password in AWS Secrets Manager, and the Amazon CloudWatch Logs log groups of every Lambda function and of the agent runtime.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how to share an agent and a knowledge base across a company and still limit each user’s searches to the documents they’re allowed to view. As the primary defense, a request interceptor injects userContext from the verified token, and ACL awareness in Managed Knowledge Base scopes the search. Based on your requirements, Policy in AgentCore validates the injected value independently, and a resource-based policy denies searches that bypass the gateway.
The underlying design principle is to not let the LLM generate values that affect authorization. This principle also applies to a multi-tenant SaaS architecture where multiple customers share a knowledge base. It also applies to MCP tools other than Managed Knowledge Base that take arguments affecting access control. Deploy the CDK stack from the GitHub repository and try it with your own data sources and IdP. To learn when to use interceptors and when to use policies, see Secure AI agents with Policy and Lambda interceptors in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway.
The architecture in this post uses the built-in AgentCore Gateway connector for Managed Knowledge Base. If you’re considering migrating from a Customer-managed Knowledge Base to a Managed Knowledge Base, the amazon-bedrock skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS includes a migration procedure to help you evaluate and plan the transition. It works in coding agents that you already use, such as Kiro, Claude Code, and Cursor. The agent reads your current configuration with read-only calls and writes a migration plan, optionally with a cost comparison based on your measured usage. After you approve the plan, it creates the new knowledge base next to the original and doesn’t change or delete the original. For the benefits of Managed Knowledge Base and a step-by-step migration walkthrough, see Migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base with your coding agent.

articles.title: EU's proposed Digital Fairness Act takes aim at Duolingo streaks, autoplay, and manipulative apps
articles.text:
In brief: Plenty of apps work hard to retain users, whether it's a pop-up claiming only two items are left or even something like a Duolingo streak you're scared to break. On Wednesday, the European Commission proposed a Digital Fairness Act that would outlaw many of those manipulative "dark patterns." Surprisingly, it doesn't stop at protecting kids. Adults would get to switch off addictive features like autoplay and streaks, too.
That off switch could reach well beyond social media. As WIRED notes, it would cover the daily streaks in apps like Strava and Duolingo. That could sting, since streaks are how those apps keep people coming back. Duolingo once wrote that a new streak animation alone made brand-new learners 1.7% more likely to stick around for a week.
Until now, Brussels could only really chase these designs on online platforms through the Digital Services Act. Last Friday, it accused TikTok of trapping users in "rabbit holes" through its For You feed, months after flagging the app's infinite scroll and autoplay. Its proposed Kids Act targets addictive design too, but only for children.
Beyond addictive features, the new act also names specific dark patterns. Fake claims that a product is almost sold out would be banned, along with opt-out buttons worded to make you feel bad for declining.
Subscriptions get a cleanup as well. Free trials couldn't roll into a paid plan without your active approval. Canceling one would have to be easy, too. If something still goes wrong, you'd have the right to speak to an actual human customer service representative.
Ticketmaster users won't get nearly as much relief. Despite years of fury over surge-priced concert tickets, the act doesn't ban dynamic pricing outright. Instead, officials settled on transparency, as The Irish Times reports. So people waiting in a virtual queue would see the current price and the highest it could climb, in real time.
To make all this stick, the Commission wants the power to investigate large cross-border cases itself. In those instances, fines could reach 6% of global annual turnover. None of it is law yet, though. The European Parliament and member states still have to agree on the text, and the rules would only apply a year after the law enters into force.
Meanwhile, Google, Meta, and TikTok sued last week to block a California law will ban addictive feeds, endless scrolling, and autoplay starting in January. That one only covers kids under 16. Europe's version would hand the same off switch to adults as well.

articles.title: Chainguard defends its choice to break the PHP security embargo: "We own the decision."
articles.text:
Chainguard defends its choice to break the PHP security embargo: “We own the decision.”
At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 this week, Chainguard co-founder and CTO Matt Moore defended the company’s decision to release patched PHP images before an agreed-upon embargo with other partners had lifted.
When Chainguard shipped patched PHP container images more than six hours ahead of an October 21 coordinated security release, PHP’s maintainers accused the company of giving attackers a head start. Chainguard argues attackers already had one.
In an interview with The New Stack, Moore said, “We own the decision that we chose to do it. Nobody could force us to do it — but we did not do it in a vacuum.” He also described, in discussions with TNS, other participants in the embargo and security vendors’ reports of activity targeting the vulnerabilities before Chainguard released its images.
Chainguard was not saying that they patched it faster so they shipped it first. According to Moore, Chainguard believed attackers could already exploit the bugs, or were at least close to figuring out how — or were trying to figure it out.
The two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 (out-of-memory corruption) and CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state), collectively known as PHP2Shell, were serious memory-management and error-handling flaws. Under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker could execute code on a PHP server.
The two bugs involved PHP’s handling of memory exhaustion and its failure to clear references to freed memory between requests. In the first, reaching a memory limit at the wrong moment could interrupt PHP before it finished setting up internal data. Later processing could mistake that unfinished data for valid information. In the second vulnerability, an error could leave PHP holding a reference to memory from an earlier request that had already been freed. A subsequent request could then access that invalid memory. Under exploitable conditions, these failures could let an attacker run code inside the server’s PHP process.
Researchers demonstrated remote code execution through both Apache/mod_php and application-level PHP-FPM paths for the first vulnerability, and against a real-world Apache/mod_php application for the second.
These were problems in PHP itself, not something an administrator could fix by simply updating a WordPress plugin. It was a fundamental and nasty security hole.
How bad were the flaws?
PHP’s advisories rate both vulnerabilities 9.2, or critical, under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0. Exploitability depends on the PHP build, server configuration, extensions, and application behavior. The advisories do not establish that every PHP installation can be compromised. PHP released fixes in versions 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12. The potential exposure is substantial: As of November 11, W3Techs reported that PHP powered 68.8% of websites whose server-side programming language it could identify.
According to the PHP Foundation’s account, a developer investigating issues from a 2024 security audit spotted the out-of-memory problem, but no concrete attack path was established then. Proposed fixes risked compatibility breaks, new denial-of-service problems, or changes across PHP extensions.
On August 11, Calif researcher Ryan A. reported remote code execution from the same underlying problem. From that date, fixing it became the PHP Foundation security team’s top priority. OpenAI independently reported the same underlying flaw. Wiz supplied additional attack vectors on August 24, and OpenAI reported more on September 18.
How the PHP security patch came apart
In response, PHP’s maintainers coordinated fixes with researchers and distributors. Then details about the release process began leaking.
On October 20, the CVE identifiers circulated publicly, accompanied by an incorrect release time and severity score. PHP responded by issuing a warning and moving the release forward a day, to October 21 at 14:00 UTC. Calif, one of the reporting security companies, then mistakenly published a video demonstrating its proof of concept. Although the video was deleted, copies circulated. PHP also acknowledged that mitigation advice given to critical infrastructure providers might have leaked.
In short, the information environment was already a mess before Chainguard published anything.
But the PHP Foundation maintained that its remaining coordination window still served a purpose: specifically that distributors were packaging the fixes, and releasing immediately would leave many users without a straightforward update path. At 07:41 UTC on October 21, Chainguard published its patched images anyway — six hours and 19 minutes before the agreed-upon time.
The PHP Foundation criticized this move: “Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix.” That meant, it argued, that “any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release.”
A patched binary protects the person who installs it. It can also tell an attacker where to look.
That was the PHP Foundation’s central objection. A patched binary protects the person who installs it. It can also tell an attacker where to look.
Moore’s defense: The advantage had already shifted to the attackers
Moore doesn’t dispute that releasing patched binaries can help attackers. He argues that, by then, the advantage an embargo was supposed to preserve had already eroded.
While defenders alone know about a vulnerability, he told The New Stack, confidentiality gives them time to prepare. Once attackers have enough information to exploit it, withholding available fixes can reverse that advantage: attackers can act, while users outside the embargo cannot protect themselves.
“If we see exploitation in the wild, it’s incumbent upon us to release it,” Moore said. In his account, reports from other security vendors were what pushed Chainguard toward that conclusion.
Moore said Chainguard learned on the Friday before the release that PHP had a vulnerability, pointed its vulnerability-hunting harness at the software, and found the vulnerability or produced a proof of concept within hours. That is Chainguard’s account of its own research. But it helps explain the company’s thinking in breaking the embargo: If your tools can find the bug quickly, you have to consider whether attackers’ tools can too.
He also disputed the implication that Chainguard simply went off on its own. According to Moore, other embargo participants woke Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc to discuss the situation while PHP maintainers in Europe were asleep. Moore declined to identify those participants.
Moore accepted that Chainguard made the final decision. It does, however, distinguish the company’s account of a disputed emergency decision from an account in which it ignored everyone else without discussion.
The evidence supports concern, not certainty
Public evidence supports Chainguard’s concern that attackers were already targeting the flaws. For example, Amazon Threat Intelligence reported a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt against its MadPot honeypot network on October 17, four days before public disclosure. It also reported proof-of-concept exploits beginning around 02:00 UTC on October 21, followed by additional attempts from anonymized infrastructure over the next six hours. Some of that activity clearly preceded Chainguard’s 07:41 release.
Cloudflare likewise reported observing attack traffic targeting its customers before the official release. It said its free and paid web application firewall protections were enabled by default starting at 03:02 UTC on October 21.
So, no, Chainguard was not imagining hostile interest in these bugs.
But Amazon included an important qualification: “Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems.” The PHP security team, meanwhile, said it examined the circulating proofs of concept and “did not identify any functional exploits at the time of release/public disclosure.”
Those statements are not necessarily contradictory. A honeypot can record a request intended to exploit a vulnerability without establishing that it can achieve remote code execution against a real application. Likewise, PHP’s failure to find a functional public exploit does not prove that no attacker privately possessed one.
Subsequent evidence should not be confused with what was known that morning. On October 26, CISA added both vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. That confirms exploitation was known by then; it does not establish when the first successful compromise occurred or whether Chainguard’s early release enabled it.
Welcome to security incident response. The evidence rarely arrives neatly labeled.
Did the binaries give attackers something they lacked?
Moore’s second argument is narrower. Attackers were already probing the relevant code, so publishing patched binaries might not have helped much.
“I don’t see any evidence that what we did helped the attackers in ways that they didn’t already have,” he told TNS. He acknowledged that comparing patched and unpatched binaries can identify vulnerable code, including with AI-assisted disassembly. But identifying the code, he argued, isn’t necessarily the same as building a working exploit.
Fair enough. Locating a memory-corruption bug and reliably turning it into remote code execution are different engineering problems.
Still, this defense has limits. Evidence that some attackers knew where to look does not establish that every prospective attacker did. Nor does it establish that the patch contained no useful clues beyond the vulnerability’s location. Chainguard’s argument depends on how much actionable information was already available and how reliable it was.
The same restraint applies to the accusation against Chainguard. Publishing the binaries created an opportunity to study the changes. It does not, by itself, demonstrate that a particular compromise happened because Chainguard released early.
The two sides were assessing different risks. Chainguard emphasized the danger of withholding a ready patch from users while hostile activity was visible. PHP emphasized the danger of distributing new information before the wider ecosystem could update. Both risks were real.
AI makes the timing problem worse
The broader concern is that AI-assisted vulnerability research could shorten the time defenders have to respond. The public reports cited here do not establish whether the pre-release PHP2Shell attempts used AI, or that this was the first incident of its kind.
For Moore, the PHP dispute fits a larger problem: attackers’ ability to turn vulnerability information into an exploit may outrun defenders’ ability to build and distribute a fix.
He described a scenario in which a Chromium patch becomes public, and an attacker develops an exploit faster than it takes to compile the browser. That was a warning about where the industry is heading, not a claim that this exact scenario had occurred.
“You literally cannot produce builds fast enough,” he said. And the build is only the beginning. Even if Chainguard produces an updated image quickly, customers still have to incorporate it, rebuild their applications, test them, and deploy.
Faster does not mean instantaneous, and a supplier’s release time is not a customer’s remediation time.
That is the uncomfortable part of the “patch faster” answer. Faster is useful. Faster does not mean instantaneous, and a supplier’s release time is not a customer’s remediation time.
Moore’s proposed longer-term response is to reduce the number of vulnerabilities that require this race in the first place. He discussed with TNS the work toward ABI-compatible replacements for foundational software components in Rust, along with formal verification techniques intended to rule out particular classes of defects. These remain engineering ambitions to evaluate.
They also do not settle, in the eyes of Chainguard’s critics, what the company should have done on October 21. A future with fewer memory-corruption bugs would be welcome, but administrators dealing with the current bugs still need a workable disclosure process, they would argue.
The lesson is bigger than Chainguard
It would be easy to see this incident as only a story about one vendor breaking the rules. It would be equally easy to see it as a story about an agile security company rescuing users from a slow-moving upstream project. It’s not that simple.
PHP’s own postmortem acknowledges a deeper failure. The foundation calls that delay “a structural failure,” involving both decision-making and insufficient resources.
Finding bugs faster doesn’t automatically provide the engineers needed to fix them safely. And getting a patch ready at one company doesn’t mean an ecosystem of distributions, hosting providers, extensions, and applications is ready to deploy it.
Many people jumped to attack Chainguard for its call. For instance, Jay Gazlay, CISA’s acting associate director for vulnerability management, said at an October 28 Red Hat conference in Washington: “that type of behavior is dangerous, and we’ve got to be careful about holding embargoes.”
There may still be room to repair the relationship. Federal News Network, citing Politico, reported that PHP Foundation Executive Director Elizabeth Barron expressed disappointment with Chainguard but hoped to restore trust and continue collaborating.
Moore called it “a really tough call” between “two really, really bad choices.” He’s right.
Maintainers and distributors need to agree in advance on when to lift an embargo early, who makes that decision, and how other distributors will get fixes to their users.
We need to do this as soon as possible. Otherwise, the next incident will end the same way, with vendors arguing about who broke the embargo. At the same time, administrators try to work out whether they can patch before somebody breaks their servers.
Learning Path

articles.title: Vanta launches AI Governance, Risk Quantification and a Vanta Agent for entire jobs - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Vanta launches AI Governance, Risk Quantification and a Vanta Agent for entire jobs
Compliance automation company Vanta Inc. today launched AI Governance by Vanta, a product on its Agentic Trust Platform said to give security teams a single view of every artificial intelligence system in a company.
Also making their debut at VantaCon 2026 in San Francisco this week are Risk Quantification, Autonomous Vendor Assessments and a new version of the Vanta Agent that the company claims can take on entire jobs.
Vanta is pitching the new products at security teams that are under pressure to move faster on AI. According to job-title data compiled by Vanta, the number of AI security engineers and architects has tripled so far this year compared with all of 2025.
AI governance roles, which did not appear in the company’s figures before 2024, have grown tenfold in two years. A complete inventory of the AI tools in use is still out of reach for many security teams, Vanta said.
Chief Product Officer Jeremy Epling, who is due to demonstrate the products at a keynote later today, said security teams are usually being held accountable for AI with the same headcount they had before it arrived.
“Plenty of tools can list the AI running in your company,” Epling said. Vanta also checks whether that AI is doing what a customer approved, he added, with the Vanta Agent taking on the follow-up work once someone signs off.
Designed to follow an AI agent through its full life cycle, AI Governance by Vanta is said to cover discovery, vulnerability testing, behavior controls and proof of governance. Vanta’s early access program for the product, opened in July, has become its most requested to date, with the waitlist now six times oversubscribed.
Point products for AI security often detect threats without the business context to judge how much they matter, according to Vanta. The company claims to be the only vendor tying an AI agent’s live security telemetry directly to an organization’s compliance controls.
On the risk side, Vanta’s unified risk view, which draws on live signals from across a customer’s compliance program, now includes Autonomous Vendor Assessments. According to the company, Risk Quantification, also added to the view, is meant to show leaders the financial impact of their most critical risks.
Entire jobs can now be handed to the latest version of the Vanta Agent. Once it has learned how a customer runs its program, the agent is said to bring staff in when a decision calls for human judgment. Users can also reach it natively inside Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and Slack.
Vanta also named Fredrick “Flee” Lee its new chief information security officer. Lee joins on Nov. 16 from Reddit Inc., where he led security before, during and after the company’s initial public offering. Gusto Inc., where he ran security before Reddit, was a Vanta customer at the time. At Vanta, he is expected to act as what the company calls “customer zero” in pushing the product road map.
The company has been valued at $4.15 billion since July 2025, when it raised $150 million in a Series D round led by Wellington Management Co. LLP.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit New N-central Zero-Day Hours After PoC Publication
articles.text:
Threat actors started exploiting a new zero-day vulnerability in N-able N-central hours after a disgruntled security researcher released it publicly.
Dubbed 4EverAble2Shell, the security defect could allow unauthenticated attackers to gain remote code execution (RCE) with root privileges on N-central servers running the latest patches.
The zero-day was dropped on GitHub by security researcher Sean Bales two days after N-able rolled out fixes for several other unpatched flaws he released publicly over the weekend.
4EverAble2Shell, Bales says, chains an exploit for a recent Apache Axis vulnerability (CVE-2026-90436, CVSS score: 9.8) with an exploit for an unspecified security hole in N-central deployments that have Legacy API enabled.
The exploit chain targets the Axis bug to achieve RCE, and then attempts to elevate privileges to root and run a shell script.
According to Bales, the exploit chain works against N-central servers that have been updated this week to 2026.4 HF2 (build number 2026.4.1.26), which contains fixes for the previously released Able2Shell zero-days.
N-able reacted immediately to the new zero-days and restricted certain N-central features and integrations, including Legacy API and Intune integration.
“Through our ongoing investigation today, we have identified additional indicators of compromise (IoCs) and are working closely with those specific customers to assess and mitigate any potential risks,” N-able said on November 13.
On November 12, Bales published proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit code for 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell, a set of roughly a dozen zero-day flaws that could allow attackers to execute commands on managed Windows agents with System privileges.
4EverAble2Shell exploited within hours
Threat actors started using the 4EverAble2Shell PoC in attacks hours after it landed, early-warning threat intelligence platform Previdian (formerly KEVIntel) said.
“New N-able zero-days are out, and WatchTowr Intel is already seeing probes for ‘4EverAble2Shell’, which affects builds with the Legacy API enabled,” preemptive attack surface management firm WatchTowr warned.
Lupovis and Huntback observed attackers successfully compromising N-central servers roughly 5 hours after the PoC publication. They deployed an XMRig miner with systemd or cron persistence.
“Each victim’s miner is named after its IP address,” Lupovis told SecurityWeek, explaining that the attacker’s wallet showed 21 rigs linked to compromised N-central servers in the US (9), South Africa (4), Canada (4), the UK, Germany, France and Sweden.
“Our decoys never execute anything, so none of the listed rigs are ours. Every one is a real server that ran the chain to root,” Lupovis said.
In a technical write-up, Huntback notes that 19 of the victims had applied the latest patches from N-able.
“The miner is the only payload we have seen, but the escalation hands the operator root on a host that manages your customers’ endpoints. Treat a hit as a full compromise, not a cleanup job. Applying Hotfix 2 is not enough on its own,” Huntaback says.

Related: Critical Xen Orchestra Flaws Exploited in Attacks

articles.title: Man's secret use of synthetic testosterone for cows nearly destroyed his heart
articles.text:
For 11 years, a Massachusetts man had an alarming array of health problems, most notably that his heart kept failing. He landed in the hospital over and over again, needed life support at one point, spent years going to specialists, and underwent a barrage of tests along the way.
But through it all, he never revealed a key detail behind his ailments: He was taking powerful, illicit synthetic testosterone derivatives (aka anabolic-androgenic steroids, or AAS). One of the drugs he took was approved only for use in animals; it’s primarily used to beef up cows.
Left in the dark, his doctors had to puzzle this out on their own. In a case report in this week’s issue of the New England Journal of Medicine, they explain how they did it. They also offer a warning: These cases will only become more common, and clinicians need to know what they look like.
“Use of AAS has now become a major international substance use disorder,” they wrote. In the US, it’s estimated that between 2.9 and 4 million people, mostly male athletes, use AAS. To put this in a public health perspective, this is more than the number of people in the US with an HIV infection.
“Clinicians should be prepared to encounter increasing numbers of patients presenting with the long-term effects of AAS exposure, including cardiomyopathy, atherosclerotic disease, and anabolic steroid–induced hypogonadism.”
Patients also need to be prepared for what recovery looks like, which they described as being “lengthy and varied.” The man’s case offers a stark example.
Troubling tale
The problems started when he was 39. He fell ill after returning from a trip to the Caribbean and went to Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston with a fever, chills, and trouble breathing. Tests suggested he had an acute kidney injury, liver damage, and an injured heart. Testing of his heart showed that the left chamber was pumping out just 21 percent of its blood in a beat (a normal amount is above 50 percent). His heart only got worse from there, and within hours, he ended up on a type of life support called ECMO (venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation), a machine that does the work of both the heart and lungs in dire circumstances. He luckily recovered—and quickly. But doctors were baffled by the cause.

articles.title: United Airlines blocks AI agents from booking flights, citing cybersecurity risks | TechCrunch
articles.text:
United Airlines said it will restrict access to AI agents seeking to book flights and manage reservations on their users’ behalf, citing a risk to cybersecurity and undermining federal regulations.
The airline is the latest American corporate giant to prevent customers from using AI agents and autonomous assistants to access their systems. The move comes as airlines and banks are struggling to differentiate between real customers and AI systems operating on their behalf, such as when users share their logins with their AI assistants. Sharing passwords with apps and assistants can create security risks if those credentials get leaked or exposed.
United warns that “sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles.”
The airline also warns of a risk of violating federal aviation rules, such as requiring that a human completes flight check-ins to acknowledge that their bags do not contain banned substances.
“As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants,” the airline said in a statement. “This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing and distribution policies.”
The airline’s move follows a warning from banks, including Bank of America, which last week urged customers not to share their passwords with their AI assistants.

articles.title: Google reworks TPU silicon into specialized systems for agents and security
articles.text:
Google adds two new specialized chips for AI agents and security to 8th-gen TPU lineup — TPU 8i Max puts two chips on one package for long-context work, TPU 8tx swaps Arm hosts for AMD EPYC
Google has yet to share specs, prices or ship dates for either new system.
Google's eighth-generation TPU family has now expanded further. Back in April, the company announced TPU 8t for training AI models and TPU 8i for general-purpose inference workloads. Google has now introduced TPU 8tx, built on the same silicon as the previously announced 8t, for confidential, hardware-isolated inference aimed at regulated enterprises and governments, and TPU 8i Max, which combines two 8i chips on one package for long-context agentic work.
TPU 8tx swaps the Arm-based Axion hosts of the 8t and 8i for a 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPU, adopting a Boardfly network, and the 8i Max doubles the compute, SRAM, and HBM bandwidth of the original 8i. The original split, the TPU 8t and 8i, made natural sense. The 8t targets large-scale training, while the 8i leans toward low-latency inference and reasoning. TPUs have become a fast-growing business, with the company claiming nearly 100 customers, including Meta’s recent move to TPUs. The more modular approach is flexible and can deliver specialized systems “in a matter of months rather than years,” helping that popularity along.
| Google’s eighth-generation TPU systems |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Header Cell - Column 0 | TPU 8t | TPU 8i | TPU 8tx | TPU 8i Max | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Built for | Large-scale pre-training | Sampling, serving and reasoning | Secure, confidential inference; small-scale training | Long-context agent work | 
| Silicon | TPU 8t | TPU 8i | Same silicon as TPU 8t | Two TPU 8i chips on one package | 
| Host CPU | Arm Axion | Arm Axion | 5th Gen AMD EPYC | Not stated | 
| Network | 3D torus | Boardfly | Boardfly | Not stated | 
| Peak FP4 PFLOPS | 12.6 | 10.1 | Not stated | About 20.2 (derived) | 
| HBM bandwidth (GB/s) | 6,528 | 8,601 | Not stated | About 17,202 (derived) | 
| HBM capacity (GB) | 216 | 288 | Not stated | Not stated | 
| On-chip SRAM (MB) | 128 | 384 | Not stated | 768 (derived) | 
| Availability | Coming soon | Coming soon | Coming soon | Coming soon | 
For the new parts, the TPU 8i Max isn't innovative on the surface, as it’s just two TPU 8i chips combined into a single package. The result is twice the theoretical compute, but more importantly, it fits twice the silicon within the “existing rack footprint,” and Google claims more compute per square foot and per watt.
Doubling both SRAM and HBM bandwidth helps keep things scaling, which would put the 8i Max at about 20.2 FP4 PFLOPS, 768 MB SRAM, and about 17.2 TB/s HBM bandwidth. This compares to Nvidia’s Rubin R200 GPU at a rated 50 FP4 PFLOPS for inference and 22 TB/s of HBM4 per socket, or AMD’s MI455X with 40 FP4 PFLOPS. The compute gap is closing.
The memory bandwidth doubling is also potentially one way around moving to HBM4. The memory wall, as Google calls it, or the bandwidth bottleneck, is a real concern “when dozens of AI agents work together across an entire software codebase.” Larger context windows — with larger models targeting 1 million tokens — mean larger KV caches, partly held in SRAM, and each new token has to read that cache back from memory, which is where the extra HBM bandwidth helps. It’s a different route from Nvidia’s LPX: more bandwidth in one package, rather than a second chip type for decoding and a storage tier for context.
Google also provides useful software for agents to get the most out of its hardware. TPU Sync is an open-source “model-state layer for TPU clusters” that moves KV caches off the chip’s HBM, “automatically tiering massive KV caches off the chip in milliseconds” down to host DRAM and, experimentally, shared storage. Google says this can cut KV transfer latency by “more than 90%,” with time-to-first-token gains that vary by workload. The company has also announced the Agent Compute Engine, a Google Cloud service that pauses idle agent sessions and moves their working memory aside until they’re needed again, another memory-saving effort.
Google credits its vLLM-TorchTPU stack with “state-of-the-art price-performance marks” on InferenceX and AgentX, which test realistic agentic coding and long-context work. However, the only published third-party numbers so far are for the last-generation Ironwood TPU. In SemiAnalysis’s InferenceX tests in September, running Qwen3.5 397B in FP8, Ironwood delivered 50.4% more tokens per dollar than Nvidia’s B200 and 96.0% more than the B300 at 20 tokens per second per user. One issue with that, however, is that Ironwood lacks native FP4, although newer November results show its FP8 beating Nvidia’s FP4 GB300 NVL72 on the same model, at 1.67 times the performance per dollar. There is also no eighth-gen result yet to compare how the new generation differs.
In contrast to the 8i Max, which is designed for long-context work, the new TPU 8tx, “built on the same silicon as TPU 8t,” is “optimized for secure and confidential inference” as well as small-scale training. The security is built into the hardware with isolation to prevent snooping on sensitive data, including model weights. Normally, data has to be unlocked in memory during processing, which is the step this isolation is meant to cover.
This chip is intended for areas where security and confidentiality are high priorities, which means regulated enterprises and governments, particularly those who are using frontier or proprietary models. In that case, the operators may want to “fine-tune models using their private data, distill large models into smaller ones, and train their agents,” without having to move sensitive data between clusters. Agents and security meet here for “secure agent execution.” Back in April, the Pentagon and Google reportedly held discussions for TPU usage in classified settings, although the 8tx chip is not specifically named.
Google’s Private AI Compute, its “hardened TPU platform” with protections “comparable to a typical TEE,” per its September technical brief, already runs confidential serving on TPUs. The 8tx appears to be that capability turned into a product for customers. Alternatives include Nvidia’s NVL72, with one security domain across 72 Rubin GPUs, 36 Vera CPUs, and the interconnects, and Intel’s TDX, which is adding trusted I/O to cover data moving to accelerators.
The TPU 8tx hosts are based on 5th Gen AMD EPYC boards, instead of the Axion hosts on the 8t, which replaced x86 in April. There's one Axion for every two TPUs on the 8i, compared with one Xeon per four on Ironwood. Google gives no reason for the change, but its Confidential VM configuration list has both AMD and Intel series chips, with no Arm-based ones listed. Private AI Compute uses “an AMD-based hardware Trusted Execution Environment” for its CPU workloads, suggesting Google swapped something it already runs on its confidential stack.
The 8tx also adopts the 8i’s Boardfly network over the 8t’s torus, which Google claims can deliver “up to 2x lower latency compared to TPU 8t” with almost no performance penalty, although it’s not clear what measure Google is using. The alternative torus network suits training, since chips mostly swap data with neighbors in a predictable manner, but inference on large mixture-of-experts and reasoning models can send smaller messages between distant chips, with every hop adding delay. With Boardfly, it’s at most seven hops against 16 at 1,024 chips.
What is lacking is a full specifications table, the amount of HBM capacity, pod sizes, an availability date, pricing, and customers for either system. Details on attestation, that is, the ability for the customer to verify confidentiality, are also missing for 8tx. The 8tx and 8i Max are currently listed, along with the 8i and 8t, as “coming soon” on Google’s Cloud TPU page.
Delivering two new TPU systems nearly seven months after April’s pair shows Google wants to turn out specialized systems much more quickly than has been the case in the past. Now, it just needs to prove them, through benchmarks and an availability date when the hardware is actually in customers’ hands.
Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

articles.title: Nintendo finally lets you gift games -- with some big limitations
articles.text:
Nintendo will finally allow digital game gifting on Nov. 16, albeit with some catches.
To start, this feature will be limited to Switch and Switch 2 users within the same family group. For context, a family group includes up to eight accounts and is naturally only intended for family members, making it difficult to gift most people unless they already happen to be in your group. There’s no option to send gifts to anyone on your Friends List.
Further, Nintendo says only “eligible” games, DLC, and upgrade packs will be available for gifting, although it’s unclear exactly which titles are excluded. Other restrictions include supervised accounts not being able to send digital gifts and the number of gifts being limited “in a given period.”
To send a gift, visit the Nintendo eShop page of the desired title and select the ‘Give as a Gift’ checkbox. From there, complete the purchase and select the gift recipient from the list of members of your family group. Note that gifts are sent immediately, so plan accordingly for when you want the recipient to get it.
All in all, these are the sorts of weird limitations you’d expect from Nintendo. If nothing else, though, you can still buy Nintendo eShop gift cards from most retailers as an alternative. It should also be noted that PlayStation doesn’t offer any digital game gifting at all, although Xbox and Steam do, and with far fewer restrictions than Nintendo.
In related news, Nintendo just announced its 2026 Black Friday deals for Canada, which include some decent savings on a Switch 2 bundle and various games.
