articles.title: Mira el tráiler del remake de 'El secreto de Thomas Crown', la nueva película de Michael B. Jordan como director después de ganar el Oscar
articles.text:
Michael B. Jordan ya está de vuelta. El actor regresa a los cines después de levantar su primer Premio Oscar el año pasado por su papel doble en Los Pecadores. Y esta vez lo hace con un proyecto muy especial. Se trata de El secreto de Thomas Crown, que acaba de lanzar su nuevo tráiler. El filme será el segundo remake de la mítica película de 1968 con Steve McQueen. El anterior, la icónica versión de 1999 con Pierce Brosnan.
Además de dirigir, Michael B. Jordan también produce y protagoniza El secreto de Thomas Crown. La cinta promete ser un thriller de robos de guante blanco visualmente deslumbrante, sensual y conmovedor, donde según indica el Amazon MGM Studios. "el hombre más peligroso es aquel al que nadie está observando".
Por el momento, la sinopsis oficial se mantiene en secreto, pero el tráiler de El secreto de Thomas Crown confirma que volverá a ser una auténtica cacería, un juego del ratón y el gato. Y es que, en la película original, el protagonista es un verdadero galán que se dedica al robo de obras de arte. En su aventura se cruza con una detective que le seguirá muy de cerca la pista a la vez que ambos empiezan a sentir una peligrosa atracción mutua.
Mira el tráiler de El secreto de Thomas Crown
Junto a Michael B. Jordan, el reparto de El secreto de Thomas Crown lo componen Kenneth Branagh, Adria Arjona, Lily Gladstone, Danai Gurira y Pilou Asbæk, entre otros. "Es un bebé mío que llevaba mucho tiempo queriendo hacer, así que estoy muy ilusionado, declaró Jordan hace unos meses en una entrevista a Deadline.
Creo que tampoco va a ser exactamente lo que la gente espera. Cuando reimaginas algo, no se trata de un remake. No es un reboot. Es una reinterpretación, y estoy muy ilusionado con ello porque me importa mucho esta película y su título", añadió.
El secreto de Thomas Crown se estrena en cines el 5 de marzo de 2027.

articles.title: Techie uses voltage glitching hack to turn $2,500 Nvidia 8GB cryptomining GPU into a full-fat $20,000 A100 with 80GB of VRAM — hack carefully blows onboard fuses to unlock entire VRAM and shader modules
articles.text:
Techie uses voltage glitching hack to turn $2,500 Nvidia 8GB cryptomining GPU into a full-fat $20,000 A100 with 80GB of VRAM — hack carefully blows onboard fuses to unlock entire VRAM and shader modules
The most dangerous thing in the world is a bored engineer with a screwdriver. If you see a soldering iron, run for the hills.
Enterprising techies looking to build their own local AI cluster have far more interesting options than buying DGX Sparks or Apple Mac Studios. Used data center GPUs are everywhere, and a server rack's garbage is an enthusiast's treasure. This option has become even more popular with CMPunlocker, a soft-mod for Nvidia CMP-170HX cards that unlocks abilities well beyond stock. Now, a techie has taken it a step further, blasting through the remaining limitations with voltage glitching and creating a card faster than the actual $20,000 Nvidia A100 GPU with 80GB of VRAM... but from an $2,500 8GB CMP-170HX mining card.
The volt-mod was done by Kate (GitHub link here), who got her starting point from a paper that described how one could exploit GA100 cards' microcode. She turned her attention to the normally protected onboard fuse controller. Although it's rarely discussed, a "fuse box" has been integral in most any CPU and GPU for a while — though it's normally used once at the factory to break physical connections in chips to parts that have tested poorly, thus disabling them so they can be sold as a lower-end model.
If you're wondering how people are getting 80-40GB of VRAM out of 8-10GB, the explanation is simple: the GA100 silicon actually includes all the corresponding HBM2e VRAM dies within; but they get disabled at the factory like the shader modules. The smaller version is more desirable, as it's based on the variant of GA100 with 80GB of HBM2e within, while the 10GB cards spawn from the 40GB GA100.
The Nvidia cards in question have quite an elaborate eFuse controller (16,384 in a 512 x 32 array) — which can be read to obtain the card's current configuration. Most every part of the card has related fuses: VRAM sections, individual shader modules, PCIe 4.0 and NVLink, and even video codec hardware. However, as Kate succinctly put it: Nvidia's design is insecure, as popping fuses can grant access to more features, not fewer.
Under normal conditions, these fuses can't be popped, or "written to," by the user — but a geek armed with a soldering iron isn't a normal user. Kate had GPT-6 Astra design a simple circuit board based on an $8 STM32G4 microcontroller to tap into the power signals on the card's PCB.
The voltage regulators (VRMs) on the card "speak" PWMVID, an Nvidia standard, and Kate's board intercepted the PWM signals sent into the VRM controller, forcing it to produce voltage glitches on the line feeding the GPU, where the fuse controller lies.
Remember when we said the fuse controller was read-only? With the voltage glitches, many fuse-status reads in a tight loop, and she managed to set the controller to a state in which its security bit flags allowed writes through. From that point, it was "easy" to reconfigure her card. She was careful to force-disable any shader modules previously marked as defective, because these are physical fuses — there's no "undo" button.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
She applied the mod to her cards and, after testing with multiple workloads, found that nine had the full 80 GB of VRAM working, and one card "only" had 64 GB usable. Most interestingly, unlocking all the shader modules (SM) nets her FP16 FMA performance 20% beyond a regular A100 card. She thinks this is due to the chips often having 120 or more usable SMs — over the 108 on the spec sheet. The GA100 die starts with 128 SMs to account for defects, which is normal in chip manufacturing.
The CMPUnlocker soft mod is required for enabling the "new" features on the drivers, but it doesn't unlock the card's full potential: the VRAM upper limit is 40-64GB (depending on the variant), many shader modules remain locked, and PCIe bandwidth only goes to 2.0. Additionally, there's no ECC, NVLink, or multi-instance GPU support, all of which are critical in a server setup and are also used for product segmentation.
Kate's volt-mod does away with all of these limits, and her best test card is happily working at PCIe 4.0 speed with the full feature set. She didn't test the video encoder bits, but it's unlikely anybody using these cards cares much for that.
As for the cost, a CMP-170HX 8GB is currently hovering around $3,000, and the 10GB variant costs around $2,500. A full-fat Nvidia A100 80GB in a PCIe configuration can reach $20,000 or more. The SXM server-module versions are cheaper, but they require infrastructure around them. Note that these prices will likely vary significantly, especially as people become increasingly aware of the mods.
Kate says she's publishing her research now because another person independently found the same issue. She has informed Nvidia of the vulnerability, though there's not much the company can do for existing cards already on the market.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: With $23M in funding, Luminal is the latest startup to put Nvidia's CUDA moat in its crosshairs - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
With $23M in funding, Luminal is the latest startup to put Nvidia’s CUDA moat in its crosshairs
Luminal AI Inc. has outlined a plan to tear down Nvidia Corp.’s formidable software moat in the artificial intelligence chip industry after raising $23 million in early-stage funding.
Today’s Series A round was led by Standard Capital and saw participation from existing investors such as Y Combinator, SagaVC, Liquid 2 and Felicis, bringing Luminal’s total amount raised to date to more than $28 million. It comes about a year after the startup raised $5.3 million in seed funding.
Everybody knows about Nvidia these days. The chipmaker has ridden the generative AI wave to a staggering $5 trillion market valuation, surpassing rivals such as Apple Inc., Alphabet Inc. and Amazon.com Inc. to become the most valuable publicly traded company in the world. But anyone who assumes that it’s solely Nvidia’s graphics processing units that set it apart would be mistaken, for the real reason for its dominance of the AI computing industry is not just silicon, but software.
For almost two decades, Nvidia’s proprietary Compute Unified Device Architecture or CUDA software framework has been the real differentiator, serving as a virtually impenetrable barrier that prevents rivals such as Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Google LLC and Amazon Web Services Inc. from stripping away its market lead. Though those rivals have developed some very powerful GPUs and custom application-specific integrated circuits for running AI workloads at lower costs than Nvidia’s hardware, they haven’t been able to match the scale of Nvidia’s software ecosystem.
Virtually every major AI framework, including TensorFlow and PyTorch, has been built natively on Nvidia’s CUDA software, enabling developers to run their AI models on Nvidia’s GPUs without any modifications. But to run their models on alternative chips, developers need to rewrite much of the underlying code, which is challenging and time-consuming work. That’s why the vast majority of AI workloads still run on Nvidia’s chips.
Many developers don’t want to be paying the exorbitant fees needed to rent Nvidia’s GPUs or purchase them outright, but they also don’t want to spend months at a time fine-tuning their codebases to get their AI models to run optimally on alternative hardware, and it’s this challenge that Luminal intends to solve for them.
The startup’s solution is a two-pronged architecture platform that consists of its proprietary search compiler and a fully managed inference cloud that combine to eliminate the hassles of bringing AI workloads onto different chips.
Co-founder and Chief Executive Joe Fioti told SiliconANGLE that the compiler works by systematically exploring different ways of running neural networks on the target chip in order to come up with the most optimal path. It benchmarks each variation until it finds the best possible solution, and then it automatically generates the code developers need.
Once the code is ready, it caches the implementation so it can be reused across recurring inference workloads. In this way, it allows developers to run their AI applications across heterogeneous chip architectures with minimal fuss, Fioti said.
“We started out building in the open on GitHub as AI adoption took off, and quickly saw how much demand there was for a more efficient way to run AI models across different hardware,” Fioti said of the company’s origins.
Luminal’s compiler and inference cloud are designed primarily for running high-throughput, continuous-uptime AI applications that demand massively scalable inference. Think applications such as AI coding tools, automated image generation engines, AI video generators and real-time voice agents.
“The cost of running AI shouldn’t limit who gets to build it,” Fioti said. “We’re building the infrastructure to make high-performance inference more accessible, giving developers more choice beyond Nvidia’s ecosystem without forcing them to compromise on speed or cost.”
Luminal launched its compiler and public cloud-based inference infrastructure just four months ago and adoption is growing rapidly. It’s already processing more than 45 trillion tokens per month – a number that’s roughly equivalent to 10% of the total tokens consumed so far by Together AI Inc., an $8 billion-valued infrastructure unicorn that has been serving the market for more than four years already. The startup has established a strong partnership with AWS, and runs a significant amount of its workloads on that company’s Tranium processors.
Going forward, Luminal’s plans include expanding its engineering team, scaling its go-to-market operations and optimizing its compiler and inference infrastructure to support more chip hardware and AI models.
Standard Capital’s Dalton Caldwell said he’s betting on Luminal because AI inference is the fastest-growing market in the world. “We backed it because of its deep technical expertise and its demonstrated proof that it can squeeze fantastic performance out of heterogeneous hardware,” he said. “Luminal’s ability to get the most out of GPUs that have already been purchased … is incredibly high leverage.”
Though Luminal has had a promising start, it’s certainly not the only company trying to break Nvidia’s CUDA stranglehold on the AI industry. Both Google and AWS have their own things going on, notably launching alternative AI frameworks to PyTorch that make it easier for developers to create AI models and applications that can run on their native processors.
Luminal also faces competition from startups such as Spectral Compute Ltd., which offers a programming toolkit and compiler that enables CUDA-based code to run natively on any AI-accelerated chip. There are also open-source efforts such as the UXL Foundation’s OneAPI, which converts CUDA code into software that can easily run on any silicon.

articles.title: Switch-Bastler aufgepasst: Nintendo lässt Modchip-Software sperren
articles.text:
Nintendo hat bei GitHub insgesamt 144 Repositories mit Firmware für Switch-Modchips sperren lassen. Im Mittelpunkt steht der quelloffene Modchip Picofly. Mit ihm lassen sich auch Switch-Konsolen öffnen, die gegen reine Software-Hacks abgesichert sind. Damit ist dann eigene Software („Homebrew“) möglich, aber auch der Verstoß gegen Urheberrechte, so der Vorwurf von Nintendo.
Nintendos Argumente
Den Antrag nach dem US-Urheberrechtsgesetz DMCA – es erlaubt Rechteinhabern, Inhalte schnell sperren zu lassen – hat Nintendo of America auf den 6. November datiert. GitHub hat ihn am Dienstag in seinem öffentlichen DMCA-Archiv veröffentlicht. Formal richtet er sich nur gegen das Repository Ansem-SoD/Picofly. Weil das Netzwerk aus Forks – also Kopien und Abwandlungen des Projekts – mehr als 100 Repositories umfasst und Nintendo alle davon als rechtsverletzend einstuft, sperrte GitHub gleich das gesamte Netzwerk, berichtet TorrentFreak.
Nintendo argumentiert, die Firmware umgehe die technischen Schutzmaßnahmen der Konsole, damit sie illegale Spielekopien ausführen kann. Konkret geht es um die Bootsequenz der Switch. Diese prüft Nintendo mit eigenen kryptografischen Schlüsseln ab, der Modchip hebelt die Prüfung aus. Neben Picofly nennt Nintendo auch die Firmware der Modchips SX Core, SX Lite und HWFLY.
So funktioniert der Modchip
Konsolen, die Nintendo seit Mitte 2018 produziert, sind gegen die Sicherheitslücke „Fusée Gelée“ abgesichert. Über diese Lücke ließen sich ältere Geräte per Software für eine eigene Firmware öffnen. Auf allen gepatchten Konsolen klappt das nur noch mit einem Modchip. Bastler löten den Chip in die Konsole ein. Beim Start erzeugt er gezielte Spannungseinbrüche, ein sogenanntes Voltage Glitching. Dadurch überspringt die CPU die Firmware-Prüfung. Statt des Original-Bootvorgangs lädt die Switch dann eine Datei von der microSD-Karte.
Picofly basiert auf dem Mikrocontroller RP2040 von Raspberry Pi und ist laut Anleitung quelloffen. Die Autoren unterstützen ausschließlich diesen Chip. Bei kommerziellen Modchips wie HWFLY oder SX Core helfen sie nur beim Aufspielen neuer Firmware, nicht beim Einbau oder beim Kauf. Custom Firmware lässt sich für Schwarzkopien nutzen – aber eben auch für Homebrew, also selbst programmierte Software, die Nintendo offiziell nicht zulässt. Das geht nun schwerer.
Wie Nintendo das Vorgehen begründet
Zur Begründung seiner Forderung verweist Nintendo auf das US-Strafverfahren gegen mutmaßliche Mitglieder der Hackergruppe Team Xecuter. Sie verkaufte die Modchips SX Core und SX Lite, die auf allen damals erhältlichen Switch-Modellen funktionierten. Gegen Verkäufer dieser Hacks zog Nintendo 2020 vor Gericht. Der Betreiber der Seite UberChips stimmte schließlich einem Urteil über zwei Millionen US-Dollar Schadenersatz zu. Nach der Strafverfolgung stellte Team Xecuter den Betrieb faktisch ein. Die Chips lebten in kompatiblen Alternativen wie HWFLY und Picofly weiter.
Der Betreiber des Picofly-Repositories kann mit einer Gegendarstellung gegen die Sperre vorgehen. Im Archiv von GitHub ist laut TorrentFreak aber bisher keine verzeichnet.

articles.title: Rethinking Memory For AI Inference
articles.text:
Processing data closer to memory could reduce power and boost performance, but software, thermal, and architectural challenges remain.
Key Takeaways:
The shift from AI training in data centers to AI inferencing at the edge will require a fundamental rethinking of where and how data is processed and stored, how it is prioritized, and what needs to be traded off in terms of power and performance to stay within a limited power budget.
At the center of these efforts is a recognition that the explosion of data — especially in physical AI where data is being live-streamed from sensors — requires much of that data to be processed as close to memory as possible. This has been a topic of discussion since the inception of the Internet of Things, but it really began gaining traction with AI due to the flood of data and concerns about the amount of power required to move and process it. In battery-electric vehicles and drones, for example, the less energy spent on processing data, the greater the range per charge and the more energy that can be allocated to critical and not-so-critical functions.
The challenge is understanding what data needs to be kept, what can be discarded, and what needs to be acted upon. Those are very different priorities. Making those choices requires advanced processing, and the quickest path to results using the least amount of energy is to minimize the distance data needs to travel between processing and memory.
“The realities of these LLMs getting into physical devices are causing everyone to rethink how they architect their memory,” said Frank Ferro, group director for product management at Cadence. “Even with conventional memory — without even talking about processing in memory — how do I partition these models to maximize the performance both of the overall processor and memory subsystem?”
Solving those issues will require several new approaches, such as processing near memory (PNM) and processing in memory (PIM), as well as improvements across multiple technologies and approaches. Compilers and operating systems will need to catch up, and standards will need to be established.
“AI in the data center and all these large language models have been the focus of everyone’s attention for the last couple of years, and now these models have been trained and pushed out into the field, into the edge of the network and physical AI,” Ferro said. “The reality is you have limited compute power and limited memory.”
AI inferencing at the edge presents different challenges than training AI models in AI data centers.
“Training almost always involves highly variable memory access patterns, and mostly involves the use of interpreted code — for example, Python to PyTorch — which necessitates the complexities of coherence across layers of memory,” said Steve Roddy, chief marketing officer at Quadric. “Once inference begins, the use model changes dramatically. Whether you are looking at big LLMs running in a data center, or models running locally, such as smaller LLMs or VLAs (vision-language-action) in cars, the model is known before you run it. That means the data access patterns are known ahead of time. This is where ahead-of-time compilation can start to take great advantage of the various at-memory, processing-in-memory, or in-memory-compute (IMC) options. The system knows exactly where, when, and how the compute is going to occur. There is no need for one element of a compute solution to guess if something manipulated the data while it was in another memory subsystem, because the entire system orchestration was planned out hours, days, or weeks before, when the AI inference model was compiled.”
Certain stages of the AI inference pipeline benefit from near-memory solutions more than others.
“Pushing the compute into the DRAM or near the DRAM has interesting implications,” said Sharad Chole, chief scientist and co-founder of Expedera. “You’re moving your communication pattern — my activation goes to memory, rather than my memory goes to activation — and that changes how much communication you need to do. These sort of solutions are okay for low-batch decode. For example, if you have batch one and you are trying to do decode and you are not reading all the weights, as soon as we move to large-batch decode, which is cost-optimized, or prefill, which is large-batch execution, the activation communication becomes the challenging part. These are the two ways to think about it. In the end, you have to break your execution into parts that are either storage-sensitive, in terms of how much data you need to store, or bandwidth-sensitive, or batching-sensitive.”
Either way, bringing compute closer to data can reduce the time and the energy spent moving it, and processing in the same memory package (custom HBM), or on the same memory die (LPDDR6-PIM), provides two fundamental advantages. “One of them is performance,” said Kos Gitchev, product marketing director at Cadence. “If we’re looking at a CPU or a core sitting inside the SoC, and every time you need to do an operation you’ve got to go out to memory, there’s a transaction that says, ‘Okay, get me some data from the memory that’s going to hit a cache somewhere in the SoC.’ That will eventually go to memory. It will come back to the cache and eventually come back to the processor. This operation really takes some time.”
So while chip architects can get compute running quickly on an SoC, the SoC has to wait for data to arrive. “Processing in memory to a large degree addresses this,” said Gitchev. “Now you can say, ‘I have this chunk of memory data in the memory, go do something with it, and I’m just going to go read the results. I’m going to skip this whole step of reading it, compute again, and putting it back. I’m just going to do a read, and that’s all I need.'”
| Term | Domain | What it means | Where the math happens | Data form | Examples | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CIM (compute-in-memory) / IMC (in-memory computing) | Hardware | The memory array itself performs the computation | Inside the bit cells and bitlines | Often analog (currents/charges summed on bitlines); digital variants also exist | Analog multiply-accumulate on SRAM or ReRAM bitlines | 
| IMC (in-memory computing) | Enterprise software | Databases or analytics run on data held in RAM rather than on disk | Conventional CPUs | Digital | SAP HANA. Not the meaning used in this article | 
| PIM (processing-in-memory) | Hardware | Logic placed on the same DRAM die as a standard memory array | Digital logic beside the banks | Digital, read out of the array | LPDDR6-PIM (JEDEC standard nearing completion) | 
| PNM (processing-near-memory) | Hardware | Logic placed in the memory package but on a separate die | Digital logic on the base/logic die | Digital, read out of the array | Compute on custom HBM4/HBM4E base dies (roadmap) | 
Fig. 1: Compute-in-memory vs. processing-in/near-memory — where the math happens and what each term means. Note that CIM and IMC are used interchangeably in hardware to describe architectures that perform computational tasks directly within the memory array, but IMC also has a separate software meaning. Source: Semiconductor Engineering
Reducing data movement
Ultimately, the entire system needs to be optimized to make this scheme work.
“The framing has shifted from, ‘We need more memory,’ to, ‘We need fabric that keeps memory fed without starving other traffic,'” said Nandan Nayampally, chief commercial officer at Baya Systems. “More recently it’s, ‘How to architect around scarcity itself.'”
Others agree. “AI systems are increasingly limited by the ability to move data efficiently between compute, memory, accelerators, chiplets, and dies,” said Andy Nightingale, vice president of product management and marketing, at Arteris. “This makes the interconnect and memory architecture as important as the memory device itself. This reinforces the need for scalable NoC, chiplet, cache coherence, and system mapping technologies that help customers optimize data movement before silicon.”
Interconnects, caching schemes, and packaging all play increasingly significant roles at the edge, but choosing the right combination while also keeping costs down is a challenge. So while new versions of high-bandwidth memory are enabling more processing in the base die of a multi-die stack, an LPDDR6-PIM that places slices of compute alongside the DRAM banks may be more attractive, depending on the cost.
“Near-memory computing is still using an external channel interface,” said Hoshik Kim, senior vice president and fellow at SK hynix.[1] “But by putting processing units near memory data, we can actually get rid of or remove a lot of data movement and have higher energy efficiency. Also, we can offload the compute function from the CPU or GPU, so that we can have better utilization of the host CPU or GPU.”
Typical use cases involve memory controllers inside the base die. “We are integrating some useful near-memory processing units to offload simple MAC operations,” said Kim. “Because, if you think about inference workload operations, most function computation is a simple MAC operation. So we could put MAC operations inside the base die to expand for and then work with the GPU for a more complex, compute-intensive operation.”
Multi-year process
Some of the necessary technologies are available today. Others will take years to develop, or improve enough to the point where they can make a difference.
“We are looking at in-memory applications in three to five years, maybe around 2030,” said Vishal Chandrasekar, director of product management at Ayar Labs. “You want to be able to connect up many GPUs so that you are able to have different GPUs access the memory of others. People are trying to ramp up the amount of memory per GPU, but you’re limited by packet size and HBM bandwidths and the like. Compute in memory is one path, which makes it so the base die of your memory now has compute capabilities of some kind.”
Still, that technology is not quite ready for commercialization. “It’s a little aggressive to say that we’re already seeing it out in the market,” said Cadence’s Ferro. “There might be some very specific embedded applications that are using a type of processing in memory, but as a broad usage, it’s still pretty early.”
Processing-in-memory solutions are slowly moving from research to commercialization. For example, Samsung announced the architecture and performance benchmarks for its LPDDR6-PIM chip aimed at low-power, mobile on-device AI applications.
“LPDDR-PIM is the one that has got the most attention within JEDEC,” said Randy White, memory solutions program manager at Keysight. “There is active development and discussion around LPDDR-PIM, but there are challenges for both the hardware and software. From a hardware standpoint, you’re mixing logic process with DRAM process, and they’re optimized for different metrics, so that innovation itself makes the manufacturing process more complex and expensive. You have to be very selective and make sure you know your application can sustain the added cost of that.” Applications for LPDDR6-PIM will range from fixed-node edge servers optimized for performance to mobile phones and tablets optimized for efficiency.
Trickier than hardware?
The software challenges may be even more difficult. “How do you manage workload skew and load balancing?” White noted. “Let’s say you take a checkerboard-style memory array or core, and every 10 columns or so of memory, you stick a vertical slice of logic silicon. If you were to take that PIM die, put it under a microscope, you’d see a checkerboard with slices repeated every certain number of rows. That by itself has some timing constraints. While you’re accessing one row, you have to wait for calculation to an instruction to be complete on the compute engine. So it’s not just a matter of fetching data and balancing timings between different bank accesses. Now you have memory access coupled with waiting for compute data. The whole point is that I don’t have to move data as much. I’m moving data between adjacent cells, and that’s great. From a hardware standpoint, you get lower power, etc. But for the engineer who’s writing the BIOS, who has to create the scheduler for synchronizing, that has just exploded in terms of complexity.”
PIM architectures need to be considered in terms of the impact on the rest of the system. “The hardware has to be designed and optimized so you have the right number of compute coefficients and things like that,” said White. “Then the memory has to be segregated in a way that you don’t have too fine resolution, so you have the right coarse and fine trade-offs in terms of separation.”
Fig. 2: What must be solved for near-data computing to achieve its potential. Source: SK hynix/DAC
Additionally, memory programming models are still in flux, particularly with the rise of non-traditional memory systems such as PIM, CIM, CXL-attached tiered memory, and heterogeneous memory architectures.
“I don’t think the industry will settle on a single programming model and coherence implementation,” said Steven Woo, fellow and distinguished inventor at Rambus. “Over the last 40 years, different programming models, coherence protocols, and consistency models have been implemented that provide different trade-offs to systems designers and application developers. The diversity of architectures and coherence implementations is driving the need for more high-performance libraries to be developed that allow programmers to call common functions that are implemented in ways that are optimized for different systems. High-performance libraries maintain a level of abstraction that improves program portability and performance scalability without burdening the programmer with understanding all details of the underlying hardware.”
Compiler and memory controller considerations
Software innovations are needed to support new memory architectures.
“The question is no longer whether a PIM is viable or makes sense,” said SK hynix’s Kim. “It’s a reality. The problem is how to make a software compiler framework and system software. All of the ecosystem needs to follow up.”
Cadence’s Gitchev agreed. “The real challenge is that currently the systems are designed so that the compilers, operating system, and everything works with a processor core or an accelerator sitting inside your SoC, and everything is designed for this processor to do all the work,” he said. “That’s the infrastructure. Now, essentially, you can offload some of that processor work and say, ‘I need to do this operation, and I don’t really need the processor to do it.’ There’s a whole infrastructure behind that to be able to do that. There’s a software aspect. The operating system and the processor need to understand, ‘These operations I can send to memory, they’ll do it, and I’ll just get the results, but these operations I still have to do locally because the memory I have may not be able to do it, or my system is not as efficient.'”
There’s also the need for standardization inside the chip. “How do you connect these things together?” said Gitchev. “Today we don’t really have a good way to say, ‘Go and do this operation in memory,’ as far as the type of transactions that move from the processor to the SoC fabric to memory. This infrastructure is not there. We need the hardware and protocol to be able to tell memory to go do this stuff, and then we need the software and the operating system to support the system to be able to do this and decide what’s efficient.”
This comes down to two streams of data. “I’ve got a stream of data that’s storing and reading and writing,” explained Ferro. “Then I’ve got a stream of data that’s compute, and that’s not native to the way operating systems and processors are built. You now need cooperation with the processor companies, the interface between the processor and the fabric, the system, and then of course the operating system. All those pieces need to get adjusted. It may or may not be a big adjustment, but without standardization, everyone’s system is going to be highly customized.”
Home agents and memory controllers
Near-memory and in-memory architectures introduce distinct pressures to traffic management and system coherence.
“In traditional hardware coherent systems, home agents are responsible for tracking where shared data is being used throughout the system and making sure processing elements have correct copies of the data,” explained Rambus’ Woo. “Hardware coherency eliminates the need for programmers to manage the updating of data across processing elements, simplifying programming. Synchronization primitives like locks and barriers, and software coherence give applications an additional level of control over how and when data is updated. Together, these hardware and software mechanisms enable efficient algorithms to be designed that maintain a level of hardware abstraction that hides the details of the underlying hardware, easing the task of programming and managing the way data is updated to maintain coherence in systems.”
That means software engineers increasingly need to understand the hardware, and vice versa.
“Achieving good, scalable performance as problem sizes grow and the number of processing elements increases is becoming more difficult,” said Woo. “While home agents remove the burden of managing coherence from the programmer, the messages sent by home agents to maintain coherence can become performance bottlenecks. Programmers increasingly need to understand the underlying structure and functions of the hardware to achieve good performance. Algorithms are often modified to shard data in ways that maximize the independence of tasks and minimize the amount of coherence traffic traveling in the system. In some systems, utilizing no hardware coherence mechanisms results in the best performance, but complicates the task of programming.”
The memory controller faces a twofold challenge. “One part is the memory subsystem, which consists of a PHY and a controller,” said Cadence’s Gitchev. “The controller itself is where these commands need to actually do the work. But now you have a different set of commands. Before that, you fundamentally had two different commands — read data, write data, and that’s about it. The control is a lot more complicated than that, but at a high level, that’s what it does. It reads data and writes data in the most efficient way possible. Now a different challenge is coming in where we need a different set of commands and rules to say, ‘Hey, now can you go take this data and multiply it, and take this data inside the memory and divide it, or do an operation.’ It’s not a significant challenge for a controller to do that. We add more commands, and we’ll figure out how that works, and try to make it efficient.”
The second challenge is harder. “The processor needs to be able to send those commands,” said Gitchev. “It needs to prepare a memory inside the memory subsystem to say, ‘If I’m going to multiply this data by that data, do I have the right data in the right place? Do I have the results in the right place? This operation is complete.’ The controller manages some of that, but it also has to have very close collaboration with the overall system.”
Thermal, physics, and CIM
Processing near memory can help reduce data traffic, but it could amplify existing physics problems, such as thermal issues.
“The memory shortage is partially due to current state-of-the-art design and use of available memory,” said Satish Radhakrishnan, head of global field applications and solutions at Vinci. “Innovative design can help reduce demand per unit and improve utilization. The most viable solutions to increasing memory utilization — including higher HBM stacks, custom HBM, near-memory, in-memory compute, and chiplet-based disaggregation — all share one property. They trade a bandwidth problem for a physics problem. Stacking memory closer to compute concentrates heat in exactly the places it’s hardest to remove. Heterogeneous material stacks and micron-scale interconnects create thermo-mechanical stress and warpage behavior that doesn’t respect the boundaries between die, package, and board. Heat doesn’t stop at the chip, and neither do the constraints that come with it.”
For this reason, memory companies tend to announce new thermal technology with their new architectures. For example, SK hynix announced an integrated HBM (iHBM) solution that embeds integrated cooling elements (ICEs) within the HBM package. Micron’s recent roadmap included vertical HBM (vHBM) with thermally aware design and a heat spreader over the PHY. Samsung is tackling heat issues with a range of solutions, including hybrid copper bonding (HCB) and a heat path block (HPB), which it plans to include in HBM5. [2]
SK hynix’s Kim proposed in-memory compute to reduce heat in the HBM base die. “If you put DRAM on top of logic, DRAM is very sensitive to temperature,” he said. “Logic is very prone to hot spots. Basically, the hot spots happen at the bottom of memory. Thermal can be a real challenge, and you need to resolve these issues. In-memory computing can be an answer. It has extremely low power consumption, so you can probably put in-memory computing at the base die or the bottom of memory.”
In practice, IMC/CIM could work with custom HBM4 or HBM4E because the base die is built on a foundry logic process. SRAM is the native memory, meaning that SRAM CIM macros can be built there. CIM does multiply-accumulate inside the SRAM array, so weights aren’t repeatedly moved between memory and a separate MAC unit. Data movement is where most of the energy goes, which is why SRAM CIM macros report far better energy efficiency, in operations per watt, than conventional digital accelerators. Less energy per operation means lower power density, so fewer hot spots under the DRAM.
Conclusion
Software support remains the missing link between near-memory hardware and its promise for AI. For compilers and AI frameworks, processing-near-memory and in-memory architectures are emerging targets that could let developers offload mathematical operators directly to the memory subsystem, but the software needed to support that shift is still catching up.
The available compute — and the limits on it — differ by architecture. LPDDR6-PIM is limited to MAC units or simple ALUs suited to matrix-vector multiplication and element-wise math. A custom HBM4/HBM4E logic-process base die can add other memory-control functions. But that flexibility comes with a thermal ceiling — how much compute fits depends on the heat it adds beneath the DRAM.
“We have spent a lot of time over the last two years talking about custom HBM and how to use that base layer,” noted Cadence’s Ferro.
AI is driving the push to bring compute closer to memory, but proximity alone will not deliver the gains. Broader adoption depends on matching workloads to the hardware, managing heat, and giving compilers and operating systems the tools to decide what to offload. Moving the compute is only part of the solution; making the system use it efficiently is the next test.

There is no one-size-fits-all — yet.

articles.title: La batterie solaire murale Samduo Nex E6000 à 1 599 € pour le Black Friday
articles.text:
Pour le Black Friday, la batterie solaire murale Samduo Nex E6000 passe à 1 599 € au lieu de 1 999 €, soit 400 € d’économie. Le compteur intelligent Samduo Smart Meter, d’une valeur de 129 €, est également offert avec chaque commande. On vous explique le pourquoi du comment de cette solution de stockage domestique qui mise autant sur sa compacité que sur sa simplicité d’installation.
Produire sa propre électricité grâce à des panneaux photovoltaïques, voilà une perspective qui séduit de plus en plus de particuliers. Pouvoir en profiter une fois le soleil couché, c’est encore mieux. C'est précisément la promesse de la Samduo Nex E6000, une batterie domestique de 6 kWh conçue pour stocker le surplus d’énergie solaire afin de le restituer lorsque le foyer en a besoin.
Mais plutôt que de s’imposer comme un équipement encombrant dans le garage ou le cellier, elle adopte un format mural particulièrement fin. Et à l’occasion du Black Friday, son tarif devient nettement plus intéressant.
Une batterie solaire de 6 kWh qui sait se faire discrète
C’est probablement le premier élément qui distingue la Samduo Nex E6000 : son format. Avec seulement 11,9 cm d’épaisseur, pour 84,25 cm de hauteur et 50 cm de largeur, cette batterie de 59 kg peut être fixée directement au mur grâce au kit de montage fourni. Un choix esthétique et pratique, qui permet de limiter l’encombrement au sol. Un vrai plus dans les espaces où chaque mètre carré compte. Elle a d'ailleurs reçu le Red Dot Design Award 2026, l'European Product Design Award 2026 et le German Design Award 2027.
Un autre détail appréciable au quotidien, c’est son fonctionnement, annoncé à moins de 25 dB, ce qui permet de l’installer sans transformer la pièce en local technique particulièrement bruyant.
Derrière cette silhouette relativement discrète, on retrouve une capacité de stockage de 6 kWh, extensible jusqu’à 90 kWh en associant plusieurs unités. De quoi envisager une installation évolutive à moyen ou long terme, en fonction des besoins énergétiques du foyer.
Une installation Plug & Play et un pilotage intelligent de l’énergie
La Nex E6000 entend également simplifier l’installation. Pas besoin de faire intervenir un électricien pour la raccorder : l’onduleur est directement intégré et la batterie se branche sur une prise secteur classique, en trois étapes, sans recâblage de l’installation électrique existante. Sa puissance bidirectionnelle atteint 2 600 W, avec une injection réseau certifiée de 800 W.
Concrètement, la batterie va se charger d’emmagasiner pendant la journée le surplus d’électricité produit par les panneaux solaires, pour le restituer en soirée, lorsque les besoins du foyer augmentent au même rythme que la production photovoltaïque diminue.
L’application Samduo prend ensuite le relais avec un plan de charge sur 24 heures, qui tient compte des habitudes de consommation et des tarifs de l’électricité. Que l’on dispose d’un contrat à prix fixe ou d’une offre à tarification dynamique, le système adapte son fonctionnement sans imposer de changer de fournisseur.
Le compteur intelligent (offert avec la batterie) joue ici un rôle important, puisqu’il mesure les flux d’électricité entrants et sortants du logement. Ces données permettent à la Nex E6000 d’affiner progressivement son pilotage et de mieux gérer l’autoconsommation. Les amateurs de domotique apprécieront également la compatibilité avec Home Assistant et Homey.
Une batterie pensée pour durer, avec une offre Black Friday à la clé
Côté fiabilité, Samduo mise sur des cellules LiFePO4, annoncées pour au moins 10 000 cycles de charge et de décharge. La batterie bénéficie d’une garantie de 10 ans et d'une certification IP65, pour une protection contre la poussière et les projections d’eau. Elle dispose également de deux prises de secours pour alimenter certains équipements en cas de coupure de courant.
Reste la question du prix. Pour le Black Friday, la Samduo Nex E6000 est proposée à 1 599 € au lieu de 1 999 €, soit 400 € de remise. Le compteur Samduo Smart Meter, habituellement vendu 129 €, est également offert pour l’occasion. L’offre est valable sur le site français de Samduo jusqu’au 30 novembre, sans cumul possible avec d’autres codes promotionnels.
Enfin, chaque commande donne également accès à un concours organisé le 21 décembre prochain, avec 12 iPhone à gagner (pour autant de gagnants) : 3 iPhone Duo 256 Go et 9 iPhone 18 Pro 256 Go. Attention, l’inscription n’est pas automatique, et il est impératif de s’inscrire avec son adresse e-mail et son numéro de commande.

articles.title: Google built an AI model that can't write a sentence — and that's the point
articles.text:
Google built an AI model that can’t write a sentence — and that’s the point
Google’s new Gemini Decisions API, introduced Wednesday, is designed to handle the routine decisions that AI applications make thousands of times a day, with lower costs, and faster response times than traditional generative models.
…the routine decisions that AI applications make thousands of times a day, with lower costs and faster response times than traditional generative models.
Instead of using a generative model to work through each decision and produce a text response, the API uses a new model, Gemini Decision 1, to evaluate predefined options in a single pass.
According to Google, response times range from 150 to 250 milliseconds for tested workloads, while pricing starts at $0.10 per million input tokens with no output-token charges.
The release comes just weeks after OpenAI launched its own Decisions API, joining TypeSafe AI and Microsoft in a growing market for models built to make specific decisions without generating text.
One pass, no generated text
The API supports a 256,000-token context window and can evaluate up to 1,000 independent questions against a single input, including multimodal content. Its responses include probabilities and confidence scores that developers can use to select between predefined options, evaluate information against specific criteria and decide how an application should proceed.
Google CEO Sundar Pichai described the model in a post on X as “built for closed-set choices,” while Google DeepMind product manager Min Choi and principal scientist Felix Yu characterized the API as providing “purpose-built primitives for bounded choices” in the launch announcement.
Where Google already uses it
Google is already using the model internally, including in Gemini Notebook, where real-time model and reasoning-level routing has reportedly reduced latency by up to 40%. Google Search also uses it to detect potentially adversarial behavior involving MCP tools.
Benchmarks come from Google
Google’s benchmark results show Gemini Decision 1 outperforming OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna, although the competition with TypeSafe’s Jev 1.14 is closer.
Logan Kilpatrick, who leads product for Google AI Studio and the Gemini API, described it on X as “our new frontier decision model in the Gemini API.” On JevBench, Google’s model scored 92.2%, compared with 90.9% for Luna and 90% for Jev.
But Jev came out ahead on two of the seven shared tests and was cheaper to run, costing $0.68 for the full benchmark suite compared with $0.88 for Gemini Decision 1. Google’s model also recorded the lowest calibration error among those tested.
All of the benchmark figures come from Google’s own testing, and independent evaluations have yet to establish how the models compare in production. SiliconANGLE also noted that Jev is cheaper than Google’s model on a per-token basis.
All of the benchmark figures come from Google’s own testing, and independent evaluations have yet to establish how the models compare in production.
What developers actually pay
Developers only pay to send the shared context once, even when they’re asking multiple questions about it, although the questions themselves still count toward token usage. The API evaluates each question separately, so a workflow that needs to use one answer to decide what to ask next requires another call.
Gemini Decision 1 is available through Google AI Studio, with a free prototyping tier and integrations through OpenRouter, LangChain, Vercel, and LiteLLM. Support for Gemini on Google Cloud is also planned, although Google has not announced a release date.

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s exit puts Nvidia’s African AI bet to the test
articles.text:
Three weeks before he resigned as Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang singled out Egypt and other African markets in an interview about where US technology companies should compete.
“There’s a reason why we’re in Africa,” he told Yahoo Finance at Nvidia’s conference in Berlin. “We want to compete everywhere.”
Huang resigned after Nvidia’s board met on Wednesday to consider removing him following reports of two extramarital affairs. One involved a Chinese businesswoman whom US authorities suspected of working for Beijing’s intelligence services, an allegation China denied. The other involved a senior Nvidia executive who reported to Huang, according to the New York Times.
Huang’s departure on Thursday comes as Nvidia’s most prominent African partner, the Zimbabwean billionaire Strive Masiyiwa’s Cassava Technologies, is trying to turn a GPU cluster in Cape Town into a business spanning five countries. The US chipmaker supplies the processors and owns a stake in Cassava, giving it a financial interest in whether African companies will pay for computing power closer to home.
Cassava is the first test
Nvidia became both a supplier to and a shareholder in Cassava Technologies, the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure group founded by Zimbabwean billionaire Strive Masiyiwa. Cassava disclosed the equity investment in October 2025 without disclosing the size.
Its rollout could cost up to $720 million and plans to deploy 12,000 Nvidia GPUs. Its first data centre is running in Cape Town. Cassava and Vodafone have announced a project in Egypt, while Kenya, Nigeria and Morocco remain part of the expansion plan.
The Nvidia investment in Cassava matters because it would give African companies a way to rent the computing power needed to train and run AI models on the continent. South Africa already offers an example beyond the planned Cassava centres.
South Africa’s Altron said its Nvidia-powered facility went live in October 2025 with five customers, including Lelapa AI, which develops speech tools for languages such as isiZulu and Sesotho.
A consortium that includes Nvidia and South Korea’s Naver also plans a data centre near Casablanca with up to 500 megawatts of capacity, aimed in part at serving European customers.
What changes for Africa
It’s still early to predict what Huang’s exit will have on the deal with Cassava. The question is whether Nvidia’s next leadership continues to take equity stakes in regional operators and gives them timely access to newer chips.
If Nvidia becomes more selective, African operators could must rely more heavily on outside financing or secure large customers before expanding.
Local data centres give African customers more control over where their data is processed. But the development of compute power still depends on hardware and software supplied by US companies, such as Nvidia.
Nvidia decides future chip supply and investment, while African operators have to make the economics work through local demand, power costs and pricing. Huang’s departure could affect such development if the leadership changes its approach to the continent.

articles.title: Vi la NFL en el Bernabéu y llegué a una conclusión: el fútbol americano se ha convertido en un 'videojuego' lleno de datos
articles.text:
El pasado domingo, tuve la oportunidad de disfrutar en vivo y en directo del NFL Madrid Game, que ha celebrado este año su segunda edición. El partido de fútbol americano entre los Cincinnati Bengals y los Atlanta Falcons se disputó en un Bernabéu vestido de gala para la ocasión (plagado de controles de seguridad, por cierto) y acabó con un 34-17 a favor de los Bengals.
Pero el resultado, para mí, fue lo de menos. Era mi primera vez en un partido de la NFL y, como en Xataka nos gusta buscar el lado tech de cualquier evento, acudí al estadio acompañada del equipo de AWS (Amazon Web Services). ¿Por qué AWS? Pues porque es el socio tecnológico de la NFL desde hace más de una década.
Con AWS, la NFL ha pasado de medir estadísticas básicas a analizar cada movimiento en el campo en tiempo real y traducirlo en lo que ellos denominan 'Next Gen Stats' (NGS), unas métricas avanzadas que ayudan a los espectadores a entender el juego, a los equipos a planificar estrategias y a los jugadores a prevenir lesiones.
La irrupción de los chips en el terreno de juego. Durante más de un siglo, el fútbol americano solo se medía por resultados, como las yardas ganadas, los touchdowns o los placajes, pero esos datos no mostraban todo lo que ocurría realmente en el campo. Y ahí es donde aparece AWS, que se alió con la NFL en 2015.
A raíz de ese acuerdo, se empezaron a colocar pequeños chips de rastreo (RFID) en las hombreras de los jugadores, dentro del balón y en los marcadores, además de instalar más de 20 antenas en cada estadio. Así nació 'Next Gen Stats' (NGS), que registraban la posición exacta (con precisión de centímetros) de los jugadores 10 veces por segundo y del balón 25 veces por segundo.
La explosión de los datos. Al principio, los datos obtenidos por los chips solo servían para medir cosas sencillas, como la velocidad máxima de un jugador o cuánto tardaba el quarterback en lanzar el balón. Pero en 2018, la NFL amplió su alianza con AWS y entró en juego el aprendizaje automático (machine learning).
A partir de ahí, la NFL y AWS convirtieron todos esos datos de seguimiento de jugadores en una plataforma de datos en tiempo real que hoy en día puede reconocer patrones, generar estadísticas avanzadas y ofrecer una visión mucho más amplia de lo que ocurre en el campo.
Más de 200 estadísticas por jugada. Uno de los mejores ejemplos de esas estadísticas avanzadas es la métrica de 'probabilidad de pase completado' (Catch Probability). En ella, un algoritmo analiza en tiempo real factores como la presión sobre el pasador, la distancia del lanzamiento o la cercanía del defensor al receptor para calcular el porcentaje de dificultad del pase y mostrarlo en la retransmisión del partido.
Para hacernos una idea de la evolución, en la última década, Next Gen Stats ha pasado de medir únicamente la velocidad a ofrecer más de 40 modelos estadísticos, como Pressure Probability (probabilidad de presión) o Tackle Probability (probabilidad de placaje), que permiten generar más de 200 estadísticas distintas por jugada.
La revolución en la retransmisión del fútbol americano. Actualmente, 75 modelos de inteligencia artificial procesan millones de datos por partido en menos de un segundo. Con toda esa información, las retransmisiones de televisión muestran a los aficionados gráficos y estadísticas avanzadas al instante que ayudan a entender la dificultad de cada jugada. Y eso es algo que, personalmente, agradecí bastante durante el partido de los Bengals y los Falcons.
Además de ser útil para las retransmisiones, los entrenadores usan toda esa información para, por ejemplo, evaluar fichajes, diseñar estrategias y preparar los partidos. Y la NFL también combina los datos con simulaciones basadas en IA para analizar los impactos y el esfuerzo físico que sufren los jugadores, y reducir así el riesgo de lesión. Ellos lo llaman 'NFL Digital Athlete'.
Una misión imposible que ya no es imposible. Otro de los aspectos que más me llamó la atención es la dificultad que entraña elaborar el calendario de la NFL. Según AWS, es uno de los retos computacionales más complejos del deporte profesional porque, para distribuir 272 partidos en 18 semanas, la NFL debe tener en cuenta más de 26.000 factores: desplazamientos, disponibilidad de estadios, rivalidades de división, partidos en horario de máxima audiencia, criterios de competición...
Dicho así, no suena exagerado, pero cada temporada, más de 4.000 instancias de Amazon EC2 ejecutan unas 1.000 permutaciones al día que permiten a la NFL analizar más de 100.000 calendarios posibles de entre unos mil billones de combinaciones. Casi nada.

articles.title: SoftBank’s billion-dollar loss may have put a cap on AI's natural gas ambitions | TechCrunch
articles.text:
SoftBank might not be the first to invest in a hot trend, but when it does, it goes big.
Witness its $30 billion bet on OpenAI in early 2025 or its announcement in February that its SB Energy subsidiary would spend $33 billion on a 9.2-gigawatt natural gas power plant. If you can’t be first, be biggest, I guess.
That philosophy apparently spilled over into procurement, where orders were also supersized. Starting about two years ago, SoftBank reportedly put down deposits on more than 13 gigawatts of turbines, almost 50% more than it needed.
The decision to over-order undoubtedly helped secure turbines and speed up SoftBank’s projects.
“SB Energy did not have a choice except to overbook turbines in the future if they wanted some turbines right away,” Peter Gardett, CEO of Noreva, told TechCrunch via email.
The energy world was caught off guard by the swiftness and magnitude of AI’s rising power demands. Queues for turbine orders now extend into the early 2030s. As natural gas was shaping up to be a go-to power source for the AI boom, CEO Masayoshi Son bet that by deploying his investment firm’s significant war chest, he could corner a portion of the market. If the AI world wanted power for its data centers, it would have to come to him.
Now that bet appears to have fizzled. SoftBank announced a $7.1 billion quarterly loss on Tuesday, with over half of that stemming from losses related to power-generating equipment. The investor had paid turbine manufacturers nonrefundable deposits to secure orders, and now it considered much of those worthless.
The move was also a costly bit of price discovery, Gardett said. Rather than overpay and potentially still be short of turbines, SoftBank overpaid and over-ordered.
“This charge is just that price discovery finally happening,” Gardett said.
The magnitude of that misplaced bet — over $3 billion — reflects some of the electricity mania that has overtaken the AI world. Faced with years-long waits to connect to the grid, many hyperscalers and developers have turned to natural gas as a sort of energy security blanket, something that is proven and familiar.
As AI data centers spend more time in operation, their operators are getting a better feel for what’s required to keep them operating. Natural gas might seem like a safe bet, but there are still risks, including winter curtailments when supplies dip and demand spikes, Brent Nelson, senior managing director of markets and strategy at Ascend Analytics, told the Equity podcast Wednesday.
In light of that, Nelson said the grid might still be their best bet. Most data centers would be best served by a grid connection, albeit a smaller one than they might normally request. To make up for the shortfall, large batteries are a cost-effective choice, Nelson said. They’d help shave peak loads or ride out requests from the utility to curtail electricity use.
Data center operators might be coming to that same conclusion, leading the natural gas market to develop more slowly than SoftBank expected.
SoftBank’s natural gas-related losses are unlikely to have a domino effect, leading to mass cancellations of gas power plants. AI’s power demand appears to be too large for that. For now, natural gas is riding high, though SoftBank may have found its ceiling.

articles.title: Jumpstarter platform helps SA entrepreneurs raise seed capital from their communities - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
South African civic-fintech Jumpstarter Crowdfunding is helping entrepreneurs, creatives and social impact organisations raise seed funding directly from their communities through a reward-based, all-or-nothing crowdfunding model.
Founded in 2012 and operating as a registered non-profit company (NPC), Jumpstarter allows project creators to run campaigns of between one and 60 days, with funds only released if 100 per cent of the target is reached. If a campaign falls short, pledges are returned to backers and the creator pays no platform fees. Backers receive non-financial rewards such as pre-ordered products, experiences or project perks, rather than equity or debt.
“South Africa has over 2.5 million micro, small and medium enterprises, and the vast majority of them face an early-stage funding gap estimated at between ZAR80 billion (US$4.8 billion) and ZAR100 billion (US$6 billion),” co-founder and chief operations officer Derek Whitehead told Disrupt Africa.
“Commercial banks demand collateral and historical balance sheets that grassroots innovators simply don’t have, while venture capital is concentrated in late-stage or hyper-scalable tech. Global platforms like Kickstarter and Indiegogo, meanwhile, lack native rand payment rails and add foreign exchange friction.”
Jumpstarter is led by Whitehead alongside co-founder and director Yaseen Kriel and director Zaid Kriel, supported by a network of advisers, digital marketing contributors and technology partners. The platform runs on Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure, is managed via Salesforce CRM, and pairs campaigns with digital marketing support funded through a US$10,000-per-month Google Ad Grant.
That marketing support is central to how the startup differentiates itself from local rivals such as Thundafund, BackaBuddy and Uprise Africa.
“Unlike platforms that function purely as passive software directories, Jumpstarter acts as an active launchpad,” Whitehead said. “Our all-or-nothing model protects backer capital, our non-profit charter lets us charge lower fees, and we actively subsidise creator outreach through our Google Ad Grant.”
The model appears to be gaining traction. Jumpstarter has facilitated more than ZAR1.34 million (US$80,000) in community-backed capital across over 36 successfully funded campaigns, spanning food and beverage, creative arts, software, publishing, green-tech and community development. Notable campaigns include helping Cape Town’s Charly’s Bakery survive lockdown disruptions and backing the commercial launch of the Pirate Masters card game.
“Campaigns that engage our structured preparation and ad-subsidisation workflows regularly achieve between 100 and 108 per cent of their targets,” Whitehead said.
Jumpstarter charges a seven per cent fee on successful for-profit campaigns and five per cent for registered NPOs and schools, with third-party payment gateways PayGate and SnapScan deducting additional processing fees. As a non-profit, all surplus revenue is reinvested into infrastructure, campaign support tools and community pilot programmes. The organisation is self-sustaining, with operations also subsidised through partnerships with AWS, Salesforce.org and Google.
The startup was recently selected for the CATAPULT: Inclusion Africa 2026 cohort run by the Luxembourg House of Financial Technology (LHoFT), and while its operations are currently focused on South Africa, it accepts pledges from backers globally, including diaspora communities. It plans to expand its infrastructure and mobile money integrations into markets such as Kenya and Nigeria within the next 24 to 36 months.
The biggest challenge, Whitehead said, has been overcoming the “cold-start” problem faced by first-time creators.
“Many entrepreneurs mistake crowdfunding for a passive lottery, assuming that publishing a campaign will automatically bring in traffic. In reality, crowdfunding amplifies pre-existing momentum. Projects must rally their first 20 to 30 per cent from their immediate networks within 48 hours to trigger the social proof needed for broader discovery,” he said.
“Because unreached goals generate zero revenue for us, educating creators on narrative clarity, realistic budgeting and early community mobilisation remains our most hands-on task.”
The startup is also working to reduce checkout friction on mobile by integrating lower-friction payment options such as PayShap and instant EFT.
