articles.title: Deadpool y Lobezno (Wolverine), confirmados oficialmente en 'Avengers: Doomsday': así se ha revelado su cameo secreto
articles.text:
Lo que durante mucho tiempo ha sido un secreto a voces parece que ya es oficial. Ryan Reynolds y Hugh Jackman, los actores de Deadpool y Lobezno (Wolverine) estarán en Avengers: Doomsday. Ambos intérpretes regresan a Marvel para la próxima película de los Vengadores, que se estrena en diciembre y que se ha convertido en uno de los lanzamientos más esperados del año.
En realidad, Marvel había tratado de mantener en secreto su participación en la película. Incluso se ha jugado al despiste llevando al propio Ryan Reynolds solamente como público a convenciones en las que se presentaba el proyecto. Pero ahora, se ha revelado definitivamente que sí son parte de la historia de Avengers: Doomsday. Lo curioso es que no ha sido cosa de Marvel ni de los intérpretes.
Resulta que el Sindicato de Guionistas (WGA) ha actualizado los créditos de Avengers: Doomsday bajo el concepto "Additional Literary Material". Esto se utiliza cuando se quiere acreditar a personas que han trabajado en un guion pero en un porcentaje demasiado pequeño como para ser considerados guionistas del filme. Y resulta que entre los nombres incluidos en este nuevo listado están los de Ryan Reynolds y Hugh Jackman.
Por tanto, ya está confirmado que ambos han participado en el guion de la película. Y, evidentemente, ha tenido que ser para sus propios personajes. Es decir, que gracias a esta nueva información ya sabemos que Deadpool y Lobezno (Wolverine) tendrán al menos un cameo en Avengers: Doomsday.
Más guionsitas para Avengers: Doomsday
En realidad, Ryan Reynolds y Hugh Jackman no son los únicos añadidos por el WGA. Con el mismo concepto de "Additional Literary Material" están Eric Pearson (Thunderbolts*), Chris McKenna y Erik Sommers (Spider-Man: Brand New Day), Jeff Loveness (Ant-Man y La Avispa), Andrew Lanham y Destin Daniel Cretton (Shang-Chi y la leyenda de los Diez Anillos).
Pearson es un habitual de Marvel al que la compañía le suele encargar que ayude a que un guion encaje dentro de la gran narrativa del UCM. Ya ha colaborado en películas como Los 4 Fantásticos: Primeros pasos o Viuda Negra. En cuanto a Loveness, fue quien debía escribir originalmente Avengers 5, titulada por aquel entonces La dinastía de Kang.
Uno de los nombres más destacados de la lista es el de Cretton, que acaba de dirigir Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Pero aunque esto podría anticipar el regreso del arácnido, la presencia de Lanham, guionista de Shang-Chi y la leyenda de los Diez Anillos, da a entender que lo más probable es que ambos hayan trabajado codo con codo en el arco narrativo del propio Shang-Chi.
Avengers: Doomsday se estrena en cines el 18 de diciembre.

articles.title: From prototype to production: Engineering agents with Agent DLC | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
From prototype to production: Engineering agents with Agent DLC
Over the past year, AI agents have moved from exploration into engineering. Enterprise teams are shipping large language model (LLM) systems that call tools, orchestrate APIs, and answer questions over internal knowledge.
A successful demo can show what an agent is capable of. Before release, the team needs to answer a further question: “Is this agent ready for production?” The person responsible for that decision needs evidence that the agent meets the agreed requirements.
To make that decision consistently, teams need a repeatable, affordable way to assess the agent’s current behavior and whether the latest change has improved it.
In traditional software development, teams answer these questions with unit tests, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD), and passing builds. Those mechanisms are necessary but not sufficient for agents, for three reasons, each requiring additional checks. This post explains these three properties and presents a measured case where an aggregate metric hides a coverage problem. It then introduces the Agent Development Lifecycle (Agent DLC): one lifecycle, two loops, and a single explicit standard for judging every change.
A note on terminology: Throughout this post, gold standard means one specific artifact: the bundle of verifiable criteria, their thresholds, and the approved examples they are checked against. Business owners approve this standard as the basis for acceptance decisions.
1. Three properties of agents that require additional engineering practices
Conventional software testing and CI/CD still apply to agents, but three properties require additional checks. First, agents are non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different outputs and execution paths. Second, changes to prompts, tool descriptions, retrieval settings, or memory configuration can alter behavior in ways that a text review alone can’t reveal. Third, model endpoints, knowledge bases, and external APIs can change independently of the repository and affect agent behavior. Table 1 summarizes the engineering practices needed to address each property.
Table 1. What each property invalidates, and what it requires instead.
| Property | The conventional answer | Why it falls short | What Agent DLC requires | 
| Non-determinism | One assertion per case in CI | Measures a single sample of a distribution. Passes and fails for reasons unrelated to your change | Run each example k times. Judge on pass rate and failure distribution | 
| Prompts are source code | Review the diff, approve the change | Behavior can’t be read off the text of a prompt | Every prompt, tool, retrieval, and memory change is versioned with an evaluation attached, and the lineage is kept | 
| Dependencies move on their own | Pin versions, validate on upgrade | Doesn’t fire because nothing in your repository changed | Re-run the standard on a schedule and alert on deviations from the baseline | 
2. A measured example: High retrieval precision can hide missing information
The following example shows how the choice of metrics affects diagnosis.
We built a reference implementation to exercise the method end to end: an internal policy assistant answering HR policy questions over a document knowledge base. We chose a narrow, well-scoped domain to make the evaluation and diagnosis straightforward to follow. The following results were measured on this reference implementation. It isn’t a customer outcome and it isn’t a benchmark result.
The accompanying AWS Samples repository includes infrastructure deployment, the HR agent, custom evaluators, and scripts for baseline evaluation and prompt-change re-evaluation (09-run-eval.sh and 10-optimize-prompt.sh). It also includes optional checks for judge repeatability, model comparison, cost, and latency. The scripts reproduce the workflow. Scores can vary across runs and repository versions.
Three golden questions, five measures each:
- Groundedness: Decompose the answer into claims and check each against the retrieved sources.
- Chunk-level source precision: Is each retrieved chunk, as a whole, necessary for this question?
- Fact-level source precision: Decompose each chunk into individual facts and check whether each fact is necessary.
- Retrieval coverage: For each sub-question, does any retrieved chunk answer it?
- Response precision: Of the claims in the answer, how many are necessary?
Table 2. First evaluation round. Measured on the reference implementation. Not a customer outcome.
| Question | Groundedness | Chunk-level precision | Fact-level precision | Retrieval coverage | Verdict | 
| Performance review | 0.83 | 1.00 | 0.59 | 1.00 | Pass | 
| Benefits enrollment | 0.90 | 1.00 | 0.53 | 1.00 | Pass | 
| Sick-leave certificate | 0.39 | 1.00 | 0.09 | 0.00 | Fail | 
Chunk-level precision is 1.00 for all three questions. A release gate based only on this metric would accept all three answers.
Fact-level precision tells a different story: 0.59, 0.53, 0.09. For the third question, roughly nine out of ten facts in the retrieved material are irrelevant to what was asked. Chunk-level precision only asks whether a passage is on topic. It doesn’t measure how much of the passage is relevant.
Then we changed exactly one thing: the system prompt. We added three constraints: ground strictly in retrieved content, ignore irrelevant retrieved content, and keep answers focused. The agent, the knowledge base, the evaluators, and the questions were untouched, so the before-and-after differs by one variable.
Table 3. After a prompt-only change. One change, two opposite outcomes.
|  | Performance review, before | Performance review, after | Sick leave, before | Sick leave, after | 
| Groundedness | 0.83 | 0.87 | 0.39 (fail) | 0.31 (still fail) | 
| Fact-level precision | 0.59 | 0.85 | 0.09 | 0.04 | 
| Response precision | 0.58 | 0.73 | 0.33 | — | 
The first question improved substantially. The third got worse.
The evaluation suggested where to investigate before we made the change. Look at the third row of Table 2 again: chunk-level precision 1.00, fact-level precision 0.09, retrieval coverage 0.00. Together, these scores suggested a knowledge-coverage problem: the retrieved material was nominally on topic but didn’t answer the question. Telling the model to “ground strictly in retrieved content” couldn’t supply the missing information.
We checked that diagnosis against the source documents used in the experiment. The corpus lacked a dedicated sick-leave policy document, although the leave-management policy contained brief references to sick leave. The next step was to address policy coverage and then check retrieval, rather than keep changing the prompt.
In this case, the source material lacks the information needed to answer the question, so prompt changes alone can’t resolve the failure.
In this example, evaluation helped identify what needed investigation before further changes.
Another result shows why groundedness needs to be checked alongside other criteria. The benefits-enrollment answer passed with groundedness 0.90, and it contained this sentence: “I also noticed from your profile that your preferred contact method is Social Media.” No such profile exists.
The policy document lists contact preference as an option inside a process step. The public, crowd-sourced, noisy FAQ corpus contains a pair answering that question with “social media”. The model combined a policy option with an unrelated FAQ answer and presented it as a fact about the user. The high groundedness score didn’t catch this false personal claim. Passing a quality threshold doesn’t establish that responsibility constraints have been met.
These scores can vary between runs, and a borderline Pass can become a Fail. Interpret score differences alongside repeated runs and the underlying evidence. Section 5 discusses how to check evaluator reliability.
This small reference-implementation example illustrates how evaluation can guide diagnosis. It doesn’t establish a general improvement rate or validate a production release.
3. Agent DLC: One lifecycle, two loops
Agent DLC connects six activities around one explicit gold standard: Define, Build, Evaluate, Release, Observe, and Feed Back.
Evaluation-driven development has been described in earlier work, including Xia et al.’s Evaluation-Driven Development of LLM Agents: A Process Model and Reference Architecture. Agent DLC applies this approach to delivery through six activities with explicit acceptance conditions, release authority, and evidence requirements.
The acceptance-first approach also appears in Fotor’s published AWS customer case study. The team defined scalability, cost, isolation, and architectural flexibility criteria before migrating to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, then validated changes against operating data. The case reports workflow overhead falling from minutes to seconds, excluding model inference, and support for thousands of concurrent active sessions. It documents Agent DLC-guided architecture delivery. Quality evaluation is identified as the next step.
Define translates business objectives into criteria, thresholds, and approved examples. Build designs the prompts, tools, context, memory, and runtime mechanisms that must satisfy them. Evaluate produces the evidence that says whether a candidate version does. When it does, the version goes to a controlled release. Observe watches it in production. Feed Back returns what production teaches to Define.
Figure 1 shows how each activity uses or updates the standard, making its role in development and release explicit.
Inside that outer loop runs a faster inner loop: score → inspect the path → change one thing → re-evaluate. It operates on one candidate version and answers two questions: where to change, and whether the change helped.
The two loops do different jobs, and the difference matters. The inner loop improves the agent against a fixed standard. The outer loop lets the standard change. Finding during development that the agent recommends products without checking inventory is an inner-loop problem. Suppose production users ask the agent to look things up on behalf of a family member, but no criterion covers this case. This requires the outer loop: define the authorization boundary and add examples. Then use the inner loop to meet the updated standard.
Confusing the two can lead teams to try to fix a missing criterion with a prompt change. Teams might also widen the standard during an improvement cycle, leaving them unable to tell which change moved the score.
Both loops build reusable assets: business criteria, approved examples, evaluators, and the record of how past failures were handled. These assets outlive the model and the framework. When you change models, evaluate the replacement against the same criteria and examples.
The next four sections explain how to define good so it can be checked (section 4) and improve the agent against that standard (section 5). They then cover updating the standard through production feedback (section 6) and designing the architecture to provide evaluation evidence (section 7).
4. Define good: Five dimensions, three tiers
Start with a business outcome defined by its owner. For a recommendation agent, this might be: “Recommend suitable products to returning customers while protecting their information.” Translate that requirement into verifiable criteria across five dimensions.
Table 4. Consider all five dimensions when defining criteria.
| Dimension | Key question | Areas of focus | 
| Domain understanding | Does it actually understand your business? | Terminology, aliases, multi-hop relationships, internal enterprise knowledge | 
| Quality | Is it correct, complete, and consistent throughout? | Correctness, completeness, consistency, support for citations | 
| Responsibility | Are permissions, boundaries, compliance, and auditability addressed? | Unauthorized access, information disclosure, compliance hard constraints, traceability | 
| Cost | What does each run cost, and does it stay economical at scale? | Token consumption, evaluator cost, redundant steps | 
| Performance | Is it fast, stable, and able to carry the load? | Latency, throughput, stability, availability | 
For each criterion, specify how it’s verified and who approves it. “It must be accurate” is a goal. “Every factual claim must be traceable to a retrieved source” is verifiable. Business experts should approve examples that make the expected behavior concrete.
Table 5. Criteria fall into three tiers. The tier, not the dimension, decides whether a criterion blocks a release.
| Tier | Blocks release? | How it’s expressed | Example | 
| Hard constraint | Yes | Boolean, evaluated per run | Disclosing another customer’s information | 
| Release gate | Until it’s met | Pass-rate threshold over k runs | At least 95% of cited clauses traceable to a source | 
| Monitoring only | No | Tracked and reviewed, promoted later | Tone appropriateness, until its evaluator is calibrated | 
Assign each criterion its own tier and, where applicable, threshold. Never let a high score elsewhere offset a hard-constraint violation.
In the recommendation example, recommendation quality is a release gate under Quality, while protecting another customer’s information is a hard constraint under Responsibility. One business requirement produces criteria in different dimensions and tiers. Assess each against its own acceptance condition.
These criteria also determine what evidence the system must expose. The next section uses that evidence to improve the agent and decide whether to release it. Section 7 explains how evidence requirements shape the architecture.
5. The inner loop: Evaluate, diagnose, and improve
Score. Match the evaluator to the criterion. Use code for unambiguous rules, runtime telemetry for cost and latency, and load tests and operating data for capacity and availability. Use model-based judges for criteria requiring judgment, calibrated against human-reviewed examples. Include authorization and cross-user isolation tests alongside checks for prohibited fields when evaluating information protection. Run each example k times to assess variable behavior.
For model-based judges, repeat evaluations to measure scoring variability and compare their judgments with human-reviewed examples. Small score gains need supporting evidence before they count as improvements.
Inspect the path. Locate a failure at three levels: session, trajectory, and step. If a recommendation exposes a phone number, follow the affected session to response composition and inspect where profile fields entered the draft. The cause might be upstream of the visible symptom, as section 2 showed.
Change one thing, then re-evaluate. Correct the identified cause and repeat evaluation against the unchanged standard under the same conditions. Verify that disclosure stopped and recommendation quality still meets its gate.
Assess release readiness separately for each task type, or intent. Release only those that meet their criteria, with any fallback for an unreleased intent also meeting the agreed release conditions.
Table 6. Release decisions by dimension, tier, and intent.
| State of the grid | Decision | 
| Any hard constraint failed | Don’t release. | 
| All hard constraints pass, but one or more release gates missed | Don’t release the affected intent unless a limited rollout was approved in advance with explicit safeguards and stop criteria. Otherwise, route it to a human. | 
| All hard constraints pass, and all release gates met | Full release. | 
A limited rollout needs acceptance conditions, safeguards, and stop criteria agreed before evaluation. It can’t override a hard constraint or lower a threshold after a failed result.
Before release, include blocked and refused requests in the evaluation, checking whether each was handled as expected. Record the criteria, thresholds, evaluator versions, and release decision so the team can trace why a version was approved.
Passing these checks supports release within the tested scope. Production monitoring then checks whether the agent continues to meet the standard as usage and dependencies change.
6. The outer loop: Keep the data flowing
Record execution traces from the first test request so failures can be diagnosed in development and production. Sample and evaluate production interactions to identify failures, then review them with the business owner to confirm the expected behavior. Add cases covered by existing criteria to the regression set. When a case reveals a missing requirement, update the standard and use the inner loop to meet it.
Run evaluations regularly to catch behavior changes caused by external dependencies. When the standard changes, compare results under both versions to distinguish agent regression from broader test coverage. Link each result to its standard, test set, evaluator, and agent version.
7. Design the architecture to support evaluation
The evaluation and feedback loops need evidence that the architecture must provide. Work backward from each criterion to the system behavior and records needed to verify it.
For example, to distinguish a tool-selection error from an execution failure, define the tool’s purpose, accepted inputs, outputs, and error conditions. Expose the actual inputs, results, and errors in traces so evaluators can locate the failure.
Acceptance criteria therefore shape both evaluation and architecture. With those foundations in place, start with one business task and establish a baseline.
8. Getting started on AWS
Choose one clearly scoped business task and aim to establish an initial evaluation baseline within a week.
- Days 1–2. Have the business owner and engineers agree on acceptance criteria, tiers, and thresholds. Prepare 20–30 golden examples covering common requests and important edge cases, with expected behavior approved by the business owner.
- Days 3–5. Implement the evaluators described in section 5 and run the golden set repeatedly. Publish the baseline, including failures and the evidence needed to investigate them.
- Week 2. Change one thing and re-evaluate under the same conditions. Record the release decision and its supporting evidence.
After reviewing the baseline, integrate evaluation into the release process and run it regularly to detect drift. Assign an owner to review production failures and feed confirmed cases back into the standard.
On AWS, use models available through Amazon Bedrock to build the agent. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, assesses agent behavior with built-in evaluators and supports custom evaluators for business-specific criteria. AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, provides execution visibility, complemented by Amazon CloudWatch for runtime monitoring and diagnostics. AgentCore runtime, Gateway, Identity, and Memory support execution, tool integration, identity management, and memory management.

    Pour aller plus loin
Quelles sont les meilleures barres de son testées en 2026 ?
            
Cette restriction tranche avec la Beosound Theatre, un modèle plus sophistiqué et nettement plus cher (environ 7 000 dollars aux États-Unis, à partir de 10 100 euros sur le site européen de la marque), qui accepte des enceintes de plusieurs générations. La Premiere, elle, se limite à quatre enceintes supplémentaires, quand la Theatre peut en piloter jusqu’à 16.

Ce que prévoit la mise à jour
D’après le revendeur britannique Bang & Olufsen of Birmingham, cité par FlatpanelsHD, une mise à jour en bêta doit lever en partie ces limites. Les anciennes enceintes seraient reliées par câble à des boîtiers Beosound Core, eux-mêmes associés à la barre de son. Il deviendrait ainsi possible d’ajouter, par exemple, une paire de Beolab 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 17, 18, 20, 6000 ou 8000 à l’avant ou à l’arrière.
Côté graves, un seul caisson serait accepté, à choisir parmi les Beolab 2, 11 ou 19. Il occuperait toutefois deux des quatre emplacements disponibles. Il resterait donc de la place pour une paire d’enceintes, à l’avant ou à l’arrière. Or il s’agit d’un caisson de basses. Une confirmation officielle de la liste complète reste donc nécessaire.
Disponibilité et prix
Aucune date de sortie n’a été annoncée pour cette mise à jour. Le passage en bêta indique seulement que son développement est bien avancé. Bang & Olufsen n’a pas encore confirmé ces informations, qui proviennent d’un revendeur. La Beosound Premiere est proposée en trois finitions, Natural Aluminium, Gold Tone et Black Anthracite, à partir de 3 900 euros sur le site européen de la marque, contre 4 900 euros à son lancement. Il faudra en outre au moins un boîtier Beosound Core pour profiter de cette compatibilité étendue dont le coût est de 1 099 euros…
Enfin, notez que la barre de son Beosound Stage, modèle d’entrée de gamme de Bang & Olufsen, n’est pas concernée par cette mise à jour et reste privée de toute possibilité d’ajouter des enceintes externes.

articles.title: El regulador de medios del Reino Unido multó a Meta con unos USD 600.000 por datos inexactos sobre WhatsApp Business
articles.text:
El regulador de medios y telecomunicaciones del Reino Unido, Ofcom, impuso a Meta una multa de 450.000 libras esterlinas (unos USD 597.000, según Reuters) por dar información inexacta sobre WhatsApp Business. La sanción responde a datos que la empresa entregó al organismo durante una revisión del mercado de mensajes de texto para empresas.
Ofcom emitió su decisión el 9 de noviembre y la publicó el 12 de noviembre. Concluyó que Meta incumplió cinco veces su obligación de responder con precisión: dio datos incorrectos a cinco preguntas, incluidas en dos requerimientos formales de información.
WhatsApp Business es la versión de la aplicación de mensajería pensada para empresas, que la usan para hablar con sus clientes. Según Ofcom, los requerimientos pidieron una serie de datos sobre ese servicio, entre ellos los volúmenes de mensajes y los ingresos, y se enviaron entre julio de 2024 y agosto de 2025.
Un descuento del 25% por admitir la falta
La multa incluye una rebaja del 25% porque Meta reconoció su responsabilidad y completó el proceso de acuerdo con el regulador. Ofcom abrió la investigación el 23 de enero. Los requerimientos que originaron el caso son del 31 de julio de 2024 y del 19 de junio de 2025.
El regulador calificó las infracciones de graves. Explicó que sus facultades para pedir datos son esenciales para cumplir sus funciones y que las fallas, repetidas en varias solicitudes, ponen en riesgo la integridad del sistema y los intereses de los consumidores.
Los errores también obligaron al organismo a dedicar más recursos a detectarlos, pedir aclaraciones y verificar las cifras, lo que afectó su análisis del mercado, dijo Ofcom. Según Reuters, algunas discrepancias persistieron hasta 11 meses antes de que Meta entregara datos corregidos.
Meta afirmó que considera prioritario cumplir con sus obligaciones y que colaboró por completo con la investigación, según medios que citan la comunicación de la empresa.
La revisión del mercado de SMS
Ofcom revisó en 2025 el mercado de los mensajes de texto masivos que las empresas envían a sus clientes, como avisos o códigos de verificación. En enero de ese año propuso un tope a los precios que cobran los operadores de telefonía móvil por entregar esos mensajes.
En septiembre de 2025, el regulador publicó una nota de corrección tras un aviso de Meta: la empresa le había informado errores en los datos sobre las conversaciones de WhatsApp Business vendidas. Ofcom retiró entonces una corrección anterior y la reemplazó.
Ofcom decidió después no continuar con la revisión por ahora. El organismo mencionó como motivo, entre otros, las rebajas de precios recientes de WhatsApp Business y compromisos voluntarios de cuatro grandes operadores. El comunicado no vincula esa decisión con los errores de Meta.
Según el estudio jurídico Bratby Law, el máximo para este tipo de infracción es de 2 millones de libras, más 500 libras por día si continúa. En 2024, Ofcom multó a TikTok con 1,875 millones de libras por datos inexactos en otro caso.
La sanción a Meta ya está publicada en el sitio de Ofcom, junto con una versión no confidencial de la decisión.

articles.title: Norwest closes $4B fund to back AI, healthcare and financial infra
articles.text:
Norwest closes $4B fund to back AI, healthcare and financial infra
Norwest’s $4 billion fund signals a long-term bet on AI, healthcare and technology, as the investment firm looks to back businesses across markets, stages and sectors.
Norwest, an investment firm focused on venture capital and growth equity, has closed a $4 billion fund, Norwest 18, the largest in its 65-year history. It will back companies in technology, healthcare and consumer markets across the US, India and Israel, from early-stage ventures to established businesses.
Founded in 1961, Norwest says it has invested in more than 750 companies and currently works with over 275 portfolio businesses. Its Indian investments include OfBusiness and Swiggy, and it has a Mumbai office. The firm notes its multi-stage approach is intended to support companies as they move from early development to expansion.
Norwest 18 follows Norwest 17, launched in April 2024. Since then, the firm says it has made more than 87 investments and worked with over 30 portfolio companies to achieve liquidity events, when investors can realise value from a holding. These include stock market listings by Amagi Media Labs and Swiggy, and acquisitions of businesses including Qualified by Salesforce and Veza by ServiceNow.
The firm believes its role extends beyond providing capital, particularly as businesses face more complicated growth decisions. Senior Managing Partner Jeff Crowe said companies are staying private for longer, expanding across markets and navigating increasingly complex decisions involving technology, talent and growth.
“Capital is only one part of what they need,” he said, emphasising the importance of long-term support, industry experience and networks.
Norwest expects AI to create opportunities across its established sectors and newer areas, including financial infrastructure, physical and voice AI, cybersecurity for AI agents, industrial technology, aerospace and healthcare. Norwest cites Beltic, Rain and Stablecore in payments and digital-currency infrastructure, and LlamaIndex and Generalist AI in intelligent systems.
The strategy comes as Indian technology investment becomes more concentrated. AI startups in the country raised $1.6 billion in the first nine months of 2026, compared with $677 million a year earlier, but funding rounds fell 43%. Four large deals accounted for 72% of the total, indicating that capital is flowing disproportionately to infrastructure and model developers, while application businesses struggle to convert interest into paying customers.
Recent Indian fundraises show activity across related sectors. Bengaluru-based Even Healthcare raised $50 million in October from Khosla Ventures and Alpha Wave to expand its managed-care and hospital operations, while wealth technology startup PowerUp Money raised $10 million in November, led by Flourish Ventures, to develop AI-enabled wealth management.
Policy is also shaping the market. The IndiaAI Mission has expanded shared computing capacity to more than 45,000 graphics processing units, and selected 20 proposals for locally developed foundation AI models. In July, the Cabinet approved Semicon 2.0, with a Rs 1.275 trillion budget for semiconductor design and manufacturing.
Norwest is also strengthening support beyond funding by doubling its Senior Advisor Network, adding operating executives and launching the Norwest Operator Collective and Norwest Kinetic.
Managing Partner Jon Kossow said Norwest’s investment approach was built around maintaining long-term relationships with businesses as their requirements evolve. Its multi-stage strategy allows the firm to “meet companies where they are” and continue supporting them as they grow, he said.

articles.title: New Windows SignDrop zero-day gives hackers SYSTEM privileges
articles.text:
Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri (also known as Nightmare Eclipse) has released a new Windows zero-day exploit that can let attackers gain SYSTEM privileges.
Named SignDrop, it exploits mitigations Microsoft introduced in October 2025 to defend against authentication attacks targeting vulnerabilities in the Common Log File System (CLFS) driver. Naceri added that attacks exploiting CLFS vulnerabilities dropped sharply after the mitigation, but that Microsoft's mitigation itself introduced this new vulnerability.
According to Naceri, the flaw is in how CLFS handles creating the authentication file (".cnpf") when it creates a new log file. He said that CLFS enforces access checks correctly at the start, but the logic can be abused if a different, privileged process later opens the log file.
He also added that privileged processes such as Windows Defender can be forced to open the files, so the authentication file gets created with SYSTEM privileges, and CLFS creates it with the original file's access permissions.
Naceri noted that Microsoft implemented the mitigation properly but that "the logic allows abuse" and said the technique works against any antimalware engine's self-defense (tamper protection), because the file-creation request appears to come from the engine's own legitimate process.
"If everything is chained correctly, funnily, this legit security mitigation can be used against itself and allow an elevation of privileges. Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse," the security researcher said.
"What makes it funnier is the fact that it can be used against any antimalware engine to bypass their self defense (or tamper protection) mechanism, as you can trigger arbitrary file creation in the context of their own antimalware process so from the perspective of their kernel drivers, the file creation request is coming from their own legit process so it passes, this makes this vulnerability unique as it can be used to turn off any antivirus/EDR."
While SignDrop can't be used against all Windows machines, Naceri tested the exploit on Windows 11 26H2, Windows 11 26H2 Experimental, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental and estimates that 80% of Windows installations are vulnerable.
Naceri recommends running the proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit to check if a Windows device is vulnerable to SignDrop attacks or to check the CLFS authentication mode under the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode registry value.
If the PoC exploit spawns a SYSTEM shell, the machine is vulnerable. Additionally, if the registry value is 0 or 1 (learning mode or enforcement mode), the computer is vulnerable.
Naceri added that there is currently no solution except waiting for a patch from Microsoft, since disabling the CLFS mitigation would expose the devices to attacks exploiting memory corruption vulnerabilities.
The security researcher, who says he is a former Microsoft employee, has disclosed a long list of other zero-day flaws in Microsoft Defender, BitLocker, and other Windows components since April, including BigDiskBuster, ShieldCrash, ShieldBreak, LegacyHive, RoguePlanet, BlueHammer, RedSun, YellowKey, GreenPlasma, MiniPlasma, and UnDefend.
Five years ago, Naceri released several zero-day exploits that allowed privilege escalation on various Windows versions.
After Naceri publicly disclosed the zero-days without first attempting to report them privately, Microsoft warned of legal action against anyone engaging in "malicious activity causing real harm" to the company's customers, leading many in the infosec community to see the company's actions as a direct threat to the security researcher.
While Microsoft has fixed some of the security flaws Naceri disclosed since the start of the year (including ShieldBreak, RoguePlanet, YellowKey, GreenPlasma, and MiniPlasma flaws), the other zero-day bugs still lack an official patch.

articles.title: La inteligencia artificial resucita las cintas magnéticas, la tecnología de las VHS
articles.text:
La cinta magnética, la tecnología de los antiguos VHS, vuelve a crecer gracias a la inteligencia artificial. Si creciste entre los ochenta y los noventa, seguramente te acuerdas de rebobinar las VHS antes de devolverlas al videoclub, de las cintas que se enredaban dentro del vídeo o de meter un lápiz en una casete para recogerla. Y quizá pensabas que todo aquello había quedado enterrado por el CD, el DVD, la memoria flash, la nube y el streaming, pero resulta que están volviendo con fuerza, aunque no al ámbito doméstico..
Cinco veces más cinta. Fujifilm ha anunciado una inversión de unos 10.000 millones de yenes, 57 millones de euros al cambio, para multiplicar por cinco su capacidad de producción de cinta magnética para almacenar datos en el ejercicio fiscal 2028. Eso sí, no hay que esperar videocasetes para el salón, porque se trata de cartuchos profesionales cuyo uso, según el mismo comunicado, está creciendo sobre todo entre los grandes proveedores de servicios en la nube y los operadores de centros de datos.
Una VHS muy evolucionada. El principio físico, de hecho, es pariente del de las viejas cintas de vídeo y de audio, ya que la información se graba como estados magnéticos sobre una capa de partículas pegada a una cinta muy larga, aunque los sistemas LTO (Linear Tape-Open) actuales son muchísimo más sofisticados. Según el comunicado de la inversión, la compañía japonesa lanzó en 2025 la generación LTO Ultrium 10, con unas partículas magnéticas híbridas muy finas, y desde enero de 2026 vende la versión que llega a los 40 terabytes sin comprimir.
El viejo peaje del rebobinado. Pero la cinta arrastra el mismo problema que conocía cualquiera que haya utilizado una VHS: es un soporte secuencial. Vamos, que para llegar a un dato hay que hacer correr la cinta hasta el punto en el que está grabado, mientras que un disco duro accede en milisegundos a archivos repartidos en diferentes posiciones, tal y como explica la misma fuente. Por eso nadie se plantea instalar Windows o abrir documentos a diario desde un cartucho, aunque para datos que hay que guardar mucho tiempo y consultar pocas veces resulta ideal.
El hambre de datos de la IA. Y es que entrenar y utilizar grandes modelos implica acumular cantidades enormes de información, que se suman a las que genera la digitalización de las empresas y que, según Fujifilm, hay que poder guardar de forma segura y eficiente. Tenerlo todo disponible en discos duros obliga a mantener muchos equipos encendidos y refrigerados, porque los discos consumen energía de forma continua, según el fabricante de bibliotecas de cinta Spectra Logic. Un cartucho, en cambio, puede sacarse de la unidad una vez escrito y quedarse en una biblioteca automatizada, donde no necesita electricidad para conservar los datos hasta que vuelvan a hacer falta.
Barata y desconectada. Además, la compañía defiende en su comunicado que la cinta permite guardar grandes volúmenes de datos durante mucho tiempo a bajo coste. También hay una ventaja de seguridad, porque un cartucho separado físicamente de la red crea lo que se conoce como “air gap”, un aislamiento que, según Fujifilm, sirve para proteger los datos frente a amenazas como el ransomware, un tipo de software malicioso.
Se da así una curiosa vuelta en la historia de la tecnología. Fujifilm, que trabaja con cinta magnética desde 1954 y asegura tener la mayor cuota del mercado mundial, destinará la inversión, la mayor que ha hecho nunca en instalaciones dedicadas a LTO, sobre todo a la última generación. Las cintas VHS no van a volver, pero la IA ha acabado tirando de un soporte con décadas a sus espaldas.

articles.title: Apple tire un trait sur son forum d’entraide, une institution vieille de près de 28 ans
articles.text:
En octobre 2023, Apple retirait ses spécialistes rémunérés de son forum d’entraide et cessait de répondre aux clients sur X et YouTube. Trois ans plus tard, la firme ferme le forum lui-même, sans préavis. Le bandeau apparu dans la nuit de mardi à mercredi fixe l’échéance au 20 novembre, pour un espace né il y a près de 28 ans.
Un forum verrouillé du jour au lendemain
« La communauté d’assistance AppleCare fermera définitivement le 20 novembre 2026. À compter d’aujourd’hui, le site n’accepte plus de nouvelles publications et reste disponible en lecture seule. » Le bandeau, qui accueille désormais chaque visiteur, redirige vers les pages d’assistance officielles. Au moment de sa découverte, le dernier sujet publié remontait à moins d’une heure, signe d’un site resté actif jusqu’au bout.
Les discussions existantes restent consultables, votes et mentions « Moi aussi » compris, et le bouton de connexion subsiste, quoiqu’il mène désormais à un portail interne réservé aux employés. Apple n’a pas précisé si les archives resteraient lisibles après le 20 novembre ou si elles disparaîtraient avec le site. Le bandeau parle au passage de communauté « AppleCare », un intitulé qui tranche avec la marque publique Apple Support Community.
Mercredi matin, les déclinaisons francophone et germanophone du forum affichaient toujours leurs boutons de publication, sans le moindre bandeau : le périmètre exact de la fermeture reste à préciser.
Une institution née en 1998, abandonnée par étapes
L’espace a ouvert en 1998 sous le nom d’Apple Tech Exchange, avant de devenir Apple Discussions en 2000, puis Apple Support Communities en avril 2011, refonte accompagnée de profils personnalisés et d’un système de réputation. Des clients y dépannaient d’autres clients, du réglage de la batterie d’un iPhone aux problèmes de stockage. Les membres y gravissaient des niveaux à force de réponses utiles, jusqu’à un salon fermé réservé aux plus gradés. Lancé en 2022, le programme Community+ distingue encore chaque année les contributeurs les plus actifs, dont les profils arborent toujours le millésime 2026.
Le 1er octobre 2023, la firme avait pourtant déjà retiré ses propres employés du jeu. Les messages adressés au compte d’assistance sur X, fort d’un million et demi d’abonnés, ne recevaient plus de réponse humaine, le suivi technique des commentaires YouTube s’arrêtait, et le poste de spécialiste rémunéré du forum disparaissait. Les centaines de salariés concernés s’étaient vu proposer une reconversion dans l’assistance téléphonique, présentée à l’époque comme le canal préféré des clients.

articles.title: Microsoft enfrenta dificuldades para normalizar Outlook e outros serviços após pane global
articles.text:
A Microsoft está enfrentando dificuldades para restabelecer seus serviços após uma pane global que afetou plataformas, como Outlook, Teams e Copilot. Em atualização divulgada nesta sexta-feira (13), a empresa afirmou que as medidas adotadas para solucionar o problema não estão apresentando os resultados esperados.
Segundo a companhia, as alterações implementadas para melhorar o funcionamento dos serviços não estão evoluindo conforme o planejado. A Microsoft está testando outras alternativas para permitir que mais usuários voltem a acessar suas plataformas sem provocar uma sobrecarga nos sistemas.
A empresa também alertou que alguns serviços que já foram reiniciados podem voltar a apresentar instabilidade quando recebem tráfego de usuários. Isso significa que a recuperação parcial ainda não representa uma normalização definitiva.
Microsoft descarta ataque hacker
- Em meio à interrupção, a Microsoft descartou que a pane tenha sido provocada por um incidente de segurança cibernética;
- Charles Lamanna, executivo da companhia, afirmou que a falha global não foi causada por atividade maliciosa ou invasão de sistemas. Em publicação no X, ele lamentou os transtornos provocados pela interrupção e disse que a empresa trabalha para resolver o problema;
- O ministro australiano de Assuntos Internos e Cibersegurança, Tony Burke, também afirmou ter conversado com representantes da Microsoft no país. Segundo ele, os funcionários não acreditavam estar diante de um incidente cibernético;
- Burke comparou a situação à pane provocada por atualização defeituosa da CrowdStrike em julho de 2024. Na ocasião, milhões de pessoas foram afetadas em diferentes países depois que uma atualização da empresa de cibersegurança provocou o congelamento de computadores com Windows;
- A comparação, porém, não significa que os dois episódios tenham a mesma origem.
Pane também afeta serviços públicos e empresas
A interrupção não ficou restrita aos usuários das plataformas da Microsoft. Empresas, como OpenAI e Anthropic, também relataram problemas relacionados à indisponibilidade dos serviços.
Na Austrália, algumas estruturas governamentais foram afetadas. O Service NSW, plataforma que reúne serviços públicos do Estado de Nova Gales do Sul, recomendou que os cidadãos adiassem visitas presenciais a centros de atendimento e priorizassem transações pela internet, quando possível.
Hospitais e instituições de saúde australianas também relataram dificuldades administrativas. Segundo Michael Bonning, presidente da Associação Médica Australiana, os problemas não atingiram diretamente o atendimento aos pacientes. Algumas instalações, entretanto, precisaram voltar a utilizar papel para emitir receitas.
Em Singapura, autoridades confirmaram que sistemas governamentais também foram afetados. Os serviços de emergência, por outro lado, permaneceram operacionais.
O Downdetector, portal que acompanha o status de sistemas e plataformas online, destaca que a interrupção afetou 74 países, tanto usuários comuns como estruturas críticas, especialmente nas Américas, Europa e Austrália.
Grandes partes de Ásia e África não sofreram interrupções, o que inclui, ainda, China e Rússia, regiões onde, como a BBC lembra, apps Microsoft possuem forte restrição de uso ou foram removidos em prol de soluções locais.
Especialistas alertam para dimensão da falha
A extensão da interrupção chamou a atenção de especialistas em tecnologia e segurança digital.
Paul Spain, analista de tecnologia da Nova Zelândia, afirmou à BBC que a pane pode representar um dos maiores impactos sobre a produtividade já registrados na região da Ásia-Pacífico. Segundo ele, se a interrupção chegar a 24 horas, os prejuízos operacionais podem alcançar bilhões de dólares.
Já o especialista em segurança cibernética Troy Hunt alertou que os efeitos vão além das pessoas que utilizam diretamente os produtos da Microsoft. Como o e-mail ainda é fundamental para atividades profissionais, autenticação de contas, compras e comunicação sobre compromissos, a indisponibilidade pode afetar diversos serviços que dependem dessas ferramentas.
Hunt também destacou a importância de empresas manterem planos alternativos para situações em que plataformas essenciais deixam de funcionar.
Instituições alertam para golpes durante a pane
Outro efeito da interrupção é o aumento do risco de golpes. Bancos, universidades e órgãos públicos estão orientando seus usuários a desconfiar de mensagens que oferecem suposto suporte técnico para solucionar os problemas.
O ING Australia, por exemplo, recomendou atenção especial a mensagens inesperadas que contenham links para baixar aplicativos ou convites para chamadas telefônicas e de vídeo.
A Universidade Old Dominion, nos Estados Unidos, também alertou estudantes sobre possíveis tentativas de phishing por e-mail e mensagens de texto.
A orientação é utilizar apenas canais oficiais de comunicação e evitar compartilhar informações confidenciais por contas pessoais ou plataformas não autorizadas.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: The amazing disappearing exoplanet
articles.text:
One nice thing about discovering exoplanets is that, once you work out how long their orbits take, they continue to show up like clockwork. The timing is so regular, in fact, that we can use variations to detect the gravitational influence of additional planets in the same exosolar system. And the precise timing is useful in that we can rely on it to point telescopes at the system when we know some of the light we detect has passed through the planet’s atmosphere.
Except when we can’t.
On Monday, researchers reported on an exoplanet that simply stopped showing up. TOI-2535b is a hot Jupiter-sized planet we’ve been observing as it transits between its host star, TOI-2535, and Earth for about seven years now. But it recently stopped showing up, and researchers suspect that’s due to an unseen companion orbiting in a different plane.
Big changes
TOI-2535 is one of the many stars with exoplanet candidates identified by TESS, the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite. It’s a K dwarf, meaning it’s somewhat smaller than the Sun. And TESS found signs of a Jupiter-sized planet orbiting it every eight days, an orbit close enough to make TOI-2535b a “hot Jupiter” exoplanet. At that point, there was nothing especially unusual about it.
But a closer look at the data showed two very strange things. First, the timing of when its transits occurred could shift by as much as six hours, a substantial variation for an orbit this brief. That’s typically a sign of gravitational interactions with another planet; depending on the details of that second planet’s orbit, it may slow the first one or accelerate it through a transit more quickly. Since the second planet doesn’t show up in TESS data, it appears to orbit in a slightly different plane, so it doesn’t pass between its host star and Earth.

articles.title: J'ai essayé la nouvelle Dacia Spring : simple Twingo au rabais ou vraie bonne affaire ?
articles.text:
Depuis 2021, la Dacia Spring a fait passer à l’électrique des automobilistes qui n’y auraient jamais pensé. Dacia en a vendu plus de 210 000 dans une quarantaine de pays, et 93 % de ses acheteurs n’avaient jamais roulé en électrique, selon la marque. En échange, il fallait accepter une petite auto aux pneus étroits, à mi-chemin entre la voiturette et la citadine.
La deuxième génération, présentée début septembre, ne garde de la première que le nom. Elle utilise dorénavant la plateforme RGEV Small de Renault Group, qu’elle partage avec la Renault Twingo électrique, au même titre que ses chaînes de montage à l’usine slovène de Novo Mesto, bien logiquement. Alors vaut-il mieux acheter la nouvelle Twingo ou cette nouvelle Spring ? Pour avoir la réponse, j’ai pu la conduire sur 182 km dans sa finition Journey pendant les essais presse organisé par Dacia, non loin de Lisbonne.
| Caractéristique | Dacia Spring | 
|---|---|
| Modèle / version testée | Dacia Spring Journey | 
| Prix | À partir de 17 900 € (Expression), 19 400 € (Journey) | 
| Autonomie WLTP | 250 km | 
| Autonomie constatée (essai) | Environ 230 km | 
| Consommation relevée | Environ 12 kWh/100 km sur 182 km | 
| Capacité batterie | 27,5 kWh utiles (LFP) | 
| Puissance / couple | 82 ch / 175 Nm | 
| 0 à 100 km/h | 12,1 s | 
| Vitesse maxi | 130 km/h | 
| Puissance de charge max (DC) | 50 kW (pack de charge en option, 500 €) | 
| Temps de charge (DC) | 28 min de 15 à 80 % | 
| Temps de charge (AC) | 2 h 55 à 7 kW (de série), 1 h 55 à 11 kW (option), de 15 à 80 % | 
| Dimensions (L x l x h) | 3,85 x 1,74 x 1,52 m | 
| Coffre | 337 l (1 283 l banquette rabattue) + 18 l à l’avant en option | 
Design extérieur de la Dacia Spring : un petit cube aux airs de SUV
Si vous n’avez pas déjà découvert, faisons d’abord un rapide tour du propriétaire (promis ça va aller vite). Déjà, la Spring a pris pas mal en carrure dans le passage à sa nouvelle génération : 3,85 m de long, 1,74 m de large et 1,52 m de haut. Rendez-vous compte, c’est 15 cm de plus en longueur et 18 cm de plus en largeur que l’ancienne ! Elle adopte le nouveau langage stylistique de Dacia, avec une carrosserie taillée en cube comme le Duster ou le Bigster. On n’arrive pas tout à fait au SUV miniature, mais on s’en approche pas mal.
Les designers ont réussi à l’éloigner nettement de la Twingo. Seuls les vitrages (pare-brise, vitres latérales et forme arrondie des vitres arrière) trahissent la parenté avec la citadine au losange. Par ailleurs, les pneus de 195 mm de large, contre 165 mm sur la première génération, jouent beaucoup dans cette nouvelle allure moins micro-voiture.
Les roues restent en tôle avec des enjoliveurs, en 15 pouces sur l’Expression et en 16 pouces sur la Journey ici à l’essai. La Twingo, quant à elle, peut recevoir des jantes en alliage en option sur sa version haute. Dacia propose quatre couleurs (Agave, Gris Schiste, Noir Étoilé et Blanc Glacier), et seul le bleu Agave, facturé 550 €, apporte un peu de gaieté. La marque promet d’autres teintes en cours de commercialisation. Il ne faudrait pas faire de l’ombre à sa cousine. Bref, vous l’aurez compris, quand la Twingo joue la carte du design coloré et fun, la Spring mise davantage sur la sobriété et la robustesse.
Design intérieur de la Dacia Spring : la Twingo n’est jamais loin
À l’intérieur, Dacia n’a pas pu faire de miracle, et l’habitacle ressemble tout de même beaucoup à celui de la Twingo. Le volant, le sélecteur de marche, les commandes de climatisation, les accoudoirs, le compartiment central et les écrans (7 pouces derrière le volant, 10,1 pouces au centre) sont tous identiques ou presque.
La Spring se distingue avec sa sellerie en tissu bleu et ses appuis-tête avant en forme de virgule. En revanche, elle n’a pas les éléments couleur carrosserie de la Twingo qui ajoute un peu de gaiété à l’ensemble. Ici, l’ambiance est sommaire et ça ne bouscule pas les codes de la marque. Cela n’affecte en rien l’espace intérieur, en témoigne le 1,38 m de largeur au niveau des épaules. Côté options, les sièges avant chauffants coûtent 250 € et sont réservés à la Journey.
À l’arrière, Dacia a fait un choix malin : la banquette certes ne coulisse plus, mais la voiture a été allongée pour agrandir le coffre sans enlever de place aux passagers. Ainsi, on trouve un volume correct pour ce gabarit de 337 litres ou 1 283 litres banquette rabattue. À noter que l’abaissement à plat du siège passager avant de la Twingo (finition haut de gamme) n’a pas été repris non plus. On peut y ajouter un coffre avant de 18 litres, en option à 150 €, bien pratique pour ranger le câble de recharge, et que la Twingo n’a pas.
Technologies embarquées de la Dacia Spring : multimédia basique, sans Google
En version entrée de gamme Expression, la Spring fait l’impasse sur l’écran central. Elle se contente à la place d’un support de smartphone et de l’application Dacia Media Control, qui transforme le téléphone en écran multimédia. La Journey reçoit un écran tactile de 10,1 pouces avec la connectivité Apple CarPlay et Android Auto sans fil.
L’interface est basique mais fait le travail, comme sur la Twingo, avec des graphismes refaits à la sauce Dacia. En revanche, la Spring n’a pas de services Google intégrés, tandis que c’est Here Technologies qui s’occupe de la partie navigation.
Pour les aides à la conduite, le traditionnel bouton « My Safety » permet en un appui de passer à ses réglages personnels à chaque démarrage, par exemple pour couper certaines alertes. Pendant l’essai, le freinage d’urgence automatique s’est déclenché une fois sans raison, comme s’il avait vu un obstacle. Étonnamment, la voiture n’a pourtant pas freiné. La finition Journey embarque une caméra de recul, dont la qualité d’image est digne d’une autre époque… Vous en jugerez par vous-même, mais à c’est à tel point qu’on peut s’en passer, d’autant plus qu’elle grossit trop la vision périphérique.
Au volant de la Dacia Spring : une citadine rassurante
Sous le capot de la Spring, il s’agit donc du bloc conçu en Chine de la Twingo, fort de 82 ch pour 175 Nm de couple et qui lui permet de passer de 0 à 100 km/h en 12,1 secondes. On ne peut pas dire qu’elle est rapide, mais elle est capable de suivre sans problème le flot de la circulation jusqu’à sa vitesse maximale de 130 km/h.
Sur la route, elle se comporte vraiment comme la Twingo. Stable dans les virages et rassurante, elle fait clairement ressentir le progrès face à l’ancienne Spring et à ses pneus étroits. Avec un rayon de braquage de 4,95 m ainsi qu’à sa direction légère, elle se montre aussi facile à garer et à manœuvrer en ville.
Des bons points de la Twingo, la Spring hérite également de ses bémols. Cela concerne notamment le train arrière, lequel rebondit pas mal sur les routes bosselées donnant un léger effet de pompage. Toutefois, rien de dramatique. Ça vaut aussi pour les bruits d’air en provenance des montants avant, se faisant entendre dès 90-100 km/h. À ce propos, ces montants sont assez épais et peuvent gêner un peu la visibilité dans certains virages. Enfin, dans certaines conditions, le moteur électrique émet un très léger sifflement.
De la Twingo, la Spring n’hérite pas non plus de mode One Pedal ni de palettes et ce, peu importe la version. Il y a le choix entre un peu de régénération au lever de pied en mode D et un freinage assez marqué en mode B, sans aller jusqu’à l’arrêt.
Autonomie et consommation de la Dacia Spring : mieux que l’homologation
Sur les 182 km de l’essai, j’ai relevé une consommation moyenne d’environ 12 kWh/100 km, encore mieux que les 12,7 kWh/100 km annoncés par Dacia. Avec 27,5 kWh utiles, cette consommation donne une autonomie réelle d’environ 230 km, contre 250 km sur le papier. Il en conviendra de vérifier à nouveau les consommations dans d’autres conditions.
Pour la recharge, la Spring a de série un chargeur de 6,6 kW en courant alternatif, celui de la maison et des bornes lentes. Il recharge la batterie de 15 à 80 % en 2 h 55 sur une wallbox de 7 kW, en 5 h 40 sur une prise renforcée et en 9 heures sur une prise classique.
Pour aller plus vite, il faut payer le pack de charge à 500 €, comme sur la Twingo. Celui-ci permet de recharger en courant continu sur les bornes rapides jusqu’à 50 kW, ce qui fait passer de 15 à 80 % en 28 minutes. Il monte aussi la charge en courant alternatif à 11 kW (1 h 55) et ajoute le V2L, qui permet de brancher de petits appareils électriques sur la voiture. Par contre, la version d’entrée de gamme Expression n’y a pas droit et ça c’est vraiment dommage.
Prix et concurrence de la Dacia Spring : plus intéressante que la Twingo ?
La Dacia Spring coûte 17 900 € en version Expression et 19 400 € en version Journey, hors primes. Avec le montant garanti pour tous, la facture tombe respectivement à 14 280 € et 15 780 €. Toute la gamme reste donc sous 20 000 €, à conditions de ne pas cocher d’options. Une Journey avec le bleu Agave (550 €), le pack de charge (500 €), le coffre avant (150 €) et les sièges chauffants (250 €) revient à 20 850 €.
Sa principale concurrente vient du même groupe. La Renault Twingo, elle aussi vendue sous les 20 000 € en version entrée de gamme Evolution (19 490 €) et à 21 290 € au niveau supérieur Techno. L’écart entre les deux modèles s’établit à 1 590 €.
En face, on trouve également la BYD Dolphin Surf, qui vient de gagner une cinquième place et qui promet 507 km WLTP (!) pour 24 490 €, hors remise constructeur. Toujours chez les Chinois, il y a la Leapmotor T03 avec son équipement généreux et ses 265 km WLTP pour 17 210 €. De retour en France, la Citroën ë-C3 autonomie urbaine se positionne à 20 390 € (215 km WLTP).
Le verdict
Dacia Spring (2026)
Voir la fiche
On a aimé
- Parenté avec la Twingo bien camouflée
- Tenue de route stable plus rassurante qu’auparavant
- Coffre de 337 litres et un coffre avant en option
- Consommation prometteuse
On a moins aimé
- Pas de mode One Pedal
- Option charge rapide indisponible en entrée de gamme
- Bruits d’air dès 90 km/h
- Train arrière rebondissant sur routes bosselées

articles.title: Beyond Bandwidth: AI Inference Is Reshaping The Memory Wall
articles.text:
Longer contexts, higher concurrency, multimodal models, and AI agents will continue changing where memory pressure appears.
AI infrastructure has spent the past several years in a race for compute. More accelerators, larger heterogeneous clusters, and higher peak performance have enabled increasingly capable models. As AI moves into large-scale deployment, infrastructure must support more users, larger models, longer context windows, and more complex applications. Performance still matters, but so do latency, power, utilization, predictability, and cost per inference.
The challenge extends beyond bandwidth. AI systems must balance memory capacity, bandwidth, latency, power, data movement, utilization, and cost. Improving one dimension can create pressure elsewhere. The key-value (KV) cache illustrates this trade-off. KV cache reduces repeated computation during generative AI inference, but requires the system to retain and repeatedly access growing amounts of data. As context lengths and concurrent requests increase, the trade-off becomes more significant.
The result is not simply another memory bottleneck. It is a coordination problem across compute, memory, interconnect, and software. Adding capacity or bandwidth helps only if the system can place, move, and retrieve data without allowing latency, congestion, power, or complexity to erase the benefit.
The memory wall predates AI. Processor performance historically has improved faster than the ability of memory systems to supply processors with data. AI magnifies that problem. Increasing arithmetic throughput delivers limited benefit if accelerators spend more time waiting for data.
But bandwidth is only part of the constraint. AI systems also need sufficient capacity for models, intermediate data, application context, and inference state. Latency affects responsiveness. Power constrains how much data can be moved economically. Packaging and physical connectivity limit how much high-performance memory can be placed near compute.
These requirements frequently conflict. High-bandwidth memory close to an accelerator can deliver tremendous bandwidth, but its capacity, power, and cost are constrained. Larger-capacity memory may be more economical but may not provide the same bandwidth or latency. Moving data among tiers can expand effective capacity, but consumes bandwidth, power, and time.
The memory wall is therefore becoming a multidimensional system constraint.
Fig. 1: AI scaling turns the memory wall into a system-level trade-off among bandwidth, capacity, latency, power, cost, and utilization.
A system may have substantial aggregate memory, but not all of that capacity is equally useful. Data in a lower tier may technically be available, yet still be too distant, congested, or costly to move within the application’s service-level objective (SLO).
The practical limit is not installed capacity alone. It is usable capacity within the workload’s latency, bandwidth, and power envelope.
Training large models requires enormous compute resources and memory bandwidth, but it is fundamentally a process of building or updating a model. Inference is dynamic and ongoing. Every prompt, generated token, agent action, and application interaction consumes infrastructure resources.
Inference also is not one workload. A conversational assistant may emphasize latency. An enterprise AI assistant may process substantial proprietary context while supporting many users. AI agents may retain information across multiple steps. Consumer services may prioritize throughput and cost per token. Batch inference may emphasize utilization.
Each creates a different balance among bandwidth, capacity, latency, power, and cost. The architecture must follow the workload.
During transformer inference, attention mechanisms generate key and value representations for tokens in a sequence. Retaining those representations allows subsequent decoding steps to reuse prior states rather than recomputing them for earlier tokens. That improves inference efficiency, but reduces repeated computation while increasing pressure on memory capacity and data movement.
Longer context windows increase the KV-cache footprint of each sequence. Higher concurrency multiplies that requirement across simultaneous requests. An optimization intended to reduce compute demand therefore creates more data that must be retained and accessed.
Fig. 2: Reducing repeated computation improves efficiency, but longer contexts and greater concurrency increase the data that must be retained, moved, and managed.
KV state also has a lifecycle. It is created during prefill, repeatedly accessed during decode, and may be retained for reuse. Depending on the serving architecture, it may be moved, replicated, compressed, or evicted. Each phase places different demands on bandwidth, capacity, latency, and control.
KV cache is therefore a data-lifecycle problem, not only a memory allocation. Moving KV state to a lower-cost tier is beneficial only when the higher-tier capacity it frees, or the recomputation it avoids, outweighs transfer latency, bandwidth consumption, energy, and the risk of missing an SLO. In other words, every movement of data must earn its cost.
A latency-sensitive assistant may benefit from keeping frequently accessed data close to the accelerator. A long-context enterprise application may emphasize capacity. AI agents may require longer-lived state and more frequent reuse. Large-scale consumer inference may prioritize throughput, utilization, and cost per token.
Frequently accessed data may justify residing near compute. Other data may tolerate additional latency for greater capacity or lower cost, or move among tiers as access patterns change. The objective is not to eliminate the memory hierarchy. It is to coordinate that hierarchy efficiently.
Bandwidth remains critical, but optimizing exclusively for bandwidth ignores other constraints. Capacity determines how much model and inference state can remain accessible. Latency affects response time. Power determines whether increasing data movement is sustainable. Utilization indicates whether expensive compute resources are working or waiting for data.
High aggregate throughput can hide unacceptable time to first token, inter-token latency, or tail latency during congestion. A more meaningful measure may be tokens per watt or dollar while meeting latency targets. Headline bandwidth alone does not solve the memory wall.
The relevant question is: Which combination of compute, memory, interconnect, and software delivers predictable performance within the available power and cost envelope?
High-bandwidth memory can supply data quickly near accelerators. Larger-capacity tiers can complement it where capacity matters more than maximum bandwidth. Expansion and pooling can provide capacity beyond the memory next to an accelerator. Software can place, reuse, compress, move, or discard KV state according to workload requirements.
But every additional tier introduces more decisions. A useful architecture must address four questions:
Moving data to a larger-capacity tier may increase effective capacity but add latency. Replicating state may avoid recomputation but consume bandwidth and capacity elsewhere. Pooling may improve utilization, but only if contention and quality of service remain controlled. The advantage comes not from maximizing one memory specification or adding another tier. It comes from coordinating the hierarchy as a system.
Higher-bandwidth memory, greater capacity, faster interconnects, compression, and smarter cache management can relieve constraints, but not eliminate the challenge. As one bottleneck improves, applications and models use the additional resources. Longer contexts, higher concurrency, multimodal models, and increasingly sophisticated AI agents will continue changing where memory pressure appears. Hardware-software co-design is therefore critical because every layer influences data movement.
The next phase of AI infrastructure scaling will not be defined by compute alone or solved simply by adding memory. The harder task is coordinating where inference data resides, when it moves, and whether moving it is more efficient than recomputing it. The memory wall is becoming something broader: a test of how effectively the system converts distributed memory resources into predictable AI performance.

articles.title: Nigeria’s Raenest acquires UK-based payments company Remitise - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian fintech startup Raenest has completed the acquisition of Remitise, a UK-based payments company, for an undisclosed amount to expand its regulatory footprint and gain greater control over its global payments infrastructure.
Founded in 2022 by Victor Alade, Sodruldeen Mustapha, and Richard Oyome, Raenest initially operated as an Employer of Record (EOR) before evolving into a platform that redefines global banking for Africans, helping businesses and freelancers receive international payments, convert between currencies, operate a multi-currency wallet, while managing transactions seamlessly.
The platform also enables customers to open global bank accounts in their names, access physical and virtual dollar cards, and manage payments in USD, EUR, and GBP. To date, the company has amassed over one million individual customers across more than 50 countries, processed over US$2 billion in payments, and served over 300 businesses. It also offers a consumer-focused product, Geegpay, which provides Africa’s gig economy with efficient payment solutions.
Raenest raised US$11 million in Series A funding in February 2025 to expand its reach in existing and new markets, and its acquisition of Remitise is linked to that ambition.
“Acquiring Remitise is part of our long-term strategy to build a global financial company. We want to own more of the infrastructure behind our products, deepen our relationships with financial institutions and create a stronger foundation for the customers and businesses we serve,” said Victor Alade, Raenest’s CEO.
The acquisition builds on Raenest’s regulatory footprint and includes a money services business (MSB) and payment service provider (PSP) licence in Canada, as well as an international money transfer operator licence in Nigeria.

articles.title: Canonicus Capital raises Rs 192 Cr in its first close of Special Situations Fund
articles.text:
Canonicus Capital raises Rs 192 Cr in its first close of Special Situations Fund
The firm will focus on deploying capital into selected opportunities across the National Capital Region (NCR), while continuing to build towards its Rs 500 crore target.
Investment platform Canonicus Capital has announced the first close of its Special Situations Fund at Rs 192 crore, against a target corpus of Rs 500 crore.
Launched in 2025, the Special Situations Fund builds on the work of Canonicus Capital's Fund I through which it had raised and deployed Rs 311 crore. Together with Fund I, the first close takes Canonicus Capital's cumulative fundraising across its two funds to Rs 503 crore.
In a statement, the firm had said it will focus on deploying capital into selected opportunities across the National Capital Region (NCR), while continuing to build towards its Rs 500 crore target.
The fund will focus on situations where disciplined capital allocation, strong governance and active execution can help unlock value.
The firm's international fundraising programme, which included roadshows across the Middle East and Singapore, was temporarily paused due to the West Asia conflict. As conditions improve, Canonicus Capital plans to resume its international investor outreach and build on the momentum of the fundraise.
“Raising commitments is only half the job. The Rs 192 crore first close gives us the flexibility to approach the next stage with discipline, and our focus now is deploying capital prudently and delivering returns for our investors. We are not passive capital providers; we are execution partners," Rajan Gupta, Managing Director, Canonicus Capital, said.
“NCR is a competitive market, with significant capital competing for a limited pool of quality projects. Yet several fundamentally sound businesses and projects remain overlooked due to governance gaps, capital constraints and execution challenges,” he added.

articles.title: Police dismantle Gootloader, CastleRAT, StealC malware infrastructure
articles.text:
Europol and law enforcement partners from nine countries have seized hundreds of servers and domains used by the Gootloader, CastleRAT, and StealC malware operations.
Gootloader is a malware loader active since 2020, StealC is an infostealer that helps exfiltrate credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, and other sensitive information from victims' devices, and CastleRAT is a remote access trojan that surfaced last year. All three malware families have been used by various cybercriminal operations, including ransomware gangs.
The joint action is part of Operation Endgame, an international law enforcement effort targeting cybercrime and "cybercrime-as-a-service" networks. This stage of Operation Endgame included law enforcement agencies from Bulgaria, Canada, Denmark, Germany, Moldova, the Netherlands, Poland, the United Kingdom, and the United States, with Europol and Eurojust coordinating the effort.
Together with private partners who helped identify, take down, seize, and block infrastructure tied to the three malware operations, the authorities seized 257 domains and 235 servers.
They also identified 6.4 million victim datasets on the targeted criminal infrastructure, stolen from malware-infected systems for use in other cyberattacks, including ransomware breaches.
"During the action, over 6 million victim credentials were identified in the criminal infrastructure owned by the cybercriminals and seized by the authorities during this week. The suspects were using these credentials, stolen from the victims after they infected them, to sell them and later be used for other cyber-attacks such as ransomware," Europol said.
"Victim data will be made available via platforms HaveIBeenPwned, DIVD, CheckjeHack, NoMoreLeaks, Sekoia, The Shadowserver Foundation, and NL-NCSC, alerting victims of stolen credentials caused by the CastleRAT malware. WordPress users are urged to update credentials, enable multi-factor authentication, and patch vulnerabilities."
Previous Operation Endgame actions
In June, as part of the same operation, law enforcement agencies also cleaned nearly 15,000 malware-infected WordPress websites and seized 106 servers used by the SocGholish botnet and the Evil Corp Russian cybercrime group.
Later that month, Operation Endgame disrupted malicious infrastructure used by the Amadey and StealC malware operations, taking down 326 servers and 142 domains and recovering around 27 million credentials stolen from more than 385,000 compromised systems.
One year ago, the same joint law enforcement action also took down over 1,000 servers used by the Rhadamanthys, VenomRAT, and Elysium botnet malware operations.
Previously, Operation Endgame targeted Smokeloader botnet customers and servers, ransomware infrastructure, the AVCheck site, and various other major malware operations, including DanaBot, IcedID, Pikabot, Trickbot, Smokeloader, Bumblebee, and SystemBC.
