articles.title: Anthropic's Dario Amodei uses IPO pitch to promise AI will eliminate cancer and Alzheimer's within a decade
articles.text:
Facepalm: AI still hasn't cured cancer, or any disease, for that matter. Don't worry, though, because Anthropic boss Dario Amodei has assured us that the technology will not only eliminate this disease but also Alzheimer's, heart disease, and mental illness in a decade. The fact that this bold and heavily mocked statement came as part of his IPO pitch is absolutely unrelated, because who among us wouldn't want to invest in a company that is going to "create an age of miracles?"
Amodei made his latest wild prediction during an IPO roadshow video the company released yesterday. It's around 42 minutes long, but the part receiving the most attention is his ambitious plan for the future of medicine.
"You know, if today we look at things like cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease, mental illness, these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade."
If that wasn't enough to emphasize the godlike power of AI, Amodei added that the technology, presumably Anthropic's, will catapult us into a utopia where illness vanishes.
"I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia," he gushed.
 – NIK (@ns123abc) November 10, 2026
The CEO obviously had to include something about where his own AI giant fits into all this. "And I believe that the company which gets the risks right will also be the company that has the license to operate that society trusts and society believes can build the benefits in the right way," he said. Given the number of rogue AI incidents and Amodei's many prophecies of AI-related destruction, society probably wouldn't trust Anthropic even if it did cure cancer.
Needless to say, Amodei is being pulled apart by the medical community over his claims. While some experts have acknowledged that AI could play an important role in the fight against cancer and Alzheimer's, they say there is no chance a complete cure will be available within 10 years, given the long-term trials involved. That will likely come as a disappointment to the AI researchers who, according to Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar, have taken up smoking because they're so confident AI will cure cancer.
 – Melinda B. Chu (@MelindaBChu1) November 10, 2026
There's also been criticism over Amodei using such comments in an IPO pitch. Biotech executive Rami Elghandour said it reeks "of desperation."
 – Rami Elghandour (@RamiElghandour) November 11, 2026
In fairness to Amodei, he's not the only one framing AI as a future magical cure-all/fountain of youth. Last week, OpenAI president Greg Brockman said AI will make significant strides in biology and health, including the treatment of diseases, over the next 12 to 18 months. He said that eventually, it could even make death a choice. At the moment, most people would be happy if AI just stopped hacking other companies and worrying everyone.

articles.title: The death of the 14-day patch: Surviving machine-speed vulnerability discovery
articles.text:
The death of the 14-day patch: Surviving machine-speed vulnerability discovery
For decades, enterprise vulnerability management ran on human time: A security researcher manually dissected a binary, traced execution paths, built a proof of concept, and filed a coordinated disclosure. Engineering leads evaluated the CVSS score and prioritized the fi before working it into an upcoming sprint schedule. Then, finally, they shipped the update.
That deliberate cadence is a thing of the past.
In the first nine months of 2026, publishers recorded 75,242 CVEs, representing roughly 20% of all vulnerabilities published since the CVE program was established in 1999.
The acceleration is steepening: according to the Cyber Strategy Institute, nearly 38,000 of those flaws surfaced in Q3 alone.
“The pace of vulnerability discovery has outpaced the human capacity to remediate it. Engineering organizations face a stark operational reality: the traditional two-week patch cycle is dead.”
The pace of vulnerability discovery has outpaced the human capacity to remediate it. Engineering organizations face a stark operational reality: the traditional two-week patch cycle is dead.
Why vulnerabilities exploded in 2026
This surge is not caused by developers writing worse code. It is the direct result of vulnerability hunting transforming from an artisan craft into an autonomous, distributed compute problem.
- Autonomous codebase traversal: Legacy SAST tools flooded dashboards with noisy pattern matches. Modern agentic security systems run full-context semantic analysis: cloning repositories, tracing asynchronous data flows across microservices, constructing dynamic exploit payloads in sandboxes, and confirming exploitability before ever raising an alert.
- Exhaustive compute at scale: Compute does not tire. Swarms of automated agents continuously traverse open-source package registries and public repositories, decompiling transitive dependencies, auditing legacy C/C++ utilities, and testing modern Go, Rust, and Node.js runtimes for concurrency bugs, deserialization flaws, and memory leaks.
- Focus on foundational infrastructure: Autonomous discovery focuses heavily on high-leverage software targets, identity layers, reverse proxies, parsers, and container runtimes.
“This surge is not caused by developers writing worse code. It is the direct result of vulnerability hunting transforming from an artisan craft into an autonomous, distributed compute problem.”
When machines search exhaustively across the entire public software graph, they will discover every reachable flaw.
The operational cascade
The deluge of machine-discovered CVEs creates severe structural friction across risk management, engineering velocity, and compliance:
- The exposure gap becomes unmanageable: As detailed in analysis on the expanding CVE exposure gap, the critical hazard is the elapsed time between public exploit discovery and downstream production deployment. When agentic frameworks generate working zero-day or N-day exploits within hours of a code push, a multi-day patching window is an open door.
- Alert paralysis and triage debt: Engineering teams are trapped between CVSS scores (which measure theoretical severity) and EPSS metrics (which predict real-world exploitation likelihood). Discerning whether an alert represents an unreachable helper function or an active, weaponizable zero-click flaw has turned routine triage into continuous crisis management.
- Compliance and audit deadlock: Frameworks like NIST SP 800-53 (Control SI-2), PCI-DSS 4.0, and DORA enforce strict timelines for critical and high-severity issues. When 9.0+ CVSS scores arrive in weekly batches, security and platform leads spend more time writing risk-acceptance waivers than hardening production architecture.
Can internal IT teams keep up with patching and push innovation?
The short answer is no.
Enterprise development exists to deliver business value: ship differentiated features, enhance platform reliability, and expand market share.
Yet today’s software supply chains rely on thousands of dependencies. When a critical flaw lands in foundational infrastructure, such as an authentication engine, an API gateway, or a database driver, feature roadmaps freeze. Development teams are forced into fire drills:
- Halt active sprint work.
- Trace internal dependencies to determine real exploitability.
- Reconcile dependency breaks, merge conflicts, and integration regressions.
- Execute emergency deployments across multi-region production clusters.
Defending against automated, machine-speed discovery using manual human labor is an economic dead end.
The architectural shift: Decoupling architecture from maintenance
Open-source software (OSS) remains a foundation of enterprise computing, but self-hosting foundational components introduces an unsustainable operational tax: you become the de facto maintainer of every layer you host.
To withstand the automated vulnerability era, forward-looking engineering teams are changing their operating model: preserve open standards and architectures, but outsource the patching burden.
1. Managed platform tiers for critical edge and identity
Foundational edge components, such as identity and authorization planes (e.g., Ory Kratos/Hydra) or ingress proxies (e.g., Envoy), form an organization’s perimeter. When implementation flaws or protocol vulnerabilities hit these layers, maintaining self-hosted community forks requires constant emergency rebuilds. Shifting these layers to managed vendor clouds offloads zero-day mitigation, regression testing, and upstream backporting to teams dedicated entirely to that software layer.
2. Commercial subscriptions with contractual backporting SLAs
For organizations restricted by strict data sovereignty, air-gapped data centers, or zero-trust VPC policies, public SaaS is not always an option. However, relying purely on raw community repositories leaves internal teams subject to unpredictable release cycles and breaking updates.
A viable hybrid approach is adopting commercial open-source enterprise subscriptions backed by formal CVE remediation SLAs (such as Red Hat Enterprise Linux, enterprise distributions of Kubernetes, or commercial licenses like the Ory Enterprise License). Organizations retain full control over their data plane while outsourcing patch engineering:
- Predictable remediation SLAs: Contractual response windows for High and Critical vulnerabilities replace upstream community best-effort timelines.
- Non-breaking LTS backports: Vendors backport security fixes directly to long-term support branches, eliminating the breaking schema changes and API refactors that accompany major upstream updates.
- Verified distribution streams: Access to signed SBOMs and hardened enterprise container images reduces internal triage friction in CI/CD pipelines.
3. Continuous delivery automation and runtime shielding
For internally maintained services, teams must automate the path from patch to production. This requires pairing automated GitOps workflows (e.g., ArgoCD, Renovate) with progressive deployment controllers (like Flagger or Argo Rollouts) and eBPF-based runtime shielding (such as Cilium Tetragon). Automated canary verification and kernel-level network enforcement isolate vulnerabilities in flight, buying engineers time to test and deploy updates without emergency rollouts.
Fighting automation with automation
The volume of vulnerability disclosures will not return to human scale. As autonomous models and agentic fuzzing advance, exploit discovery and weaponization will move faster still.
“The volume of vulnerability disclosures will not return to human scale. The sustainable path forward requires matching automation with automation: modernize the stack so upstream infrastructure partners absorb the patching burden.”
Attempting to absorb this flood with manual Jira tickets and emergency weekend deployments guarantees developer burnout and security breaches. The sustainable path forward requires matching automation with automation: modernize the stack so upstream infrastructure partners absorb the patching burden, allowing internal engineering teams to focus on what matters… shipping product.

articles.title: Computer vision startup Tristar AI pulls in $12.4M to automate quality control for manufacturers - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Computer vision startup Tristar AI pulls in $12.4M to automate quality control for manufacturers
All too often, manufacturing defects seem to slip past human eyes, with the result that high-speed production lines turn into expensive scrapheaps. Computer vision startup Tristar AI Inc. has just raised $12.4 million in early-stage funding in order to try to put an end to these costly mistakes.
Today’s Series A round was led by Isogon Ventures and saw participation from Blackhorn Ventures, Ford Street Ventures, NextView Ventures, TenOneTen and Capgemini’s ISAI Cap Venture Fund.
Tristar AI is gearing up to transform quality assurance in manufacturing at a critical moment for the industry. Manufacturers have found themselves squeezed by a combination of rising raw material costs and growing labor shortages, and these problems have been made even more acute by the U.S. government’s insistence on bringing more manufacturing back home.
According to data from the Capgemini Research Institute, 48% of U.S. companies have invested in reshoring projects this year. But 83% say they’re worried about the lack of skilled industrial workers needed to fulfill those initiatives.
One of the major challenges for manufacturers is that they’re still encumbered by inefficient inspection protocols that rely on either manual checks, or in a best-case scenario, rigid, rule-based machine vision systems. Quality control is essential for any manufacturing operation, but the inefficiency of these protocols makes it a significant roadblock too.
It forces companies to take skilled workers off production lines and sometimes even bring their entire operations screeching to a halt. Yet there are many occasions where they still miss subtle flaws in their products, resulting in wasted materials, downtime, missed deadlines and sometimes even very expensive customer claims.
Founder and Chief Executive Salem Karani is all too familiar with the inefficiency of manual inspection. He told SiliconANGLE that while growing up, he would often accompany his father to his family’s plastic film manufacturing plant in Houston, turning up at all hours of the day and night in order to troubleshoot production issues that could spring up at any moment. Because the company’s margins were so tight, any period of extended downtime could threaten its profitability, so he would spend hours with his dad frantically troubleshooting line errors.
It was this experience that ultimately inspired Karani, who studied computer vision at Harvard and MIT, to develop an automated quality inspection system that can operate continuously without slowing down production. “The problem was never that people didn’t care about quality,” Karani said. “It’s that people catch problems after the fact, once they’ve already cost time, materials and customers. Tristar gives every production line a live record so teams can act when it matters most.”
Computer vision in manufacturing operations is not a new concept, but where Tristar differs is through its use of more sophisticated artificial intelligence models that can adapt to changing conditions, materials and defect types. The startup’s platform looks at machine telemetry, the quality of the products coming off the line and the activity of human operators, allowing it to uncover issues the moment they emerge and immediately understand where the problem is, and why it occurred.
Best of all, the system can integrate with factories’ existing systems, such as cameras, sensors, programmable logic controllers, enterprise resource planning systems and so on That enables them to get up and running without an expensive overhaul.
Isagon Ventures General Partner Paco Riberas said he’s backing Tristar because manufacturers are losing far too much money to avoidable defects. “In today’s industry, precision isn’t optional, and Tristar makes it possible,” he said. “Its AI vision catches defects in real time, directly on existing production lines. Salem and his team are building the quality standard for modern manufacturing.”
Tristar’s early traction has been encouraging. Its system already monitors more than 500 production lines across North America and Europe.
Customers include global packaging giants such as Amcor, DuPont and Klöckner Pentaplast, and also some of the biggest suppliers to automakers such as Toyota, Honda and Mercedes, Karani said. Those customers report defect detection accuracy rates of between 95% and 99%, and say the platform pays for itself in an average of just four months.
Karani said the goal now is to expand Tristar’s platform into new manufacturing sectors and enhance the capabilities of its computer vision AI to try and improve its accuracy even further. Ultimately, he sees the company as the operational system of record for factory floors, giving manufacturers more visibility into everything about their production operations, from the raw materials to the finished product.
“Physical AI will play a critical role in the future of manufacturing,” said Capgemini Ventures’ Matthieu Eyriès. “Tristar combines advanced AI capabilities with a strong understanding of industrial environments, addressing concrete manufacturing challenges with measurable impact.”

articles.title: FBI Says US Seized $1.2 Billion Worth of Cryptocurrency Stolen From Binance
articles.text:
The FBI said Thursday that it had seized more than $1.2 billion of cryptocurrency reported stolen last month from Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange.
The theft of about $6.3 billion from Binance is regarded as the biggest crypto heist in history, and the FBI has previously attributed it to a North Korean hacking group known as TraderTraitor. The U.S. government and private sector have so far combined to freeze more than $2.7 billion of the stolen funds, and the Justice Department said Thursday that it has now obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of that total.
Typically in those situations, the U.S. government will file a claim of forfeiture with a judge, who will then determine who has a legitimate claim to the recovered funds.
[ Read: North Korea Launches Missiles Toward the Sea to Protest Binance Hack Claims ]
Also Thursday, the FBI blamed North Korea for a separate social engineering scheme that officials say resulted in the theft of $400 million worth of cryptocurrency over the last 18 months. That scheme, known as FaceStealer, involves a complicated chain of events combining the hijacking of popular messaging apps and the recording of deepfake videos.
U.S. officials have repeatedly accused North Korea of using cyber schemes to generate funds for its regime, including its illicit weapons program.
Related: Rigged Coding Assignment, Abused AI Tool Opened Path to $6 Billion Binance Heist
Related: Chainalysis Discloses Data Breach Following AI-Driven Cyberattack

articles.title: Google pushes privacy angle as Gemini-powered smartglasses debut starting at $395
articles.text:
Smartglasses have always faced an uphill road to acceptance. Not only is propping a computer up on your nose an uncomfortable proposition, but the privacy aspect has been vexing people since the Google Glass days. Now, Google is ready to take another swing at “intelligent eyewear” for the Gemini era after previewing its plans a couple of times. The first glasses are up for preorder today from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, but they’re no impulse buy.
These devices are a collaboration between Google, Samsung, and the aforementioned eyewear designers. Gentle Monster and Warby Parker have each designed a few different frames, with options for transparent and tinted lenses. Samsung is providing the computing hardware that fits inside them, and Google has the software covered.
Warby Parker has designed three frames for Google eyewear, called Alden, Reid, and Wren (see above). They are available with both standard optical and sun lenses in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black colors at $395 and higher. Warby Parker is only selling devices in the US. Gentle Monster has gone a bit further with six styles, but Google hasn’t told us any names for those yet. They come in dark red, pink, gray, and yellow colors and are available with clear, tinted, blue, or brown lenses. The Gentle Monster styles start a little higher at $449, and they will be available in the US and South Korea.
Google says the frames all weigh about 41 grams, which is not terrible but is definitely near the top for glasses generally. They will, naturally, weigh much more when you account for lenses. That will also determine the final pricing. So far, we only have the starting prices for these devices, including non-prescription lenses.
The setup here is similar to the Ray-Ban Meta glasses we’ve seen for a few years. There are no screens in the lenses, but you can interact with the AI system via voice or by activating the integrated camera. The experience should be similar to using Gemini Live on your phone, but it will be a lot easier to fire up the AI. You can say “Hey Gemini” or tap a touch-sensitive area of the frame to start interacting with the robot.

articles.title: Phota Labs uses AI to turn everyday photos into professional-looking shots | TechCrunch
articles.text:
A new iOS app called Phota Labs gives users access to a personal AI photo assistant that turns everyday snapshots into images that look like they were taken by a professional photographer, all while preserving the authenticity of the image.
Rather than giving consumers yet another photo-editing tool, Phota Labs aims to use advances in AI to automate the editing process so it’s easier for anyone to get access to better photos.
The a16z-backed startup was founded by Cecilia Zhang and Zach Xia, who met at Adobe while working on computational photography products, including Project Indigo, Lightroom, and Photoshop.
The duo saw a gap in the editing tools on the market and believed that although editing tools can be powerful for enhancing photos, they aren’t very effective at fixing a photo that wasn’t captured well in the first place. Phota Labs changes that by focusing on fixing the shot itself while preserving the natural appearances of those in the image.
“Phota is your personal photo assistant that can make great photos for any moment you want to keep before you even ask, which means that it’s a very proactive experience,” Zhang told TechCrunch in an interview. “Think of it almost like a photographer or virtual photographer who looks over your camera roll and tries to understand what’s happening and how they could have taken that photo for you on the spot for that scene.”
The idea is to use AI to transform photos, whether that’s turning a wide-angle group photo into a tighter portrait or transforming a selfie into a regular shot.
Users can choose from different photography styles that determine how AI transforms their images, ranging from subtle edits that preserve the original lens and composition to more dramatic transformations that introduce effects like fish-eye lenses, alternative angles, and entirely different perspectives.
While some people turn to ChatGPT and other generative AI tools to enhance or edit images, these tools can often alter a person’s appearance, especially when working with blurry photos because they don’t know what that person actually looks like.
“For Phota, we built our own tech,” Zhang said. ”We built this personalization technology that actually learns about people’s identity and is able to preserve them in any transformation we do to a photo.”
Images edited with Phota Labs feature invisible watermarks that identify them as altered by AI when shared on social platforms.
The startup is initially targeting people who take tons of photos and like to share them on social media, but don’t want to deal with the tedious process of editing photos. Over time, the founders envision a broader audience, from retirees looking to create beautiful photos for their grandchildren to parents who want to share polished family albums with friends and relatives.
“We have this obsession with authenticity,” Xia said. “I think there’s so much value in connecting AI with real moments and making sure those photos are not perfect, in a sense. That’s why we spend a lot of research into understanding personal context, into building this identity model because we want to make sure the photos are authentic. They’re just better photos of the same moment, rather than saying, ‘Oh, this is an AI image’.”
Xia said beta users were excited to see better versions of moments they had actually lived and saw the results as photos of real memories rather than AI-generated images. The founders discovered that users were taking more photos because they knew Phota Labs could enhance them later.
“We’re turning something that’s unusable into something that people want to print,” Zhang said. “People who just love photos but never really got into editing can now experience professional quality that could never have been possible. So, I think that meant so much to us. There’s so many cherished moments for photos, and we really want them to be actually meaningful and something that you can remember.”
In terms of funding, the company raised a $5.6 million seed round led by a16z last year.
Phota Labs is launching as a free app to build an initial user base before exploring a freemium model. The startup also plans to launch an Android app in the future.

articles.title: Struggling marijuana farms pivoting to becoming AI data center sites to escape falling weed revenue — existing water and power infrastructure makes cultivation sites ideal for decentralized ‘mini data center nodes’
articles.text:
Struggling marijuana farms pivot to becoming AI data center sites to escape falling weed revenue — existing water and power infrastructure makes cultivation sites ideal for decentralized ‘mini data center nodes’
Let's get high... on AI.
The AI data center boom is bringing hope to struggling cannabis farmers as they face increased competition, costs, and taxes amid reduced demand for marijuana. According to Arizona Public Media, the cannabis industry is in decline, with sales peaking in 2024 and oversupply driving prices down. And now, several growers are considering selling their cultivation facilities or converting them into “mini data center nodes.” These facilities already have many of the ingredients needed for AI data centers, such as the increasingly hard-to-get supply of electricity and water infrastructure.
"For some reason, there's a lot more cannabis grown in Arizona than Arizonans use. And so, a lot of folks are getting out of that business, like myself, at least on the cultivation side. But these facilities can potentially be repurposed to be mini data center nodes," Moe Asnani, the former owner of two Tucson D2 Dispensaries, told the public broadcaster. He also added, "The whole idea is if you create these smaller nodes where people control their own data, where they're not at the mercy of other people's updates and things like that — that's kind of where the idea came in, because I believe in decentralization."
Cannabis farming is both power- and water-intensive. Forbes looked at a 32,850-square-foot cannabis facility in Kalamazoo, Michigan, which is currently wired for 1.5 megawatts, which can be expanded to 2.5 megawatts in under a year and 15 megawatts in the long term. It's also provisioned for fiber internet and equipped with a state-of-the-art HVAC system for climate control, which should make it a tempting property for anyone wanting to put up a small data center — something that even OpenAI and Anthropic are interested in as massive hyperscale sites face opposition from the community.
This concept is dubbed "adaptive reuse," with Tucson City Council member Paul Cunningham saying that it’s a more palatable alternative to massive, purpose-built sites sitting on the outskirts of town. "Data centers are dirty words, and everybody knows that. And no one wants to build a brand-new data center anywhere," the politician said. "But if we have buildings that were using that amount of water and that amount of energy already in their previous function and [it] can be done without being invasive, I'm OK with exploring that option."
There is massive demand for data centers, but it’s not a guaranteed payoff for struggling cash-strapped growers looking to unload their unprofitable properties. Niki Krear, vice president of acquisitions of real estate investment trust New Lake Capital Partners, said that there’s a sweet spot between connectivity, costs, and regulation that data center operators look for in a site.
"It’s a combination of finding affordable power, dense fiber networks, and favorable tax policies," Krear told MJBizDaily. Even though many cultivation facilities already boast higher-than-average power capacity for lighting and climate control, data centers often demand twice to thrice more, with upgrades possibly taking up to five years.
Data center operators looking for smaller sites may also have to contend with NIMBY — not in my backyard — fights from neighbors. Additionally, there may be zoning restrictions, moratoriums, and regulatory hurdles, and the lack of economies of scale could end up costing operators more.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
This is particularly important as AI chips are expected to increase in power and efficiency in the next five years. As these new AI GPUs become available, data centers will need to sell their existing equipment and buy new hardware to remain competitive. Because suppliers usually offer favorable pricing for larger orders, upgrading these smaller sites will likely end up being more expensive on a per-unit basis. That said, growing opposition toward large new projects could make these former cannabis farms suitable alternatives for operators desperate to get more compute online quickly, provided they check all (or most of) the boxes they need.

articles.title: The Jensen Huang saga isn’t just a tech-world soap opera — it could change the entire future of AI
articles.text:
The Jensen Huang saga isn’t just a tech-world soap opera — it could change the entire future of AI
The wrong relationship at the wrong time
Update: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO at 9:00 AM ET. The company's CFO, Colette Kress, is the interim CEO.
The Jensen Huang scandal is one of the most remarkable tech stories in recent memory, and, in my view, it’s less about the now ex-Nvidia CEO’s alleged affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy than the tsunami-grade ripple effects of one man’s questionable choices.
We do not know, nor do we have proof, that Jensen Huang's (whose departure was confirmed by Nvidia on Thursday morning) alleged relationship with Alice Huang resulted in any kind of quid pro quo, or in state or industry secrets being leaked or traded. Even so, Huang is surely smart enough to know the perception: the incredible irresponsibility of an extramarital affair, allegedly with a woman who, even if she isn’t a spy, is an influential businesswoman in China, the biggest economic and strategic rival to the United States.
Nvidia chips are, according to a 2025 report by IOT Analytics, in 92% of all Data Centers. Ironically, virtually every AI-generated meme currently doing the rounds featuring Jensen Huang and Alice Huang (they’re not related) — and there are hundreds of them — has probably been generated using Nvidia hardware.
Nvidia is a publicly traded company, and its fortunes impact global markets — and right now everyone is nervous. Jensen Huang’s actions are the latest PR disaster for an industry that’s already struggling with major trust issues. Many people already worry that AI is not being developed or employed in our best interests, and that the companies creating these foundational models are chasing money, rather than dreams of heroic medical breakthroughs, climate change solutions, and occasionally finding previously unseen Mayan ruins. (I think they may be doing all of the above, but that’s just me.)
I get it if you think that one person's infidelity can't possibly have any bearing on an entire tech industry. I disagree. Huang’s fortunes are inextricably tied to those of AI. There might not be an AI industry without Nvidia and Huang (again, see Nvidia's AI market share numbers above), and so you have to question what the future of the industry looks like without his specific vision for AI hardware over the next few years.
What's love got to do with it? Not much
This is about much more than the fact that Jensen Huang had an affair. It's about who he had the affair with, when it happened, what information might have been shared, and how, if any of this is true, Jensen Huang might have been used to steer US chip policy in relation to AI, and reshape the global AI race to favor or assist China. The fallout from all that boggles the mind — and it may reshape our AI future.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Let’s make one thing clear: this is not about Jensen Huang’s matters of the heart. He’s not the first powerful business figure to have an affair. But Alice Huang — if indeed the two were romantically involved — is not just anyone. She is described in numerous reports as a high-powered executive at Megaspeed, an apparent Nvidia cloud partner since 2023 that, up until a few years ago, was part of a Chinese gaming company known as 7Road International.
When Megaspeed was spun off as a separate company, Alice Huang became the de facto boss (she had majority shares), but NBC reports that her role with the company is less clear; as of May, she was reportedly still ‘the boss’ and running operations.
Right now, the FBI is trying to figure out if Alice Huang is a Chinese spy. Whether she is one may not matter. After all, it’s widely accepted that some Chinese companies are only nominally independent of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), which reserves the right to set aside a company’s privacy and ensure that its goals, strategies, and operations align with the CCP’s goals.
Jensen Huang and Alice Huang may have known each other for a decade, but if their deepening relationship aligned with recent events, it’s a bad look, whether or not Alice Huang is in fact a spy.
You see, Jensen Huang spent part of 2025 lobbying the White House and, specifically, President Donald Trump to relax his Chinese export rules so Nvidia could keep selling its chips to China. Those conversations happened while Jensen and Alice were, if not in a relationship, seemingly business partners (Megaspeed reportedly became an Nvidia cloud partner in 2023).
It stands to reason that Megaspeed and Alice Huang would want Nvidia to continue selling the chips Nvidia custom-designed for the region to China.
Jensen Huang succeeded, but in doing so, may have put the White House in a difficult position. After all, Jensen would have had a duty to disclose any partnership with Megaspeed, if only because the White House is well aware that Chinese companies are not independent of the Chinese government, which is that administration’s stated reason for banning so many Chinese tech products from coming into the US market.
Did he? Who knows? That's one of the questions the FBI and others will be looking to answer.
A long tech history
I often think back to my first meeting with Jensen Huang some 30 years ago, when he still went by Jen-Hsun Huang. Back then he was focused on — checks meeting notes — “a graphics chip that incorporated graphics acceleration, sound (can play two WAV files at once) and 3D acceleration.” It was a simpler time, and Huang was scrappily competing with companies like Matrox and ATI. He was a smart guy, although at the time he left no lasting impression on me.
I was impressed and maybe a bit confounded, though, when Jensen Huang started focusing on the AI capabilities of his chips more than a decade ago. Initially, a lot of the work was going into supporting autonomous vehicles. It was the discovery by others that Nvidia GPUs and their native math-iness could power model training and generative operations that transformed his business — and which may have also transformed Jensen Huang, who has now resigned from the company he helped found.
I don’t recall a leather jacket in 1996 (it was firmly in place by 2015), but Jensen’s signature style seemed to coincide with his transformation into a high-profile industry rock star. He still seemed humble, but by 2024, as the AI boom was starting to take off, his customers, and the industry, knew he was effectively the most important tech CEO in the world.
And with that came great responsibility. Like it or not, the AI industry was hugely reliant on him. But he shirked that responsibility, and made, it seems, some very messy choices that may have unforeseen ramifications for all of us.
Crossing a rubicon
Become a TechRadar Insider by simply clicking 'Join Now' at the top of this page. Have a question? Please email membership@techradar.com
Regardless of what the FBI discovers, expect a chilling effect on further sales of AI chips to China. Huang argued to the White House that Nvidia losing access to the Chinese market might help Chinese AI competitors and thereby hurt the US in the AI race. He might be right, but Jensen Huang’s say in the future of the AI industry may now be diminishing by the minute.
Jensen’s admission and how he handles the next few days, weeks, and months will influence the stock market, the AI industry, and how tech companies conduct business on the global stage, as well as whoever will succeed him as Nvidia's CEO (Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, has been named as an interim boss for now).
Nvidia’s role as the AI chip leader may remain undiminished, but only if it figures out its leadership picture. As it stands, the company cannot make AI chips fast enough. A stumble here will alter the course of foundation model development, future AI capabilities, and even robotics. It might also hinder the potential good work that all those AI CEOs keep promising. Another company could pick up the slack, but it won't happen quickly enough for most people's tastes.
Let’s face it, while nothing else seemed capable of slowing the inexorable march of AI, I think this scandal might do the trick — and what comes next could have implications far beyond the tech world.

articles.title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
articles.text:
Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
The Chip Security Act is getting renewed attention following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.”
Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.”
But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them.
“They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public.
Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling.
Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization.
In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.”
The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.
The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option.
Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so.
But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.
In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”
Deep Dive
Artificial intelligence
Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason

articles.title: Donald Trump really wants Tim Cook to run Nvidia
articles.text:
Jensen Huang resigned this morning as Nvidia’s CEO following reports of affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Right now, the company is being led by its CFO on an interim basis. But President Donald Trump is already throwing around one person he thinks should take over the chipmaking giant: former Apple CEO Tim Cook, who stepped down from leading the company on September 1st and moved into an executive chairman role.
Donald Trump really wants Tim Cook to run Nvidia
Nvidia is looking for a new CEO, and President Trump says the former Apple CEO would be ‘a great candidate.’
Shortly after Huang’s resignation was announced today, Trump posted his idea about Cook on Truth Social: “NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump said. “A Legend replaces a Legend!”
In a new episode of Stephen A. Smith’s Straight Shooter podcast published today, Trump made his pitch for Cook again, saying that Apple “would never be what it is today” if Steve Jobs was still “around”:
Can [Huang] be replaced?
Well, you know, the expression, Anybody can be replaced? So it’s very hard to replace him, but I had an idea this morning that I sort of just released: Tim Cook. He just sort of semi-retired from Apple. He’s done one of the greatest jobs in the history of business.
I think if Tim Cook, who built Apple… If Steve Jobs were around, Apple would never be what it is today. Tim Cook took a lot of these brilliant ideas and designs and everything else from Jobs and others, and he made it into one of the great companies of the world in a fairly short period. I think Tim Cook would be a great candidate to run Nvidia.
Apple and Nvidia didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. Cook is well-known for his ongoing relationship with President Trump, including gifting the president a 24k gold and glass statue last year. (Trump, after Cook announced his transition plan earlier this year, posted a story about having “the head of Apple calling to ‘kiss my ass.’”)
During the podcast, Trump said he spoke to Huang yesterday and that Huang is “going through hell”:
Should [Huang] have stepped down?
Well, the big thing is, was the woman a spy, and I don’t know if that’s been determined yet, but if the woman was a spy, yes, if the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different.
But I can tell you this. Somehow, he’ll end up on his feet. I mean, I know him, I know him pretty well. I always thought of him as a fine man.
I spoke to him yesterday. He’s going through hell. What he feels most badly about is his wife and family. That’s what he is, really… that’s what he told me. I’m president, and he called me. And he said, What I’ve done to my wife and family is... That’s what he talked about.
Trump, on the podcast, called Huang a “tremendous talent.” Other tech leaders have also publicly supported Huang following his resignation.

articles.title: Jensen Huang renuncia como CEO de NVIDIA
articles.text:
Bombazo en NVIDIA, que acaba de anunciar la renuncia de Jensen Huang como presidente, CEO e integrante de la junta directiva. La decisión del empresario tiene efecto inmediato y se produce tras los escándalos que salieron a la luz en las últimas semanas por sus relaciones extramatrimoniales, una con una empleada de la empresa y otra con una supuesta espía de China.
Colette Kress, quien se desempeña como jefa de finanzas y vicepresidenta ejecutiva de NVIDIA, servirá como CEO interina tras la salida de Jensen Huang. El anuncio se produce apenas horas después de que un reporte de The New York Times expusiera que la junta de la empresa estaba analizando la destitución de su cofundador y jefe.
El anuncio de NVIDIA no revela los motivos detrás de la renuncia de Jensen Huang como CEO y principal cara visible. No obstante, es evidente que la determinación se desprende de la consecución de escándalos que lo tuvieron como protagonista en el último tiempo.
El pasado domingo, la firma anunció el inicio de una investigación interna por las afirmaciones de que Jensen Huang había mantenido un vínculo cercano con una supuesta espía china llamada Alice Huang. El empresario reconoció haberle sido infiel a su esposa, aunque puertas hacia adentro negó cualquier conocimiento sobre una operación de espionaje en su contra. El FBI también abrió una pesquisa para determinar el alcance del asunto.
Ayer, en tanto, un reporte reveló que Jensen Huang también había tenido una aventura con una empleada de NVIDIA. Esto complicó todavía más al empresario, debido a que la situación habría infringido las políticas de la compañía respecto de las relaciones entre ejecutivos y subordinados.
Jensen Huang abandona NVIDIA envuelto en escándalos
De más está decir que este panorama era imposible de imaginar hace apenas un par de semanas. Pensar en una NVIDIA sin Jensen Huang al comando era totalmente inverosímil. Después de todo, estamos hablando no solo de uno de los fundadores de la empresa, sino del responsable de convertirla en la más importante del mundo gracias a sus innovaciones en el campo del hardware avanzado para IA.
Claro que los escándalos de Jensen Huang no demoraron en impactar de forma directa sobre la economía de NVIDIA. El lunes, la acción de la compañía experimentó una caída que barrió 190.000 millones de dólares de capitalización bursátil en solo un día. La bajada se pronunció en la continuidad de la semana. Hoy, el valor de la acción mostraba una caída del 11 % antes de la apertura de los mercados.
A diferencia de otras renuncias, Jensen Huang no ha brindado comentarios públicos, ni tampoco se sabe si los dará con el correr de las horas. NVIDIA ha incluido una tibia referencia a su legado en el anuncio de su salida. "Las contribuciones de Jensen a NVIDIA son profundas. NVIDIA es una de las empresas tecnológicas más trascendentales del mundo. El Consejo de Administración y la firma agradecen a Jensen sus inestimables contribuciones a la compañía y al sector", indicaron desde el gigante verde.
Cómo sigue NVIDIA sin su líder
Colette Kress, la nueva CEO interina de NVIDIA, se unió a la compañía en 2013. Se trata de una veterana con una vasta experiencia en grandes tecnológicas, habiéndose desempeñado previamente en Microsoft y Cisco. Pese al nuevo cargo temporario, Kress continuará ejerciendo sus roles actuales como jefa de finanzas y vicepresidenta ejecutiva. De hecho, la compañía ha ratificado que planea presentar sus resultados financieros del último trimestre el próximo 17 de noviembre.
Todavía no se sabe si Kress tiene posibilidades de asumir el rol de CEO de NVIDIA a tiempo completo. La junta de la compañía informó la puesta en marcha de un proceso para definir al reemplazante de Jensen Huang, considerando tanto a candidatos internos como a externos.
Otro cambio notorio que llega con la renuncia de Jensen Huang es que la junta de NVIDIA ha nombrado un presidente por primera vez en su historia. Dicho rol ha recaído sobre Harvey C. Jones, inversor y exCEO de Synopsys, una empresa estadounidense dedicada al desarrollo de software para el diseño de circuitos integrados complejos.
"La fortaleza de NVIDIA siempre ha residido en su gente. Junto con nuestro equipo directivo, me comprometo a seguir construyendo sobre la base extraordinaria que Jensen ha forjado a lo largo de los últimos 33 años. Seguiremos impulsando el trabajo que ha convertido a NVIDIA en un referente en computación acelerada e inteligencia artificial, y aprovecharemos las oportunidades que tenemos por delante. Nuestro objetivo sigue siendo servir a nuestros clientes, socios, desarrolladores y accionistas", remarcó Colette Kress tras la salida de Jensen Huang.

articles.title: Here are Nintendo's Canadian Black Friday 2026 deals
articles.text:
Nintendo of Canada has revealed its lineup of Black Friday 2026 deals.
Notably, Canadians will be able to save on Switch 2 bundles and some marquee games. The main promotion is a discounted Nintendo Switch 2 + Mario Kart World bundle, which includes the Switch 2 console (regularly $679.99), a full download of Mario Kart World (regularly $109.99) and a three-month Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership (regularly $11.99).
This bundle costs $749.99, which works out to savings of $51.98. On top of that, Nintendo is offering this bundle for $679.99 ($70 off) between Nov. 19 and Dec. 2, working out to total savings of $121.98. This comes two months after Nintendo raised the Canadian price of the Switch 2 by $50 to $679.99.
Outside of hardware, Nintendo is offering deals on various games, including $25 off Donkey Kong Bananza and Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2 (both $74.99, regularly $99.99). These discounts will run from Nov. 26 to Dec. 2 at participating retailers.
And finally, the Nintendo eShop and Nintendo Store website will offer various deals on games from Nov. 19 to Dec. 3. Nintendo didn’t tease what will be offered in these sales, but we’ll update this story once the promotion goes live.
All of these Switch 2 promos come after the console just got one of its biggest games, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. The remake launched last week and has already sold over 5.2 million copies, making it the Switch 2’s fastest-selling game.
In addition to Ocarina of Time, this year’s Switch 2 holiday lineup includes the recently released Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave and Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, as well as this year’s Star Fox remake, Splatoon Raiders and Mario Tennis Fever.
Some of next year’s 2027 Switch 2 titles, meanwhile, include Metroid Ravenous (Jan. 18), the recently delayed The Duskbloods (TBA), Pokémon Winds and Waves (TBA) and Kirby and the World Beyond (TBA).

articles.title: Perplexity peut désormais accéder à vos comptes en banque et gérer votre argent
articles.text:
Anthropic a récemment annoncé la possibilité pour ses utilisateurs de connecter Claude à leurs comptes en banque. C’est maintenant au tour de Perplexity de pouvoir avoir accès à vos comptes bancaires afin de se transformer en conseiller financier. Cette fonctionnalité est disponible dès à présent en France.
Perplexity peut dorénavant accéder à vos comptes bancaires
À partir d’aujourd’hui, il est possible de connecter Perplexity à ses comptes bancaires, via la plateforme Plaid. Une fois la connexion établie, l’assistant IA se transforme tout simplement en conseiller financier en fournissant des réponses basées sur les données bancaires de l’utilisateur. L’intelligence artificielle peut par exemple élaborer un suivi budgétaire ou un graphique des dépenses, qui se mettent à jour automatiquement à chaque nouvelle transaction. Les différentes transactions sont par ailleurs divisées par catégories (loyer, courses, abonnements, cafés, etc.).
L’utilisateur peut par exemple poser les questions suivantes : « Combien ai-je dépensé en plats à emporter le mois dernier ? », « Combien ai-je dépensé en café le mois dernier ? », « Est-ce que je paie encore des abonnements oubliés ? », « Est-ce qu’il me reste suffisamment d’argent pour payer le loyer ? », etc. L’IA fournira alors une réponse sur la base des données bancaires de l’utilisateur.
L’assistant IA ne peut pas effectuer d’actions sur vos comptes
L’accès de Perplexity à vos comptes bancaires est en lecture seule, c’est-à-dire que l’assistant IA ne peut pas effectuer d’actions, comme faire des virement, faire des investissements ou déplacer de l’argent. Il peut seulement lire les données des comptes bancaires dont vous lui avez donné l’autorisation d’accéder. Notons également que l’IA n’a pas accès à vos mots de passe bancaires.
Il est possible de connecter Perplexity à ses comptes bancaires via Plaid dès aujourd’hui dans 17 pays européens, dont la France, l’Allemagne, l’Espagne, l’Italie, l’Irlande, la Pologne et les Pays-Bas. À noter que l’entreprise Perplexity définit cette fonctionnalité comme une étape vers ce qu’elle appelle « la finance intelligente », c’est-à-dire l’intégration de l’intelligence artificielle directement dans les questions financières. Petit à petit, l’IA s’immisce dans la plupart des services que nous utilisons, et nos comptes bancaires ne font pas figure d’exception.

articles.title: The Semiconductor Singularity: When AI Starts Accelerating The Silicon That Accelerates AI
articles.text:
Use evidence from silicon to improve the tools and decisions that create the next generation of hardware.
AI is entering the inner loop of semiconductor engineering by reducing the effort required to develop software, operate software tools and carry out engineering analysis.
Ray Kurzweil described the broader pattern as the Law of Accelerating Returns: accumulated technical capability helps create the next computing paradigm. In my recent white paper, The semiconductor singularity: Accelerating IC innovation with AI, I applied that idea to semiconductor engineering. Better computing improves the tools used to design and manufacture semiconductors, and those tools help create the next generation of computing.
Figure 1 places that loop in the longer history of computing. The technologies change, but each generation contributes tools, knowledge and capacity that help create its successor.
Fig. 1: Successive computing paradigms have built the technical capacity used to create the next generation.
Progress in semiconductor engineering never follows a smooth exponential curve. It advances when a bottleneck is overcome sufficiently for engineers to try something that previously cost too much money, time, computation or organizational effort.
I saw this firsthand with machine learning in computational lithography. Early demonstrations were exciting, but production adoption required developers who understood both ML and semiconductor applications, representative data, model management, IP controls and customer confidence. Production adoption followed only after the model, data, deployment environment and customer requirements matured together.
Generative AI relieves many of the user-complexity bottlenecks characteristic of EDA flows. When I created my original SPIE machine-learning course for lithography, the prototype work took roughly 200 to 300 hours, including some help generating training data. In a later experiment, I used generative AI to recreate and expand a surprising amount of that prototype functionality in roughly 30 hours. These were notebook-level prototypes, not production computational-lithography tools, but the change in exploratory effort was striking.
The practical effect is more engineering exploration within the same schedule. Experienced silicon engineers can examine more alternatives and produce more usable results while spending less time on software and workflow mechanics.
Agentic AI extends this effect from delivering predictions or analyses to carrying out sequences of engineering work. The LLM interprets intent, assembles the workflow, retrieves relevant context and coordinates specialized tools. Engineering authority remains in the EDA tools, models, qualified data and deterministic analysis.
Semiconductor workflows have traditionally depended on experienced engineers who know which analysis to run, which data matters, when a result is credible and when something requires closer examination. That expertise takes years to develop and cannot expand as quickly as computational capacity or engineering demand.
Agentic systems can increase the reach of that expertise. In computational lithography, an agent might collect recent SEM data, configure model calibration, invoke the appropriate analysis, inspect convergence and runtime, and return exceptions to the engineer for judgment. More computation, data and tool activity can operate under the direction of each expert.
Siemens Fuse EDA AI implements this architecture by connecting AI models to EDA tools, engineering knowledge, specialized languages and data formats.
Computational lithography shows how this works. A fab collects wafer and metrology data, calibrates models, uses those models to drive correction, measures the resulting silicon and feeds what it learns into the next calibration and process change. The model improves through repeated comparison with physical evidence.
Different parts of that loop require different computational methods. Physics-based simulation predicts physical behavior. Qualified models, rule decks and deterministic verification establish engineering and signoff authority. Specialized machine learning supports prediction, classification and optimization. Generative AI improves access to knowledge and tools. Agents coordinate workflows. Accelerated computing expands the analyses that fit within practical schedules.
The result of these workflows is usually the conversion of physical understanding and manufacturing observations into evidence-backed engineering interventions. Simulation directs exploration, metrology records what happened, models reconcile prediction with observation, and engineering action changes the design or process.
As EDA tools, manufacturing systems and digital twins become accessible to agents, this loop can operate across more of the workflow. Agents can explore design-technology tradeoffs, run simulation and computational-metrology flows, evaluate alternatives and organize evidence for the next engineering decision.
As engineering cycles accelerate, the value of trust increases. AI can generate hypotheses, assemble workflows and explore alternatives quickly. Semiconductor development advances through evidence that engineers can responsibly act on: verified designs, qualified models, measured silicon and data whose origin and applicability are understood.
Agentic EDA needs engineering context, secure data access, traceable actions, deterministic authority and human control over consequential decisions. These properties belong inside the workflow and provide a foundation of trust.
A Calibre nmOPC model earns trust through calibration against physical metrology data and continued comparison with what appears on the wafer. The model, calibration data, process conditions and physical evidence together establish where the model can be relied upon. As conditions change, the model is recalibrated and the evidence base grows. AI-enhanced metrology tools such as Canopus can strengthen that foundation by increasing the quantity and quality of SEM data available for calibration.
Calibre, together with foundry-qualified rule decks and verification flows, establishes that a design complies with the physical requirements of manufacturing. Agents can orchestrate more work and explore more possibilities, while trusted engineering tools determine which results are allowed to move forward.
With access to more tools within a well-designed trusted software foundation, engineering analysis may encounter bottlenecks in the larger organization or ecosystem. The time required to establish data access, protect IP or authorize a production change can become the limiting factor on acceleration. Reducing the time required to establish access, protection and authority becomes the next engineering problem.
Figure 2 summarizes how the limiting constraint moves as the engineering workflow accelerates. Physical evidence, deterministic authority, data access, IP protection, validation and human control account for a larger share of the remaining cycle time.
Fig. 2: As development and analysis accelerate, physical evidence, deterministic authority, data access, IP protection, validation and human control account for more of the remaining end-to-end cycle time.
Better hardware expands AI capability. AI expands what engineers can explore and automate. Manufacturing supplies physical evidence, and verification establishes which results can move forward.
Each improvement changes the limiting constraint. The semiconductor singularity is the continuing acceleration of this engineering loop: identify the next constraint, preserve authority where physics and signoff require it, and use evidence from silicon to improve the tools and decisions that create the next generation of hardware.

articles.title: Les Anneaux de pouvoir : voilà les Nazgnagôl (Nazgûl) déjà identifiés dans la saison 3
articles.text:
Dans les livres de J.R.R. Tolkien comme dans l’adaptation au cinéma de Peter Jackson, les Nazgûl ne sont plus que des spectres au corps invisible. Des silhouettes nimbées de ténèbres, qui furent autrefois neuf rois humains, asservies au pouvoir de l’Anneau unique. Ce sont les esclaves de Sauron.
Sur ces neuf serviteurs, l’auteur n’a identifié que deux membres. Plutôt que de se contenter de ces deux-là, la série Les Anneaux de pouvoir a choisi de remplir les cases vides avec ses propres personnages, pour étoffer le récit – qui se déroule au Deuxième Âge de la Terre du Milieu, des milliers d’années avant Le Seigneur des anneaux.
La saison 3, dont la moitié des épisodes est en ligne sur Prime Video depuis le 11 novembre, fait d’ailleurs la part belle à quatre de ces futurs spectres de l’Anneau, avant leur transformation finale. Sur ces quatre-là, un seul sort vraiment des textes de Tolkien. Les trois autres sont des créations de la série.
Attention, la suite de l’article dévoile des éléments de la saison 3.
Ce ne sont pas encore des Nazgûl, mais des Nazgnagôl
À l’époque où la série se passe, les Nazgûl n’existent pas encore. Comme ces rois humains viennent tout juste d’entrer en contact avec les anneaux maudits, leur déchéance démarre à peine. Les showrunners J.D. Payne et Patrick McKay ont donc créé un mot pour désigner cet état intermédiaire de pré-corruption : Nazgnagôl.
Ce terme a été bâti à partir du noir parler, la langue du Mordor imaginée par Tolkien : « nazg » y veut dire anneau, et les showrunners en ont déduit « nagôl », serviteur, un mot que Tolkien n’a jamais écrit mais qui suit sa logique. Des serviteurs de l’Anneau encore humains, donc, de chair et d’os, car, dans la chronologie de la série, Sauron n’a pas encore forgé l’Anneau unique qui fera d’eux des spectres. Chez Tolkien, c’est l’inverse : l’Unique existe déjà quand les Neuf apparaissent.
Dans le premier épisode, la série résume leur état en une phrase : quand il porte son anneau, un Nazgnagôl est à la fois de ce monde et d’un autre.
Le Roi-Sorcier et Khamûl, les deux seuls noms laissés par Tolkien
Le Roi-Sorcier d’Angmar
Tolkien n’a jamais dressé la liste exacte des Neuf. L’encyclopédie Tolkiendil, référence francophone sur son œuvre, résume ce qu’on en sait : ils étaient des seigneurs, dont trois Númenóréens et un Orientais, et sont apparus vers l’an 2250 du Deuxième Âge. Surtout, seuls le Roi-Sorcier d’Angmar et Khamûl l’Orientais ont droit à un nom, ou au moins à un titre.
Le Roi-Sorcier est le chef des Nazgûl et le plus célèbre des Neuf.
Vers l’an 1300 du Troisième Âge, il s’installe en Angmar, au nord, pour faire la guerre aux royaumes des Dúnedain, et prend la cité de Fornost en 1974. C’est lui qui poignarde Frodon au Mont Venteux, et c’est lui que tuent Éowyn et Merry à la bataille des Champs du Pelennor, le 15 mars 3019. Tolkien n’a jamais dit qui il était avant de porter l’anneau au doigt.
Pour le dire autrement, l’un des méchants les plus connus et marquants de la fantasy n’a ni nom ni visage, et la série n’a encore désigné personne pour ce rôle.
Khamûl l’Orientais
Khamûl est un peu mieux servi.
Dans les textes, il est le second du Roi-Sorcier, un ancien Orientais, que Sauron envoie en 2951 du Troisième Âge dans sa forteresse de Dol Guldur, située dans la Forêt Noire (Mirkwood). La série en fait le premier Nazgnagôl qu’on voit naître à l’écran. Joué par Zubin Varla, Khamûl y est un seigneur de guerre du Rhûn, à l’est, qui a perdu le pouvoir face au mage ténébreux.
Dans la saison 3 des Anneaux de pouvoir, Sauron fait s’affronter à mort des représentants de Rhûn, avec la promesse de confier un anneau au survivant. Khamûl tue ses anciens compagnons, soigne ses blessures grâce au pouvoir de l’anneau et promet en échange cent mille hommes au Seigneur des ténèbres.
Le roi des Lossoth, le roi des Haradrim et Theo, les ajouts de la série
Le roi des Lossoth
Le tout premier porteur d’anneau à apparaître dans la saison n’existe pas chez Tolkien.
Dès l’ouverture de l’épisode 1, un colosse en armure noire et en fourrures domine Galadriel au combat, au point qu’elle doit battre en retraite avec Arondir. De retour à Fondcombe, elle l’identifie devant Elrond : c’est le roi des Lossoth (joué par Paul Hickey), un peuple des terres gelées du Forodwaith, tout au nord du monde.
Il avait promis d’aider les Elfes avant que Sauron ne le retourne. Il a reçu son anneau avant le début de la saison, pendant l’ellipse de cinq ans qui la sépare de la précédente.
Le roi des Haradrim
Son homologue du Sud est présenté à partir de l’épisode 2.
Dans l’épisode 1, Gil-galad et Círdan constatent que Sauron s’est tourné vers les hommes pour grossir ses rangs, « les Lossoth au nord, les Haradrim au sud ». Les épisodes 1 et 2 citent un roi des Haradrim, peuple du Harad (ceux qui chargeront à dos d’oliphant au Pelennor, quelques millénaires plus tard), parmi les porteurs d’anneau.
Les deux Nazgnagôl (le roi des Haradrim et le roi des Lossoth) sont décrits un peu plus précisément dans l’épisode 2, lorsqu’ils se présentent à Durin IV. Ils ont même droit à des lignes de dialogue, et retirent leur masque pendant qu’ils tentent d’amadouer Durin IV avec de belles paroles. Une manœuvre qui ne prend pas, et la discussion finit par mal tourner.
Theo
Theo, lui, est le seul personnage déjà connu des spectateurs à rejoindre les Neuf.
Le fils de Bronwyn, joué par Tyroe Muhafidin et présent depuis la saison 1, coupe désormais du bois pour les navires des Númenóréens à Pelargir, où il prend douze coups de fouet. Il entend des officiers parler de l’offre de Sauron, se présente à l’épreuve à la fin de l’épisode 1 et reçoit son anneau dans l’épisode 2, avec « l’aide » de Sauron.
On apprend aussi qu’il est de lignée noble, fils de Fäldred, lui-même fils de Hammerthreg (les loyaux intendants du Mordor, selon Sauron), et qu’il aurait pu régner sur les terres du sud.
À la fin de l’épisode 4, Arondir, qui l’a presque élevé, se retrouve face à un Nazgnagôl masqué. C’est Theo qui le tue, sur ordre de Sauron. Ce dernier lui assure qu’il est né pour être un conquérant, un sorcier et un roi (il lui avait dit plus tôt qu’il avait accès à « certains pouvoirs »). Une piste vers le Roi-Sorcier ? Rien n’accrédite cette thèse pour l’instant.
Cinq anneaux donnés, quatre porteurs connus
Le site américain Nerdist a compté les anneaux. Dans l’épisode 1, le coffret de Sauron en contient six avant que Khamûl ne reçoive le sien. Dans l’épisode 2, il en reste cinq, dont celui de Theo, juste avant que Sauron ne le lui remette, puis quatre.
Sauron a donc déjà distribué cinq anneaux aux hommes, sur les neuf, alors qu’on ne connaît pour l’instant que quatre Nazgnagôl (les rois des Lossoth et des Haradrim, Khamûl et Theo). Un cinquième porteur manque donc à l’appel. Qui est-il ?
Nerdist mise sur Kemen, le fils de Pharazôn, l’actuel dirigeant de Númenor, l’une des principales puissances militaires du monde connu. Kemen balaie à deux reprises l’idée même d’anneau magique. Le site relève aussi que, malgré ses tenues couvertes de broches, il ne porte aucune bague. Mais peut-être y a-t-il anguille sous roche. Or, chez Tolkien, trois des Neuf étaient des seigneurs númenóréens.
Sur r/LOTR_on_Prime, le forum Reddit consacré à la série, les fans tiennent d’ailleurs un fil pour identifier les Neuf épisode après épisode.
Il reste donc quatre anneaux dans le coffret, et quatre épisodes à diffuser. Les épisodes 5 et 6 arrivent sur Prime Video le mercredi 18 novembre, et les deux derniers le 25 novembre.
