articles.title: Author Q+A: finprim is a Case for One Financial Validation Library in TypeScript
articles.text:
finprim, which is an MIT-licensed TypeScript library that puts IBAN, BIC, card, sort code, VAT, routing number and loan calculations behind one API, has published its fifth release, 0.1.4. The repository has 81 stars.
InfoQ asked author Oluwatosin Adelaja what pushed him to build it, and where he wants it to stop.
InfoQ: What pushed you to build finprim?
Adelaja: Honestly, it came from doing the same work too many times. At Sprint Technology Solutions we had several products, and each one ended up with its own copy of the same financial validation, sort code checks in one place, IBAN formatting in another, card validation somewhere else, all written slightly differently by whoever got there first.
The moment it really landed for me was on a payout flow. We had account and sort code validation on the web side, and then the mobile app needed the same thing. Rather than share it, the validation got rewritten for mobile, and the two copies drifted. One of them was a little stricter than the other, so a bank detail that the web form accepted would get rejected on mobile, and we had people re-entering details that were actually fine. It took longer than it should have to track down, because nobody thinks to check whether two "identical" validators are actually identical. The fix was easy once we found it, but the real problem was that there were two of them at all.
I hit the same shape of thing again later building a daily pay feature for NHS workers, where the same rules needed to hold on web and on mobile. That is when I stopped treating it as a one-off chore and started thinking it should just be one library, written once and tested once, that any product could pull in and trust.
InfoQ: What was missing that justified a unified library rather than assembling existing single-purpose packages?
Adelaja: You can absolutely wire together a pile of single-purpose packages, and plenty of teams do. The problem is what you are left maintaining. Each package has its own API shape, its own types, its own idea of what a valid result looks like, and often its own dependencies. So you end up writing a layer of glue code just to make them agree with each other, and that glue becomes its own thing to test and keep working.
finprim's bet is that financial validation is coherent enough to live behind one consistent API. The same shape of input, the same shape of result, and the same typing approach across IBAN, sort code, card, VAT, all of it. And zero runtime dependencies, so there is no tree of other people's packages to audit or keep patched. For something sitting in the path of a payment, I wanted fewer moving parts, not more.
InfoQ: What concrete class of bugs do branded types prevent, and why not rely on plain runtime validation?
Adelaja: The bug class is the one where a string that was never validated gets used as if it had been. To the compiler, a validated IBAN and a random string are both just a string, so nothing stops you passing the wrong one into a function that assumes the value is good. It compiles fine, and then it fails at runtime, which in this domain means it fails in the middle of a live transaction.
Branded types close that gap. A validated IBAN comes back as its own distinct type, not a plain string, so if you try to use an unchecked value where a validated one is required, the compiler rejects it before the code ever runs. The runtime validation still happens, that does not go away. The branding just guarantees it actually happened and that nobody quietly skipped it on some code path. It moves a whole class of "we forgot to validate this one route" mistakes from production back to compile time.
InfoQ: For something handling payment data, how do you think about trust, what can you guarantee, and where do you draw the line?
Adelaja: The honest answer starts with being clear about what finprim is and is not. It validates and formats financial data. It does not store anything, it does not send anything over the network, and it does not process payments. No database, no telemetry, no outbound calls.
So the guarantees I can actually make are narrow and specific. It checks values against published standards, IBAN structure, checksum rules, card network ranges, and tells you whether they are well formed, deterministically, without logging the sensitive values it is handling. That last part is deliberate. You do not want account numbers or card numbers turning up in logs, so the library does not put them there.
Where I draw the line matters just as much. finprim does not tell you a payment is safe to make, it is not a compliance tool, and it is not a replacement for the checks your payment provider runs. It confirms the data is shaped correctly before it goes anywhere. Treating a validation library as more than that would be the real mistake.
InfoQ: How do you source and maintain the correctness of 80+ IBAN formats, VAT quirks and card ranges, and how is it tested?
Adelaja: The rules come from the published standards rather than from me guessing. IBAN is checked against the ISO 13616 country formats, card numbers use Luhn plus the published network ranges, VAT uses the documented per-country formats, and so on. Where there is an authoritative spec, that is the source of truth.
On testing, each validator runs against known-good and known-bad values taken from those reference sources, so the tests check behaviour against the standard, not just against themselves. Overall coverage is around 91% of lines and 88% of statements. The core validation modules are the most heavily covered, the IBAN, card, VAT, routing, BIC and sort code logic sits around 94% of lines with full function coverage, and the thinner coverage is in the optional React bindings rather than the validation itself. I would rather be straight about that split than quote one headline number, because the part that actually handles financial data is the part that is tested hardest.
Keeping it correct over time is mostly manual, I update the formats as the standards change, and this is one place the outside contributors have genuinely helped, because people using it in different countries spot edge cases I would never hit on my own.
InfoQ: SEPA and ACH generation is a big jump from validation into transaction generation. Where do you want finprim to end up?
Adelaja: That is a fair thing to push on, because generation is a genuinely different job from validation, and I do not want to pretend otherwise. Validating an IBAN is self-contained. Producing a SEPA credit transfer file or an ACH batch means taking on formatting rules, sequencing and a lot more responsibility for getting something exactly right that is going to be submitted to a bank.
Where I want finprim to sit is as a validation and formatting toolkit first. I am deliberately cautious about the generation side. If it does move into producing standard file formats, I would want that to be safe, well-tested generation of documented formats, not finprim turning into a transaction engine or a payments platform. I would rather it did one layer really well than spread itself thin doing a half version of what a payment provider already gives you.
Narrower tools exist, such as ibankit for IBAN and BIC alone, and on DEV a commenter called the Dinero.js approach solid while warning that teams get burned when a library's precision assumptions diverge from the processor's.
Adelaja is a senior full stack engineer. All five releases have stayed within 0.1.x, so upgrading has meant patch releases rather than code changes, and there is no dedicated migration guide, so the README and release notes are the reference.

articles.title: Clipto enables ChatGPT and Claude to search and analyze years of people's meetings and video calls - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Clipto enables ChatGPT and Claude to search and analyze years of people’s meetings and video calls
Artificial intelligence assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude have become essential tools for millions of workers worldwide, helping them compose emails in seconds, generate complex code and draft reports by looking at whatever data that person has access to.
But there’s one thing that’s missing from those chatbots’ knowledge. Ask them what was discussed in the previous week’s team meeting or on yesterday’s call with a client, and it will be stumped.
It’s this shortcoming that a startup called Clipto Inc. is trying to solve with the launch of a new AI chatbot memory platform called Clipto Studio, which enables AI assistants to listen in on calls, presentations and meetings and search through them or analyze them upon request.
Clipto argues that this is going to be an important capability as AI becomes more pervasive in daily work. Though AI chatbots can sift through email inboxes and corporate databases in seconds, that’s not where many companies’ most valuable knowledge is actually stored. Rather, Clipto says the most important business insights are trapped in raw video and audio files.
Most of the big decisions are made during Zoom calls, customer interviews and team meetings, but the details of those discussions are stored in heavy, unstructured data formats that are incredibly expensive for AI to process. But AI can potentially provide much more meaningful help to workers if it has a way to access this knowledge.
That’s where Clipto Studio comes in. It’s a native skill set that integrates directly with ChatGPT, Claude and other AI assistants using the Model Context Protocol, powered by proprietary models that run locally on user’s Mac and Windows computers.
The software works by pre-indexing speech, individual speaker’s voices, facial expressions and other on-screen visuals before transforming the raw footage into a structured and easily searchable dataset that’s optimized for AI chatbots. Then, when the user asks a question about one of their recent conversations, or even one from two years ago, it can quickly find the answers it needs by searching through the metadata of those recordings.
Clipto founder and Chief Executive Henry Kang said AI knows basically everything that has been posted online, but has barely scratched the surface of the terabytes of audio and video data that’s sitting in people’s hard drives.
“The next generation of AI will need to understand the conversations, experiences and knowledge that never makes it into a text-based document,” he said. “That’s the future we’re building, giving AI the memory it needs to move beyond answering questions from the internet and start getting real world done with what we ourselves have seen and heard.”
Clipto Studio can be thought of as a kind of instant-replay service. For instance, a management consultant could ask ChatGPT to pinpoint the exact time when a project’s scope changed by looking at more than six month’s worth of calls and meetings, and it will surface the exact moment when that occurred. Alternatively, a researcher might prompt Claude to identify the most common problems with a particular product or service by looking at thousands of customer calls, and pull out direct quotes that illustrate the depth of those issues.
There are other use cases too. For instance, users could ask Clipto Studio to look at dozens of hours of event presentations they’ve attended and create a highlight reel that surfaces the most interesting or relevant moments from them.
Clipto Studio’s official launch is a big moment for the startup, which recently signaled its ambitions with the hiring of former Google LLC research scientist Dr. Mei Han as its new chief scientist. Han, who holds a doctorate in robotics from Carnegie Mellon University, has been tasked with leading the development of Clipto’s lightweight multimodal AI architecture.
Han said she believes in Clipto’s mission because it’s trying to help AI perceive the world in the same way as humans do, by seeing and listening to what’s going on around them.
“The challenge isn’t just recognizing speech or identifying what’s on screen,” she said. “It’s connecting that information across thousands of recordings so AI can understand the context and use it. We’re building the technology to make video and audio as accessible and as useful to AI as text, opening up an entirely new generation of applications.”

articles.title: Coraltalk wants universities to stop chasing AI cheaters and start measuring learning | BetaKit
articles.text:
“Show your work” is an instruction known to just about anyone who has gone to school.
With generative AI now capable of producing entire assignments, universities have good reason to revisit that old classroom principle. Asking students to explain their reasoning can help instructors establish what they’ve actually learned, but in a large university class, that’s easier said than done.
Suppose a university professor wanted to sit down with each of their 75 students and ask them a few questions about their latest assignment. If they were to dedicate 15 minutes per student, the exercise would take close to 20 hours, before accounting for preparation, scheduling, or grading. Melissa Morgan, co-founder and CEO of Toronto-based EdTech startup Coraltalk, believes technology could make these kinds of assessments achievable on a much larger scale.
“A detector estimates whether text may have been produced by AI,” Morgan said. “It cannot tell a professor whether the student understands the argument, could explain a decision, or would know what to do if the facts changed.”
Coraltalk is using conversational AI to bring oral examinations into the digital age. Instructors provide the platform with course materials, assignments, and grading criteria, which the software uses to question students about their work. As students respond, the AI asks follow-up questions to probe their understanding.
A new take on an old-school approach
Consider a business student who has submitted a class assignment recommending that a company expand into a new market. Coraltalk’s platform would ask the student to explain their recommendation and identify its underlying assumptions before introducing a new constraint to see how they respond.
Once the assessment is complete, instructors can review the conversation in video form, as well as the transcript and feedback aligned with their rubric. Importantly, the instructor retains the final say over grades. Coraltalk’s role is to handle the labour-intensive part of the assessment and make individualized questioning practical for professors who would otherwise have to conduct dozens of interviews themselves.
Smita Bakshi, an investor in Coraltalk, said she took oral exams known as “vivas” during her university days. “That was possible with a class of 50, but is not possible today without the use of a technology like Coraltalk,” Bakshi said.
There are obvious technical complications that come with putting an AI system in charge of questioning students, particularly when the same technology has a well-documented tendency to hallucinate or misinterpret information. Oral exams can also disadvantage students whose language proficiency, confidence, or communication style affects their ability to answer questions aloud.
Coraltalk co-founder and CTO Adhikansh Mittal said developing the platform presented several technical challenges. One was latency, since conversations need to flow naturally between students and the AI system. Another was ensuring the privacy and security of student voice recordings and assessment data, which meant accounting for institutional requirements early in the platform’s development.
Mittal said it was also important to ensure questions draw on an instructor’s course materials, and that faculty can review results and make their own assessments.
“Those safeguards reduce risk, although no AI system can eliminate bias or hallucinations entirely, so ongoing evaluation and human oversight remain essential,” Mittal added.
Finding traction in the classroom
Coraltalk was founded in 2025 but has already found a receptive audience. The company says it has reached users in more than 60 countries without spending money on paid marketing.
Educators associated with institutions including York University and James Madison University are among those who have engaged with the platform. The company has also raised $768,000 CAD ($570,000 USD) in funding, and this year won the Higher Ed Shark Tank competition at New York’s EdTech Week.
Morgan attributed much of the early interest to professors recommending Coraltalk to colleagues, often out of frustration with the limitations of conventional assignments.
“They did not want another tool that accused students of cheating,” Morgan said. “They wanted something practical that worked with the courses they already teach.”
David Kwok is familiar with this need. Alongside his position as Director of Entrepreneurship and Innovation at York University’s YSpace, he teaches at the Schulich School of Business, where AI is changing the way students approach their coursework.
“While AI is a powerful tool, we need to ensure students continue developing the critical thinking, problem-solving, and communication skills essential to their future careers,” Kwok said, adding that he sees promise in Coraltalk’s focus on students’ ability to explain and apply their knowledge, skills that will remain relevant long after graduation.
International by necessity
Building Coraltalk has required the founders to work across several countries, and not entirely by choice. Morgan is Canadian, while Mittal is based in New Delhi, India. When Mittal was unable to obtain a visa to visit Canada, the duo began looking for other places where they could develop the company. Their travels have taken them to Vietnam, Indonesia, Malta, and Mexico.
“It has made us resourceful and given us an international perspective, although I wish it were easier for Canadian startups to collaborate in person with exceptional global talent,” Morgan added.
Coraltalk participated in various YSpace programs, including the ELLA Women Accelerator, a program supporting women-led businesses. Through YSpace, the startup gained access to experienced entrepreneurs and support with fundraising and partnerships.
Marlina Ramchandran, ELLA Entrepreneurship Manager at YSpace, said Morgan’s ability to overcome obstacles is characteristic of the adaptability YSpace wants to cultivate among entrepreneurs in the program.
“From shifting primary markets due to visa restrictions to building a business in a completely new language, she has consistently adapted, overcome every barrier, and emerged stronger,” Ramchandran said.
Back to the business of learning
Coraltalk is now looking at how its technology might be incorporated into existing education platforms. The company has developed an integration with Canvas, a widely used learning management system, and is pursuing a broader strategy to embed its technology in third-party platforms.
“Schools and learning platforms already have workflows they rely on,” Mittal said. “An API can bring conversational assessment into those products without asking everyone to adopt a separate system.”
The startup’s longer-term ambitions include applications beyond higher education, including hospitality training, where employees could practice handling difficult customer interactions, and professional development programs focused on communication and decision-making skills. Language education is another potential market the company is watching.
In a 2025 survey by the York University Faculty Association, 60 percent of respondents reported spending more time dealing with academic integrity issues than they had five years earlier. With generative AI further complicating the assessment process, Morgan believes universities need a better way to establish what students actually understand.
“AI is changing what students can produce, and that makes human skills like reasoning, communication, judgment, and adaptability even more important,” Morgan said. “My hope is that we build a future where students are invited to demonstrate those skills, teachers have meaningful evidence of learning, and using AI does not automatically turn every learner into a suspect.”
PRESENTED BY
YSpace is building a stronger Canadian tech ecosystem by fostering a community of innovators, entrepreneurs, and change makers with dedicated programs for women (ELLA) and Black (BEA) entrepreneurs, and sector-specific initiatives like SmartTO for automotive and mobility-related ventures. articles.title: Five ways Jensen Huang’s ouster from Nvidia could damage the AI industry | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s confession that he had an affair (and reports of another one with a direct report) that led the board to oust him on Thursday isn’t just your run-of-the-mill salacious billionaire CEO sex scandal.
In this case, one of his lovers is suspected by the U.S. government of being a spy for China. She’s also an executive of a Singapore-based neocloud that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China.
These affairs show undeniably poor judgment by Huang and, I’d argue, unchecked hubris on many levels. Such choices are not only a betrayal of his wife of 40 years, they’re also a liability for his company. Sleeping with any Nvidia partner is bad enough, but he also chose one in a tinderbox of a geopolitical situation. Even if Alice Huang’s company wasn’t suspected of helping Chinese firms evade chip restrictions (and he was somehow unaware of this), it was still exploiting a legal loophole by renting powerful AI infrastructure to Chinese companies.
It’s those potential national consequences that may land him in a hellscape of ongoing public humiliation. Republican committee chairs are already summoning him to testify in closed-door sessions about the security ramifications.
Will Democrats, who are set to take over key committees when the new Congress convenes in January, also haul him in to testify on the Hill? No one knows yet, but Huang has flaunted his close relationship with President Trump. Remember when Trump called him while he was onstage at the All-In Summit in September? Nvidia also donated $25 million to Trump’s ballroom, a deeply unpopular project with American voters. Several Democratic lawmakers have already vowed to investigate the money behind it.
In other words, he is a billionaire close to Trump. He was — until Thursday — the face of AI and data centers (also a deeply unpopular political topic with voters), and he has publicly admitted to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Even though he’s no longer CEO, that seems too juicy a target for Democrats to ignore.
Beyond whatever may be coming, Huang’s influence has been lost right when he was using it to push the tech industry in a number of directions. These areas have now lost their biggest champion.
Open-weight AI models as competitors to closed-source labs
Huang has been the biggest, loudest advocate for open-weight AI models in the tech industry and among government policymakers. Nvidia not only offers its own open-weight models, it also offers a lot of other open source tech for agents, AI security, and more. It has even agreed to acquire the biggest site that hosts them, Hugging Face, for $12.9 billion. (That deal is supposed to close in the first half of next year, pending regulatory approval.)
In July, when Anthropic and OpenAI were reportedly urging the Trump administration to ban Chinese open-weight models, Huang organized a letter of support for open-weight models generally (if not Chinese models specifically), signed by hundreds of tech companies.
Open-weight models give enterprises choice in the market and reduce costs. Without Huang, the next biggest advocate for them is perhaps Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, but he’s not out there organizing the industry to speak up.
Pushing the AI industry to clean up its security
Both OpenAI and Anthropic revealed incident after incident this year as their AI agents hacked into others’ networks or performed other misdeeds. Huang loudly proclaimed the AI industry still didn’t need regulation and would deal with safety itself.
As the industry mulled over what they should do (auditors? a FINRA-like board?), Huang rallied the tech industry again. Nvidia got over 100 companies to sign on to his Open Agent Safety Platform, a largely open source effort to solve the epidemic of misbehaving AI agents.
Naturally, this effort hasn’t instantly solved the problem, and now the top spokesperson for self-regulation via technology solutions is out of his position of influence.
Arguing AI is a tool, not a life form
Huang has also been among the loudest voices insisting that AI is an engineered system that creates products, and so can be controlled like any other engineered system. This viewpoint counters the AI doomers and even the big AI labs themselves, which sometimes position their models as on the verge of consciousness (Anthropic) or as alien minds (OpenAI).
While Huang deals with the fallout of his actions, the loudest voice of this counter-narrative is, for the foreseeable future, silenced.
A new Nvidia-powered AI PC industry
Huang also just convinced a long list of PC makers to buy into his long-time dream of providing CPUs (the main processor chips) for them. In this age, when most Americans have not experienced AI beyond a chatbot, he orchestrated a new line of high-end AI PCs geared for running agents locally.
These new PCs are due out this holiday season, and they may sell well for their intended targets: creators, developers, and others already savvy with agents. But now that Huang has become a meme for cheating on his wife with an alleged spy, he’s perhaps not the best choice to help market these devices as a cool alternative to the Mac mini.
Financial engineering to fund data centers
Huang demolished his reputation right as bond underwriters (lenders) and bond buyers are pretty much over AI build-out-related debt. Of roughly $80 billion in data center bonds issued this year, nearly half were rated high-risk “junk,” Forbes reports.
Undeterred, Huang has been coming up with ways to continue financing the boom and keep his company’s revenues growing. Certainly, he’s authorized a mind-boggling number of so-called circular deals, where Nvidia buys stakes in companies to fund their expansion so they can buy chips. By some accounts, the company had committed to $750 billion in such deals as of July, Bloomberg reported. In August, Nvidia got even bolder, agreeing to backstop $105 billion in financing for an OpenAI data center in Ohio, CNBC reported.
Huang also convinced a whole new set of financiers to pony up. In August, he announced that deep-pocketed PE firms Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR had committed up to $500 billion for data center build outs. He promised them that the data centers’ Nvidia GPUs could be used as collateral because Nvidia was guaranteeing the chips would retain value.
Huang sold a vision of Nvidia as “investable infrastructure” with a long resale cycle, like airplanes. Then he made the rounds with the financial press, as he often did, to pitch his vision. Now, however, Wall Street is concerned that Nvidia’s stock will crash and take their portfolios, and possibly the economy, with it.
Nvidia has lost its top salesperson and the AI industry has lost its top hype man. Even if Huang somehow comes back into the public eye to champion AI again, every interview and meeting will be about his sex life, choices, and national security — not his vision for the industry.
We’ll have to wait and see how Nvidia navigates the scandal Huang heaped onto it, but now that the company is finally in its post “founder mode” era, and hunting for a new CEO, it’s doubtful it has the cache to push the industry the way Huang was.

articles.title: Review: Apple's M6 iMac is pricey, but it's still a good choice for a clean desk
articles.text:
The Apple Silicon iMac got its fourth refresh this month.
Every other Apple Silicon Mac has found a way to move forward over the last half-decade—we’ve gotten a more Pro design for the MacBook Pro, a mini-er design for the Mac mini, and a Mac Studio that has finally made Apple admit it doesn’t want to make the Mac Pro anymore.
But the Apple Silicon iMac has always been more interested in looking backward. It’s the thin, screen-on-a-stand iMac design by way of the original Bondi Blue G3 iMac. It’s a clean and pretty desktop computer, one I see all the time in small offices and on TV shows that depict small offices. We’re long past the days when it was Apple’s primary workstation computer.
So I wanted to write about this new iMac from the perspective of that entry-level iMac buyer, who chooses the iMac because it’s simple and then uses it until it breaks. What does a new iMac get you if you’re stepping up from the M1 model or comparing it against an older refurbished M4 model? Without any real external updates, what makes this iMac iteration interesting?
Same friendly face
If you haven’t used an Apple Silicon-era iMac before, here’s a brief primer.
The new iMac is much thinner than the older aluminum Intel models. Its front is mostly one big 24-inch screen, surrounded on all sides by a relatively thick white bezel (I still wish black were at least an option, but Apple apparently doesn’t agree).
White bezel aside, it’s by far Apple’s most colorful computer. The iMacs ship with color-matched fronts, backs, stands, keyboards, mice, trackpads, and cables. Apple has tweaked the color offerings and changed the tints of each specific color a few times over the years, but the M6 iMac uses the same six color tints (plus silver) that the M4 iMac did.
The basic $1,499 iMac is essentially a MacBook Air in terms of ports—it has two Thunderbolt ports on the back and a headphone jack on the left side. Choosing this model also locks you into a lesser version of the Apple M6 with 10 CPU cores and 10 GPU cores instead of 12 of each, a maximum of 24GB of RAM, a minimum of 256GB of storage, and a maximum of 1TB. Its default keyboard doesn’t have Touch ID support, and the only way to get it is to buy the version with the built-in number pad, an $80 upsell.
The M6 iMac still comes with either two or four Thunderbolt 4 ports. The four-port version can run two external displays; the one-port version is limited to one. Ethernet is available on the power brick for an extra $30.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
The M6 iMac still comes with either two or four Thunderbolt 4 ports. The four-port version can run two external displays; the one-port version is limited to one. Ethernet is available on the power brick for an extra $30.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
The $1,699 version is the one to get if you still intend to use the iMac as a workstation. It includes the full-speed version of the M6 with all its CPU and GPU cores intact (though there are performance caveats here we’ll talk about later), plus options for 32GB of RAM and up to 2TB of storage. This version also includes four Thunderbolt ports on the back for connecting additional accessories. Both available keyboards on this version have Touch ID.
A 2.5 gigabit Ethernet port can be added to any iMac for $30. This port is located on the desktop’s power brick rather than the iMac itself, an elegant solution that keeps even a wired Internet connection hidden beneath your desk with the other cables. All iMacs also offer a VESA mount adapter option in place of the default stand at no extra charge.
I still really like the effect created by the color-matched keyboard, mouse/trackpad, and cables—even the white bezel complements the white keycaps and mouse. Just know you’re paying quite a lot for how the desktop looks. The $899 Mac mini is $800 cheaper than the iMac with the same chip, the same amount of RAM, and the same amount of storage. Sure, it would cost something to add a nice-looking 4K monitor, but not $800, even if you go for extra frills like a high refresh rate.
It’s fine that the iMac upcharges you for style and convenience. That’s the point of the computer. Just make sure that’s what you want to pay for.

Here are the basic specs for every entry-level iMac Apple has shipped, going all the way back to the last of the Intel models.
The iMac’s evolution has been slow and gradual during the Apple Silicon era. The computer has never gotten a base storage upgrade, and the base M4 and M6 models still only support a single external display (the upgraded models support two external displays, finally surpassing the old Intel model).
If you have any kind of Apple Silicon iMac and you’re happy with how it’s performing and you’re not hankering for more RAM or more displays, I don’t think the M6 model really adds anything worth upgrading for. It’s definitely faster, but even six years on, the Apple M1 remains perfectly serviceable for daily use, especially when it’s attached to 16GB of RAM.
And if you’re in the market for an iMac now, I think the M4 model still gets you the best bang for your buck if you can find one refurbished or on sale. That one still gets you a minimum of 16GB of RAM, Thunderbolt in all four ports for the four-port model, the 32GB RAM option, the nano-texture display option, and support for multiple external displays (again, in the four-port model).
The M6 iMac builds on that, and it comes with real performance benefits (more on that shortly). But the brightest dividing line in the Apple Silicon iMac model history is between the M3 and M4 model, not the M4 and M6 model. And that’s true despite the two-generation silicon upgrade.

A quick recap on the M6: a total of 12 CPU cores (two super cores, four performance cores, six efficiency cores), either 10 or 12 GPU cores, 16/24/32GB RAM options, and a doubled Neural Engine NPU with 32 cores instead of 16. For the iMac, the M6 also introduces some of the architectural tweaks introduced with the Apple M5, including the addition of neural accelerator hardware to the GPU cores. This boosts the speed of some kinds of local AI workloads compared to the M4, including MetalFX upscaling and frame generation in games.
The M6 in the Mac mini and the M6 in the 14-inch MacBook Pro both perform similarly within a roughly 28 W sustained power envelope. The version with 16GB of RAM will perform slightly worse in games and other workloads sensitive to memory bandwidth—the 16GB M6 offers 153 GB/s of memory bandwidth, and the 24GB and 32GB versions offer 170 GB/s. But that’s a pretty minor difference.
The iMac is slower than either of those two Macs, particularly in multi-core CPU benchmarks and graphics benchmarks, and the HandBrake video encoding test shows the likely culprit. The iMac’s M6 consumes an average of 18 W of power under sustained heavy load. It won’t throttle its speeds as aggressively as a MacBook Air because the iMac still includes an active cooling fan, but the reduced power envelope does mean that the Mac mini or MacBook Pro are 5 to 8 percent faster than the iMac in heavy multi-core CPU tasks and about 8 to 12 percent faster in graphics benchmarks.
One benefit of the smaller power envelope is that the iMac’s chip is even more power-efficient than the regular M6 and the iMac’s version of the M4, using much less power to do the same amount of work.
That still makes it a solid upgrade over the M4. The iMac’s M6 is 15 to 20 percent faster in our single-core CPU benchmarks, between 20 and 30 percent faster in multi-core CPU benchmarks, and between 20 and 40 percent faster in graphics benchmarks (the Blender GPU benchmarks do even better—they seem to like the neural accelerators in the M5 and M6 GPUs). Especially with 24GB or 32GB of RAM, it’s perfectly capable of being the heart of a multi-monitor workstation setup or a light photo/video editing rig.
What meets the eye
The M6 iMac changes almost nothing about who the iMac is for, its position in Apple’s lineup, or what it’s technically capable of. It’s a box-ticking upgrade, and the box being ticked is “keep the insides up to date.”
That means today’s iMac is best for the same kinds of computer users it was good for in 1998: people who don’t want a laptop, people who need a friendly and approachable kiosk or office computer, and people who just want something pretty that doesn’t require a lot of fussing with screens or cables.
That’s the main thing I miss about being an iMac user. I like how my current Mac Studio desktop works, and I need flexibility and complexity in my specific setup to get the Mac and a gaming PC connected to all the same stuff. But despite my best efforts, the cable situation has always been a barely managed mess.
If someone you know has a cable management problem and doesn’t need the complexity, congratulations, you’ve found someone the iMac is for. I just wish Apple would use these kinds of pretty, saturated colors in a laptop or desktop that meets my needs, you know?
The good
A pretty and capable desktop computer that minimizes the cable mess that most desktops make
Energy efficient and quiet, on the rare occasions when you can hear the fan spinning at all
Apple M6 is fast, and especially with 24GB or 32GB of RAM, will be more than capable of handling most tasks
Like the M4 version, it can support multiple external displays if you pay for the faster chip
The bad
Limited port selection
Costs $200 more than the M4 model did when it launched
Still just 256GB of base storage
Slightly slower than M6 versions of the Mac mini and MacBook Pro
Andrew is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica, with a focus on consumer tech including computer hardware and in-depth reviews of operating systems like Windows and macOS. Andrew lives in Philadelphia and co-hosts a weekly book podcast called Overdue.

articles.title: Chrome, Firefox Updates Patch Over 180 Vulnerabilities
articles.text:
Google and Mozilla have released fresh Chrome and Firefox security updates that resolve more than 180 vulnerabilities.
The Chrome refresh fixes 83 security defects, including five critical-severity use-after-free issues in ServiceWorker, CSS, Layout, Skia, and Accessibility.
All the remaining 78 bugs are high-severity weaknesses, mostly use-after-free (24), out-of-bounds read/write (10), type confusion (9), uninitialized resource (9), and incorrect/missing authorization (8).
Google discovered 52 of the vulnerabilities internally, and Anthropic and OpenAI researchers reported 18 more. No monetary reward will be handed out for any of these flaws.
The internet giant has paid a $4,000 bug bounty reward for a high-severity use-after-free in V8, but has not determined the amounts to be handed out for the remaining 12 externally reported flaws.
The latest Chrome iteration is now rolling out as versions 157.0.8103.78/.79 for Windows and macOS, and as version 157.0.8103.78 for Linux.
Firefox 160 arrived this week with patches for 99 vulnerabilities, including 57 high-severity security weaknesses.
Most of the flaws are use-after-free, incorrect boundary, and sandbox escape issues. The browser refresh also resolved invalid pointer, privilege escalation, information disclosure, and same-origin policy bypass bugs.
Mozilla included patches for most of these security defects in Thunderbird 160, which landed this week with 103 fixes. Thunderbird 153.7, Firefox ESR 153.7, and Firefox ESR 115.45 also rolled out with dozens of vulnerability patches.
Google and Mozilla make no mention of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild.

articles.title: Apple TV 4K: Siri AI and a mic are welcome additions
articles.text:
Among my Apple ecosystem, the device I use the most is my iPhone (currently the Duo), but my second most-used product from the Cupertino tech giant is my Apple TV. So, when the new Apple TV 4K was revealed, I was pretty ecstatic. I don’t even need an Apple TV; my TV is smart, but I’ve always liked using the Apple TV remote and seeing how it’s all organized.
Siri AI is here
This new Apple TV 4K is one of the most exciting yet, with a microphone directly on the streaming box. What does a microphone on the Apple TV get you? Siri, and in my case, Siri AI. While AI could potentially one day lead us to our inevitable end, Siri AI on a set-top box is pretty nice. However, it’s worth mentioning that the Apple TV always had Siri, but you needed the remote to activate the assistant. With the new Apple TV, you can activate the AI just by saying “Hey Siri.”
And because I’m using it with Siri AI, the assistant has access to broad world knowledge, allowing the Apple TV to answer questions about anything, alongside personal context, which works with your handset to answer personal queries.
Most importantly, you can use Siri on the Apple TV to ring your remote, which has already saved me countless minutes in searching for the remote. Yes, the Siri Remote now has a little speaker so that you can ring it when you can’t find it. You can also use Find My for Precision Finding on the remote, which is one of the most useful features ever.
Personalized experience
After setting up Siri AI and ‘Personal Content,’ I was able to get Siri to talk about shows and movies that my partner sent me. And even just asking Siri, “What are some shows that have been recommended to me?” and it listed different shows that I’ve talked about in my texts.
I could ask Siri AI to recommend shows with LGBTQ characters, and it’ll list various series that it considers popular. If you’re already watching something, you’ll see Siri answer in the top right corner, but if you’re not, Siri AI will take over the whole TV and populate a page with thumbnails about the different options.
Honestly, I’ve really liked this. I’m always looking for the next show to watch, and I like that I can ask Apple TV for recommendations. Because it’s Siri AI, you can keep talking to the assistant without having to say the command phrase again. I also have a horrible memory, so I like that it can recall shows from my text messages, and because of broad world knowledge, you can ask something like “what’s the name of that funny vampire show?” and you’ll get a list of comedic vampire shows; surprisingly, there’s more than you’d guess. You can follow up with “put on What We Do in the Shadows,” and the Apple TV will direct you to the series.
And to keep things private, no one can just ask Siri about the messages you’ve received because Siri can recognize each user’s voice. For instance, when my partner asked Siri what shows were recommended via text, Apple couldn’t populate the answer because it didn’t recognize him.
Probably, the worst part of the Siri AI experience is that after you invoke the AI, the text bubble doesn’t just go away. I need to press the back button, or tell Siri to go away. Another negative, though, is that if you have too many devices, Siri can activate the wrong device, which can be a bit annoying.
You can also use Siri AI to view and control smart home accessories, but I don’t have anything to test this out. And if you have four HomePods (including the 2023 HomePod or the 2026 HomePod mini), you can set up surround sound. Unfortunately, I didn’t get the chance to try this out either.
Faster, stronger, smoother
The Apple TV 4K is powered by the A19 chip and offers up to 50 per cent faster CPU performance and 2x faster GPU performance. This is the same chip that powers the iPhone 17, and you can tell how responsive the Apple TV 4K is compared to its predecessor. Navigation is faster, and animations are quick; I really like how smooth the experience is. Especially with Siri AI, it pulls up information incredibly fast too, or tells you it can’t find that answer.
The Apple TV 4K also obviously offers 4K output, high dynamic range (HDR) and supports Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos. Of course, this isn’t new to the Apple TV 4K, and I’ve had an experience with the previous set-top box. Other features include controlling your Apple TV with ‘Remote Control’ on your iPhone or Apple Watch. Private listening with your earbuds is still available as soon as you pull out your earbuds.
You don’t need this Apple TV 4K; I don’t need it either, especially considering its $429. However, I like the experience, especially being able to find the remote simply with my voice. I also never dreamed of the day that I’d use AI on the Apple TV, but when I forget the name of a show I wanted to watch or am looking for my next series, the assistant has come in clutch.
It’s worth mentioning Siri AI is still in beta, and you’ll need to change your language to U.S. English to try out the experience. If you’re seeing the same ol’ Siri on your iPhone, it’s likely because you haven’t made this change yet. And you’ll need to make sure you’re updated to iOS 27.2.
The new Apple TV 4K is available Friday, November 13, for $429. Alongside the Apple TV 4K, Apple’s new HomeView is also out on Friday.

articles.title: Mass Effect 1 and 2 composer speaks out against AI, says ‘machines can never be artists as they aren’t human’ — ‘The entire purpose of art is to be a human form of communication. Full stop’
articles.text:
‘AI is not an artist’ — Mass Effect 1 and 2 composer shares his stance on AI replacement in video games, says ‘Machines can never be artists as they aren’t human’
"I think as long as it’s a creative tool to get you going, it’s fine"
- Original Mass Effect composer Jack Wall shares his stance on AI in video games
- Wall believes the tech shouldn't replace human creativity, and "as long as it’s a creative tool to get you going, it’s fine"
- He adds that "Machines can never be artists as they aren’t humans"
Mass Effect and Mass Effect 2 composer Jack Wall has shared his stance on AI music and the technology being used as a replacement in video games.
It's hard to ignore how rampant artificial intelligence has become in everyday life. It's become controversial and, as many continue to object to the tech, an unwelcome part of the entertainment business, dramatically changing the gaming landscape.
As AI becomes increasingly popular, some studios have been called out for their egregious use of AI, and tech companies like Nvidia have taken advantage of it to push AI-enhanced upscaling technology.
In an interview with TechRadar Gaming, the original Mass Effect composer shared his opinion on AI — something that wasn't around 20 years ago during the creation of BioWare's iconic sci-fi series — and believes the tech shouldn't replace human creativity, but only be a "creative tool" to help.
"I think as long as it’s a creative tool to get you going, it’s fine," Wall said. "I’m not a fan of AI music. AI music is just copying what’s been done before. But if you use it as a tool, and you’re still making the creative decisions, I think it’s fine."
The composer was firm on his stance that AI can never replace the work of real people, adding, "AI is not an artist."
"Machines can never be artists as they aren’t human," he said. "The entire purpose of art is to be a human form of communication. Full stop."

"Music is not just a bunch of notes strung together," Graves told TechRadar Gaming.

articles.title: Jensen Huang aceita depor ao Congresso dos EUA sobre caso de suposta espionagem
articles.text:
Jensen Huang, que deixou o comando da Nvidia nesta quinta-feira (12), aceitou prestar esclarecimentos ao Congresso dos Estados Unidos sobre suas relações com Alice Huang, apontada por autoridades estadunidenses como uma possível agente de inteligência chinesa. O depoimento será realizado a portas fechadas, mas a data ainda está sendo negociada pelos parlamentares e representantes do empresário.
A confirmação foi feita pelo deputado Brian Mast, presidente do Comitê de Relações Exteriores da Câmara dos Representantes. Segundo ele, Huang concordou em comparecer depois de receber solicitação conjunta de três comissões do Congresso.
A reunião deve envolver os colegiados de Relações Exteriores, Inteligência e assuntos relacionados à China. Mast afirmou que espera que o encontro seja gravado em vídeo e transcrito, embora não seja aberto ao público.
O presidente do Comitê Seleto sobre a China, John Moolenaar, afirmou que os parlamentares querem ouvir Huang o mais rápido possível para esclarecer os fatos. Caso o ex-executivo não compareça, os três comitês estão dispostos a recorrer ao poder de intimação do Congresso.
O que o Congresso quer saber de Jensen Huang?
- Em carta enviada em 4 de novembro, Mast, Moolenaar e Rick Crawford, presidente do Comitê de Inteligência da Câmara, solicitaram que Huang participasse de reunião conjunta em 18 de novembro. Os parlamentares pediram que ele confirmasse a data ou apresentasse alternativa até o dia 11;
- O documento aponta dois temas principais: as interações de Huang com Alice Huang, ex-executiva da empresa Megaspeed, e os protocolos de segurança da Nvidia contra operações de espionagem estrangeira;
- A preocupação dos parlamentares é que a suposta relação entre os dois possa ter sido usada para obter informações sensíveis da fabricante de chips. Também há questionamentos sobre a possibilidade de tecnologia estadunidense ter sido desviada para a China, em meio às restrições de exportação impostas por Washington;
- A Megaspeed, empresa sediada em Singapura que comprava chips da Nvidia, está sob investigação nos Estados Unidos e em Singapura por suspeitas de facilitar o envio de componentes avançados para a China. A companhia nega irregularidades e afirma cooperar com as autoridades.
Parlamentares divergem sobre exportação de chips para a China
Além das suspeitas de espionagem, o depoimento pode abordar a política estadunidense de exportação de semicondutores. Huang já teve divergências públicas com Brian Mast sobre as restrições à venda de chips para clientes chineses.
O deputado afirmou que os dois estiveram em lados opostos nesse debate, mas destacou a importância da Nvidia para os Estados Unidos e disse que o executivo tem questões sérias a responder.
O deputado John Moolenaar, por sua vez, afirmou que a principal preocupação é saber se Huang poderia ter sido influenciado por uma agente chinesa e se informações estratégicas da indústria estadunidense chegaram à inteligência de Pequim.
Nem todos os parlamentares, porém, consideram que a vida pessoal do executivo deva dominar a discussão. O deputado Jay Obernolte defendeu que o debate permaneça concentrado nas consequências da política de exportação de chips e não em questões particulares.
Leia mais:
- Nvidia tenta acalmar funcionários após saída de Jensen Huang
- Nvidia: agência de notícias revela novo relacionamento atribuído a Jensen Huang
- Suposta espiã chinesa ligada a Jensen Huang tinha negócios conectados à Huawei
Saída da Nvidia não encerra pressão sobre Huang
A concordância em depor ocorreu no mesmo dia em que a Nvidia anunciou a saída imediata de Huang do cargo de CEO. O empresário liderou a companhia por mais de três décadas e deixou a posição em meio à repercussão de relatos sobre relacionamentos extraconjugais, incluindo um supostamente envolvendo Alice Huang.
A saída não encerrou os questionamentos políticos. O líder da maioria no Senado, John Thune, também afirmou que deve haver interesse em investigação parlamentar sobre o caso.
Do lado democrata, o líder da minoria no Senado, Chuck Schumer, defendeu que o Congresso cobre explicações não apenas de Huang e da Nvidia, mas também do governo de Donald Trump sobre o que sabia a respeito das suspeitas.
Os republicanos ainda controlam a Câmara dos Representantes até janeiro de 2027 e querem avançar com a apuração antes da mudança de maioria. Por enquanto, não há data definitiva para a reunião com o ex-CEO.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Microsoft Outlook is still down
articles.text:
Since just before 1PM ET on Thursday, reports have come in from around the world that people can’t access their Outlook email, either through the web or apps. Microsoft quickly acknowledged the issue from its Microsoft 365 Status account, saying that “We’ve determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors.”
Microsoft Outlook is still down
Microsoft 365 issues have been cutting people off from their email since early Thursday afternoon, and they still aren’t fixed.
There were also some reports of problems with Teams, but not to the same extent, while Microsoft’s official updates said customers may experience issues across its suite of 365 business services. Microsoft comms director Ben Hope said in a statement that “We are aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues with Exchange Online. We appreciate our customers’ patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible.”
Several hours later, Microsoft has gone through several variations of update notes regarding the issues and its attempts to fix them, saying it’s had problems rebooting servers and being able to monitor their health. As of about 6PM ET, Microsoft has a note saying it’s managed to get some of the affected servers running:
We’ve begun returning a portion of the affected servers to service, and they’re remaining stable so far. We’ve also shifted traffic and connections to alternative pathways wherever possible and have observed limited recovery in some regions.
We’ve streamlined our recovery process to expedite returning the remaining affected servers to service. To further support recovery, we’re implementing protective traffic management measures in a specific location to reduce load on the affected infrastructure, and we’ll expand these measures to additional locations if we observe positive results. As capacity is restored, users may experience a gradual recovery as their clients reconnect to the service.
There’s still no ETA for full restoration, but we will continue to monitor this ongoing outage.
Update, 6:23PM ET: Added latest status update from Microsoft.

articles.title: NVIDIA podría destituir a Jensen Huang como CEO tras el escándalo con la espía china
articles.text:
Jensen Huang podría perder su puesto como director ejecutivo de NVIDIA. De acuerdo con The Wall Street Journal, la junta directiva estaría preparando una reunión para decidir el futuro del fundador y CEO de la compañía. Las cosas se complicaron para Huang luego de que una investigación interna descubriera vínculos con una supuesta espía china.
Según el reporte, el consejo de administración considera destituir a Huang después de que salieran a la luz dos relaciones extramaritales. Hace unos días, el CEO reconoció que había sido infiel a su esposa y pidió disculpas por traicionar la confianza de su familia y de la organización. La figura en el centro de esa polémica es Alice Huang, una ejecutiva de la compañía Megaspeed y con vínculos con el gobierno de Xi Jinping.
Los primeros rumores apuntaban a que Megaspeed habría ayudado a desviar chips de IA hacia China. La compañía, con sede en Singapur, se convirtió en uno de los principales clientes de NVIDIA para la construcción de centros de datos de IA en el sudeste asiático. No obstante, las autoridades estadounidenses sospecharon que Huang ayudó a contrabandear tarjetas gráficas, por lo cual abrieron una investigación a finales de 2024.
La relación entre Jensen Huang y Alice Huang comenzó en 2023 y permitió que la ejecutiva china desviara 240.000 placas gráficas H100, H200 y A100 hacia el gigante asiático. The Information reveló que Huang montó una red de empresas en China junto con su hermana y esposo, incluyendo una que le ayudó a convertirse en socio preferente de NVIDIA. Este movimiento le garantizó acceso prioritario a los chips y al CEO de la empresa.
Jensen Huang se metió con una espía china y con una empleada de NVIDIA
Hace unas semanas surgió un reporte de que Alice Huang estaba vinculada a los servicios de inteligencia chinos. El Departamento de Justicia abrió múltiples investigaciones relacionadas con ella y el mundo se le vino encima al jefe de NVIDIA. Según informó el New York Times, Alice Huang (también conocida como Huang Le) trabajaba para el Ministerio de Seguridad del Estado de China mientras mantenía una relación romántica con el directivo de la empresa de tarjetas gráficas.
Los investigadores temen que pueda haber accedido a detalles técnicos sobre el hardware de IA de NVIDIA y las discusiones internas con la Casa Blanca. Hasta ahora, las autoridades se han centrado en su papel como ejecutiva de Megaspeed, donde aprovechó su cercanía con Jensen Huang para ayudar a eludir los controles de exportación estadounidenses.
Además de esta relación, el New York Times señaló que el jefe de NVIDIA mantuvo un romance con otra empleada de la compañía. Kimberly Powell, vicepresidente del área de atención médica de NVIDIA, fue captada en un vídeo con Jensen Huang mientras se encontraban en un hotel de San José, California. Las políticas internas de la compañía prohíben este tipo de acciones, sobre todo cuando se trata de una relación extramarital entre un jefe y su subordinada.
Hasta el momento de esta publicación, el futuro de Jensen Huang permanece en el aire. Si la junta decide apartarlo del cargo, NVIDIA perdería al hombre que transformó la compañía y la convirtió en una de las más valiosas del mundo. Huang ha sido el rostro visible de la empresa por más de tres décadas, primero en su etapa gamer y ahora en el desarrollo de chips para centros de datos, por lo que encontrar un sucesor será un trabajo complejo.

articles.title: Anthropic-IPO: Banken drängen auf höheren Startpreis der Aktie
articles.text:
Anthropic hat am Dienstag die Roadshow für den Börsengang gestartet. Dabei wollen die begleitenden Banken offenbar einen besseren Startpreis für die Aktie durchsetzen und die Bewertung auf 1,5 Billionen Dollar oder mehr erhöhen, wie die „Financial Times“ unter Berufung auf Insider berichtet.
Laut aktualisiertem Börsenprospekt peilt Anthropic eine Gesamtbewertung von über einer Billion Dollar an. Zunächst sollen rund 825 Millionen Aktien für einen Preis von 70 bis 78 Dollar angeboten werden. Strategische Investoren wie Alphabet, Nvidia oder Microsoft können für weitere 26 Milliarden Dollar besondere stimmrechtslose Aktien zum IPO-Preis kaufen. Insgesamt könnte Anthropic so bis zu 90,4 Milliarden Dollar einnehmen.
Damit würde die Bewertung des KI-Unternehmens inklusive Mitarbeiteroptionen und reservierten Aktien auf bis zu 1,4 Billionen Dollar steigen. Das ist deutlich mehr als die 965 Milliarden Dollar, mit denen Anthropic bei der letzten Finanzierungsrunde von Investoren bewertet wurde, aber auch deutlich weniger, als Investoren noch im Sommer erhofft hatten. Damals stand eine Bewertung von bis zu zwei Billionen Dollar im Raum.
Banken wollen höheren Startpreis
Die Banken streben laut dem Bericht einen Aktienpreis von rund 83 Dollar an. Zu welchem Preis die Aktie in den Handel startet, entscheidet sich voraussichtlich am 18. November. Einen Tag später könnte Anthropic an der Nasdaq unter dem Kürzel „ANT“ an die Börse gehen. Bis zu 20 Prozent der angebotenen Papiere sollen dann an Privatanleger gehen. Auch in Deutschland werden Anleger Anthropic-Aktien zeichnen können.
Trotz der hohen Bewertung wird Anthropic damit den Mega-IPO von SpaceX im Juni dieses Jahres nicht überflügeln. Das Raumfahrtunternehmen von Elon Musk nahm bei seinem Börsengang 75 Milliarden Dollar bei einer Bewertung von rund 1,75 Billionen Dollar ein.
In den vergangenen Jahren ist der Umsatz bei Anthropic rasant gewachsen: 2023 setzte Anthropic noch 41 Millionen Dollar um, 2025 waren es knapp 4,6 Milliarden. In den ersten neun Monaten 2026 stieg der Umsatz auf 33,2 Milliarden Dollar. Die Run Rate, also der aufs Jahr hochgerechnete aktuelle Umsatz, lag Ende Oktober bei 81 Milliarden Dollar. Allerdings warnt Anthropic selbst im Börsenprospekt davor, dass sich das Tempo des Wachstums so nicht halten lässt.
Was Analysten erwarten
Die Analysten von Goldman Sachs rechnen für 2030 mit rund 685 Milliarden Dollar Umsatz, wovon 586 Milliarden allein aus dem Geschäft mit Unternehmenskunden kommen sollen. Das entspräche mehr als dem Achtfachen der aktuellen Run Rate. Diese optimistische Einschätzung stammt allerdings von der Bank, die den IPO federführend begleitet, also am Verkauf der Aktien entsprechend mitverdient.
Die Analysten von Morningstar rechnen dagegen im Basisszenario mit einem Wachstum von 47 Prozent pro Jahr für die Jahre 2027 bis 2031, wenn das KI-Unternehmen noch mehr Unternehmenskunden gewinnen und bestehende Kunden an sich binden kann.
Im optimistischen Szenario gehen sie von einer Wachstumsrate von mehr als 60 Prozent über einen Zeitraum von fünf Jahren aus, wenn es Anthropic gelingt, erhebliche Marktanteile zu gewinnen und an Konkurrenten wie OpenAI vorbeizuziehen. In diesem Fall könnte die Aktie um über 150 Prozent auf bis zu 188 Dollar steigen, mehr als doppelt so hoch wie im Basisszenario.
Finanzprofessor Aswath Damodaran von der New York University hält eine Bewertung von 1,5 Billionen Dollar für möglich, falls der Umsatz bis 2036 auf eine Billion Dollar wächst. Im schlechtesten Fall könnte Anthropic allerdings auch erst in zehn Jahren 200 Milliarden Dollar Umsatz erreichen, während hohe Rechenkosten die Marge auf zehn Prozent drücken.
Knappe und teure Rechenkapazitäten könnten eine Wachstumsbremse für Anthropic werden. Laut Börsenprospekt hat sich das KI-Unternehmen Rechenleistung und Infrastruktur für rund 895 Milliarden Dollar vertraglich gesichert, und im dritten Quartal machte das Unternehmen auch wegen kurzfristig zugekaufter Kapazitäten wieder einen operativen Verlust.
Damodaran sieht außerdem „Warnsignale“ in der ungewöhnlichen Führungsstruktur von Anthropic. Das KI-Startup ist als Public Benefit Corporation (PBC) strukturiert und damit nicht nur dem Profit, sondern auch dem Gemeinwohl verpflichtet. Ein unabhängiges Gremium, der sogenannte Long-Term Benefit Trust, darf Vorstandsmitglieder ernennen und abberufen. Außerdem haben sich die Gründer um die Geschwister Dario und Daniela Amodei über Sonderaktien 50,1 Prozent der Stimmrechte gesichert.
Tech-Werte erholen sich, Nvidia bricht ein
Anleger hatten in der vergangenen Woche pessimistisch auf KI-Unternehmen geblickt. Tech-Aktien verloren nach dem überraschend deutlichen Sieg der Demokraten bei den US-Midterms zeitweise zweistellig, da sich der Ausbau von Rechenzentren aufgrund einer strengen Regulierung nun verlangsamen könnte.
Angesichts des Anthropic-IPO steigt die Laune bei Tech-Werten nun aber wieder. Ausnahme ist Nvidia: Die Aktie brach am Mittwoch nachbörslich um mehr als acht Prozent ein, nachdem Berichte aufkamen, der Verwaltungsrat erwäge wegen der Affärenvorwürfe die Ablösung von CEO Jensen Huang.

articles.title: The Memory Challenge Of Physical AI
articles.text:
Right-size the memory hierarchy around the device’s data streams, reuse patterns, latency requirements, and operating constraints.
Most AI hardware conversations start with compute, which is understandable since accelerators are visible, easy to compare, and often tied to headline performance metrics. Physical AI broadens that conversation by placing greater emphasis on how compute, memory, and data movement work together under real-world operating constraints. For intelligent systems that must see, interpret, decide, and act in the physical world in real time, it’s critical that the right data reaches the right engine at the right time.
As a result, data movement has become an increasingly important consideration when architecting physical AI systems. A physical AI device may simultaneously handle sensor streams, model weights, activations, temporary buffers, control loops, and safety functions. If memory access becomes unpredictable, compute engines can stall. Power consumption rises when data is moved too often, and poorly planned buffering can cause latency accumulation that is hard to recover from later.
As physical AI workloads become more complex, architects must now consider how predictably the complete system performs when multiple real-world workloads are active simultaneously.
Physical AI systems rely on a memory hierarchy that coordinates on-chip memory with larger-capacity external memory. LPDDR or GDDR may hold model weights, sensor data, activations, and other working data, while on-chip SRAM and cache keep the portions currently needed by the NPU, CPU, DSP, ISP, or other processing engines close to compute.
As workloads move through the processing pipeline, required data is transferred from external memory into on-chip memory, where it can be accessed and reused with lower latency and energy. The more effectively the architecture reuses that local data, the fewer times it must retrieve the same information from external memory. However, because SRAM and cache consume silicon area, their capacity is limited. Data that does not fit on-chip, or is used less frequently, remains in LPDDR or GDDR until it is needed.
This coordination is important because every unnecessary transfer across the memory hierarchy consumes energy, adds latency, and uses external-memory bandwidth. Physical AI systems are also constrained by device size, package complexity, power delivery, and thermal headroom. The goal is therefore not to eliminate external memory access, but to keep the right data close to compute for as long as it is useful and avoid moving it more often than necessary.
A well-planned dataflow coordinates compute engines, on-chip SRAM and cache, external LPDDR or GDDR, buffering, and interconnect around the workload. This helps keep compute resources productive while using external-memory capacity and bandwidth efficiently.
Humanoid robots, drones, autonomous vehicles, smart cameras, inspection robots, industrial robots, and autonomous mobile robots may all run local intelligence, yet each stresses memory and interfaces differently. Their architectures must determine which data should remain close to compute for immediate access and which should reside in higher-capacity external memory.
Humanoids may combine cameras, depth sensing, audio, inertial data, balance control, object recognition, path planning, and actuator feedback within a limited power and thermal envelope. If perception data arrives late, control decisions may be delayed. In addition, sustained performance drops and power rises if model weights and intermediate data are reloaded too often. In this kind of system, memory efficiency affects how smoothly the robot can perceive, decide, and move, all of which are key to successful real-time operation.
A drone or autonomous mobile robot has a different set of constraints. It may need visual navigation, obstacle avoidance, stabilization, object tracking, wireless communication, and video processing, all while staying within a limited power and thermal budget. Unnecessary external memory accesses reduce operating time, add heat, or introduce latency into the control loop. For these physical AI systems, bandwidth per watt is as important as raw bandwidth.
Autonomous vehicles and advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) present an even greater challenge. With cameras, radar, lidar, ultrasonic sensors, vehicle telemetry, map data, and control functions, competition for memory access is fierce. Some data streams need continuous throughput, while others need fusion across sensor domains. Retaining relevant data long enough to support planning and decision-making is also an important consideration. In this environment, memory behavior affects both throughput and response predictability.
When building a memory architecture, architects should begin with the behavior of the physical AI workload itself. The objective is not simply to select the fastest external memory technology or provision the greatest possible bandwidth. It is to right-size the complete memory hierarchy, including local storage, external memory capacity, bandwidth, power, buffering, and integration, around the device’s data streams, reuse patterns, latency requirements, and operating constraints.
LPDDR and GDDR address different architectural priorities. LPDDR is often a strong fit when bandwidth per watt and memory capacity are needed to sustain local inference performance. When continuous image or sensor-stream bandwidth is the primary requirement, GDDR may be a viable option because its high bandwidth can meet those performance needs with fewer DRAM devices.
Available solutions give architects considerable flexibility in making this tradeoff. For example, Cadence offers LPDDR6/LPDDR5X PHY and Controller IP supporting data rates up to 14.4Gbps, as well as GDDR7 PHY IP supporting data rates up to 36Gbps for high-bandwidth applications. These options allow the external memory interface to be aligned with the workload rather than treated as a one-size-fits-all design choice.
A humanoid robot may prioritize power-efficient access to model weights, perception data, and control information. A smart camera or autonomous-vehicle perception processor may place greater pressure on sustained vision-stream bandwidth. In each case, the architecture should keep frequently reused and latency-sensitive data close to compute while selecting an external memory interface sized for the remaining capacity and bandwidth requirements. This helps avoid both memory bottlenecks and unnecessary over-provisioning.
| Device context | Examples | Primary pressure | Likely memory fit | 
| Mobile physical AI devices | Humanoids, drones, autonomous mobile robots, robotic modules | Sustained local inference under size, capacity, bandwidth, and latency limits | LPDDR for bandwidth-per-watt and high DRAM capacity design; GDDR selectively for heavy vision streams | 
| Vision-heavy physical AI devices | Autonomous vehicles, smart cameras, inspection robots, industrial vision systems | Continuous image or sensor streams with predictable response | LPDDR where memory capacity matters; GDDR when stream bandwidth dominates | 
Before selecting an external memory interface, architects should evaluate how the device’s dataflow and operating constraints affect five key areas:
A balanced memory architecture aligns data locality, traffic management, external memory selection, buffering, and latency predictability with the device workload. Together, these decisions help reduce unnecessary data movement, keep compute resources productive, and maintain predictable performance when multiple workloads operate concurrently.
Physical AI places intelligence inside devices that operate continuously, interact with real-world signals, and respond under power, thermal, latency, and reliability constraints. Meeting these demands requires compute, memory, and data movement to function as a coordinated system. Predictable data movement is crucial for physical AI devices to operate effectively under real-world conditions, making memory architecture an important part of the overall design. Selecting the right memory requires a careful balance of latency, power efficiency, bandwidth, buffering, and workload requirements. Architects must keep frequently used data close to the engines that need it, use external bandwidth efficiently, keep compute resources productive, and maintain predictable system behavior as workloads operate concurrently.
Learn more about how to architect physical AI systems with design IP in Cadence’s “Designing Physical AI Systems Under Real-World Constraints” white paper.
