articles.title: Claude alcanza 1.300 millones de visitas antes de salir a bolsa y se consolida entre las tres IA más utilizadas del mundo
articles.text:
Claude, el asistente de inteligencia artificial desarrollado por Anthropic, alcanzó aproximadamente 1.300 millones de visitas durante octubre, una cifra que lo consolida como uno de los tres servicios de IA conversacional más visitados del mundo. El crecimiento se produjo mientras la compañía prepara su salida a bolsa en Wall Street, una operación que podría convertirla en una de las empresas tecnológicas más valiosas del sector.
Los datos de la firma de inteligencia digital Similarweb, compartidos con Forbes, muestran que el tráfico de Claude aumentó un 23,8 % respecto a septiembre, cuando había registrado alrededor de 1.000 millones de visitas. El avance también representa un crecimiento interanual del 536,3 %, una expansión que supera el ritmo de sus principales competidores en el mercado de asistentes de inteligencia artificial.
Con estos resultados, Claude subió seis posiciones en el ranking global de sitios web más visitados y alcanzó el puesto número 25. Dentro de la categoría de chatbots, se ubicó en el tercer lugar, detrás de ChatGPT y Gemini, las plataformas de OpenAI y Google, respectivamente.
Claude crece mientras ChatGPT y Gemini mantienen sus posiciones
El aumento del tráfico de Claude contrasta con el comportamiento de otros asistentes de inteligencia artificial durante octubre. Según los datos de Similarweb, ChatGPT registró aproximadamente 6.000 millones de visitas, frente a los 5.900 millones contabilizados en septiembre. Esto representa un incremento mensual del 2,2 %.
La plataforma de OpenAI mantiene el liderazgo mundial y concentra el 81,2 % de la cuota de tráfico del sector, de acuerdo con las cifras citadas en el informe.
Por su parte, Gemini, la inteligencia artificial de Google, alcanzó los 2.600 millones de visitas. Su actividad prácticamente no presentó cambios respecto al mes anterior, con una ligera caída del 0,1 %.
Estas cifras muestran que, aunque ChatGPT continúa dominando el mercado, Claude consiguió acelerar su crecimiento y reducir parte de la distancia frente a las plataformas más populares.
Sin embargo, es importante distinguir entre visitas y usuarios únicos. Las cifras de Similarweb contabilizan accesos a los sitios web y no necesariamente representan personas diferentes, ya que un mismo usuario puede ingresar varias veces durante el mes.
Anthropic prepara una salida a bolsa multimillonaria
El crecimiento de Claude coincide con los preparativos de Anthropic para ingresar al mercado bursátil estadounidense. La compañía trabaja en una oferta pública inicial (OPI) que podría alcanzar una valoración de 1,4 billones de dólares, según la documentación citada en la información original.
La operación contempla la colocación de 825 millones de acciones, con un precio estimado de entre 70 y 78 dólares por título. Si se concretan esas condiciones, la empresa protagonizaría una de las mayores salidas a bolsa de la historia tecnológica.
El movimiento también permitiría a Anthropic adelantarse a OpenAI, su principal competidor. Aunque esta última compañía habría iniciado trámites confidenciales para preparar su debut bursátil, decidió postergar sus planes más allá de 2026.
La posible salida a bolsa representa un momento importante para Anthropic, que busca demostrar que su crecimiento en inteligencia artificial puede traducirse en un negocio sostenible y atractivo para los inversores.
Las controversias también impulsaron la atención sobre Claude
El crecimiento de Claude se produjo en un contexto de discusiones sobre el uso de inteligencia artificial en organismos públicos y aplicaciones militares.
Anthropic ganó notoriedad tras protagonizar una disputa contractual con el Departamento de Defensa de Estados Unidos, además de recibir cuestionamientos públicos del presidente Donald Trump.
La compañía ha defendido una estrategia centrada en la seguridad y el desarrollo responsable de sus modelos, un enfoque que forma parte de su posicionamiento frente a otros competidores.
No obstante, el aumento de visitas también refleja el interés de los usuarios por herramientas capaces de resolver tareas cotidianas, desde redactar documentos y analizar información hasta ayudar con programación y trabajos complejos.
Gil Luria, director gerente de la firma D. A. Davidson, señaló que, pese a los cuestionamientos reputacionales que enfrentan las grandes compañías de inteligencia artificial, los usuarios siguen priorizando la potencia y utilidad de estas herramientas.
Con 1.300 millones de visitas en octubre, Claude demuestra que Anthropic ha conseguido ampliar su presencia internacional. El siguiente desafío será mantener ese crecimiento y convertir la popularidad de su asistente en una ventaja competitiva frente a ChatGPT y Gemini, especialmente mientras prepara su posible debut en Wall Street.

articles.title: LinkedIn Replaces Argo CD with a Custom GitOps Engine for Kubernetes Deployments
articles.text:
In a recent post, LinkedIn revealed it has replaced Argo CD with its own GitOps engine. This new system deploys applications across over 250 Kubernetes clusters. It supports more than 4,000 services and manages over 100,000 deployments each week. According to a post, deployment infrastructure failures fell from 925 to 63 despite a 3.7x increase in deployment volume. The median time to detect and conclude a failed deployment dropped from 16.1 to 2.45 minutes.
LinkedIn started with one Argo CD instance per cluster, a topology it chose because Argo CD already managed its cluster add-ons that way. Clusters run up to 5,000 nodes each. A central deployment orchestrator spawned an ephemeral pod per deployment, with Argo CD hidden behind it. The team lists seven problems that emerged at scale. Argo CD doesn't have an observedGeneration, so you can't link sync and health status to a specific deployment. LinkedIn created a Lua health check that uses a tracking annotation to address this. A Synced and Healthy application could also resolve to an unintended revision when stale repo-server cache entries were used.
Two of the issues were architectural. Argo CD maintains one watch per group-version-resource across Applications. LinkedIn’s clusters have low resource-type diversity. This means etcd churn from one app can slow syncs for all apps. In one test, sync took under 3 minutes on a cluster with 60,000 pods and over 10 minutes with more than 80,000. The second was server-side-apply PATCH. Kubernetes truncates managedFields once an object has had more than 10 distinct field managers, and the API server then forgets who owns a field. In LinkedIn's AI workloads, which run multiple containers per Pod, a container removed from a manifest could therefore survive on the live Pod. The team had pruning disabled because destructive operations in production require approval. The remaining problems were CRD schema changes that required controller restarts across the fleet. Some OutOfSync states did not reflect real drift. Error messages were buried in boilerplate.
LinkedIn evaluated Flux but found it shared the same controller paradigm, so it built the engine as a library. Each deployment runs in its pod, with no shared controller state. Updates use PUT for full replacements, not PATCH. They retry on resourceVersion conflicts with exponential backoff. A 3-way diff across the live object, the previously deployed manifest, and the newly rendered manifest detects drift, and genuine drift fails the deployment. The same pod then watches the object's status until it converges or times out, and the API server unwraps errors for the user. Objects missing from the rendered manifest become deletion candidates, subject to delete protection, and convergence logic for LinkedIn's CRDs is built in.
The comparison uses the same calendar month a year apart. The migration ran from July 2025 to April 2026, which makes May 2026 the first clean post-migration month. The infra failure count covers only failures caused by the deployment system and excludes drift errors, since the two systems define drift differently. LinkedIn states that the improvement isn't solely due to the new engine. The orchestrator's error classification and reliability also got better during this time. The median duration for successful deployments is similar for both systems. However, the mean and tail have improved. The team attributes this to a namespace-scoped informer cache.
The engine is internal, and no open-source release is mentioned. Argo CD remains in use at LinkedIn for cluster add-ons and system services. The team had also found that maintaining 200+ Argo CD instances made each upgrade a multi-week project.
Teams running Argo CD at scale can check two things without a rewrite. Count the field managers on long-lived objects, since managedFields truncation can leave orphaned containers that produce no error. Then check whether sync latency tracks total pod count on shared clusters, which points to watch contention. LinkedIn concludes that the build-or-extend decision relies on the operational model. They say that per-deployment isolation, not controller tuning, allows the system to scale with compute.
LinkedIn is not the only large operator to build deployment logic around Kubernetes rather than adopt a general-purpose GitOps controller. Uber’s Up platform assigns each deployment to a dedicated controller. This is the Uber Deployment Controller. It translates the intent into Kubernetes primitives and sends status updates. This helps the workflow move forward. Uber keeps a long-running controller, while LinkedIn runs one ephemeral pod per deployment with no shared controller state.
Airbnb went further back and built its own tooling years earlier. In a talk at QCon London 2019 on InfoQ, infrastructure engineer Melanie Cebula introduced kube-gen. This internal framework creates Kubernetes configuration from one versioned project file. It also includes a deploy tool that applies or replaces objects and restarts pods, so changes take effect right away. Airbnb's deploy tool also returns an atomic success or failure, and a container that restarts for 30 seconds at the start of a rollout counts as a failed deploy. Airbnb was then at roughly 125,000 production deploys a year.

articles.title: Attacker Targets 60,000 GitHub Repositories in Credential Theft Campaign
articles.text:
An attacker has tested stolen access to more than 60,000 GitHub repositories and inserted credential-stealing code in thousands of them, several security firms report.
Aikido Security said the operation, which it calls wfx-loot, began on November 10. It identified roughly 4,800 compromised accounts behind probe pull requests submitted to 61,764 repositories.
The requests were used to establish whether the stolen access permitted changes to a repository. “The pull request does nothing by itself,” StepSecurity explained, noting that malware was subsequently deployed in repositories where the permissions and configuration allowed it.
Aikido found signs that the stealer ran in more than 1,800 repositories. SafeDep separately counted 8,093 public repositories that received malicious commits, a figure that does not necessarily indicate successful execution.
“The attacker does not exploit a bug in GitHub Actions,” StepSecurity noted. The intruder instead relies on valid tokens belonging to developer and bot accounts.
The attacker placed the malware in existing or new GitHub Actions workflows, shell scripts run by CI systems, and npm installation hooks. The npm method also poses a risk to developers who install dependencies while the malicious changes are present.
The script looks for GitHub tokens, repository secrets, cloud credentials and AI service keys. It also reads GitHub Actions runner process memory and has functionality designed to expand access and establish persistence in AWS and Azure.
The attacker usually reversed the code changes and deleted workflow runs to conceal the activity.
StepSecurity traced 173 probe pull requests to tokens issued to the Fly.io GitHub app. The firm said it could not determine how the tokens were obtained and had no evidence that Fly.io’s infrastructure had been breached.
Affected software releases include a Packagist package and versions of two Go modules.
Aikido identified similarities with October’s GhostAction campaign but assessed that the two operations probably involved different actors.
The security firm warned that organizations should assume all accessible secrets were compromised if the malware executed. Organizations have been advised to revoke compromised tokens, rotate exposed secrets, and check for unauthorized cloud changes.
Related: Notion Customer Data Compromised in Fireworks AI Hack
Related: 500,000 Active Credentials Left Exposed on GitHub
Related: Meta Says Hackers Took Code, Personal Data of 1,500 in GitHub Breach

articles.title: BluWave-ai secures $8.1 million for energy grid software as data centres strain load | BetaKit
articles.text:
Heading into its 10th year as a company, energy grid management startup BluWave-ai has raised fresh funding as it anticipates a surge in demand thanks to an AI data centre build-out.
The Ottawa company announced on Thursday that it has secured $8.1 million in a mix of equity from several angel investors and family offices, non-dilutive federal government funding (though it did not disclose through which department), and debt from Royal Bank of Canada and Bank of Montreal. Founder and CEO Devashish Paul said the financing was 40 percent debt facilities but did not break down the split further.
Founded in 2017, BluWave-ai is a cleantech startup that uses AI to help utility companies add renewable energy sources to their electricity grids and to manage energy loads more broadly. The 40-person company is led by Paul, who was a longtime tech executive and Royal Canadian Air Force officer before founding BluWave. The company has raised more than $24 million since its founding.
Despite a difficult few years for the cleantech sector, BluWave sees a renewed opportunity to help utilities manage energy fluctuations with AI software.
“All the data centres that are coming on board around the world are adding strain to the grid,” Paul said in an interview. Despite a difficult few years for the cleantech sector, BluWave sees a renewed opportunity to help utilities manage energy fluctuations with AI software.
Nearly 10 years ago, BluWave bet on the need for technology to help utilities manage a green energy transition. The company built an app that tracks energy loads and optimizes renewable energy usage and electric vehicle (EVs) charging. This summer, it partnered with four electricity utilities in Ontario to provide a provincial regulation system for EV charging.
It has established a global presence, with operations in Japan and in Europe. BluWave has also amassed a broad portfolio of patents for its energy management technology, allowing it to build a business out of licensing the patents to customers who want to create their own tailored products.
Paul said that changes in US administration leadership have swayed the clean-energy market over the years. When former President Joe Biden was in power, companies similar to BluWave cropped up to meet demand for smart solutions to renewable energy management, raising money along the way. But since then, through President Donald Trump’s second term, as he has slashed environmental regulations, Paul said some of BluWave’s competition has thinned out.
Then came the generative AI era: projected demand has exploded for data centres to supply computing power for AI. Canada has been no exception; Québec’s provincial utility suggested that electricity demand could increase by more than 30 percent by 2041, in part due to new data centre demand. In last week’s federal budget, the government pledged to enable domestic access to 500 megawatts of “sovereign AI compute.” At the same time, US data centre builders are eyeing Canada as an attractive destination, with projects underway from Anthropic, Meta, and Microsoft.
RELATED: Cleantech startup BluWave-ai closes $3.9 million in seed funding
All of this will undoubtedly make balancing provincial electricity grids more tricky, something BluWave argues it was built to help with. “We’ve played a bit of a long game,” Paul said.
While its main customers are utilities, Paul said it’s also targeting data centre operators and tenants. BluWave has developed a product tailored to data centre operators it claims would allow them to shift compute-intensive workloads to periods of low demand on electrical grids and consume less electricity in the process.
Along with the round, which BluWave is describing as “Series A2,” the company has added two board members: Suzanne Grant, the executive director of the Capital Angels Network, and former board member Mario Montana, a former semiconductor company entrepreneur. Montana stepped away in 2023 due to his professional and family workload, but Paul said the opportunity has since arisen to bring him back on.
Feature image courtesy Unsplash. Photo by Matthew Henry.

articles.title: Canadian tech gifts driven by nostalgia, physical ownership: survey
articles.text:
Canadians are leaning into the nostalgia factor for tech holiday gifts, driven by a growing desire to own physical products, according to a new survey.
Named the Holiday Tech Gifting Report, the study was done by Best Buy and Angus Reid. It surveyed 1,500 Canadian adults between Oct. 16-20, 2026, who were members of the Angus Reid Forum.
Starting things off, the study shared that four in ten (40 per cent) of Canadians are likely to buy a tech gift because of the nostalgia factor. To make it specific, Best Buy notes that Millennials (53 per cent) are the most likely generation to do so, while Boomers (22 per cent) are almost half as likely to do so. Millennials are also the most likely to say that it reminds them of a certain time in their life (20 per cent), almost double that of Boomers (11 per cent).
The survey also noted that if Canadians could bring back one piece of tech, the iPod (15 per cent) was the highest voted, with the physical keyboard-sporting BlackBerry, Nintendo 64, or Super Nintendo all following behind. In terms of age groups, Gen Z favoured the iPod (22 per cent), while Millennials chose the Nintendo 64/Super Nintendo (24 per cent). Boomers on the other hand, were most likely to pick VCR/VHS tapes (17 per cent).
Why the rise in nostalgia? Well, according to the survey, one in three Canadians say their main reason for being drawn to old tech is a preference for owning physical products — with nearly one in four (23 per cent) having bought music, movies, or games within the last year. Interestingly, Millennials (32 per cent) and Gen Z (30 per cent) were more than twice as likely to have purchased physical media within the last year.
The survey also said that 46 per cent of Canadians are considering a tech product as a holiday gift this year. These people also said that what matters most is that the recipient will use it regularly and that it reflects their interests (both at 46 per cent), that it is a good value (36 per cent), and that it lasts for years (30 per cent).
Of course, the survey notes that Boomers (24 per cent) were more than twice as likely as Gen Z (9 per cent) to say that ease of setup matters most.
Image Credit: Shutterstock

articles.title: Whoop just launched a social network | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Whoop, the maker of screen-less fitness bands, is launching a social network on Thursday that lets its members follow friends and family and share their health data.
The network, called Whoop Humans, will be rolled out in the Whoop app to members at every membership tier at no extra cost. Members can follow anyone on Whoop and choose what to share, from sleep and recovery to workouts and achievements. Followers can react and comment; members can also attach photos and commentary to their data. It’s all opt-in, CEO Will Ahmed tells us.
Whoop already has a social feature, Teams, which a little more than half its customers use, according to the company. But Teams is built around groups and leaderboards, and everyone in a group sees everyone else’s information. Humans is meant to be more intimate. Members decide who follows them and who sees what, so a trainer can track a set of clients without the clients seeing one another’s data, for example.
I found myself questioning how much a spouse wants to know about the other’s sleep score when Ahmed mentioned this particular scenario, so I asked him how else beta members used these newer social features. He said the company learned that people were more engaged when someone reported a low recovery score than a nearly perfect one, suggesting that the new feature may be particularly helpful for understanding when someone is struggling and might need attention.
Indeed, the bigger story here is where Whoop continues to be headed, which is into medical wellness. Like its most direct rival, Oura, the company is pushing faster and more aggressively into the wellness opportunity that an aging population presents.
Whoop had already added FDA-cleared ECG and atrial fibrillation detection, blood pressure insights, blood testing, and medical-record uploads. Asked if older customers are gravitating to Whoop, Ahmed said, without offering specifics, that Whoop has seen “huge growth” among people over 60 over the past 18 months. He also said his was among the first companies accepted into a Medicare program that reimburses qualifying wearables that can show they improve health outcomes, and that it now has Medicare members.
He added that he expects families to be big users of Humans. (You can imagine adult children checking in on aging parents.)
But the company’s efforts to be thought of as the “brand for personal health” raises questions, naturally, about privacy. Ahmed said members choose which metrics to share, can remove followers, and can switch on “stealth mode” to go dark for a few days without changing their settings. Activities marked sensitive aren’t shared by default, and Ahmed said health alerts and medical information aren’t shared at all. Members can also report any comment or photo that they deem disturbing, and the company said reported content is reviewed.
As for minors, Whoop’s minimum age is 13 for all members (higher in some countries), meaning customers of that age can share their data subject to consents and privacy settings. Asked whether a parent could follow a teenager’s data, he didn’t answer directly and pointed to the privacy controls.
Ahmed also said Whoop doesn’t sell member data. “Our product is not you; it’s the membership,” he said, adding that the company doesn’t license data to third parties.
He was candid about dealmaking. Asked about Oura’s announcement this week that it will pay $625 million for Counsel Health, a service offering on-demand physicians, Ahmed said he expects “more consolidation” among AI-focused, clinician-focused, and wearable companies, and that Whoop is always on the prowl. Its deep relationship with members, he said, puts it “in a position to be an acquirer.”
He was more guarded about the company’s own finances, declining to share revenue or say whether Whoop is profitable. He did say that the company now has about 1,200 employees, membership on its software platform has increased more than 70% a year for three years running, and that it expects to have nearly 4 million members by year-end.
As for an IPO (the company raised a very big round earlier this year), he said only that Whoop “will certainly IPO in the future.” He also wouldn’t comment on Oura, which shelved its own IPO of up to $2.2 billion in September citing market uncertainty.
In the meantime, Whoop is widening its reach. The company announced that its devices will be sold through Ulta stores beginning next March (around 500 locations of the beauty retailer to start, and a target to retail in more than a thousand stores eventually). Indeed, Ahmed said Whoop’s female audience has more than doubled from last year.
As for competition, in addition to Google’s new Fitbit Air band, Whoop may soon have to contend with Apple, which is reportedly developing a Whoop-style band. But Ahmed mostly shrugged off those concerns, suggesting that building a product doesn’t guarantee success. Instead, he said, Whoop’s job is to stay true to the “aspiring” people it serves.

articles.title: Tesouro Nacional tem dados de 30 mil pessoas e quatro mil chaves Pix acessados
articles.text:
O Tesouro Nacional identificou um acesso não autorizado a dados pessoais de aproximadamente 30 mil cadastros e quatro mil chaves Pix. O incidente foi descoberto em 4 de novembro e atingiu duas bases de dados do órgão, incluindo informações de usuários de serviços públicos e beneficiários de pagamentos do governo federal.
Segundo o Tesouro, não houve impacto financeiro nem comprometimento de sistemas estruturantes. Ainda assim, o órgão alerta que os dados acessados podem ser utilizados por criminosos para dar mais credibilidade a contatos fraudulentos.
Uma das bases afetadas reúne informações de usuários do portal e-Serviços, utilizado para solicitar e acompanhar serviços oferecidos pelo Tesouro. Nesse conjunto, foram acessados nomes, CPFs e endereços de e-mail de aproximadamente 30 mil cadastros.
A segunda base era utilizada para consultas analíticas internas e continha cerca de quatro mil chaves Pix de destinatários de pagamentos do governo federal. Também foram acessadas informações relacionadas a pagamentos já realizados.
Leia mais:
- Hackers exploram brecha no Outlook para capturar credenciais do Windows
- Ataques hackers na Europa acendem alerta para algo maior: a computação quântica
- Ataque hacker expõe CPFs de milhões de clientes da Caixa; veja dados vazados
Como os dados vazados podem ser usados em golpes?
- O Tesouro alerta que criminosos podem utilizar informações verdadeiras das vítimas para tornar abordagens fraudulentas mais convincentes;
- Uma pessoa mal-intencionada, por exemplo, pode mencionar dados pessoais ou informações sobre pagamentos para tentar se passar por uma instituição financeira ou órgão público;
- Por isso, a recomendação é ter atenção a mensagens e contatos suspeitos que solicitem informações pessoais, senhas ou pagamentos;
- O acesso a dados, como nome, CPF, e-mail e informações relacionadas a transações, pode facilitar tentativas de engenharia social, nas quais golpistas usam detalhes reais para conquistar a confiança das vítimas.
O que o Tesouro Nacional fez após o acesso indevido?
De acordo com o órgão, os mecanismos de segurança e o monitoramento da rede permitiram identificar e conter o acesso não autorizado.
Após a descoberta, o Tesouro reforçou o monitoramento, implementou medidas adicionais de proteção e iniciou investigação técnica para determinar a origem e a extensão do incidente.
O caso também foi comunicado à Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) e ao Centro de Prevenção, Tratamento e Resposta a Incidentes Cibernéticos de Governo (CTIR Gov).
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Google’s new Gemini model is better at understanding complicated questions
articles.text:
Google says its new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model can give more helpful answers to complex questions, including “questions with multiple parts, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests.” The new model can break down your questions and address each part in its responses. It’s available starting today in search, the Gemini app, all tiers of Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Gemini for business, and in Google Antigravity for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Robby Stein, VP of product at Google Search, says it’s “now the new default model in AI Mode & being used for your hardest questions in AI Overviews.”
Google’s new Gemini model is better at understanding complicated questions
Google’s Robby Stein says Gemini 4 Hydrogen is ‘the biggest model upgrade to Search yet.’
Google says Gemini 4 Hydrogen also gives users a wider range of links in its responses by “conducting simultaneous queries across all the relevant subtopics.” Its responses have more visuals, too, like images, comparison tables, graphs, and maps. One of Stein’s examples shows the AI generating an interactive animated driving simulation in response to a user’s question about how phones locate which lane of a highway a car is on in areas without cell service. Google says the new model also has improved language understanding “across all supported AI Mode languages.”
Users have more thinking level options with Gemini 4 Hydrogen, as well, including low, medium, high, and a new “xhigh” mode. According to Google, the new model “delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence” compared to Gemini Flash 3.8, and it “matches or outperforms some of the competing models in its class,” like Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Terra.

articles.title: CEOs drängen zum KI-Einsatz – und ernten "Work-Slop" von Mitarbeitenden
articles.text:
CEOs drängen zum KI-Einsatz – und ernten „Work-Slop“ von Mitarbeitenden
KI ist in vielen Bereichen der Arbeitswelt nicht mehr wegzudenken. Es gibt zahlreiche Unternehmen, die den Einsatz von KI explizit gefördert haben, um die Produktivität im Konzern zu erhöhen.
Doch dieser gutgemeinte Gedanke kann auch nach hinten losgehen. Unternehmen, die den Einsatz von KI zunächst gefördert haben, stellen nun Regeln gegen sogenannten „Work-Slop“ auf: also KI-generierte Nachrichten und Dokumente, die die Posteingänge überfluten.
Chefin an Mitarbeitende: „Hört bitte auf, wie Roboter mit mir zu sprechen“
Eine solche Unternehmensleiterin ist Michelle Volberg. Als CEO des auf den Tech-Sektor spezialisierten Personalvermittlungsunternehmens Twill stattete sie ihr zehnköpfiges Team mit einer Unternehmenslizenz für den KI-Chatbot Claude aus. Mittlerweile hat sie aber genug davon, dass ihre Mitarbeiter:innen roboterhaft mit ihr kommunizieren. Sie schickte eine E-Mail mit einer klaren Botschaft an ihr Team: „Hört bitte auf, wie Roboter mit mir zu sprechen.“
Volberg berichtete gegenüber Business Insider, dass die Slack-Nachrichten und E-Mails ihrer Mitarbeiter:innen plötzlich wirkten wie die Vorschläge ahnungsloser externer Berater:innen. Perfekte Zeichensetzung, fehlender Kontext zum Kunden und gelegentliche „Halluzinationen“ der KI.
KI-Slop am Arbeitsplatz kann auch kontraproduktiv sein
Wie verbreitet ist „Work-Slop“ mittlerweile? Laut einer aktuellen Umfrage des Stanford Social Media Lab und von Betterup Labs gaben 53 Prozent der befragten Büroangestellten an, bereits „Work-Slop“ verschickt zu haben. Der Anteil derjenigen, die solche Inhalte erhielten, sank zwar leicht von 40 auf 38 Prozent, doch die Betroffenen schätzten, dass sie monatlich drei bis vier Stunden damit verbringen, das zu korrigieren.
KI-Slop am Arbeitsplatz ist nicht nur nervig, sondern kann auch kontraproduktiv sein. Sobald Menschen den Eindruck gewinnen, dass sie nur noch mit KI-generiertem „Müll“ (Slop) konfrontiert werden – egal ob Kolleg:innen oder Kund:innen –, hören sie in vielen Fällen auf, weiter zuzuhören.
Für die interne Kommunikation ist die eigene Stimme gefragt
Volbergs neue Richtlinie in ihrem Unternehmen ist simpel: KI darf genutzt werden, um Ideen zu entwickeln oder auszuarbeiten – für die interne Kommunikation ist jedoch die eigene Stimme gefragt. „Wenn du es nicht auch persönlich, per E-Mail oder in Slack so sagen würdest, dann verschicke es auch nicht“, betonte sie.
Wer sich nicht an solche Vorgaben hält, kann durchaus Probleme bekommen. Medienberichten zufolge ist es bereits zu Entlassungen von Mitarbeiter:innen gekommen, die trotz einer ausdrücklichen Warnung weiterhin KI für Aufgaben einsetzten, bei denen dies untersagt war.

articles.title: Opportuniste, Elon Musk prêt à embaucher Jensen Huang, « Ce serait un honneur », dit-il !
articles.text:
Pendant que le conseil de NVIDIA délibère sur le sort de Jensen Huang, Elon Musk a jugé sur X qu'embaucher le cofondateur du géant des puces serait « un honneur ».
Sollicité par des utilisateurs sur son réseau social, Elon Musk n'a évidemment pas attendu la décision du conseil d'administration de NVIDIA pour se prononcer sur le dossier Jensen Huang. Le twittos ZeroHedge lui suggérait de recruter le PDG menacé d'éviction, et il a répondu « That would be an honor », traduisez Ce serait un honneur, juste après les révélations du Wall Street Journal sur un départ en préparation et préparé en coulisses. La réponse du milliardaire s'explique notamment par des années de liens avec le cofondateur du mastodonte des semi-conducteurs. Elle arrive aussi au moment où l'affaire d'espionnage présumé qui vise le patron de NVIDIA s'aggrave de jour en jour.
Elon Musk et Jensen Huang, des années de complicité à coups de GPU
Le message d'Elon Musk a été publié vers 2h20 cette nuit, heure de Paris. Dans la matinée, il affichait déjà plus de quatre millions de vues, alors qu'il ne s'agit que d'une réponse à une sollicitation. Le patron de Tesla et SpaceX n'a pas donné plus de précisions. Rien ne dit donc qu'il s'agit d'une vraie proposition, d'autant que NVIDIA n'a annoncé aucun départ. On pourrait même estimer qu'Elon Musk ne fait que rendre hommage au « talent » du dirigeant secoué actuellement. Rappelons toutefois que les entreprises d'Elon Musk comptent parmi les plus gros clients de NVIDIA, alors forcément, sa phrase ne passe pas inaperçue.
Ce qui est certain, c'est que les deux dirigeants s'admirent mutuellement, et depuis longtemps. Pour le premier supercalculateur Colossus, à Memphis, xAI a lancé l'entraînement de ses modèles 19 jours seulement après l'arrivée des premiers serveurs. Selon Jensen Huang, ce genre de chantier prend normalement quatre ans. Le patron de NVIDIA a même qualifié Musk de « GPU ultime », capable de garder en tête toutes les interdépendances d'un supercalculateur.
Leurs liens sont donc, par extension, financiers. NVIDIA aurait par exemple investi jusqu'à 2 milliards de dollars dans xAI, avant que SpaceX ne rachète la start-up en février. Cet été, Musk a confirmé que SpaceX miserait exclusivement sur NVIDIA, y compris pour ses futurs data centers en orbite. En mai, les deux hommes accompagnaient même Donald Trump à Pékin. Or, avant ce voyage, le président avait déjà été informé des soupçons sur Alice Huang.
Jensen Huang suspendu à la décision du conseil de NVIDIA
L'affaire a pris de l'ampleur à la fin du mois d'octobre. Ce jour-là, le New York Times a révélé que le renseignement américain soupçonnait Alice Huang de travailler pour Pékin, ce que la Chine dément. Elle a dirigé Megaspeed, une société singapourienne cliente de NVIDIA. D'après The Information, son réseau aurait aidé à faire entrer en Chine environ 7,5 milliards de dollars de puces. Le 8 novembre, Jensen Huang a reconnu avoir été infidèle, et le conseil a ouvert une enquête indépendante. De leur côté, des élus du Congrès veulent l'entendre à huis clos le 18 novembre.
Puis mercredi 11 novembre, ça s'est encore accéléré. Le New York Times, qui cite cinq anciens salariés, a révélé une seconde liaison, avec Kimberly Powell. Il s'agit cette fois de la vice-présidente chargée de la santé de NVIDIA, qui rend compte directement au PDG. Peu après, le Wall Street Journal affirmait que le conseil s'apprêtait à pousser Jensen Huang vers la sortie. Les administrateurs se sont réunis dans la soirée. Ce jeudi matin, ils n'avaient encore rien annoncé, à cinq jours des résultats trimestriels. Les statuts de l'entreprise NVIDIA permettent à une majorité simple des onze administrateurs de démettre le PDG, qui ne détient qu'environ 3,6 % du capital.
Le titre a perdu jusqu'à 9 % après la clôture de Wall Street. Si la baisse se confirme, la firme américaine aura perdu près de 600 milliards de dollars de valeur depuis l'annonce de l'enquête, d'après Reuters. Pour un éventuel intérim, on cite Colette Kress, la directrice financière, et Ian Buck, le créateur de CUDA. Si Nvidia ferme sa porte à Jensen Huang, celle d'Elon Musk reste entrouverte, du moins sur X.

articles.title: Hackers plant GSocket on Linux servers for persistent access
articles.text:
Multiple threat actors are abusing GSocket, a legitimate open-source remote access tool, to maintain access to Linux servers even after patching the vulnerabilities exploited to gain initial access.
Since March, detections of malicious GSocket activity have increased, particularly in attacks targeting web applications and hosting environments.
GSocket allows attackers to reach systems behind firewalls or NAT by intercepting network connections and replacing the program's conventional IP-layer communication with its own transport layer, which routes traffic through the Global Socket Relay Network.
Since both endpoints initiate outbound connections to the relay, which matches them and brokers an end-to-end encrypted session, an attacker can reconnect without needing the compromised server's IP address or hostname.
This makes it more difficult for defenders to disrupt attacks using IP- or domain-based access control lists.
According to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry, GSocket-related detections increased by 356.2% between March and August.
Microsoft explains that both the compromised server and the attacker connect outbound, hence the server needs no inbound listener implants, making the attack stealthier.
“The compromised host and the operator both connect outbound to the relay, which bridges the two sessions,” Microsoft explains.
“The host needs no inbound listener or public IP address, and network address translation does not prevent the connection.”
The same model also removes the need for attackers to use a dedicated command-and-control (C2) server.
Microsoft says inbound firewall rules don’t catch the malicious traffic, although egress filtering and outbound monitoring can.
Of the detected incidents, 87.1% related to web applications and hosting. PHP web apps and cPanel hosting accounted for 63.9%, and Apache accounted for 24.3%.
The researchers observed attackers disguising GSocket as kernel threads and using cron jobs, systemd services, and shell startup files for persistence purposes.
In some cases, the attackers attempted to exploit the “Dirty Frag” Linux kernel flaw (CVE-2026-43284) to gain root privileges on the host.
Microsoft says most targets of GSocket activity are in the education and research sector, followed by technology and communications, manufacturing, and government entities.
The researchers recommend that system administrators remove GSocket and associated files from potentially impacted servers, and verify that outbound connections to its relay network have stopped.
They also advise restricting outbound traffic to predetermined destinations and auditing cron jobs, systemd services, and shell startup files for rogue additions.
Generally, keeping the OS and applications up to date, including patching for CVE-2026-43284, is a strong measure against this and other attacks.

articles.title: Megaspeed, empresa clave en el escándalo de Jensen Huang, CEO de Nvidia, prometió cooperar con la investigación de Estados Unidos
articles.text:
Megaspeed, la empresa de centros de datos con sede en Singapur que ocupa el centro del escándalo que sacudió a Nvidia, prometió cooperar con la investigación del gobierno de Estados Unidos sobre potenciales riesgos para la seguridad nacional, según informó Associated Press (AP) este jueves 12 de noviembre.
La compañía emitió su primer comunicado público desde que el director ejecutivo de Nvidia, Jensen Huang, reconoció haber mantenido una relación sentimental con Alice Huang, una exejecutiva de Megaspeed a quien funcionarios de inteligencia estadounidenses identificaron como presunta agente reclutada por China.
En ese texto, Megaspeed afirmó que toma “muy en serio” su obligación de cumplir las leyes estadounidenses de control de exportaciones y que actuará “de manera constructiva y transparente” con las autoridades.
Jensen Huang renunció a la dirección ejecutiva de Nvidia y Colette Kress asumió de forma interina, según informó este jueves la compañía. El relevo se produjo tras una reunión del directorio que había quedado bajo la atención de los mercados, con las acciones de la fabricante de procesadores para inteligencia artificial bajo presión en las operaciones previas a la apertura.
Megaspeed enfrenta una investigación del Departamento de Justicia por elusión de controles de exportación
El compromiso público de la compañía llegó después de que su situación legal se agravara de forma significativa. El año pasado, Megaspeed fue objeto de escrutinio por parte del Departamento de Comercio de Estados Unidos por presuntamente eludir las leyes de exportación y desviar una gran cantidad de chips avanzados de Nvidia hacia usuarios chinos. La empresa negó esas acusaciones.
Posteriormente, esa investigación fue transferida al Departamento de Justicia, cuya División de Seguridad Nacional evalúa si Megaspeed violó esas normas, en una indagación que también abarca el escrutinio de Alice Huang, según una persona familiarizada con el caso que habló bajo condición de anonimato, de acuerdo con AP.
Los controles de exportación son regulaciones que impone el gobierno de Estados Unidos para restringir la venta o transferencia de tecnología sensible hacia determinados países o empresas. Cuando una compañía opera en sectores estratégicos como la inteligencia artificial o la infraestructura de datos y mantiene vínculos con ciudadanos o firmas de países considerados de riesgo, puede quedar sujeta a investigaciones que evalúen si se vulneraron esas normas.
El vínculo entre Jensen Huang, Alice Huang y los chips de inteligencia artificial
El caso adquirió relevancia pública cuando Huang admitió la relación con Alice Huang, quien se había desempeñado como ejecutiva en Megaspeed. La conexión entre el jefe de la mayor empresa de chips de inteligencia artificial del mundo y una compañía de centros de datos con vínculos en China despertó alarmas en Washington sobre posibles implicancias para la seguridad nacional. Según un informe de The Information citado por Reuters, esa relación habría facilitado el envío de al menos USD 7.500 millones en chips a empresas chinas.
Nvidia es el principal proveedor mundial de procesadores gráficos utilizados para entrenar sistemas de inteligencia artificial. Precisamente por eso, sus chips están sujetos a estrictos controles de exportación que limitan su venta a ciertos países, entre ellos China.
La senadora demócrata de Massachusetts Elizabeth Warren señaló en un comunicado que, según se informó, Nvidia había obtenido aprobaciones para exportar “cientos de miles de chips avanzados de IA a China, incluso a empresas vinculadas al ejército chino”, y subrayó que la relación de Huang con Alice Huang “plantea preguntas importantes que Nvidia debe responder”.
La junta directiva de Nvidia analiza el futuro de Huang sin anunciar una decisión
Según informó AP, la junta directiva de Nvidia celebró una reunión para evaluar la situación de Huang. Para conducir la revisión interna, el directorio contrató a Joon Kim, socio del estudio Wachtell Lipton y exfiscal federal interino del Distrito Sur de Nueva York, con experiencia en investigaciones internas y defensa en casos de delitos de cuello blanco, según Reuters. Hasta el cierre de esta nota, no trascendió ninguna decisión concreta sobre el futuro del ejecutivo.
La incertidumbre sobre la continuidad de Huang agrega una capa de complejidad adicional al panorama. Nvidia había señalado previamente que “no tiene motivos para creer” que se hayan comprometido la seguridad nacional o los secretos corporativos, y que Huang seguiría al mando mientras coopera con la investigación.
Mientras tanto, varios legisladores de ambos partidos aguardan su comparecencia ante el Congreso, prevista para el 18 de noviembre, según consignó Infobae con base en información de AP.

articles.title: Google lance Gemini sur Apple CarPlay
articles.text:
Après avoir introduit Gemini sur Android Auto et Android Automotive, Google lance officiellement son assistant IA sur Apple CarPlay. Les utilisateurs d’iPhone qui se servent quotidiennement du système d’Apple pourront profiter de Gemini Live directement depuis l’écran embarqué de leur véhicule pour lui donner des instructions sans pour autant quitter la route des yeux.
Gemini, nouveau copilote de CarPlay
Google explique avoir « conçu Gemini sur CarPlay pour fonctionner comme un compagnon de conduite conversationnel qui minimise les distractions ». Vous n’aurez ainsi qu’à appuyer sur l’icône de l’application pour lancer ou reprendre une conversation avec l’assistant intelligent de Google, tout en restant concentré sur la route.
Concrètement, Gemini étant connecté aux différents services Google que vous utilisez quotidiennement, vous pourrez lui demander, par exemple, de vous faire un résumé des rendez-vous à venir dans la journée renseignés dans Google Agenda. L’assistant intelligent de Google pourra également être interrogé pour rattraper les e-mails non lus dans votre boîte de réception Gmail, et pourquoi pas, pour y répondre.
Gemini pourra aussi, et surtout, être un copilote utile puisque vous pourrez lui demander des recommandations de lieux à visiter lorsque vous vous déplacez dans un nouvel endroit. Parmi les autres exemples d’utilisations de Gemini en voiture, Google suggère que vous pourriez même profiter de l’environnement calme de l’habitacle de votre voiture pour demander à l’assistant vocal de vous coacher avant une présentation importante ou une conversation difficile à venir. L’assistant vocal de Google étant synchronisé avec l’application Gemini installée sur votre iPhone, vous pourrez, après votre trajet, retrouver toutes vos notes et autres conversations avec Gemini sur votre iPhone.
Gemini dans CarPlay est disponible dès maintenant pour les utilisateurs du monde entier et dans toutes les langues prises en charge par Gemini Live. Pour en profiter, il vous faudra néanmoins mettre à jour l’application dans sa dernière version depuis l’App Store, mais aussi vous assurer d’avoir au préalable déjà autorisé l’accès au microphone par Gemini sur votre iPhone.

Les appareil de coiffage Shark SpeedStyle Trois accessoires passent sous les 100 € chez Amazon soit une baisse d'environ 26% sur le prix habituellement constaté.
Avec le SpeedStyle, l’étasunien Shark s’inscrit encore un peu plus dans la tendance des stylers. D’abord sèche-cheveux, l’appareil à la silhouette coudée est tout de même accompagné de trois ou cinq embouts pour mieux définir les mèches.

articles.title: Brian May, histórico guitarrista de Queen, compró un campo, plantó 100.000 árboles y creó una reserva natural privada
articles.text:
Brian May compró unos campos al sur de Bere Regis, un pueblo del condado inglés de Dorset, para devolvérselas a la fauna local. Hasta entonces, los campos comprados por el mítico guitarrista de Queen se dedicaban a lo mismo que muchas fincas de la zona, los cultivos y el ganado, pero ahora todo es diferente.
Un campo que antes fue bosque. El músico, que cumplió 79 años en julio de 2026, ya tenía algo de arbolado en Bere Regis cuando le sumó unas 63 hectáreas compradas en 2012, unas tierras de labor que hasta entonces se utilizaban para cultivos y ganado. Y es que el plan era recuperar algo que ya había estado ahí. Tal y como explicaba el propio May en la nota de prensa del proyecto, su plan era recuperar lo que había allí antes“esta tierra era bosque hace cientos de años y ahora quiero recuperarla en nombre de nuestra fauna”.
Para hacerlo tiró de Save Me, la organización de defensa de los animales salvajes que cofundó en 2010. Fue ella la que puso en marcha la transformación, con un día de plantación abierto a todo el pueblo.
El primer roble. Esa jornada fue el 28 de septiembre de 2013, y acudieron cientos de vecinos y los alumnos de la escuela local. May plantó el primer roble, y entre todos los asistentes plantaron unos 600 árboles, casi todos robles. Pero esto era solo el principio, porque el plan era el de plantar más de 100.000 árboles y arbustos en los doce meses siguientes. El bosque iba a llamarse Save Me Woods, homenaje a la canción “Save Me” de Queen, pero en el pueblo empezaron a llamarlo May’s Wood y el nombre acabó quedándose, significando “El bosque de May”.
La lista de especies prevista incluía robles, hayas, castaños, tilos, cerezos silvestres, nogales y diferentes arbustos, y el grueso de la plantación quedó para después del 1 de enero de 2014, una vez terminado el ciclo agrícola.
Huecos a propósito. Pero la idea nunca se limitó a llenar cada metro cuadrado de troncos. Entre las parcelas forestadas se dejaron franjas de flores silvestres, caminos abiertos y una zona de transición con pradera. Vamos, que se trataba de crear un mosaico de hábitats y no una plantación en fila, algo que May resumía diciendo que con el tiempo el bosque formaría un corredor para la fauna conectado con la pradera.
Lo que ha ido llegando. Con los años, esa mezcla ha acabado atrayendo insectos, aves y pequeños mamíferos que no estaban cuando allí se cultivaba, como recoge el balance del décimo aniversario publicado en la web oficial del músico. La fotógrafa Linda Lamon, que ha retratado el bosque desde el primer día, cuenta que con la vuelta de las flores las mariposas y las abejas estaban encantadas. Eso sí, la fauna tenía que llegar por su cuenta, ya que May nunca quiso traer animales de otras zonas, y en 2023 algunas partes del bosque seguían cerradas al público.
May planteó el proyecto con la idea de crear un entorno en el que “nuestros hijos y nietos crezcan y disfruten en armonía con los animales”. En 2023 se cumplieron 10 años del proyecto, y en este tiempo se convirtió en un bosque joven que ya llegaba a los 101.000 árboles y arbustos.

articles.title: RISC-V For AI: Breakthrough Or Bad Idea?
articles.text:
Custom instructions promise flexibility, but experts question whether RISC-V belongs at the heart of AI acceleration.
Key Takeaways:
Experts At The Table: Demand for parallelism and power efficiency is shifting chip design from general computing to AI, increasing the need for flexible, modular, and open hardware. This trend is bringing RISC-V into AI acceleration. Customizable hardware can implement AI computations directly instead of relying on fixed CPU designs. Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss these issues with Steve Roddy, chief marketing officer at Quadric; Francisca Tan, director of product management and product engineering for Tessent at Siemens EDA; Ewald Liess, senior vice president of sales and business development at SignatureIP; and Dave Kelf, CEO of Breker. What follows are excerpts of that conversation.
L-R: Quadric’s Roddy; Siemens EDA’s Tan; SignatureIP’s Liess; Breker’s Kelf.
SE: With AI models evolving rapidly, architects use RISC-V to design highly specialized extensions. From an IP provider standpoint, how would you balance delivering a standardized, reusable IP core with the extreme customization that customers are demanding for AI workloads?
Leiss: We don’t think that we need to configure because we provide NoC and PCI Express and CXL CHI AMBA interfaces. Based on this, we don’t need to customize. Instead, it’s the NoC that will be configured. Because we have a pre-verified NoC, we can do that with our tools. We can configure customized RISC-Vs. Of course, the customers may modify the RISC-V core with new instructions, but they will stick to the interfaces like the AMBA bus, or CXL, PCI Express interfaces, because this enables them to access the external components that they need, like memory or going off-chip. And this is where we come in. So the RISC-V guys should feel free to do whatever they want.
Tan: Custom verification and validation also become important, as does observability. For test and embedded analytics, engineers doing debug or silicon bring-up can monitor, introspect, and inspect internal signals, or calculate whether performance is being met. In my view, it’s also about hardware observability, as the industry moves into various challenges and complexity in the chip.
Roddy: We’ll take the contrarian view in this particular area. We think that starting with RISC-V to do an AI accelerator is a flat-out bad idea, because you instantly create a problem. You now have a partition between some things running on a programmable processor with good ALU capacity, and some external accelerator where you’ve now had to partition the system. The minute you partition, the minute you create a problem, you need fancy compilers to go fix it and figure out how to move data from the accelerator or accelerators across a nice NoC over to a programmable core, and back and forth. That’s a problem that scales badly. The bigger the accelerator, the worse it gets. And so now you’re compounding the problem. If you have something that’s, say, 100 TOPS and you have to have, say, 16 RISC-V processors slave to a whole bunch of accelerator blocks, sure, you need great interconnect, and you need great verification, and all those things that go with it because you’re trying to solve the underlying fundamental problem, which is starting with a CPU. And CPUs are great for chasing pointers. That’s what CPUs do. CPUs have wonderful logic to handle the fact that you’ve got 40 threads running, and on the very next clock tick, you have no idea what you’ll be running. That’s not what you’re doing when you’re doing AI inference. You know for millions of cycles in advance what’s happening. You don’t need most of the CPU hardware. DSPs are a little closer to what you need, but DSPs are vector machines — vector-by-scalar or vector-by-vector. And most of what is challenging in AI is matrix-by-matrix. So we built a matrix-native machine. The only other one I know of that’s close to that is in the data center, and that’s the big giant TPUs from Google. Literally, everybody else has a partitioned problem, and then they struggle and spend billions of dollars trying to handle that partitioning problem and figure out how to make up for the fact that they started from, we think, a bad place.
Kelf: I agree with Steve’s point, because what we’re seeing is large AI accelerators — which might be different architectures, SIMD, SIMT — are pretty common. These kinds of things basically are controlled, or have been controlled, by a complex state machine of some sort, and then there’ll be some kind of host processor driving several of these different things and telling the state machine what to do, and then driving the accelerator. What we’ve seen in four instances now, both big and small companies, is that the state machines are hopeless. So they’re taking a RISC-V processor, and they’re using that as the control function on top of these accelerators for a number of reasons. One is that they can, in fact, build in a bunch of mathematical engines — exactly what Steve was mentioning — vector type, using either the RISC-V vector instructions or those. And then they add in their own, as well, or some of the new matrix multiplication instructions. They’re also putting in their own instructions for very efficient load/store to reduce the latency that you see between partitions. So they’re trying to figure out how they can adjust these RISC-V processes to reduce that latency and to reduce that partitioning problem. We have a number of examples where some are successful, some are less so. They’re still working on this problem, but RISC-V is nice because they can add whatever custom instructions they want, still use a regular compiler, and create a mechanism to drive a very efficient load/store that they can’t with other processors. Then, of course, there are people like Arm and others who have built instructions into some of their processors, but they’re not variable. RISC-V is ideal for this, and pretty unique in its ability to create these powerful custom instructions.
SE: Regarding those custom vector instructions, are EDA tools accounting for this and automating the verification?
Roddy: I spent 17 years at Tensilica. We automated all that. The downside, of course, is that you pay a royalty. RISC-V is an opportunity to not pay a royalty, a tribute, a tax to the big guy. If you want customization, the folks at Tensilica automated that many years ago. The idea is to change instructions and instantly get compilers and simulators that match, with verification handled because it’s in a structured environment. RISC-V gives a bit more flexibility to go outside those bounds. My take on that is if you really want to use RISC-V, you better be going all out and customizing the hell out of it to go through the effort to manually create all that stuff, because if you want just a little bit of customization, my old friends at Tensilica have an automated system that makes that happen. Yes, it comes with a commercial cost. RISC-V is a very interesting technology, and it absolutely serves a purpose. The market leader doesn’t allow that level of flexibility for control and CPU functions. You can get a lot of value out of tweaking and tuning a processor for the control function at hand. We just don’t think it makes sense to do inference on it. But there are thousands of things that CPUs are used for, and RISC-V CPUs can do those things perhaps more flexibly and more efficiently, and certainly at a lower price point than fixed-function CPUs from other vendors. We just don’t think doing heavy lifting and inferencing is the right way to deploy that kind of technology.
Kelf: I tend to agree. Some companies are trying to build in the vectors and build their own mathematical sort of DSP-type instructions. I was talking with some customers who were having some issues. They had a SIMT array — single-instruction, multiple threads — and they were doing a ton of parallel mathematics and hoping one of the parallel lanes wasn’t going to diverge from the others. And then one does. The nice thing about SIMT is you can make it diverge. They were using the RISC-V control processor to do some of the mathematical processing from the divergence, leaving the rest of the accelerator to do the rest of the mathematical processing that’s going on. They’re not doing heavyweight processing inside the RISC-V. They’re just doing enough to keep the whole machine working and reduce that latency, but doing this odd thing inside the RISC-V. It took them a lot of work to get this working properly, but now they are seeing this as quite successful. I agree that there’s the business side of RISC-V, which is you don’t have to pay a royalty, and I agree on the Tensilica technology as well, which was fantastic for this kind of stuff, especially DSP communications. But they can do similar things inside RISC-V. They have to build it themselves. They have to know how to do that. But once they do, there’s a lot of flexibility, a lot of standardization around RISC-V. They can get a compiler. They can potentially shift to a different company and build some of their proprietary stuff into that RISC-V. That does allow for more flexibility, but more standardization, as well, which you may not get out of a fixed processor and a proprietary processor.
Tan: In terms of what testing and better analytics provide for custom instructions, especially from the RISC-V arena, we support debuggability for custom-instruction tracing. We support RISC-V users specifying which custom instructions they want to trace while the processor is running, to support that debuggability environment. We are also one of the members of the RISC-V organization, whereby we donated a few years back the Efficient Trace (E-Trace) specification. That is a highly compressed instruction trace catering to complex systems where there’s going to be a lot of data, and therefore we need to think about compressing all this data as well. Within our infrastructure, it’s not just about the processor. It’s about the entire system. So our infrastructure can capture instruction traces from the RISC-V core, as well as from various parts of the RISC-V SoC, such as the interconnect, bus monitoring, or specific signals we want to monitor.
Leiss: We’ve talked a lot about verifying the custom instruction set, passing the ISA-level verification, and most of the time, maybe generated IP comes with verification collateral like test benches, traffic generators, and performance models. But I look at it from a system point of view, and it means that there are typically multiple cores in one high-performance system, and when you have an accelerator in RISC-V five, or you have several RISC-V in one, then you immediately end up with a coherency problem because you use caches and so on. The coherency corner cases and traffic bursts can easily cause deadlocks in the fabric. It is therefore important that, from the NoC side, we do all this verification at the system level to check how the traffic can flow through and make sure that you don’t end up in a deadlock situation. In simple terms, an instruction can execute correctly, but the chip can still fail if the data burst needed for the instruction or the calculation isn’t available. That’s an area we’re addressing.
Leave a Reply

articles.title: Après Mass Effect, The Expanse: Osiris Reborn pourrait bien prendre la relève du RPG spatial
articles.text:
Il y a des univers de science-fiction qui semblent taillés pour se décliner sous différentes formes : romans, séries, films et jeux vidéo. C’est notamment le cas de The Expanse. Née sous la plume de James S. A. Corey, la saga littéraire a ensuite connu une adaptation en série télévisée, devenue une référence pour les amateurs de science-fiction. Et voilà désormais qu’elle s’apprête à investir de nouveau le jeu vidéo avec The Expanse: Osiris Reborn.
Après The Expanse: A Telltale Series, qui n’a pas vraiment convaincu, l’univers de The Expanse revient sous un projet ambitieux qui pourrait bien combler le vide laissé par une certaine trilogie Mass Effect.
Développé par Owlcat Games, le studio derrière les RPG Pathfinder et Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader, The Expanse: Osiris Reborn a profité des Golden Joystick Awards, le 11 novembre 2026, pour dévoiler une nouvelle vidéo de gameplay. Baptisée « Becoming a Captain », ce trailer donne un aperçu plus concret de ce que nous réserve le jeu.
Séquences d’exploration et de dialogue avec des PNJ, conséquences des décisions, fusillades et affrontements en apesanteur dans des environnements sans gravité, compagnons aux diverses facultés, The Expanse: Osiris Reborn semble de plus en plus toquer à la porte de Mass Effect.
Si Exodus nous avait semblé être le successeur parfait de la trilogie de Bioware, le jeu d’Owlcat Games pourrait bien s’imposer comme un nouveau poids lourd du space opera. Il dispose en tout cas d’un atout de taille : un univers vaste et complexe, déjà solidement établi par une riche saga littéraire.
The Expanse: Osiris Reborn peut compter dans le space opéra
The Expanse compte déjà plusieurs romans, une série télévisée de six saisons et un monde particulièrement dense. Dans cet univers, l’humanité a colonisé le système solaire, mais cette expansion n’a rien d’une utopie. La Terre, Mars et les habitants de la Ceinture d’astéroïdes entretiennent des rapports de force permanents, sur fond de tensions politiques, de luttes économiques et de méfiance entre les différentes populations.
C’est cette dimension qui rend la licence intéressante pour un RPG. Tout comme Mass Effect, ici, l’espace n’est pas simplement un décor, mais un environnement habité, avec ses conflits, ses inégalités et ses personnages aux intérêts parfois contradictoires. Si le jeu exploite cette composante, c’est un terrain idéal pour raconter une histoire dans laquelle les décisions peuvent avoir un véritable poids.
En tout cas, au vu de ces nouvelles images, Owlcat Games semble avoir compris ce qui fait la force de la licence. Reste à voir jusqu’où cette ambition ira, et si le scénario saura proposer des personnages aussi mémorables que ceux de BioWare.
Sur le papier, les ingrédients sont là. The Expanse: Osiris Reborn est attendu au printemps 2027 sur PC, PS5 et Xbox Series X|S.

articles.title: Qvyon launches with $8M to improve safety for physical AI deployments - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Qvyon launches with $8M to improve safety for physical AI deployments
Physical AI validation infrastructure and software development company Qvyon Technologies Inc. launched today with $8 million in total funding to help companies validate autonomous vehicles and robots before deployment.
MaC Venture Capital led the funding, with participation from BDC Capital, BKR Capital and Spotlight VP.
Physical AI is artificial intelligence that moves from digital brains to the real world, allowing smart machines to perceive, reason about and act within physical environments. This can include factory floors, retail shopping aisles, the kitchen or the roadway.
Before companies can deploy smart machines, such as robots or self-driving cars, into the real world, they must understand how these systems will operate under both normal and abnormal conditions. Reproducing strange, unlikely and dangerous conditions in the field is difficult and risky. For example, a car might suddenly pull in front of a truck during a rainstorm or a sensor array on a robot might become blocked or damaged while working on a production line.
To address these examples, Qvyon released Mimic Core, a platform that takes real-world sensor recordings into simulated environments to produce varied test scenarios, allowing developers and engineers to access data and test physical AI models and robotics setups in virtual environments without repeatedly collecting field data.
A single recording can allow an engineer to create many test variations to tease out where systems make mistakes. This allows development teams to catch problems before putting robots to work in the real world.
“We spent years building AI for vehicles and saw how hard it was to prove those systems were ready for the road,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Frantz Saintellemy. “Companies need to test what happens in their own vehicles and factories by using their own recordings.”
Qvyon’s system ingests camera, lidar and radar data. It uses this to reconstruct environments in 3D and time-sequence snapshots, capturing scenes and how they change over time. It uses this to generate challenging conditions to test AI models against the hardware they will drive in simulation. The platform produces traceable datasets and validation evidence that engineers can use to evaluate smart machines’ performance before deployment.
Mimic Core works alongside the same virtual testing tools that companies already use and helps them better understand the scenarios and conditions robots and smart machines will face.
The company offers the product as software-as-a-service and as a self-hosted solution for companies that want to keep everything in-house. Qvyon stressed that when using its cloud product, customer data is kept separate and is never used to train AI models for other customers.
Mimic Core is available today via Qvyon Cloud with a 14-day guided evaluation, or for companies to run on their own systems.
The company said the funding will support Mimic Core and its rollout through the United States, Europe and Japan. Qvyon is also developing Mimic Validation OS, planned for the first half of 2027, to help companies measure and document test results, and Mimic Learn, planned for late 2027, to help improve AI using information from machines already in operation.

articles.title: Beyond the first transaction: Building inclusive digital payments for Bharat
articles.text:
Beyond the first transaction: Building inclusive digital payments for Bharat
At TechSparks 2026, Sagar Kumar of PayU discussed how payment systems can improve accessibility, build user trust, and bring more consumers and small businesses into the digital economy.
For digital payments to work for Bharat, getting someone to make their first transaction is only the beginning. The bigger challenge is making sure they feel confident enough to return, whether they are shopping online in their preferred language, making a payment independently, or running a small business.
At TechSparks 2026, Sagar Kumar, Vice President of Engineering at PayU, joined Shivani Muthanna, Senior Director – Strategic Content & Video at YourStory, for a fireside chat on the engineering behind inclusive digital payments.
Balancing speed with reliability
Having worked at early-stage startups and on systems handling millions of transactions, Kumar explained how engineering priorities change as businesses scale.
In the early stages, startup teams focus on speed, launching products quickly and learning as they go. But architecture remains important. Loosely coupled systems make it easier to add new business verticals without rebuilding everything from scratch.
At scale, speed is still important, but there is less room for error. Feature flags, incremental rollouts and A/B testing allow teams to introduce changes gradually, test them with specific customer groups and limit the impact of potential problems.
“Speed is the constant. It's just that the room for error will be smaller when you grow to a larger scale ecosystem, and in that process, you have to build enough safety nets,” he said.
Building for the next 100 payments
With UPI now familiar to many users in smaller cities and towns, Kumar believes the next step is to make online payments as intuitive as offline transactions.
PayU’s checkout pages default to a scan-and-pay option, offering an experience similar to what customers are used to at physical stores. The company has also launched Checkout for Bharat, which allows users to view checkout pages in multiple languages, making it easier for those who are less comfortable with English to complete payments.
But a simpler interface is only part of the solution.
For a first-time online shopper, seeing money debited from their account followed by a payment failure message can quickly undermine confidence. Kumar explained that payment systems need safeguards such as idempotency checks, which ensure that repeating the same request does not change the outcome after the first successful attempt.
These checks help prevent duplicate debits. Clear communication about failed transactions and automatic reversals are also important so customers do not have to initiate refund requests themselves.
“The next level of inclusivity, in my opinion, is not to bring a first-time user online to make payments, but to gain the confidence so that he makes another 100 payments. We engineer our systems to achieve that kind of a goal,” Kumar said.
Making accessibility part of engineering
In August, PayU launched an RBI-compliant checkout page designed to help blind and visually impaired users make payments independently.
The features include screen-reader voiceovers that identify important information such as payment amounts, merchant details, and transaction status. The company also made changes to button sizes, text layouts, and other visual elements.
PayU tested the checkout experience with blind and visually impaired users, who were able to complete payments independently rather than rely on someone else.
The company has also made accessibility part of its software development lifecycle, treating it as a consideration alongside functionality and performance when developing new features.
Kumar pointed out that these improvements can benefit other users too. High-contrast displays, for example, make it easier for delivery partners to view payment pages in bright sunlight. Clearly labelled interface elements can also help AI agents navigate checkout pages.
Keeping transactions running at scale
PayU processes close to 20 million transactions on an average day. At that volume, even a 0.1% failure rate could mean 20,000 unsuccessful payments.
Kumar explained that the challenge of operating at this scale comes from the number of systems involved. A single transaction can depend on merchants, issuing and acquiring banks, payment networks, aggregators, and multiple gateways. A slowdown or disruption in any one of these systems can affect the payment.
PayU uses intelligent routing to manage this complexity. Its systems monitor gateway success rates across several parameters, while machine-learning (ML) models help determine the best route for each transaction.
The algorithms also send a portion of transaction traffic through alternative routes to test their performance. This gives the system a real-time view of how different gateways are functioning.
If a gateway's performance deteriorates, transactions can be redirected to another option. Kumar said PayU has patented this routing algorithm.
The aim is to manage these complexities in the background so merchants and customers can complete transactions without having to deal with them.
Turning payments into business opportunities
Kumar also discussed how payment data can create opportunities beyond transactions.
UPI payments generate transaction histories that can help businesses understand customer payment behavior and support financial underwriting for specific credit needs.
PayU’s LazyPay addresses buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) use cases, while its merchant lending product helps small and medium businesses manage cash-flow requirements, including purchasing goods at more favourable prices. Repayments can be collected through daily settlements.
The company has also launched Agent HQ, which helps small businesses automate operational tasks such as following up with customers who abandon their websites, reconciling payments and initiating refunds.
By reducing the time founders spend on these activities, such tools can allow them to focus on growing their businesses.
For Kumar, the benefits extend beyond individual merchants. As small businesses grow, the wider digital payments ecosystem stands to gain too.

articles.title: Starlink dévoile le Mini 2, une antenne satellite avec batterie pour accéder à Internet partout
articles.text:
Starlink a dévoilé le Mini 2, une antenne satellite « conçue pour l’aventure ». La principale nouveauté par rapport à son prédécesseur ? Une batterie amovible qui offrirait 4 h 30 d’Internet par satellite, sans être branché sur une prise secteur donc. Attention toutefois, son prix pourrait en refroidir certains.
L’antenne satellite Mini 2 intègre une batterie amovible
Starlink vient de dévoiler le Mini 2, soit la deuxième génération de son antenne satellite portable. L’appareil, certifié IP67 (résistant à l’eau et à la poussière), affiche un poids d’environ 1,6 kg et une épaisseur de 23,1 mm (contre 38,5 mm pour le Mini de première génération).
Mais c’est surtout au niveau de son alimentation qu’une nouveauté survient. En effet, le Mini 2 intègre une batterie amovible, fournie dans la boîte, qui promet jusqu’à 4 h 30 d’Internet par satellite sans être branché sur une prise secteur. Ainsi, en achetant une seconde batterie amovible, l’utilisateur pourrait théoriquement profiter de 9 heures d’autonomie. Bien entendu, il est aussi possible d’alimenter l’appareil en le branchant à une source d’alimentation USB-C compatible de 60 W.
À noter que l’appareil intègre le Wi-Fi 6 et qu’il peut couvrir une surface allant jusqu’à 167 m². Starlink assure que « tout ce dont vous avez besoin est une vue dégagée du ciel pour vous connecter en ligne en 60 secondes ».
Quand le Mini 2 sera-t-il disponible en France ?
Pour l’instant, les précommandes du Mini 2 sont ouvertes seulement aux États-Unis, sur invitation. Son prix ? 999 dollars. Il faut toutefois préciser que ce tarif comprend l’antenne Starlink Mini 2, une batterie amovible, les accessoires d’alimentation, mais aussi 12 mois d’abonnement Starlink Roam Unlimited, qui permet de profiter d’une connexion à l’étranger pendant 30 jours consécutifs maximum, hors déplacements au sein d’une même zone régionale.
En France, nous ne disposons pas encore de date de lancement. Le site officiel de Starlink affiche pour l’instant seulement un bouton qui permet d’être prévenu lorsque les précommandes seront ouvertes. Patience donc si le produit vous intéresse.
