articles.title: NVIDIA CEO and Co-Founder Jensen Huang Resigns, Effective Immediately
articles.text:
We pulled today’s planned review because, well, there is huge news in the world of technology. Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of NVIDIA, marking the end of an era.
In a brief press release published by NVIDIA a bit before 6:00am PT, the company announced that Jensen Huang, the co-founder and CEO of NVIDIA, has resigned from the company effective immediately. He will be replaced on an interim basis by Colette Kress, NVIDIA’s current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, while the company undertakes a search for a permanent CEO.
Jensen Huang’s Resignation
Officially, NVIDIA and its board have not commented on why Huang is resigning. However, the NVIDIA leader and his reputation have been very publicly impaired in recent weeks by the allegations of multiple extramarital affairs with significant geopolitical considerations. The first of which involved a Chinese citizen, and attracted the attention of the US government due to concerns over Huang being the target of a foreign intelligence effort. That affair was confirmed by Huang and the company on Sunday, when Huang sent out an email to the company apologizing for his actions.
The events behind that letter had already spurred NVIDIA’s Board of Directors to initiate an independent investigation, with the company hiring Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz and former acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New York Joon H. Kim to lead the investigation.
More recently, yesterday the New York Times reported on a second affair. This one involved an NVIDIA employee, Kimberly Powell, who is NVIDIA’s Vice President of Health Care. Following that news story, media reports indicated that NVIDIA’s Board of Directors held a same-day meeting to discuss the fate of Huang and the company.
But whatever the underpinning reasons, the situation has escalated to the point where Huang is resigning from NVIDIA, effective immediately. And with it, NVIDIA’s Board is taking a number of steps to ensure the continuity and stability of the company.
For the time being, NVIDIA’s CFO Colette Kress will be stepping up to lead the company on an interim basis. Kress has been a steady hand at NVIDIA for over a decade, though with a primary focus on financial matters for the rapidly growing company. NVIDIA is due to report its Q3’2027 earnings next week on Tuesday, November 17th, a call that Kress will now lead.
Meanwhile, the NVIDIA Board is initiating a search for a permanent CEO to replace Huang. With Huang having no clearly-defined successor within NVIDIA, the Board has stated that they will be looking at candidates from both inside and outside of the company.
Huang’s resignation has also triggered the Board to appoint a chairperson for the first time in its history. Harvey C. Jones, a Managing Partner at Square Wave Ventures and formerly the CEO of Synopsys, will serve as the Chair of the Board.
Replacing a Singular Leader
Jensen Huang’s resignation leaves NVIDIA in the position of trying to replace a CEO who has been a singular leader for NVIDIA since its inception. As one of NVIDIA’s co-founders (and the only still involved in the business), Huang has been with the company since its beginning and been at the center of defining the company’s vision. Huang well-known for his hands-on management style, which saw him operate with over 60 direct reports and a very centralized management structure with him at the top. This has allowed Huang to take the company in the direction he wants to go – and make risky bets on things like CUDA and automotive – but it means that his unplanned resignation leaves a large hole in NVIDIA’s managerial structure.
Looking to ensure the stability of the company, the NVIDIA Board has already stated that it has “full confidence in Colette and the leadership team,” and that they “expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.” Meanwhile in her first comment as NVIDIA’s CEO, Peters has stated that under her watch, NVIDIA “will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader.”
And whatever the circumstances are behind Huang’s resignation, publicly the company is parting with Huang on friendly terms. The announcement from the company included a brief comment thanking Jensen “for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.”
With that said, it is difficult to imagine who will – or even could – take the reins from Jensen to serve as the company’s new leader. While Patrick is out on assignment this week, I pinged him for his thoughts on the matter, which he summed up rather succinctly: “Jensen is a singular leader in the industry who made a big bet on, and then inspired the industry to develop the current advancements in AI. These will not be easy shoes for NVIDIA to fill.”
Similarly, I have covered NVIDIA’s wares for 21 years and periodically met with Huang for almost as long. NVIDIA has always been Jensen’s company, for both the good and the bad that come with a having a strong-but-demanding leader at the top. A Steve Jobs comparison might be apt here, but even as a co-founder himself, Jobs was never quite so heavily integrated into Apple like Huang is at NVIDIA. Though both were visionaries for their respective industries, which means that recent events have not just cost NVIDIA their leader, but the AI and graphics industries are similarly losing one of their biggest driving forces.
Final Words
The sheer speed of the events surrounding Jensen Huang’s resignation mean that even with today’s announcement, a lot of questions remain. More than just who will replace Huang as the permanent CEO, what kind of changes will they enact at NVIDIA as they eventually make their own mark on the company? Will Huang’s departure eventually bring about a change to NVIDIA’s dual focus on hardware and software, which has come in large part due to having a both a business-savvy and highly-capable engineer at the top? And how will this impact the AI industry, which NVIDIA’s modern fortune is built from, and which NVIDIA is currently the de facto leader of?
Answers will undoubtedly be slower to arrive than the turmoil that surrounds Huang’s departure. But as the company’s investigations move forward and the Board winnows down the field to find a new CEO, those answers will arrive. Replacing Jensen Huang will be an incredibly difficult task, but in the wide field of talent in Silicon Valley, there is someone out there who will be up to the challenge.
What a POS
I’m bit sad, will never see him and “his iconic jacket’ while proudly presenting NVidia products in any Conference and Trade Fair.
Last time in Taiwan he’s tell audience new plan for NVidia HQ in Taiwan. Unfortunately he’s never there anymore in the opening, if ever
I hope he’s well and keep pursuit in technology advancement like NVidia.

articles.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
articles.text:
A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
- Date:
- November 7, 2026
- Source:
- University of Regensburg
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.
- Share:
Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.
But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.
The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.
Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds
Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.
However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.
At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.
Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.
To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.
Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.
Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling
To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.
In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.
The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.
Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."
This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.
What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.
This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.
"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.
A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay
To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."
Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.
At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.
For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."
The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.
The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.
A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time
Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."
In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.
To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.
This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.
Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.
The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.
Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?
Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.
One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.
Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.
Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.
"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.
The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.
"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.
That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.
For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Regensburg. Original written by Karoline Stürmer. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- S. Maier, R. Spachtholz, K. Glöckl, C. M. Bustamante, S. Lingl, M. Maczejka, J. Schön, A. Riedel, K. Richter, F. J. Giessibl, F. P. Bonafé, M. A. Huber, A. Rubio, J. Repp, R. Huber. Tracking electrons at the space-time limit. Nature Photonics, 2026; 20 (8): 961 DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-01932-0

articles.title: Hackers Deploy Malware in Fresh ScreenConnect Campaign
articles.text:
A threat actor has compromised hundreds of endpoints across dozens of ConnectWise ScreenConnect customers in a fresh campaign, cybersecurity outfit Huntress reports.
The attacks were observed on November 11, when the hackers abused their unauthorized access to cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to run commands on managed endpoints.
According to Huntress, the campaign compromised at least 6 MSPs and 288 hosts across 48 organizations. The attackers hit all 288 compromised hosts within 90 minutes.
The attackers’ commands deployed rogue ScreenConnect clients and a malware toolkit called SCKit that provides persistent backdoor access, intercepts session cookies, and can self-replicate.
Initially deployed via ScreenConnect panels, it waits for a technician to connect to the compromised endpoint to infect their workstation. Next, attempts to compromise other sessions the technician has access to and spread itself to other panels.
“However, not all functionality has been observed during observed incidents; some functionality has been discovered through analyzing the payloads,” Huntress says.
As part of the attacks, the hackers exploited a vulnerability in RMM+, a third-party extension for managing ScreenConnect sessions that uses a shared access key to bypass ScreenConnect’s authentication mechanism.
The hackers likely exploited a bug in the extension’s versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, where the access key defaults to blank if not configured, thus allowing an attacker to bypass authentication with an empty value.
“Our analysis suggests that most RMM+ installations we encountered were legitimate, usually added for a project and left in place. But versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 contained a serious authentication flaw: if an administrator had never configured the extension’s access key, RMM+ would accept a blank one,” Huntress says.
The cybersecurity firm says its investigation determined that commands reached endpoints within minutes. However, there was no corresponding login activity, and the reviewed logs were linked to RMM+ instead.
In response, ConnectWise disabled five extensions from the RMM+ family across approximately 400 ScreenConnect environments, including Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+, RMM Plus Password Link, and RMM+ Password Link.
“Their presence alone does not establish compromise. These extensions provide an API capable of executing remote commands. Access to that API is protected by a passphrase configured by the partner during setup,” ConnectWise notes.
Both Huntress and ConnectWise have released indicators of compromise (IoCs) associated with the campaign and recommend that organizations disable the extensions in their on-premises ScreenConnect deployments.

articles.text:
Avec l’augmentation incessante du prix des composants pour PC, le Black Friday est une excellente occasion pour faire de bonnes affaires. C’est justement ce que fait Boulanger en retirant plus de 250 euros au prix de l’Asus Zenbook S 14 (UX5406SA-QJ722W). Pour moins de 1 050 euros, vous aurez ainsi une machine polyvalente, que ce soit pour du multitâche ou pour des activités créatives grâce à l’Intel Core Ultra 7 256V et aux 16 Go de RAM.
Les atouts de l’Asus Zenbook UX5406SA-QJ722W :
- L’Intel Core Ultra 7 et 16 Go de RAM
- Un écran OLED confortable de 14 pouces
- Une autonomie annoncée à 27 heures
Habituellement vendu pour 1 303,97 euros, l’Asus Zenbook UX5406SA-QJ722W chute à 1 049,99 euros grâce à cette offre de Boulanger.

L’Asus Zenbook S 14 vise d’abord les professionnels et les étudiants. À l’intérieur, Asus associe un Intel Core Ultra 7 256V à 16 Go de RAM, une configuration solide pour un ultraportable de ce prix. La retouche photo et le montage vidéo sont aussi possibles.
Pour ranger vos fichiers, ce PC portable possède un SSD de 512 Go. Si c’est insuffisant, les deux ports USB-C compatibles Thunderbolt et le port USB-A vous permettront de connecter un disque dur externe.
Ce PC portable dispose aussi d’un écran OLED de 14 pouces en 1 920 x 1 200 pixels, rafraîchi à 60 Hz. Sa luminosité de 400 nits (500 nits en pic HDR) suffit pour travailler dans un bureau tandis que l’OLED permet de regarder des films et des séries en profitant de noirs plus profonds.

articles.title: Microsoft Research Focus – Edition #98 - Microsoft Research
articles.text:
What’s new in research?
In this edition of Microsoft Research Focus, based on the Research Focus newsletter (opens in new tab), host Anson Ho shares some of the latest news and cutting-edge research from across Microsoft—from bringing AI-powered universal translation closer to reality and solving a 31-year-old mathematical challenge to making AI coding agents faster and more efficient.
Catch up on the ideas, tools, and discoveries researchers are exploring today and get a quick look at what’s coming next.
Chapters
0:35: Internship: Growing expertise, building community (opens in new tab)
1:28: Breaking the language barrier with AI (opens in new tab)
2:10: Solving a 31-year-old mathematics challenge (opens in new tab)
2:56: Making AI coding agents more efficient (opens in new tab)
3:57: Improving AI tokenization across 104 languages (opens in new tab)
Subscribe to the Microsoft Research Podcast:
Transcript
[MUSIC]
This is Microsoft Research Focus, your quick look at news and cutting-edge research from across Microsoft.
I’m Anson Ho, and these are some of the latest advances we’re tracking.
Coming up in this edition: how AI is bringing the possibility of a universal translator closer to reality; a breakthrough that solves a 31-year-old mathematical challenge; a new approach to make AI coding agents faster and more efficient; and more.
Here’s what’s new.
[MUSIC FADES]
Internship: Growing expertise, building community
At the Microsoft Research lab in Tokyo, research intern Lilika Makabe found opportunities to grow her expertise while helping to shape a new research community.
Makabe joined the lab with a background in computer vision and worked alongside researchers exploring robotics and physical intelligence, AI systems that can interpret information and act in the physical world.
Her experience highlights how research internships can offer more than technical training. Through hands-on experimentation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and everyday conversations with colleagues from different backgrounds, Makabe expanded her research perspective while contributing to the lab’s growing community.
You can read about her experience on the Microsoft Research blog.
[TRANSITION MUSIC]
Breaking the language barrier with AI
For decades, science fiction has imagined a world where language barriers no longer stand in the way of communication.
For example, in 1967, Star Trek introduced the fictional Universal Translator. Now, advances in AI are bringing that possibility closer to reality.
In a new conversation, Microsoft Applied Science Manager Jinyu Li explores how AI is advancing the prospect of communication across languages, the progress researchers have made, and the challenges that remain.
To learn more, catch the full episode of the podcast Our Digital Life, available to listen or watch on YouTube and podcast platforms.
[TRANSITION MUSIC]
Solving a 31-year-old mathematics challenge
For the last 31 years, the KLS conjecture has been one of the central open problems in high-dimensional geometry. But not anymore.
New research has resolved the conjecture. This removes a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing.
The breakthrough establishes a universal principle for log-concave distributions: simple flat cuts can identify their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. The results have been independently validated, and the proof has also been formally verified using computer-assisted methods.
Learn more about this breakthrough on the Microsoft Research blog.
[TRANSITION MUSIC]
Making AI coding agents more efficient
Coding agents can help when writing and modifying code, but long sessions can max out the amount of information an AI model can process at once. As a result, coding agents will summarize earlier interactions in a resource-intensive process known as context compaction.
A new study looked at 13.5 million coding sessions and found fewer than 8% required context compaction. Yet those sessions accounted for 44% of total AI processing costs.
To address this challenge, researchers developed COMPACTIONBENCH.
COMPACTIONBENCH is a benchmark for evaluating context compaction during long-running coding tasks. They also introduced APEC, a method that prepares summaries in the background instead of interrupting an agent’s work.
In evaluations, APEC improved coding performance while reducing costs by up to 25.4% and execution time by 9.6%.
[TRANSITION MUSIC]
Improving AI tokenization across 104 languages
Before AI models can process text, they break it into smaller units called tokens. How that text is divided can affect both efficiency and performance, especially across different languages.
Most tokenizers are designed to compress text as efficiently as possible. But a new study suggests that compression alone isn’t enough.
Researchers introduced the Latent Core Tokenizer, or LCT, which identifies reusable components of words before building a shared vocabulary across languages.
In evaluations spanning 104 languages, LCT produced more linguistically meaningful tokens than leading alternatives while maintaining comparable efficiency across languages. It also improved model performance across four multilingual benchmarks.
The findings suggest that better tokenization depends not just on how much text can be compressed, but on how well the underlying structure of language is preserved.
[MUSIC]
And that’s your Microsoft Research Focus.
From the research culture and the collaborations driving discovery to producing more linguistically meaningful tokens, these are just a few of the developments researchers are exploring across Microsoft.
Want to learn more and stay connected? Explore the latest research, discover the people behind it, and keep tabs on the ideas shaping what’s next by visiting aka.ms/MicrosoftResearch (opens in new tab) and follow Microsoft Research on all major social platforms.
I’m Anson Ho, and thanks for tuning in.
We’ll see you at the next Microsoft Research Focus.
[MUSIC FADES]

articles.title: Pour contrer la Citroën ë-C3, Dacia préparerait un tout nouveau SUV électrique à moins de 20 000 €
articles.text:
Dacia vient de renouveler la vieillissante Spring. Un bon début, même si la marque roumaine reste pour l’instant bloquée à un seul et unique véhicule électrique dans sa gamme. Pour réduire à l’avenir ses émissions de CO₂, cela ne suffira clairement pas. Si une Sandero à batterie est bel et bien dans les cartons, un autre invité surprise pourrait se joindre à la fête. Il s’agit d’un crossover qui n’était initialement pas prévu pour Europe…
Présenté en mars dernier, le Renault Bridger est un parfait inconnu puisqu’il ne s’agit qu’à l’heure actuelle d’un concept. Mais cette jolie étude de style sera promise à un bel avenir en arrivant dès 2027 sur les marchés émergents. Elle prendra alors la forme d’un petit crossover dépassant tout juste les 4 mètres de long, et qui sera décliné en versions essence, hybride et électrique. Ce véhicule inédit se placera ainsi sous le Renault Duster.
Objectif CO2 : pourquoi Dacia veut importer ce modèle en Europe
S’il n’était pas censé arriver chez nous, le Bridger pourrait voir sa feuille de route complètement bouleversée en raison du contexte actuel. Vu que Dacia doit rapidement électrifier sa gamme à moindre coût, adapter le Bridger au marché européen est une occasion rêvée pour atteindre les objectifs CO₂ imposés par l’Union européenne. Possible ainsi que le véhicule ait une carrière bien plus importante que prévu, portée par des horizons repoussés.
Parachuter le Bridger en Europe permettrait alors à Dacia de concurrencer frontalement les citadines électriques accessibles de Stellantis que sont les Citroën ë-C3 et Fiat Grande Panda. Ces deux véhicules ont d’ailleurs opté pour une stratégie similaire, à savoir un développement initialement pensé pour les pays émergents avant une arrivée sur le marché européen. Le Bridger se positionnerait ainsi entre la Spring et la future Sandero électrique.
4 nouvelles voitures électriques : la feuille de route de la marque roumaine
Dacia avait d’ailleurs confirmé lancer quatre modèles électriques d’ici 2030, la Spring étant la première sur la liste. Les Sandero et Sandero Stepway se placent aussi en quasi-certitudes. Le dernier membre de la vague demeure en revanche purement hypothétique. Un remplaçant du Jogger semble peu probable, au même titre qu’une déclinaison électrique du Striker. Tous les regards sont donc tournés vers le Bridger, même si le Hipster est aussi un bon candidat.
François Provost, le PDG du groupe Renault, avait d’ailleurs lâché un gros indice au Mondial de l’Automobile de Paris en affirmant que le Bridger a été « créé pour l’Inde, mais qu’il pourrait un jour arriver sur nos marchés également ». S’il est confirmé, le SUV pourrait débuter sous les 20 000 € et offrir entre 200 et 300 km d’autonomie. Son style cubique devrait être fidèle à celui du concept et Dacia ne devrait pas y apporter de trop grosses modifications.
