articles.title: Qi2 25 W et câble intégré font de la Ugreen MagFlow Pro une alliée redoutable pour iPhone et Android
articles.text:
| Capacité nominale annoncée | 10000 mAh | 
| Capacité réelle annoncée | 10000 mAh | 
| Puissance maximale de charge | 45 W | 
| Connectique | 2 x USB-C, 0 x USB-A | 
| Câble intégré | Oui | 
| Charge sans-fil | Oui | 
| Poids | 220 g | 
| Dimensions | 71 x 16 x 108 mm | 
Complétant une gamme MagFlow aux nombreuses batteries externes, l’Ugreen MagFlow Pro mêle charge filaire et charge sans-fil Qi2 à 25 W. Son twist supplémentaire est un système de refroidissement liquide au fonctionnement visible depuis la surface de l’appareil.
Spécialiste de ce type de périphériques, Ugreen propose un très vaste catalogue de batteries externes. Le fabricant chinois cède, comme ses concurrents, aux sirènes des modèles cumulant charge filaire et sans-fil, en y ajoutant un système de refroidissement liquide inédit dans l’univers des powerbanks, et tout droit venu de l’univers des smartphones et ordinateurs.
Voici donc la promesse de la MagFlow Pro, modèle annonçant une capacité de 10 000 mAh. Entre sa double casquette filaire (avec câble intégré), sa charge Qi2 et son refroidissement, l’appareil ne se classe pas parmi les plus abordables du marché. Lancée à 130 €, elle apparaît fréquemment à un peu moins de 110 €.
Ugreen propose une MagFlow Pro d’apparence assez classique. Sa batterie mesure en effet 10,8 x 7,1 x 1,6 cm, soit un format assez similaire à celui des modèles concurrents. Elle occupe ainsi quelque 123 cm³, un peu moins que la Magnetic Power Bank 10000 de Xiaomi (133 cm³). Son poids reste contenu à 220 g, soit l’équivalent d’un smartphone, ce qui permet de l’emporter assez facilement avec soi. Le modèle de Xiaomi évoqué ici pèse 229 g, donc dans la moyenne.
Cet aspect nomade est renforcé par l’intégration d’un câble USB-C faisant au besoin office de dragonne, à côté du bouton d’allumage. Plutôt pratique pour repêcher l’appareil au fond d'un sac. L’appareil joue en revanche la carte de l’économie sur le plan des connecteurs supplémentaires : vous avez droit à un unique port USB-C, et c'est tout…
Si la finition en plastique gris retenue par Ugreen n’a rien de follement original, la marque opte au dos pour un revêtement en silicone doux. Ce matériau signale la zone magnétique de la batterie et évite de rayer le smartphone auquel on la fixe. En revanche, il attire à lui toutes les fibres et poussières qui passent à sa portée.
Pour séduire davantage encore, Ugreen mise tout sur des afficheurs. Le premier est un tout petit écran LCD situé sur le flanc droit du dispositif. Dédié aux informations de charge (puissance délivrée, pourcentage de batterie restant), dommage qu’il soit si riquiqui. Il faut des yeux de lynx pour le décrypter.
Le second occupe plus d’un tiers de la façade de la batterie, mais ne nous y trompons pas : il ne s’agit pas d’un écran, mais d’une fenêtre montrant le fonctionnement en temps réel des micropompes et du liquide au sein de l’appareil. Sans doute un peu gadget et avant tout destinée à prouver à l’utilisateur que sa technologie n’est pas qu’une simple ligne sur une fiche technique, cette trouvaille a aussi le mérite d’apporter de l’originalité à un design par ailleurs très sobre.
Ugreen annonce une capacité de 10 000 mAh sous une tension de 3,92 V (ou plutôt deux cellules de 5000 mAh sous tension de 7,84 V), ce qui constitue en général le bon compromis entre la capacité à recharger des appareils électroniques variés et une compacité adaptée au transport.
Nous avons pour notre part mesuré une capacité réelle de 8 482 mAh, soit une différence de 15,18 % avec la valeur annoncée par Ugreen. Si la Xiaomi Magnetic Power Bank 10000 fait mieux, ne laissant s’échapper que 6,76 % de sa capacité, la MagGo PowerBank 2 Pro d’Anker, de 10 000 mAh également, est amputée de 16,35 % de sa promesse initiale. Bref, le modèle d’Ugreen se situe sensiblement dans la moyenne de sa catégorie.
Dans les faits, la MagFlow Pro 10 000 mAh est capable de recharger 1,7 fois un Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (ou ses aînés, les S25 Ultra et S24 Ultra, eux-mêmes pourvus d’un accumulateur de 5 000 mAh). Elle peut requinquer plus de 2,5 fois un iPhone 15 Pro — en sans-fil, profitant de l’équivalence des technologies Qi2 et MagSafe — ou encore près de deux fois une Nintendo Switch. Bien entendu, ces données restent des estimations théoriques, ne tenant pas compte des inévitables pertes d’énergie propres à la recharge de chaque appareil.
| Nb. charges Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra | Nb. charges Apple iPhone 15 Pro | Nb. charges Apple iPad Pro 13 (2024) | Nb. charges Nintendo Switch | Nb. charges Sony WH-1000XM5 | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,70 | 2,59 | 0,82 | 1,97 | 7,07 | 
La puissance délivrée par la MagFlow Pro d’Ugreen varie selon le mode de charge retenu. Concrètement, la batterie est compatible avec la technologie Qi2 à 25 W, ce qui signifie qu’elle répond en réalité à la norme Qi2.2 (la norme Qi2 classique n’excédant pas les 15 W). C’est le maximum pris en charge à ce jour par cette technologie qui, rappelons-le, est compatible avec MagSafe, le standard d’Apple.
Il est donc possible de faire appel à la batterie à la fois pour charger l’un des (rares) produits Android compatibles avec la charge sans-fil magnétique, mais aussi pour alimenter un iPhone depuis la génération 12. Point intéressant : vous pouvez aussi placer des AirPods à boîtier de charge sans-fil sur la batterie, comme nous l’avons nous-mêmes réalisé, mais aussi un appareil bien plus gourmand, tel qu'une tablette ou un ordinateur. Pour rassurer l’utilisateur, la batterie inclut une puce dédiée à la surveillance en temps réel de la température.
En filaire, en passant par le port USB-C comme par le câble (USB-C également) intégré à la batterie, Ugreen annonce une puissance maximale de 45 W. Notez que les trois connecteurs (les deux sorties USB-C et la surface à induction) peuvent fonctionner de concert, Ugreen se gardant toutefois de préciser la répartition des puissances disponibles dans ce cas de figure.
En USB-C, nous avons mesuré une puissance plus que satisfaisante, excédant même les 45 W annoncés par le fabricant. À 5 V, la batterie atteint 15,94 W. Elle monte à 29,04 W à 9 V, mais aussi à 41,91 W à 12 V et à 50,25 W à 15 V. Au maximum, à 20 V, nous avons relevé 51,22 W. Retenez tout de même que cette puissance ne peut pas être maintenue sur la durée complète d’une charge, ce qui explique le temps exigé par vos appareils pour refaire le plein complet. Quant à la batterie elle-même, elle se recharge à 30 W.
Si elle propose un design futuriste, l'Ugreen MagFlow Pro ne fait pas de l’esbroufe. La batterie externe de 10 000 mAh propose une puissance de charge élevée, peut être utilisée avec une large variété d’appareils, en filaire comme en sans-fil, et tient ses promesses de puissance. Elle compense sa capacité réelle légèrement moindre qu’annoncée par sa polyvalence et par un poids contenu, qui la rend très pratique à emporter avec soi.
La concurrence est nombreuse sur le terrain des batteries de 10 000 mAh. Les modèles proposant de la charge filaire et sans-fil se font de plus en plus courants, tel l'Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro qui mise certes sur un ventilateur un peu bruyant, mais s'affiche à moins de 80 € tout en mêlant charge sans-fil et USB-C. On peut aussi citer la Xiaomi Magnetic Power Bank 10000 with Built-in Stand qui se contente d'une charge Qi à 15 W et ne propose pas de technologie de refroidissement aussi poussée, mais bénéficie d'un tarif dépassant à peine les 40 €.

articles.title: /Plan und /Goal: Was bringen die Abkürzungen für KI?
articles.text:
/Plan oder /Goal? So nutzt du zwei KI-Modi sinnvoll im Büroalltag
Wenig eingeben, aber dennoch präzisere Ausgaben bekommen: Dafür gibt es bei KI sinnvolle Abkürzungen. Zwei davon bringen im Büro am meisten, findet Prompt Engineer Susanne Renate Schneider: Plan- und Zielmodus. Im Podcast t3n MeisterPrompter erklärt sie mit t3n-Redakteurin Stella-Sophie Wojtczak, wie sich beide unterscheiden.
/plan und /goal nutzen
Im Planmodus werden dir bei ChatGPT laut Renate gezielt Rückfragen gestellt. Darauf basierend entsteht dann ein Plan. Im Vergleich mit einem einfachen Prompt seien die Fragen im Planmodus laut Renate direkt fokussierter.
Aktivierst du den Zielmodus, beschreibst du ChatGPT oder Claude lediglich dein Ziel, inklusiv der beschreibenden Kriterien. Die KI arbeitet dann auf dieses Ergebniss hin, auch über mehrere Schritte. In ChatGPT waren die Modi wie /study zum lernen bisher auch über die Vorauswahl erreichbar, das gelingt allerdings aktuell nicht.
Am einfachsten ist es dabei, diese Chatvorgabe mit /plan und /goal anzufordern. Das funktioniert laut Renate Tool-übergreifend. Selbstläufer sind die Modi jedoch nicht. Du musst demzufolge Rückfragen beantworten und Zwischenschritte prüfen. Die Verantwortung für die KI-Ergebnisse trägst außerdem du. Anwendungsbeispiele hörst du in der verlinkten Folge von t3n MeisterPrompter.
Hier hörst du t3n MeisterPrompter – auf allen Plattformen
Den Podcast hörst du über die Podcast-Plattform deiner Wahl. Gib dafür in der Suche „t3n MeisterPrompter“ ein. Alternativ findest du direkte Verlinkungen hier:
Du hast einen Vorschlag für ein Episoden-Thema? Schreib uns unter meisterprompter@t3n.de. Renate erreichst du außerdem über Instagram und Tiktok unter @renate.gpt oder du meldest dich auf Instagram oder Tiktok unter @t3n_magazin.

articles.title: Cyberattack on Fireworks AI allowed hackers to access Notion customers' chat transcripts | TechCrunch
articles.text:
A cyberattack at Fireworks AI has exposed some of its customers’ data, the company has confirmed. Fireworks AI, a platform that developers use to access and use open AI models, said an attacker breached its cloud provider to gain access to a Fireworks development system, which allowed access to some of its customers’ data.
The company said in its latest security advisory that the cybercriminals took Fireworks’ customers’ billing information and some datasets. Fireworks touts tens of thousands of customers worldwide using its platform, including legal tech company Harvey and AI company Cursor.
At least one confirmed affected customer is online document editor and notetaker Notion, which said in a disclosure that the breach affected around 1% of its own customers.
Notion said that Fireworks alerted the company to a security incident and later confirmed that the hackers had stolen some Notion customer data. On November 3, Notion said it disconnected its systems from Fireworks, deleted the data stored in its systems, and stopped all connectivity between the two.
Notion confirmed this week that the hackers took chat transcripts of its Notion AI customers who used the “Insights” feature. The company said that the transcripts include “any input to or output from the model that was written to the chat,” but added that much of the data was unattributable and could not be determined from which customer it was obtained.
The breach at Fireworks AI shows how tech companies are reliant on other tech providers for their own offerings, and how cyberattacks can, as a result, spill over into other customers.
Fireworks said that it believes the hackers are financially motivated and that their goals are focused on selling tokens from breaching access to large language models, or LLMs. These schemes rely on selling to unauthorized third parties, who can burn through AI model usage without using their own resources.
This is the second breach affecting Fireworks in as many months, following a security incident in October.

articles.title: Un ‘USB’ universal de creación europea para dar una segunda vida a los satélites y reducir la basura espacial
articles.text:
Un ‘USB’ universal de creación europea para dar una segunda vida a los satélites y reducir la basura espacial
Un grupo de investigadores desarrolla y prueba un sistema similar a estos puertos de conexión que podría facilitar la reparación de estos artefactos en órbita
¿No resulta molesto tener que viajar con varios adaptadores durante las vacaciones? Pues lo mismo ocurre en el espacio, donde las naves espaciales y los satélites suelen utilizar diferentes conectores para transmitir energía, datos y otros servicios. Un equipo internacional de investigadores ha estado estudiando si una interfaz común puede facilitar estas conexiones. Su idea, desarrollada en el marco del proyecto Space USB, financiado por la UE, se parece un poco a los puertos USB tan extendidos en el ámbito informático: una conexión normalizada admite diferentes funciones en diversos diseños de satélites.
“Es algo que nos concierne a todos”, afirma Raphael Boissonnade, de Thales Alenia Space en Francia, quien coordinó el proyecto. “Ofrecemos los mismos enchufes, pero con servicios y tecnología diferentes”. Esta flexibilidad es cada vez más necesaria. En la actualidad, hay más de 16.000 satélites orbitando la Tierra, y su número sigue aumentando. Sin embargo, cuando un satélite se queda sin combustible o su equipamiento queda obsoleto, lo habitual es sustituirlo en lugar de repararlo o actualizarlo en órbita.
Esto genera costes y riesgos. Un satélite que ya no puede maniobrar puede convertirse en basura espacial, lo que podría suponer una amenaza para otras naves espaciales. Una sola colisión puede dispersar miles de fragmentos que supongan una amenaza para otras misiones durante décadas. Por el contrario, la posibilidad de realizar el mantenimiento y la reparación de los satélites permitiría prolongar su vida útil, evitar el riesgo de colisiones y reducir la necesidad de lanzar costosos satélites de sustitución.
Una conexión
Hoy en día, los satélites no cuentan con un método normalizado para conectar dispositivos de alimentación, datos, calor y otros servicios. No existe una interfaz única que permita conectar fácilmente equipos de diferentes sistemas. “En Europa contamos con tres interfaces diferentes”, comentó Mehmed Yüksel, del Centro Alemán de Investigación en Inteligencia Artificial (DFKI, en sus siglas en alemán). Cada una de ellas fue desarrollada de forma independiente por empresas rivales, sin ningún incentivo conjunto para que sus sistemas se comunicaran entre sí.
Los investigadores del proyecto Space USB se propusieron averiguar si era posible encontrar una alternativa común. El conector debía soportar una fuerza mínima al acoplarse, ser relativamente ligero y compacto, y fijarse en su sitio en pocos minutos. Cuando el proyecto concluyó a finales de 2025, el equipo había elaborado un prototipo funcional denominado “interfaz pasiva común” (common passive interface). Es mayor de lo que tendría que ser una versión de vuelo futura, pero sirve para demostrar el principio.
Los investigadores lo probaron con las tres interfaces europeas consolidadas —HOTDOCK, SIROM e iSSI— y demostraron que era totalmente compatible, tanto desde el punto de vista mecánico como eléctrico, con las tres. Mediante un banco de pruebas robótico de Thales Alenia Space, demostraron cómo se puede acoplar el conector a un satélite simulado para distintos fines.
“Hemos conseguido interconectar todos los dispositivos, lo que demuestra que la normalización es posible”, agregó Boissonnade. La conexión se asegura mediante un cilindro giratorio o una serie de pestillos. Su objetivo no es acoplar dos naves espaciales entre sí. En cambio, el sistema está diseñado para permitir que se conecte equipo adicional a un satélite que ya se encuentre en órbita, lo que podría prolongar su vida útil.
Una segunda vida para los satélites
Hoy en día, lo habitual es que un satélite averiado se deje caer para que se desintegre en la atmósfera o se traslade a una “órbita cementerio” más elevada, un proceso que puede llevar años. Una interfaz común podría hacer que la reparación fuera una alternativa más viable, lo que permitiría mantener los satélites en servicio en lugar de retirarlos.
Una nave espacial de mantenimiento podría acercarse a un satélite que tenga un componente defectuoso y sustituirlo. También podría incorporarse nuevo equipamiento, lo que dotaría a un satélite ya existente de nuevas capacidades. “Podría abrir nuevas posibilidades, como la incorporación de nuevos sensores, unidades de cálculo y unidades de procesamiento gráfico para la inteligencia artificial en órbita”, indicó Yüksel.
Los sensores estelares, por ejemplo, ayudan a las naves espaciales a determinar su orientación y, en caso de avería, pueden sustituirse. También podrían actualizarse otros sensores sin necesidad de sustituir todo el satélite. “Si aún queda mucho combustible en la nave espacial, sería una pena interrumpir la misión”, apuntó Boissonnade.
Una nave espacial de mantenimiento equipada con un conector compatible podría intervenir en varios satélites para sustituir o actualizar los equipos, según fuera necesario. Por consiguiente, la normalización facilita el desarrollo de un ecosistema de vehículos de servicio y componentes de recambio, en lugar de tener que diseñar cada misión desde cero.
Esta idea se refleja cada vez más en la política espacial europea. En junio de 2026, la Comisión Europea y la Agencia Espacial Europea firmaron una declaración conjunta en apoyo de una misión piloto de operaciones y servicios en el espacio (ISOS). La declaración también ha sido firmada por diez países europeos y respalda las actividades relacionadas con la inspección, la reparación, el reposicionamiento, el reabastecimiento, la fabricación y la retirada de residuos de satélites.
La Comisión está desarrollando una misión piloto, cuya puesta en marcha está prevista para 2030, como paso hacia una infraestructura europea de servicios en el espacio.
La propuesta de Ley Espacial Europea apunta en una dirección similar. Su proyecto de normativa exigiría que determinadas naves espaciales propiedad de la UE dispusieran de una capacidad mínima para recibir servicios en el espacio, incluidas interfaces de servicio específicas para naves espaciales. La propuesta sigue sujeta al proceso legislativo de la UE.
Por lo tanto, para las tecnologías como SPACE USB, el momento es clave: ahora que Europa empieza a plantearse la creación de naves espaciales diseñadas para poder ser reparadas, la existencia de interfaces comunes contribuiría a que esos servicios resultaran viables y sostenibles.
Construcción en órbita
Una conexión común también resultaría útil para un proyecto más ambicioso: la construcción de estructuras en el espacio. En lugar de lanzar un satélite grande o una plataforma completamente montada a partir de la Tierra, los módulos podrían enviarse por separado y conectarse en órbita. Las interfaces normalizadas permitirían añadir diferentes equipos en función de las necesidades.
“Si queremos construir una gran estructura en órbita y queremos acoplar elementos mediante una conexión eléctrica, ¿por qué no instalarla con una conexión normalizada?“, dijo Boissonnade. Esto podría facilitar, en el futuro, aplicaciones como la fabricación en el espacio, donde la microgravedad ofrece condiciones que resultan difíciles o imposibles de reproducir en la Tierra.
Los semiconductores y los productos farmacéuticos se encuentran entre los objetos cuya fabricación en órbita se está estudiando. Las plataformas modulares de mayor tamaño pueden proporcionar la infraestructura necesaria para este tipo de actividades.
Los investigadores del proyecto Space USB han demostrado que los equipos basados en tres interfaces europeas diferentes pueden conectarse a través de un sistema común. En el marco del proyecto, también se han elaborado unas especificaciones destinadas a servir de base para futuros diseños de interfaces a escala europea e internacional.
La transformación de dicho prototipo en una norma operativa dependerá de si los fabricantes de naves espaciales, los proveedores de equipos y las empresas de mantenimiento lo adoptan. “Si hay una gran demanda de servicios de mantenimiento, creemos que será necesaria la normalización”, afirmó Boissonnade.
Un conector común puede parecer una pequeña pieza de hardware. No obstante, a medida que Europa avanza hacia una infraestructura espacial más funcional y reutilizable, este elemento se perfila como uno de los pilares fundamentales de un futuro en el que los satélites no se utilicen y desechen sin más, sino que se reparen, se actualicen y se conecten en órbita.
Ahora mismo, en el sector espacial se utilizan diversos tipos de conectores; pero si el equipo de Space USB logra su objetivo, algún día una norma universal hará que todos ellos sean compatibles entre sí.

articles.title: The promise and peril of AI in government
articles.text:
In Taoyuan, Taiwan’s bustling industrial hub where 200 semiconductor manufacturing facilities are based, Mayor San-Cheng Chang is using AI to orchestrate an ambitious transformation. He brings a unique blend of technical expertise and government experience to the challenge of running the country’s fastest-growing city. Before becoming mayor, he served as Taiwan’s first nonpartisan premier and held leadership positions at both Google and Acer. As a former director of Taiwan’s National Center for High-Performance Computing, Chang embodies the intersection of technology and governance that helps explain Taoyuan’s embrace of AI.
As the home of Taiwan’s international airport as well as 2.2 million residents, Taoyuan must manage heavy truck traffic, air pollution, rapid population growth, and constant construction. Since March 2023, Taoyuan has run an AI-powered lung cancer screening initiative targeting citizens over 40 with risk factors that include occupational exposure and family history. Two years later, Taoyuan’s program had screened over 400,000 residents, detecting 233 lung cancer cases (90% in early stage), and achieving cost savings of NT$500 million ($17 million) through AI-aided diagnostics. To manage this volume without overwhelming local hospitals, the city deployed advanced AI software, which can predict cancer risk from a single low-dose CT scan without requiring additional clinical data, helping doctors to efficiently triage cases and focus resources on those most at risk.
When residents complained about noise from illegally modified vehicle exhaust pipes, Taoyuan developed an AI system that analyzes exhaust pipe images and matches them against a database of legal configurations. Patrol cars equipped with cameras can now identify violations on sight, and complaints are down 20% over last year. Other AI-powered cameras monitor construction sites and factory chimneys for pollution, automatically triggering water sprays when dust levels rise too high, or alerting inspectors when chimney emissions change suspiciously. AI now optimizes traffic-light cycles at busy intersections, shaving about 10 seconds off each wait. More dramatically, when ambulances approach, electronic fences detect their presence and create green-light corridors, cutting the ambulances’ average travel times from four minutes to just over two — a difference that can save lives.
While Taoyuan exemplifies the opportunities to use AI to develop practical solutions to urban problems, Mayor Chang is circumspect in his choice of projects. He will not sanction the use of generative AI chatbots that could hallucinate, and he carefully distinguishes between using machine learning to detect existing conditions and employing it to predict future outcomes. His administration embraces AI tools that can spot patterns — like identifying an existing cancer or finding vehicles with illegal modifications. Taoyuan uses AI to pinpoint potholes for faster road maintenance or identify train station elevator passengers in wheelchairs so that assistance can await them when the doors open. In these cases, AI sees what is already there faster than human eyes can, but it does not automate away human decision making.
“Black box” of algorithms
Unfortunately, governments and companies are increasingly turning to machine learning algorithms to anticipate future occurrences such as the risk of recidivism and relying on these predictive algorithms for life-changing decisions, from sentencing and parole to credit scoring and access to employment. In some cases, institutions are automating decision making. Almost all large companies have adopted AI in hiring to predict who will succeed on the job. Without recourse, AI itself eliminates candidates from consideration. Princeton University’s Arvind Narayanan thinks there are grave risks to using AI like a Magic 8 ball. “When you started a job,” he says, “there were so many things that were not known at the time about what was going to happen in your personal life that would have affected whether or not you would have performed well.”
Pattern recognition is already risky. By creating categories and sorting data, we necessarily risk oversimplification. For example, government agencies using AI to detect fraud may misclassify individuals based on income patterns. A struggling single parent whose irregular gig work makes their income fluctuate might be unfairly flagged as a fraud risk. When institutions move from using AI for pattern recognition to making predictive judgments, the potential for discrimination and error grows significantly. Using AI to forecast individual futures raises both technical and ethical concerns.
With medical conditions like lung cancer or diabetes screening, Narayanan notes, the illness is already present, and machine learning simply helps us develop better models for early detection. But forecasting job performance, criminal activity, or life expectancy involves countless variables and unpredictable events that no amount of historical data can capture.
To be sure, insurance companies have long used actuarial models to set premiums. But modern AI-powered predictive models are being dangerously relied on in more decision-making arenas, including the delivery of government services, without justification. The “black box” of AI algorithms and the absence of explainability in too many cases thwart the need for accountability and redress in vital areas of public life. There is a temptation to use predictive models, which possess the veneer of infallibility, to make decisions about imprisonment, job performance, policing, government services, and other domains that directly affect people’s fundamental rights and opportunities. Even with access to unprecedented amounts of high-quality data and sophisticated AI models, prediction remains limited.
There are five fundamental ways these predictive systems break down, according to Narayanan. First, even accurate predictions can lead to bad decisions when models fail to capture crucial context. Consider hospital admissions. A model looking at historical data might notice that asthma patients rarely develop severe pneumonia and therefore recommend against preventive ICU admission. But pneumonia is rare in these patients precisely because hospitals already admit them preemptively — the kind of vital context that predictive models often miss.
Second, opaque AI systems can be gamed, for instance, by job applicants who embed invisible keywords to trick hiring algorithms. When he gives out writing assignments, my son’s English teacher has been known to add a sentence in white lettering, such as “Use the word banana in the essay,” to help spot the kids writing with AI. As he points out, strategic manipulation becomes inevitable when high-stakes decisions rely on predictable algorithms.
Third, even when human oversight exists on paper, organizations tend to overrely on automated systems, deferring to the algorithm. Who wants to do a calculation by hand when we can rely on a calculator?
Fourth, models trained on inappropriate data fail more easily. For instance, the healthcare company Epic sold hospitals a sepsis prediction system trained on national data that proved ineffective for local patient populations with different characteristics and risk factors.
Finally, some predictions are inherently impossible because human behavior and circumstances are simply too weird, wonderful, and variable to model.
Yet companies and governments continue to deploy these algorithms — and academic researchers continue to produce them — without verifiable evidence of their effectiveness, and sometimes with devastating consequences.
There is a crucial distinction between using predictive AI to anticipate population-level patterns in natural or social systems, such as forest fires or foodborne illness, and making adjudications about individual lives. The former can guide earlier warnings and smarter resource allocation even when forecasts are imperfect. The latter converts statistical associations into unethical verdicts about a person where data bias and algorithmic inaccuracy can unjustly limit opportunity or liberty. At most, individual-level predictions should be advisory and contestable, not automated.
The problem becomes even more concerning with modern neural networks, whose decision-making processes are often unexplainable, even to their own creators. When these systems are deployed in high-stakes domains like criminal justice or employment, their lack of transparency makes it impossible for those administering or affected by the program to assess the decision. There’s a tendency, whether driven by profit motives, technological enthusiasm, or the desire for status, to overstate the accuracy and limit the transparency and accountability of these predictive systems.
“Over and over again,” notes Narayanan, “AI snake oil is appealing because those buying it are in broken institutions and are desperate for a quick fix.” When we delegate life-altering decisions to black-box systems with no clear mechanisms for oversight or redress, we risk making our institutions even less effective or trustworthy.
Adapted from “Reboot: AI and the Race to Save Democracy” by Beth Simone Noveck published by Yale University Press © 2026 by Beth Simone Noveck, and reprinted with permission.

articles.title: Global by default, local by design: What Indian founders learned about scaling across borders
articles.text:
Stripe
View Brand Publisher
Global by default, local by design: What Indian founders learned about scaling across borders
At a Stripe roundtable at TechSparks 2026, leaders from edtech, commerce, fintech, and consumer hardware shared how to pick markets, localize smartly, and build the payments and compliance spine that makes expansion repeatable
For many Indian businesses, going global does not begin with a grand strategy. It begins with a signup from a shopper in Texas, a lead from Dubai that lands at 2 a.m., or a customer in London who wants to pay in pounds. The first sale feels like proof. The harder question is whether the next market will follow the same path or demand starting from scratch. That question anchored a roundtable by Stripe on building a repeatable global growth playbook at TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s flagship event.
The table brought together leaders from organisations like Xoxoday, upGrad, Dodo Payments, Bhanzu, Borderless Access, Cuemath, FreshtoHome, Codingal, Codeyoung and Ultrahuman.
Representing the host was Manish Maheshwari, Managing Director, India, Stripe. The conversation was moderated by Madanmohan Rao, Research Director, YourStory.
Prove demand before crossing borders
The discussion opened with a shared instinct: start small and start by listening. Companies weigh customer acquisition cost, lifetime value, and operational scalability, along with whether reliable payment rails and local talent exist. One approach was to collect leads and call them before a product even existed, since online research rarely surfaces micro-level insight. A market that keeps asking for the same thing earns a place on the roadmap, while a single large client in one location is better treated as a customization. The first paying customer proves little, while repeat purchases and low dispute rates tell the real story.
Localize the edges, standardize the core
Anything that touches the end user, such as catalogs, curriculum and preferred payment modes like ACH in the United States or direct debit in the United Kingdom, can flex by market. Anything that moves money, including core fraud rules, stays standard. Legal and regulatory needs come first, followed by customer-specific requests, whether that means a bright red palette in China or tax-inclusive pricing in India. Pricing deserves equal care, as carrying Indian price points into the US took one team a long time to correct. Partnerships help too. In the UAE, a government tie-up won acceptance for credentials, while local payment partners improved affordability and brought in new customers.
Treat payments as a growth lever
Maheshwari offered a caution that resonated across the table: “Your payment failure or your checkout failure can be mistaken as a demand failure.”
Pricing in local currency is a big part of the fix, with Stripe’s data showing that 76% of customers prefer to pay in their own currency. Local payment methods and installments for large purchases help, as does a stack that is standard at the core but adaptable by country. Fraud control is a balancing act, because tightening rules too far turns away genuine buyers. Tracking chargebacks, refunds and failure rates by country also helps teams find leaks, such as overseas customers whose one-time passwords never arrived under Indian authentication rules.
Make compliance part of the product
Revenue brings obligations. US states set their own tax thresholds, Europe and India have data rules, and even text messaging follows different regulations in each country. Notices and penalties tend to arrive just as growth does, and one founder recalled how an India-only business shrank overnight after a regulatory shock. Stripe’s view was that a global stack chosen on day one costs less, since “going back and fixing it is far more expensive”.
Tools such as Stripe Atlas, helps businesses create a US entity,, set up local banking, accept payments and raise funds early in their journey, before international growth makes those decisions harder to revisit.
Let AI speed things up, with guardrails
AI is already compressing timelines. Content localization has become nearly 4X faster, with human verification and evaluation layers still in place, and engineers increasingly act as reviewers of AI-written code. Sales bots handle lead qualification and reminders across time zones, lifting funnel performance by an estimated 20-25%. Speed, however, raises questions of stability, safety and security, and cybersecurity was flagged as the topic most missing from the conversation.
Plant the flag where the pull is
Being global by default does not mean opening offices everywhere. One team that localized its curriculum and hired instructors and sales staff in Japan saw momentum fade within three months, because the effort amounted to a separate business. The lesson was to scale where strengths already exist, go deep, and then widen.
Audiences beyond the Indian diaspora need a different approach altogether, with local hiring, community events and even offline centers in the US to feel like a native brand.
A playbook still taking shape
Taken together, the repeatable playbook is clear: validate repeat demand, keep the money-moving core standard, localize what customers see, build finance and compliance muscle early, and enter markets where pull already exists.
Gaps remain. Paying individuals abroad, such as teachers, from an Indian entity is still expensive, and the infrastructure for it is thin.
As the evening closed, the shared belief was that the best learning comes from peers who work in the field. For Indian businesses, going global market by market is less a leap than a discipline, built one repeatable decision at a time.

articles.title: A guide to making Firefox the default mobile browser | The Mozilla Blog
articles.text:
An open letter to every family’s designated IT support
Almost every family has one. They’re the only ones who know which remote turns on the TV and which controls the volume and channels. They know what an HDMI cable actually does and where to plug it in. They’ve even fixed multiple phone issues within seconds through a little-known, well-kept secret procedure (turning it off and back on).
Perhaps they are a parent, tech-savvy sibling, cool aunt or uncle, or close family friend. Whatever the relation, the role stays the same. They are the unpaid, on-call tech specialist for every relative’s forgotten password, printer jam, and device settings update.
If this sounds like you, we would first like to thank you for doing a job you never signed up for. Second, we would like to share a simple way you can help your family and friends protect their privacy and security without adding more to your plate.
A small settings change that makes a big difference
With Android and iPhone’s latest releases, and Black Friday deals rapidly approaching, many people are upgrading their current phone to a newer model. As the family’s go-to tech helper, you’ll likely be setting up a few new devices in the near future. You already know the routine: connect to Wi-Fi, choose a language, and transfer data from the old phone to the new one. But beyond the steps you are prompted to take when setting up a new phone lies a quiet decision many people never think twice about: their default browser.
While people in some regions, like Europe and Japan, get to choose their default browser when setting up a new phone, this is not the case everywhere. Most phones ship with a browser preinstalled and set as the default, ready to start collecting data and monetizing off user activity the minute it’s opened. Unless deliberately changed, that’s the browser that will be used moving forward. Not because it’s the best option, but because it’s already there.
But remember, everyone can choose the browser they use, and as the designated tech whiz of the family, you can help inspire others to choose the right one.
Choosing Firefox means choosing privacy from the very first tap.
The browser is where the data lives
A browser is the door to everything you do online, and depending on how it’s designed, it can see a lot. Every site visited. Every phrase searched. Every link tapped. As we socialize, work, and explore on our phones, the browser can be the biggest funnel of personal data leaving that device, and how it’s built determines who collects that data, who can sell it, and how long it sticks around.
Privacy is the starting point for our browser, not an afterthought. Firefox is built on the principle that not even Mozilla should know which websites you visit or what you do there.
Why Firefox is the right call
Firefox is backed by Mozilla, a nonprofit-backed company with no shareholders to report to. Instead of chasing financial returns for a small group, Mozilla aims to provide an internet that truly puts people first. This means we limit the data we know about you and give you more choice about what data you share and when.
This commitment to user privacy is built into the browser itself. On both Android and iOS, Enhanced Tracking Protection (ETP) is enabled by default, blocking known trackers every time you browse. This helps prevent advertisers and data brokers from following people across sites, no setup required. You can also adjust ETP to fit different needs, including turning it off altogether or activating Strict mode for even stronger protection.
Control and choice are built in, too. Firefox has an easily accessible AI controls section where people can customize how AI features show up in the browser, or turn them off entirely – because AI should always be a choice, not a requirement.
To carry these principles and protections across every link opened on a new phone, set Firefox as the default mobile browser in just a few taps.
How to set Firefox as the default browser on Android and iOS
Downloading the Firefox mobile app isn’t enough on its own, since most phones will keep opening links in whatever browser came preinstalled unless told otherwise. Here’s how to make Firefox the browser that actually opens by default. Make sure Firefox is installed on the device you’re working with before you begin.
On Android: 
- Open Firefox
- Tap the three-dot menu button.
- Tap Settings.
- In the General section, locate the Set default browser option.
- Tap the toggle next to Set as default browser to turn it on.
- Select Firefox from the listed options.
- Tap Set as default.
On iOS:
- Open phone Settings.
- Tap Apps.
- Tap Default Apps.
- Tap Browser App.
- Select Firefox from the listed options.
Once Firefox has been selected as the default browser, links tapped from messages, email, social media, or anywhere else will open in Firefox automatically. No additional steps required by your less tech-savvy family members and friends, and no relying on them to open the “right” browser every time they want to access the internet.
A little help on day one, lasting benefits later
The way a device is initially set up tends to stick. Whichever browser is already selected as default and whatever privacy settings are (or aren’t) adjusted on day one often just…stay that way. That’s a lot of reliance on whatever defaults the phone is purchased with.
So this fall, whether you are setting up a shiny new Google Pixel 11 for your aunt, an iPhone 18 Pro for your brother, or any other model for any one of your non-paying tech support “clients,” take an extra five minutes to help them download Firefox and set it as their default browser. They can start their new device journey browsing with privacy, choice, and control built in. And you can check one more thing off your unofficial family IT to-do list.

articles.title: Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills
articles.text:
Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills
Agent skills capture repeatable engineering work in files teams can review and reuse, while tools, project context, and permissions remain specific to the host that runs them.
How many times this week did you re-explain the same task to an agent? How many times did you ask your colleague with deep institutional knowledge how to solve a specific problem? That context shouldn’t be lost in a chat or locked in one person’s head. Agent skills let you capture repeatable instructions so you and your agents can reuse them. The skill you write for yourself tonight can later become part of a team’s pipeline.
An agent skill is a versioned directory centered on a SKILL.md file that describes when and how to do a repeatable task. You can share those instructions across agents, but the environment still needs to provide the tools, credentials, and permissions to carry them out. A skill can describe how to query a database, for example, but it doesn’t grant access to that database.
A skill works best when it has a clear job, input, and output. For example, let’s say you’re building an agent that checks AI-generated changes against the original request. If the same agent assesses its own work, its explanation might influence the review. With Proof Agent, we use a separate verifier to examine the changes and provide evidence for its findings. The skill’s frontmatter names the task and describes its purpose:
---
name: proof-agent
description: Adversarial verification of AI-generated work. Spawns an independent verifier to check for false claims, broken code, and security issues.
---
At the center is a simple rule: self-verification is not verification.
The When to Verify section in Proof Agent’s SKILL.md says when to invoke the skill. The remaining instructions explain what the verifier reviews and what evidence to include in its findings.
Coordinate multiple skills for a larger workflow
When the judgment that makes a data pipeline correct lives in four different people’s heads, those four people are the roadmap. Each change to the pipeline depends on their availability and knowledge of the data. Data Forge is an example of how to capture parts of that judgment in skills that work together.
In the support-desk pipeline example, we start with a request for metrics that count incidents created and resolved. Before building the pipeline, the forge-init skill discovers details such as source tables and naming conventions, then writes them to a resolved manifest. The other skills read that manifest for the project context they need.
The forge-builder skill then coordinates the work from the issue through to a pull request. It uses forge-dbx to query the data platform and forge-lint to apply the team’s standards as it designs and builds the pipeline. A person reviews the proposed decisions along the way, and the resulting pull request contains the pipeline code, schema changes, and tests.
Each skill has a defined responsibility, and they share project context instead of rediscovering it independently. When a step changes, you can change one skill and leave the rest alone.
Skills fit bounded, repeatable work that benefits from reusable judgment, such as a checklist, release, migration, or metric pipeline. If a workflow needs a stable interface, shared state, an audit trail, long-running control, or permissions enforced outside the model, an application is a better fit.
Keep project configuration out of the skill
We don’t want to hardcode every project’s names, database, or conventions into the skills. In the Data Forge support-desk example, a manifest describes the project, metric store, and platform so the skills can use the right project details without baking them into their instructions:
With the discovered details in the resolved manifest, the other skills don’t have to make their own assumptions about the project.
Keep discovered project details separate from team standards. The forge-init initialization skill can inspect existing schemas and code patterns; the forge-lint skill supplies the rules to follow before code is generated. A pattern found in a repository isn’t automatically a rule to preserve, so make discovered details reviewable and let people confirm or change them where business judgment is needed. To check portability, ask: could another team use these skills with its own manifest without rewriting them?
Share execution paths between skills
The forge-dbx skill gives the other Data Forge skills one way to access the data platform. It reads the manifest and selects a Databricks or DuckDB adapter, so each skill doesn’t need its own connection and query logic.
The manifest can choose DuckDB for the local support-desk demo, but it can’t install the DuckDB CLI or grant database access. Those remain setup responsibilities for the environment and its user. The manifest picks the engine; the host provides the access.
Put checks and approval points in the workflow
The Data Forge support-desk workflow has seven phases, with a human checkpoint at each one. The workflow overview shows how the skills fit together. Before a phase proceeds, the workflow checks that the previous phase is complete; before schema changes run, it asks for approval.
The Proof Agent example applies the same principle to code review. A GitHub Actions workflow gives the verifier the original request and code changes, but not the coding agent’s own assessment. The verifier returns PASS, FAIL, or PARTIAL and must cite evidence in the changed files. The GitHub Action does a static review of the diff; it doesn’t execute code or run tests. In the demo workflow, we set block-on-fail: false so findings were advisory. By default, a FAIL fails the check, which blocks the merge if the check is required. The aim is to keep test results and merge requirements in your repository’s CI checks and rules.
Package for each agent client, then verify its setup
Supporting multiple clients can mean keeping several copies of the same instructions in sync. In the Data Forge example, we keep skills/*/SKILL.md as the source and use a packaging script to generate client-specific files: .claude-plugin/plugin.json for Claude Code, .cursor-plugin/plugin.json for Cursor, and .github/agents/*.agent.md for GitHub Copilot. The script also includes a check mode for CI:
node scripts/package.mjs --check
Clients can differ in their available models, tools, credentials, and permissions. After installing a skill, check that the client recognizes it for the intended task, loads its references, can use the required tools, and returns the evidence the skill calls for.
Three practices for building agent skills
Put business context in one file. Keep project-specific names, schemas, and conventions in a manifest, and have each skill read it instead of duplicating those facts. This gives the team one visible place to update configuration.
Give related skills one consistent way to use the platform. Have related skills use the same path to run queries, jobs, and schema changes instead of each defining its own commands and connection logic. This makes the workflow’s access easier to understand and its behavior easier to check in each client.
Use instructions to guide the work, and checks to verify it. A skill can tell an agent which standards to follow and when to ask for approval. Add human review at decisions that need context or judgment, and use tests and CI checks to catch issues before a change moves forward. If a check must block a merge or deployment, configure that requirement in your repository’s rules.
Start with the task you’re tired of explaining. Write down what it needs, where it stops, and what a reviewer sees. Then try it with another agent and improve it as you learn what works.
Andrea is a Senior Developer Advocate at GitHub with over a decade of experience in developer tools. She combines technical depth with a mission to make advanced technologies more accessible. After transitioning from Army service and construction management to software development, she brings a unique perspective to bridging complex engineering concepts with practical implementation. She lives in Florida with her Welsh partner, two sons, and two dogs, where she continues to drive innovation and support open source through GitHub's global initiatives. Find her online @acolombiadev.

articles.title: This is the Meta MetaRoCE Network Adapter
articles.text:
At OCP Summit 2026, we saw Meta’s new MetaRoCE network adapter. This is Meta’s answer to providing an open RDMA transport layer that has features like packet spraying, congestion control, and more. This was a presentation we saw at OCP Summit, but Meta had a NIC on display.
Meta MetaRoCE Network Adapter at OCP 2026
Here is the display from the Meta booth at OCP Summit 2026, where you can see an OCP NIC 3.0 card.
During its OCP 2026 presentation, Meta shared some of the big features of MetaRoCE:
- Per-path reliability and congestion control
- Receiver rate hints (RCN) for fast incast convergence
- Tolerates packet loss and reordering
- Single QP carries multiple streams over multiple network paths
- Runs on commodity Ethernet: ECN + ECMP, no switch (Source: Meta)
Before OCP Summit, Meta demonstrated this with the AMD Pensando NIC series. The programmability allowed it to implement the protocol without having dedicated hardware. That allows Meta to potentially source from multiple vendors.
Meta is trying to build a network protocol that can scale to million-GPU training, but also that can run on different network topologies and hardware.
As a quick aside, the NIC shown was an OCP NIC 3.0 with SFF pull tab design, which is our favorite form factor that we wish all server vendors used.
Final Words
Given Meta’s heritage of starting OCP Summit, they usually have super-cool hardware in the booth. Last year, we got the AMD Helios MI450 Rack at OCP Summit with a Different Version from Meta as an example. This year, the company brought some larger nodes, but also small items like this adapter. It is always neat to see what Meta is working on.
If you want to see what AWS is doing, for example, you can check out our Inside the Secretive AWS Networking Lab.

articles.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
articles.text:
A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
Scientists have developed a promising new method that could read quantum information with 99.85% accuracy while barely disturbing the qubit itself.
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo
- Summary:
- Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient.
- Share:
One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.
Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.
The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.
Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult
Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.
This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.
"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.
To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.
The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.
Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.
"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.
A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal
The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.
Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.
These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.
"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.
The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.
The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.
Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.
"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.
How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information
To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.
One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.
The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.
According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.
"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.
This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.
A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage
Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.
Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."
The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.
"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.
This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.
That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.
Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor
The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.
Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.
Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.
The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.
Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.
"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."
The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.
Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance
In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.
This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.
The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.
"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.
The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.
This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.
Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy
To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.
These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.
The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.
According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.
The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.
However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.
Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?
Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.
The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.
What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.
"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.
This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.
The research offers two potentially significant advances.
From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.
From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.
If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.
More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo. Original written by José Tadeu Arantes. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Xian-Peng Zhang, Chuanchang Zeng, Zhen-Biao Yang, Jose Carlos Egues, Yugui Yao. Andreev qubit readout from dynamic interference supercurrent. Physical Review B, 2026; 114 (8) DOI: 10.1103/6gkt-hghj

articles.title: A New Dawn in the Cloud: ‘Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV’ Is Coming to GeForce NOW
articles.text:
Rally the ranks this GFN Thursday. Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV is coming to GeForce NOW, allowing players to experience the battle for Kronus through cloud gaming.
There’s more on the horizon, with NVIDIA DLSS 5 technology coming to War Thunder and Where Winds Meet. Meanwhile, Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen brings new tales and encounters, alongside 10 games joining the GeForce NOW library this week.
Kronus Calls for Reinforcements
Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV, developed by KING Art Games and published by Deep Silver, is coming to GeForce NOW. Launching on Steam Thursday, Dec. 3, the real-time strategy game returns to the series’ roots with large-scale battles, base building and a renewed fight for planet Kronus.
Command the Space Marines, Orks, Necrons or the Adeptus Mechanicus, which makes their series debut. Build a base, secure resources and customize squads to the conflict across more than 70 campaign missions, playable solo or in co-op mode. The Last Stand, Skirmish and multiplayer modes offer more ways to put tactics to the test.
GeForce NOW will bring the action to supported PCs, Macs, handhelds and other devices, with game downloads and updates handled in the cloud. Save the storage space for everyday essentials and planning for the next offensive. Wishlist the game on Steam, and stay tuned to GFN Thursday to prepare for launch.
DLSS 5 Keeps on Coming
NVIDIA DLSS 5 continues to evolve, with Gaijin Entertainment’s War Thunder and Everstone Studio’s Where Winds Meet next to receive support for the technology with the 3D-Guided Neural Rendering feature.
Arriving in mid-November, War Thunder’s Eagle’s Shadow major update adds DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, dozens of new planes, ships and tanks, along with cluster bombs for planes and visual-effects enhancements increasing the realism and dynamism of battle.
In Where Winds Meet, DLSS support arrives Monday, Nov. 23, enhancing the environments and characters of its wuxia open-world action role-playing game.
Both titles will use the latest DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering model, released in October, which doubles model performance compared with the previous version. Since its initial announcement in March, model performance has improved tenfold, bringing the technology to more gamers, including GeForce NOW Ultimate members streaming with GeForce RTX 5080 cloud rigs.
Get a closer look at the DLSS updates and find more details.
A New Tale for the Arisen
Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is streaming on GeForce NOW, expanding the deep, explorable fantasy world of Dragon’s Dogma 2 with new tales and encounters. Travel to the long-abandoned region of Norgan, join the enigmatic Eir and uncover the secrets of the undying Fallen Dragon.
Unearth forgotten relics to unlock powerful weapons and skills, take on Lost Rites’ 12 dungeon challenges and explore new hairstyles and tattoos for Arisen and Pawn customization.
Delicious in Dungeon also arrives in the world of Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen with a special collaboration.
GeForce NOW keeps all the new downloadable content available across supported devices — without a single download claiming local storage on a gamer’s hardware of choice.
In addition, members can look for the following games joining the GeForce NOW library this week:
- Worst Class Ever (New release on Steam, Nov. 9)
- Ashes of the Singularity II (New release on Steam, Nov. 10)
- Cyberpunk 2077 (Xbox Play Anywhere, new release on Battle.net, Nov. 10)
- DreamWorks Shrek 2 Remastered (New release on Steam, Nov. 10)
- Warhammer Survivors (New release on Steam and Xbox, available on Game Pass, Nov. 10)
- Main Sequence (New release on Steam, Nov. 12)
- Deadly Days: Roadtrip (Steam)
- GeForce 8800 GTX – 20 Years of a Legend (Steam, Ultimate members)
- Graveyard Keeper (Steam)
- Tape to Tape (Steam)
Also this week, Ultimate members can take a trip back to 2006 with GeForce 8800 GTX – 20 Years of a Legend, a playable demo celebrating the iconic GPU’s 20th anniversary with DLSS 4.5 and path tracing in the cloud.
Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after release and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates on announced titles.
Those ready to put the next game plan into action can grab a day pass to try Performance or Ultimate, with the cost applicable toward a first monthly membership.
What’s on the gaming lineup this weekend? Let us know on X or in the comments below.
